name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell
detailed_description: 'Momodora: Moonlit Farewell' is the latest installment in the Momodora series. Join Momo, High Priestess of the village of Koho, as she embarks on a divine mission to save her people from imminent destruction at the hands of the demon hordes summoned by a malevolent bellringer. Story: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell presents the account of the greatest calamity to befall the village of Koho, five years after the events of Momodora III. Once the toll of an ominous bell is heard, the village is soon threatened by a demon invasion. The village's matriarch sends Momo Reinol, their most capable priestess, to investigate the bell and find the bellringer responsible for summoning demons. It is their hope that by finding the culprit, they will also be able to secure the village's safety, and most importantly, the sacred Lun Tree's, a source of life and healing for Koho... Features: Gorgeous pixel art and animation Action-packed gameplay focusing on melee combos, dodging enemy attacks, and firing arrows at enemies The 'Sigil' system, which allows for greatly customizable play styles Intense and core-shaking boss battles Deep exploration into a world rich in lore and atmosphere Freely adjustable difficulty levels, allowing you to relax and explore the alluring world at your own pace or take on mighty foes for a real challenge Developer's Voice: Hello! This is rdein, creator of the Momodora series. Recently my team and I have announced the latest installment in the series, “Moonlit Farewell”. This is a concluding story, following through from the events of Momodora 3. With this new tale, I also intend to close the book on many of the past games’ mysteries and questions. I’m aware that many players are more familiar with the story of Kaho, which is set in a distant past. As such, I’m designing “Moonlit Farewell” to be as enjoyable as possible without prior knowledge of Momodora 1 to 3’s stories. Moreover, the series has always been focused on action and minimal stories. So please, don’t worry too much about “catching up”! Lastly, we hope to bring you our best game with this new title, using all the knowledge we’ve learned in the past 10 years. Please look forward to it!

_childDocuments_.review: Solid metroidvania all around and the dev's best game to date. Gorgeous visuals, well tuned movement with a lot of fun upgrades to unlock, build variety with sigils and companions, and a more in depth combat system that rewards well timed dodges and stamina management. Anyone who likes action platformers definitely shouldn't miss this.

_childDocuments_.review: Count about 7 hours of play, 10 if you aim for the 111% completion, more if you want to do the post-game content.It plays similarly to Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight, and takes place after Momodora III.If you have missed other titles, the librarian lad in Koho village gives you a set of short notes that summarize (and complete!) their story and put this one in context.Way prettier, more polished, and bad*ss than its predecessors (including Minoria), it also handles better and has more gameplay depth, with the most fun and synergistic perk/item system (sigils) and best feeling powercreep in the series.It further fleshes out the characters, and does a good job at tieing loose ends and referencing the other games, making it even more enjoyable if you are a Momodora fan. Momo is virtuous yet a bit sassy, Isadora mellowed out despite her fiery temperament, godly beings aren't perfect and make dumb mistakes, and as usual, the game's narrative elegantly slithers between light-hearted interactions, gorgeous and whimsical landscapes, and very somber and monstrous events and areas. Oh, and so many cats it could be categorized as one of those "find all the cats" games that've been all the rage lately. I hope you're not allergic.There's one nail I must hammer once more: The art direction and world building are absolutely stellar, insane.Stopping to smell the roses is not really my thing, as my dumb gorilla brain is too too busy trying to brutally annihilate the movement and combat systems of every single game I touch to admire the scenery. But this? This is one of those rare games that make me realize that I, in fact, have been attached with eyes.Additionally, the soundscape goes perfectly well with it, weaving a mystical and immersive atmosphere in every single region of the game. Some tracks are also pretty memorable, with a very strong main leitmotiv and really good boss music.The combat is closer to RUtM than Minoria and it is designed to be enjoyable by both dodgeroll-focused players and those who prefer spacing, air control and positioning. Oh and I guess filthy, arrow-spamming, turtly heathens too but they lost their human rights long ago so who cares!Level and boss design are extremely varied and will always surprise you. No two bosses or areas are alike and it just never goes stale. I would even say that .It is not without flaws, however. There are two things that prevent it from being perfect in my eyes:First, (very minor mechanic spoiler) Second, and most importantly, difficulty.The difficulty curve in MF is more consistent than its predecessors, with perfectly placed spikes that are designed to challenge your gameplan in specific areas each. The problem is  difficulty, and the  the challenge.If you are new to the series or just not used to this kind of game, it'll feel just fine (heck, it even has a Lite mode with togglable adaptive difficulty!). However if you're one of those who quickly catch on to how an enemy or bossfight works, you will breeze through the game with little to no death, and left hungry for more, as . In RUtM, this was compensated for in the form of an additional reward if you beat a boss without being hit once. Here, perfecting a boss feels almost as fun (they are overall easier to cheese) but there is no incentive to it and the game even autosaves after beating some of the bosses, making it impossible to retry if you mistakenly end the fight after taking a hit.It still tries to allow you to spice things up (and prevent the aforementioned scenario) in the form of a sigil  but there's no point outside of speedrun builds and it takes a precious grimoire slot away...On the other hand, it does provide you with post-game content to test your mettle with, , it is just unfortunate that you have to finish the game to get a fitting challenge if you're a brute, a masochist or a fossilized NES/SNES-era monk like me.Mind you, those are mainly the nitpicks of a seasoned player and most people won't even be affected by them.I've been a fan of the momodora series since the second game, contributed to RUtM as a playtester and its french translator, and consider rdein to be my friend. This game was the fruit of much struggle and it came out an absolute beauty.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I'd say Moonlit Farewell was passably enjoyable, but it definitely doesn't live up to the standards rdein set with RuTM and Minoria. Far and away the biggest gripe I have has to be the map design, feeling much more reminiscent of an IGAVania than a Metroidvania that actually focuses on exploration. Just a quick overview of the map will show you that, overall, it's less interconnected than 4's, and even Minoria's. And this is to say nothing of actually traveling through it. Minoria's lack of a fast-travel system felt like it made things somewhat more tedious sometimes, but RuTM's map is one I enjoy going through even without teleporting between the bells.Moreover, the controls are definitely a departure from the previous entries. Having the bow be used with up+attack as opposed to having its own dedicated input feels like a step back. (Maybe rdein was playing a lot of Castlevania 1 during development?) Likewise with  being down+attack. The buff from spending Lunar Crystals at the bells doesn't really feel worthwhile, though I understand the devs probably wanted some use for the currency of the game beyond the single,  slowly expanding shop the game gives you, and the stat plants that, for whatever incomprehensible reason, they decided needed to have a timer on their growth? They only appear 3 times in the game if I remember correctly, all with the same 10 minute wait time, but I genuinely have no idea why the devs thought this was necessary or a fun addition, particularly given that the first one you encounter is in Koho Village, essentially the starting town, which doesn't have much of anything you'd expect from such an area, as the one shop in the game is never there, and the only reason to revisit it other than the plant is for the sanctuary area beneath it, which connects to literally nothing else. (Again, not the greatest choice for Metroidvania map design. Hell, even Blue Brinstar in Super Metroid had proper connections to the rest of the map once you got stuff like Power Bombs.)However, in terms of gameplay, all of that is relatively minor compared to the biggest issue.Every game rdein and Bombservice have put on Steam prior to this had some sort of item system, which allowed for a measure of gameplay customization. In Momodora 3, these were effectively all passive items, of which you could equip 3. In RuTM and Minoria, however, you have 5 slots total, 2 for passives, and 3 for active items, which functioned somewhat like Dark Souls Spells. In addition, from the very first Momodora entry, all these items had attached flavor text, which often made hints at lore, even if most of them didn't go anywhere with it. However, every item in RuTM, and most of them in Minoria, felt like it had some measure of value, even if it wasn't one I personally would've used. By comparison, the Sigils in this entry often feel like they just aren't all that great. A good chunk of them I would never even bother to touch, such as Dark Healing which gives you health on enemy kills (Made redundant by the Queen Of Dusk, which gives you health when picking up Lunar Crystals, which most enemies drop,) or the one that makes your Companion act more often, as that only has a substantial benefit with Brave Companions. Although there are many Companions that can be equipped, they all only ever do one of three things: Attack [Brave], Rarely bring up a large chunk of money [Explorer], or drop a 10 MP restorative [Healer]. That last category ends up being the most useless of all, as there are only a grand total of  to use your MP. The Healing Bell, which at least gets an offensive upgrade and has some Sigils that modify it to be a more useful defensive tool, (creating a shield, adding a buff if you use it twice in quick succession, allowing it to overheal you) the Sigil that enhances your powered-up arrows to inflict fire damage over time, (reduced against bosses and objectively inferior to  dot arrows which you can get later that do more damage per tick, can be stacked more easily, and doesn't require a charge shot) and the Sigil that makes your arrows explode to deal more damage, that last one burns through MP at an incredibly quick rate, and considering you can get a separate Sigil that just makes you shoot three arrows that deal half damage each instead for a whopping zero MP per shot, there's absolutely no reason to ever bother with it.In essence, you get, if you collect all the grimoires to expand your Sigil capacity, 5 slots for passives, with two actual valuable uses for MP, which in any other scenario would be a resource you'd have to manage, choosing between healing yourself or burning it for powerful attacks on the enemy. Not to mention, these Sigils have zero flavor text. You aren't going to be having the same experience as in RuTM or Minoria where reading through the descriptions of the items you collect gives you a better picture of the world and what it's like.The story overall is much more tell than show, as well. While it answers a number of questions the other games raised, if you want a clear image of the world, you'd still need to dive through rdein's posts in the Discussion Threads to find answers to other questions, including hooks raised in this very game. As one particular example:  Most of the lore we get from this is outright told to us in exposition dumps from Melilot or background signs, including one from the Fairy Queen where Credit where it's due, however, the game's art is a step up, the environments are undeniably beautiful, and the soundtrack, especially the themes for Plunia and the Tainted Serpent, as well as  is wonderful. It gets full marks for style points, even if at the cost of its enjoyability as a game.And rdein, if you happen to read all this, I do remember the Twitter post where you admitted to being tired of making Momodora games, and it shows here. Don't force yourself. If you aren't passionate about what you're making, people will be able to tell by the product, and it won't measure up to your best.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a final love letter to the Momodora series by Rdein and Bombservice. Unfortunately it feels like a love letter jotted down in haste, by someone who no longer has any love to give for their franchise, and it's a sad development to see, coming off the truly special "Momodora: Reverie Under The Moonlight" and "Minoria", which were both stellar (particularly the former).Let's start from the beginning. Momodora is a series of bite-sized Metroidvanias, the first two of which came out for free online and were heavily inspired by Cave Story, a 2004 indie game classic by Daisuke "Pixel" Amaya.These entries along with the later Steam release of Momodora 3 in 2014, cemented Momodora's niche identity as bite-sized, casual Metroidvanias. Two years afterwards in 2016, Momodora: Reverie Under The Moonlight came out and gained a cult following. It was a genuinely incredible outing and a beautiful display of a game designer maturing. Then, three years later, a new direction was ushered in by Minoria, with a completely different art style, which looked more painterly than pixel art and used what looked like 3D models in a 2D environment, much like the Ori series. Fans were a bit more critical of this spin-off, but it was still clearly a valiant effort, and even featured a story that felt like it actually had something to say, even if the conclusion seemed like it took away from some of the messaging that was attempted to be established.And now we’re here, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a game that takes ten steps backwards. Even in the series’ most banal entries, at least the game design elements did not clash with one another, but Momodora Moonlit Farewell takes away great elements from the predecessor, such as rewards for no-hit killing bosses, fun secrets and a true Metroidvania map that loops in on itself multiple times in clever ways and trades it for a half-baked linear experience with an eye-roll worthy story and a level of writing that almost feels like the entire writing team for their previous games was fired, as well as some of the most bland boss battles in the series, boring character designs and a Hardcore mode, that only exemplifies the game’s further issues with lack of control response and typical Momodora one-hit kill shenanigans.Characters in Momodora Moonlit Farewell have about as many dimensions as their in-game sprites. Stamina is a drag, and works poorly, along with your bow using up the entire gauge whenever you accidentally decide to fire it while at full stamina (which performs a lackluster, extra powerful shot). The hitboxes are (as already mentioned) wonky, there are instakill moments and areas, where the entire difficulty is enemy spam or not being able to see anything two feet in front of you (particularly during the latter half of the game). Enemies do not stagger consistently, the dodge is also inconsistent, and has a terrible delay at times, or you just straight up take damage during a part of the animation that should have I-frames, or even during a perfect dodge (a type of dodge at the last second, where your stamina is not drained in the process). Status ailments are barely visible unless you go out of your way to remember to look into the corner of your screen, same with health, unless you’re actively looking at it, you will not know whether you are at full health or on the brink of death, cause your character always behaves the same. There is a mana system that you’re mostly just gonna use for healing and nothing else. Most bosses, particularly towards the latter half of the game, can simply be out-DPSed, while you spam attack and occasionally heal during your brainless button-mashing. Sigils, this game’s signature passive upgrades, are equally bad, with a bunch of them overlapping in effect, and only like a 10th of them being of any use to you during a playthrough.Reverie Under The Moonlight, a game that’s over half a decade old at this point, features a hidden ending, actual secrets that aren’t just marked for you on the map, a map that isn’t just a boring, linear slog, masquerading as a Metroidvania, an interesting story, with characters that you can actually get somewhat invested in, a dodge roll that works, without superfluous, poorly implemented stamina mechanics, actual proper and interesting difficulty modes, that aren’t just “what if you play the game again, but now it’s mirrored and you have a three hit combo instead of a four hit combo?” and “what if we delete your save file when you inevitably die to the unresponsive controls and strange hitboxes?” The game also had interesting and memorable boss encounters, which this game lacks wholly. All of that just to say the game is half-baked, and I actually had to stop myself in listing all of the flaws and glaring design oversights, because this review would’ve been even longer. This is not what I expected after four years of development and 7 years after the team released an actual Metroidvania classic. Moonlit Farewell is a hollow husk of the greatness that came before, and it’s a damn shame. At least it runs well and has nice spritework.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell? A Beautifully Dark Tale with a Hint of Light! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"This game dazzles with its exquisite pixel art and engaging combat, yet grapples with linear progression and restrictive gameplay elements, presenting a beautiful but flawed gem in the Metroidvania genre.""Momodora: Moonlit Farewell" captivates with its enchanting pixel art and a story that weaves darkness with hope. As the latest installment in the beloved Momodora series, it stands out with its compelling narrative of Momo, the High Priestess of Koho, battling against demonic forces. The game's aesthetics are a major triumph. Every frame of its pixel art oozes charm and attention to detail, creating an immersive world that's both haunting and beautiful. The animation is fluid, bringing the action-packed gameplay to life. Melee combos, dodging, and archery feel satisfyingly responsive, making each encounter a thrilling experience.The game innovates with its Sigil system, allowing players to customize their playstyles. This level of customization adds a layer of strategy and personalization, appealing to players who enjoy tailoring their gameplay experience. However, not every aspect shines equally. Some players have expressed concerns over the linear progression, feeling it departs from the exploratory nature typical of the genre. Additionally, the stamina meter, while aiming to add a layer of challenge, occasionally feels more restrictive than rewarding. The map, though beautifully crafted, has drawn criticism for its layout, which some feel undermines the Metroidvania essence of exploration and discovery.Despite its shortcomings, "Momodora: Moonlit Farewell" delivers a compelling experience. The game's story, while more direct and less open-ended than some might prefer, is engaging and concludes the series in a meaningful way. The combat system, with its fluid mechanics and impressive art, makes each battle a visual and tactile pleasure. The game doesn't shy away from its darker themes, handling them with a maturity that adds depth to its world. In summary, “Momodora: Moonlit Farewell” is a title that offers both beauty and flaws, much like the moonlit world it portrays. It's a journey worth taking for fans of the series and newcomers alike, offering a unique blend of action, art, and story that resonates long after the screen fades to black.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: Finished my 1st playthrough so it's time to write a review.For those who have never played Momodora, you might've heard of the game .This game is  that sequel, rather, this game is the sequel to , with this, let me call this game .But don't let this confuse you, Reverie Under the Moonlight is a distant prequel to Momodora 1, so technically it's Momodora 0.Now that we got that out of the way let's start the review.Read the  part of this review for tl;dr.The gameplay is very similar to RUtM (Momodora 0), that game was the first game in the series that's considered souls-like, and Momodora 4 is no different, it's still very much a souls-like, even more so because they added stamina system, MP system, and autosaves. Like in RUtM, you have two weapons, Maple Leaf and Bow, but they don't behave the same way, which makes sense, you can no longer charge your bow, and Momo will throw her Maple Leaf to use it as a boomerang-like projectile at the end of the combo.Active Items are not a thing anymore, the only item you can use is the Healing Bell, which is not a consumable, instead, it just costs your MP to heal, but it's not broken since your MP doesn't regenerate over time, unless you have a sigil that can do just that.Passive Items returns and is more expanded, in the form of Sigils, you can craft Sigils or you can find them throughout the map.You can no longer warp from the bells, instead there's an NPC for teleportation, and it's not present in every bells, basically checkpoints and teleports are separate now.Movement wise, you don't unlock double jump right away, and later on you can unlock sprint, which is something that wasn't present in RUtM, unfortunately there's no airdash in this game.But the most important thing of it all, This game has Fishing!!If you know anything about the developer, rdein, he plays FFXIV, and the fishing minigame is similar to that in FFXIV, but it's basically level 1 ffxiv fishing, Tap to cast, tap when you see "!!", get the fish, very simple.Oh, you can also pet the cats, you can even get an achievement for it!RUtM story was quite dark and tragic, but this one is brighter and more hopeful, that's all I can say, as the dev said the series has always been focused on action and minimal stories, so I'd say don't worry too much about the story, but if you do care, the dev have left you some notes in game that you can obtain at the start of the game which explains all the events that happened in previous Momodora games, so yeah, again, like the dev said, don't worry too much about "catching up"!It's very much an improvement from the previous installment, it might be related to how the story goes but this time the music has more "colors" to it.Now since I've only finished my first playthrough, I can't really say much about this, but after you beat the game you do unlock an alternate mode and an extra difficulty, and I think the alternate mode is different enough that it might be worth replaying, the game is short anyway, about 6-7 hours long.Though I think the Sigils system is enough to make this game worth replaying, trying out different builds might be fun.And after you beat the game, you can revisit the boss fights! I think this is an important feature for speedrunners who wants to practice and fight certain bosses, or for anyone who wants to fight certain bosses over and over again, since some of them are really fun.Momodora: Moonlit Farewell, or as I'd like to call it Momodora 4, is just like Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight, but with Fishing, uh, I mean, it's a huge improvement over Momodora RUtM, with better looking graphics, more enemy varieties, more gameplay features, etc.If you don't know anything about RUtM, it's a souls-like metroidvania game, and this game is no different.And if you've never played a Momodora game before, I'd still absolutely recommend getting this, don't worry too much about the story, the game gives you notes at the beginning which explains everything that happened in previous Momodora games.If you're a fan of Metroidvania games in general, try this game, this game might be short (6-7 hours), but it's packed with quality in every part of it.Fluid gameplay, nice looking pixel graphics, and great soundtracks.

_childDocuments_.review: It's... okay.Competent enough 'vania with good exploration, story and combat. Doesn't reach the heights of Momodora: RUtM, but it's decent fun for a single playthrough.Doing additional runs however is a chore. The movement is a bit sluggish and there is tad too much dialogue and cutscenes in the game to make replaying enjoyable. The overall difficulty is also too low to make it challenging. The 2 modes you unlock after beating the game is essentially just mirror mode and "HardCore" which deletes your savefile upon single death - which works really bloody well with the fact the only boss that has 1HKO death pit in it's arena is *the last one* - and even that is just more annoying than difficult.Single playthrough lasts somewhere between 5 to 8 hours and there is not much fun to squeeze out of the game after you are done with that one run so grab it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall fine, if somewhat short and slightly hollow feeling. I finished it in one (admittedly quite long) sitting. I'm not sure what it is missing, but I didn't like it quite as much as Reverie Under the Moonlight. Maybe it is the lack of multiple endings or the lack of any real difficulty. By the end, there wasn't even any point in dodging anymore, with how easy it was to out heal the boss damage.To summarize, if you've played the rest of the series, get the game. Otherwise, get Reverie Under the Moonlight instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick note: This is the 5th game in the Momodora franchise. If you haven't played the past games and want to jump into this one, that's still perfectly fine. There are some documents in-game that you can find that briefly tells the story of the past games. If you find that you do enjoy this game, I recommend playing the other games as well. 1, 2, and 3 are all connected. The 4th game (Reverie Under the Moonlight) is a prequel to the series and can be played standalone.Reverie Under the Moonlight already impressed me and skyrocketed to the #1 spot in my list of all-time favorite games. Moonlit Farewell? Blew RUtM out of the water.The pixel art is more gorgeous than ever. The combat feels faster, smoother, and overall more satisfying. The addition of Sigils to provide new abilities and damage bonuses expanded the fun even more and gives a sense of build crafting if you'd like to go all in on defense, self-healing, offense, or even mobility.Finishing a first-time playthrough with all collectibles and upgrades for 111% completion should take around 10-11 hours. After that you'll unlock two new modes and have to complete each of those (3 playthroughs total) to get the last achievements for the modes you unlocked.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm saying this first because it will be the biggest make or break for people looking into buying this game: , despite the map design still aligning with that -vania style of game. For this reason, I am going to call this game a vania, after Metroid Fusion.That being said, this game has been well worth the wait. I have been excited for this game since I saw its initial announcement and it has lived up to the expectations I had.-Momo is a step up from Kaho in terms of movement, retaining almost all of the movement Kaho had in Reverie (including some unintentional tech like the jumping dodge roll being implemented) and getting additional movement options through the upgrades given to you.-In addition to the above point, there is now a stamina meter tied to the dodge roll and sprinting. I assume the former is to punish dodge spam while the latter is... Sprinting. It has been very well implemented and never outright gets in the way of the experience.-I really like the Sigil system. There's a lot of different ways to customize Momo with it that allow you to choose how to play the game. Want to give your leaf attacks a little more oomph? Do it. Want to make yourself more tanky? The Sigils exist for it. Want to shoot a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of explosive arrows? Go ahead! I love it because you can make an argument for the use of any Sigil, so it comes down to what you think is the most important.-This game is  The art is very fluid and detailed without any style clashing. I adore the backgrounds, scenery, and animation; as a sprite artist myself, I know this is all hard to nail down and they hit that nail on the freakin' head.-The map tells you if there are secrets in the area and how many exits a room has. This makes secret hunting easier, but I do prefer when games only hint at this information and don't disclose if there's something secret in an area outright.-Hard mode is a 1-life ordeal, and while easy to find, is not accessible from the start, instead being earned behind a fake wall.-Kinda miffed there aren't multiple endings this time around...-Some enemies, mainly at the midway point, felt a bit too damage spongey, even with obtaining all the damage upgrades up to that point.-I do not like the upgrades that require you to wait in real time for them to appear.The story and writing are serviceable. I'm not expecting every game to be a life-changing experience of course, but I'm not going to keep playing a game if the writing is Marvel-tier. Fortunately, Moonlit Farewell is competently written, and does a good job of wrapping up the story.I've never been a good music critic; I don't know the terminology for any of it, so I'm not going to go in depth. The compositions are good and atmospheric, which fits the game's overall mood.I already went over the graphics, but I could go on and gush about them forever. This game is FRIGGIN BEAUTIFUL with its art. It's fluidly animated, everything is very clearly readable (you can tell what it's supposed to be), and it all fits the atmosphere so well. I could recognize some re-used sprites from Reverie, but the artstyle between the two games is not so different that they clash.Part of me thought the maps were just slightly too big, but going back with the perspective that the game is more of a "Fusionvania" rather than your typical open-ended affair, it honestly kinda works with that type of design. It does make backtracking to get stuff you missed take a bit longer, but with the increased mobility you get as you get further in, this slowly becomes less of an issue over time.Ultimately, this game is best if you go in with the expectation that it will be a more linear adventure. That in itself is not a bad thing; I do not believe all Metroidvanias have to be open-ended, easily-broken maps. In fact, I would encourage more games to try the approach done here! I believe this sort of "Fusionvania" style is worthy of being its own subgenre.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodoras fifth entry is also its strongest.  This is not surprising, as rdein/Bomb Service have gotten more skilled between each Momodora release.  The game fully embraces its "Metroidvania-ness" this time around, with a proper map and everything.  The pixel work and sound design are, as always, exceptional.  The action is challenging and great, especially the boss encounters.  The game and the world are bigger and more ambitious than the last game, and it is very rewarding to explore.  It has taken some cues from the great Hollow Knight and is better for it.  A wonderful game, I had a great time playing through it.  10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I took a very  enjoyment from the bulk of the game, looking at the nice pixel art and animation, navigating the perfectly  map while drinking green tea and eating Turkish candy bars.  Nothing about it was offensive, but nothing in it was particularly thrilling, particularly interesting, and that made it sort of  -- it's a real come-down from , the fourth excellent installment in the series (and the one you should actually be playing instead of this, if you haven't already).  I will now launch into a series of criticisms of things that drag  down to the level of a perfectly forgettable (but not hateful) bundle game:- Clunkier character movement when compared to .  The addition of the stamina bar was a bad design decision, as Momo plods along slowly enough through these winding metroidvania corridors when she's full-out  -- but then she's also constantly running out of stamina and being reduced to an even more sluggish walk!  In keeping with the molasses-momentum theme, attack combos feel way too drawn-out and  for such a big environment, meaning you can't turn readily when you start up the leaf bash dance, which can be pretty frustrating.  If this was a game in which you constantly face-off against complexly programmed individual enemies, it would be a different matter.- Too many flashing, glowing light effects.  Along with the more detailed pixel art, this makes me think the dev concentrated too much on the visual side of things and not enough on the design aspect.  Often the magic lights and explosions occlude what you really want to see.  The spirit companions are mostly useless and distracting as well -- always zipping around or making light blooms -- and you're better off without them.- Too easy, with uninteresting, dopily programmed boss battles.  Not much to see here -- no interesting patterns of magic attacks from the big bad guardians, no real threats or temporary roadblocks of difficulty that make you back up and think about what you're doing wrong.  Usually bosses have two simple attacks that are easy to avoid while you totally  on them, and mostly kill them on the first try.  The difficulty problem is exacerbated by the plethora of perk-giving Sigil cards.  A game of this simplicity did not  all this extra, superficially complicated junk -- the Sigils or the spirit companions.- For a story that's so unremittingly , there sure is a lot of dialog to emphasize it!  But maybe it's not so much the story itself as the way it's presented . . . there should have been a little more personality involved in the telling, cool pixel art portraits with expressions, perhaps.  Definitely could have used a lot more fan service!  (I did, however, get a chuckle out of the lamia boss with the big hanging knockers; if you make more games, Bombservice, more designs like this, please!)  Dora and Momo should have been given funny little quirks in the dialog (since there is so very much), building them up to be something other than "aggressive girl-boss with upbeat attitude" and "slightly more humble girl-boss with upbeat attitude."  Everybody else is just "well-wisher" and "grumbler who becomes well-wisher after quest."If I'd known  was so middle-of-the-road, I wouldn't have rushed to buy it, and would certainly have opted for a more fun action indie to play on my vacation.  Just to make sure that my memory was accurate, I loaded up  -- and it's , still so much better than this!  I almost started playing it outright (and would have, if this one hadn't burned me out on the whole Momodora thing for a while).  Fast, punchy gameplay, clean attractive graphics, level design that makes you feel like you're on an actual .  Just better all-around!(Notice that I do not discommend the game.  It's not really that bad, and I did have some meditative, marginally fun times with it.  I just don't think it's worth full price -- and unlike the previous installment, I will never consider playing it again.)

_childDocuments_.review: It's been awhile; Almost 8 years since the last Momodora game as well as close to 5 since Minoria. And wow, rdein and the rest of the Bombservice came back with a really good game.  Phenomenal visuals. The other games already looked great but the way the style has evolved since then; smaller details, sprite work, etc elevate Moonlit Farewells presentation to a truly impressive level. The more zoomed out view, especially compared to Reverie, plays a part in this too; seeing more of the background art and of course letting you see further ahead is always nice for games like this. But that's not the only thing; the animations? Excellent! The work put into them was most certainly not unnoticed or unappreciated. Good soundtrack too! The music for each area is very nice and atmospheric. Hearing that classic bell gong sound effect after hitting it to save progress is something I never tire of.The gameplay has been a bit more streamlined and faster paced. Switching between different items to use is gone; there's a dedicated button for healing and instead you have sigils to equip which have a variety of effects that you can't freely change in and out around during boss fights. Not all are created equal, though there's enough variety for different approaches. There is no leveling in this game, you collect and eat berries to increase various stats so being thorough is always a good idea. Moonlit Farewell is definitely on the easier side; those sigils can really help you shred through a Boss' HP much faster or add greatly to your survivability depending on your load-out. Doing a run without sigils and deliberately limiting the amount of stat increases would make for quite a challenge.Overall, I had a lot of fun with Momodora: Moonlit Farewell. It feels like, and is, the culmination of the series; that the team has really applied what they've learned over the years to give the series a worthy send off; something they readily succeeded at. I look forward to whatever they decide to work on next.

_childDocuments_.review: Greatly enjoyed the experience, though, I must say, slightly less then previous series entry- Reverie. As a result, the game had less creative bosses, uneven difficulty (and by uneven I mean it was for the most part far too easy with several significant spikes here and there).However, I would not want my words to distract from the fact of this game being extremely enjoyable. Movement was done beautifully well, with the only gripe I can think of - far to sensitive walljumps, often leading to Momo doublejumping instead of walljumping.Toolkit works really good and all the main tools we get throughout the world are used frequently, but, yet again, I feel like I'm repeating myself, the progression felt a bit too guided, with few possibilities to wander off to where the dragons live. On the other hand, after ending the main campaign you get a lot of post-end content, with possibilities to fight a bit more, including an unexpected harder-than-final boss, as well as a challenge mode and additional play modes for the campaign.Artwork is very similar to previous game - it is intentionally flat, which makes for memorable style, with cute sprites of all characters and enemies.Overall - categorically recommending, good stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a game made with a lot of care from its developers and it shows. From the beautifully polished designs and animations to the smooth and well optimized gameplay, the stelar soundtrack, the nice and responsive combat and controls, as well as the charming dialogue on the sparse story moments it has.From a technical standpoint, Moonlit Farewell is a Metroidvania and, in comparison to many others, maybe a much more linear one. While finding multiple routes, sequence breaking and non linear gameplay are considered sacred pillars of metroidvania and I can't disagree on the notion of being very good features, their absense here is not too harshly felt if you're more interested in seeing what the game has to offer. It's much closer to Metroid Fusion's metroidvania than Super Metroid. A less open, though still mostly exploration driven and much more story centric than it's predecessor, Moonlit Farewell is delightful to play, to explore and to see what it has to offer.This is not a painful game to 100%, which is a complaint I have despite being a veteran of the genre, I do find the "shoot every hidden block to find every secret in the game" a dreadfully boring quest, so I like how the game tells you which rooms have puzzles worth exploring and trying instead of letting you figure everything out. In my opinion, no game should have the player spend tens of hours shooting, attacking and rolling into every pixel because of a fake wall trying to find the one last collectible pick up, so to me, games have two options remedying this: They either make the game not meant to find everything or they make it more feasible to find everything. Moonlit Farewell goes for the second round and it's still very much enjoyable.With customizable abilities through collectible and purchaseable items and a wonderful pace, as well as very relaxing and soothing artstyle, it's a great game to put some effort in and still have a good time. Selectable difficulty also helps cater for a larger audience, so that's a plus.Any self respecting Momodora fan should give this game a try, even if it's to come to their own conclusions. I see this as a stellar game and I'm glad I bought this as soon as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: While I excitedly awaited for Moonlit Farewell's release, I played through all the Momodora games and the (sadly underrated and underappreciated) Minoria. I'm a few hours, several zones and several bosses into the game and can safely say that this feels like the culmination of years of practice, improvement and iteration from the developer. Everything feels bigger, better, more thought out; there's more story to be told, and the game isn't afraid to tell it (in that sense it reminds me of Minoria more than its predecessors); bossfights and special encounters are generously peppered through each of the richly-detailed zones, which steadily provide you with augments to your exploration/movement and combat skills, in such a way that you're always only a few minutes away from some kind of improvement; the pixel art and sound design/soundtrack is at its best... and so on and so on. To avoid being even more repetitive, my point can be summed up as: this is Momodora at its best and I can't wait to play more of it. If you're a fan of the series or Metroidvanias in general, I fully recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid. Nothing more, nothing less.The graphics and animations are an iteration and a step up from Momodora4, disregarding the change in artstyle of Minoria,But everything else...it just feels uninspired, tired even, "by the numbers". And rather linear and easy. Seriously, there is ONE somewhat difficult platforming part to get a lily...and I don't know if the difficulty setting is bugged or something? Are bosses designed with no-hit runs in mind? Most of them do so little damage that you can just facetank your way to victory, and their balance is also all over the place. Is the last phase of the last boss supposed to just kinda stand there? Moreso for the nightmare versions (catgirl first fight nightmare is harder than anything else).Speaking of all over the place: Upgrades. At the beginning you'll have to find hidden walls, later you might have to go out of your way through 5 maptiles with like 3 enemies in it just to arrive at a dead end with a berry. Or they are just ...there, in plain sight. Best example is the upgrade for the leaf: Randomly step into some puddle and here you go.There is also pretty much no point in the currency you collect, there is nothing to buy except for some mediocre sigils. And there's a fish that gives 1k a pop.The fast travel system showing up late isn't really an issue, since the game autosaves your state frequently, for example when you pick up an item. That state persists through death&respawn, or quit to title, so just selecting your manual savepoints carefully when backtracking and just quit and load when you picked up what you came for.I still had fun and completed the 111% in 2 sittings, but just like with Minoria it could have been so much better.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I enjoyed this one, but would highly recommend Momodora RUtM over it if you haven't played that one yet, then play Moonlit Farewell afterwards. I beat Moonlit Farewell in 6.5 hours, with 110% completion on Normal Mode, so it's fairly short, but sweet. The art and music's at its strongest in this entry, and the atmosphere's palpable, each zone feels unique both with its scenery and the enemies that inhabit them. Also the map UI is a great improvement too, it felt way smoother to 100% the game here than in RUtM thanks to the ? marks indicating things you haven't gotten yet.Although my biggest gripe is that the game's way, way too easy (for me perhaps). You get some crazy good Sigils (abilities) even early on that're fun to customize your build with. But the bosses just can't catch up to your power as long as you're doing a reasonable amount of exploration. Most of their attacks are laughably slow compared to your much faster movement in this game, or look way more threatening than they are. And since there isn't much to spend mana on aside from healing, you're rarely ever short on heals. I actually didn't die to a single boss (okay I fell off a kill-ledge instantly on one of them because my attack sent me too far), whereas RUtM's boss fights kicked my ass.The last thing I'll mention is the difference in tone, which's interesting to me. While the atmosphere of the stages conveys a journey through a once peaceful land under attack, the actual story itself is told more directly to you, and presents Momo (the player) as a hero/chosen one who'll save her village and the world at the end of the day. It even has companions who stick with you along the way so you don't feel too lonely on your journey! You really do feel like a hero with how powerful the game makes you at the end. By contrast, Kaho in RUtM feels like a hopeless, yet ceaselessly determined cause, and its world feels far more oppressive to her, with very few NPCs who actually acknowledge her cause or even care that she exists, even forcing her to kill other humans who were only trying to do what they thought was right. To both ends, these games succeed at telling their stories, Moonlit Farewell's much more optimistic story is a great note to end off on after Reverie Under the Moonlight's grim and dreary world.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since I played the other Momodora games but I think I even 100%'ed them all. I don't consider myself a fan, but I've always appreciated them for what they are; decent little metroidvania games with their own distinguishable style. So naturally, when I saw this one was out, it was an instant buy for me. This review is mainly about warning others from making the same mistake I did.While the art, animations and music are as good as they always were, that's where the glowing positives end.The game has plenty of baffling systems and decisions which make it seem like it lacked anyone to tie it all together or ask if this or that is a good idea. Just as an example, the game has a mobile game reminiscent system where you plant seeds in various rooms around the map and have to wait 10 real life minutes for it to grow into a stat boost item. While that is a very minor thing by itself, and I wouldn't even care about it if the map was fun to explore and to come back to grab the item after a while, but it isn't. Traveling through the world is mostly a chore which makes such a minor-sounding gripe so offensive, like the developer doesn't respect your time. Hence why patching such a system out wouldn't fix the game because the problem is deeper than that. Still, nothing about the game is inherently broken. The controls are fine. The combat is fine. The bosses are fine. It just lacks anything interesting to keep you playing. I would recommend the game to two types of people: those that are hardcore Momodora fans or hardcore metroidvania fans who have exhausted pretty much all of their other options and are looking for their next fix. I belong to the 2nd group but I just didn't have a good time with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a culmination of the passion which has been poured into its predecessors. There are many places where it exceeds them and a handful of ways in which it falls short, but the latter is vastly overshadowed by the former. While I still firmly believe that Reverie Under the Moonlight is the premiere experience for this series of bite-sized metroidvanias, Moonlit Farewell is more than worthy to stand alongside it, and I sincerely hope that the team behind this is proud of their work and rewarded for their efforts. It goes without saying that I highly recommend this game, but this wouldn’t be a review of mine if I didn’t excessively elaborate:Despite my many gripes with this game’s direct predecessor, Minoria, one aspect it strongly succeeded in was combat. Much can be said about the strength of the full-screen-slash parry’s capacity to trivialize certain rooms, but let it never be said that it wasn’t a damn satisfying parry. That’s the key word here for me: combat in Momodora games has never been particularly challenging by my metric, but it has always been satisfying. Minoria added additional layers of mechanical complexity which greatly improved the gamefeel of what was already there, and it is with great delight that I can say Moonlit Farewell has taken those improvements and ran with them (while reigning them in somewhat). Highest on the list are two new resources to manage: tried and true mana and stamina.In previous Momodora games, items would be individual-use: you had X amount of heals/magic projectiles and after you used them up, you were done. This created a situation in which your best choice was to drop a thermonuclear payload the instant you walked into the room with no consequences and then carry on with the fight like usual. Moonlit Farewell instead ties all of these usual resources to a mana bar, meaning that you have to manage your resources and raw destructive potential a bit more carefully. Healing and explosive arrows (as an example) being tied to the same resource forces you to sacrifice safety for aggression: you can dish out some crazy damage, but in doing so you’re limiting your own ability to take it. Though this change limits the macabre glee that comes with nuking a boss frame one, it also adds some technical complexity to existing systems by combining them, making the game feel more cohesive as a whole. It’s smart, though not the only resource which marries existing ideas to great effect.Unlike most games stamina in Moonlit Farewell is more of a defensive reserve than an offensive allowance. Outside of a heavily empowered arrow which activates when at full stamina - once again balancing safety with aggression - the only action which consumes the bar is dodging. Gone are the days of Kaho’s endless frame-perfect frollicking (which I did miss, admittedly) and Semilla’s perpetual parry-baiting; in their place, however, is a roll which rewards you for timing it like a parry by refunding the spent stamina back alongside a one-two-punch of dopamine in the form of gold flourish and a brief time-slow. While this does feel satisfying, it unfortunately brings us to my first key gripe.One of my favorite aspects of the Momodora games is the No-Hit Bonus - if you’re skilled enough to beat a boss without taking a single hit of damage, you’ll get a unique (and often overpowered) reward for your efforts that you can’t find anywhere else in the game. It’s certainly a “rich get richer” mechanic in the sense that someone good enough to get the bonus probably doesn’t need it, but it adds an extra layer of challenge to boss fights and makes repeat playthroughs (which are essential to Momodora games) far more engaging. With that in mind, I’m sure you’ll understand my disappointment at the complete removal of this feature in Moonlit Farewell. With the inclusion of the perfect dodge and the stamina system, Moonlit Farewell is perfectly poised to encourage mechanical mastery and reward it when it's achieved, but it simply does not do so. As a result, I find myself less eager to engage with repeat playthroughs, which is rough for this series. This didn’t significantly harm my enjoyment of the game overall, mind you, but the exclusion of a system I greatly enjoyed does leave a slightly sour taste. What sweetens my palette in response, however, is the consistently delightful presentation.Moonlit Farewell returns to the gorgeous pixel art of Reverie Under the Moonlight after the experimental 2.5D style that was used (quite well, in my opinion) in Minoria. I’ve always loved the character designs of this series, and that continued charm is on full display with this newly-improved stylistic iteration. Sprites are not only more detailed and expressive, but their range of expression through animation is far stronger too: Momo acrobatically swaps grips and angles when repeatedly firing her bow as opposed to Kaho’s more static, utilitarian archery, making her feel far more energetic and active. This aesthetic fluidity keeps traversal engaging, which heavily supplements the areas you’ll be traversing in. Environments are richly-detailed, visually compelling, and - most important of all for a metroidvania - instantly distinct. The Momodora games have always boasted clear and communicative maps, but I found myself intuitively remembering the pathways within each area even on my first time through them - no map necessary. This is not, to say, however, that the map itself is not worthy of praise. It’s not revolutionary or anything, but having secrets be immediately marked on the map struck me as particularly kind. It could be argued that this level of signposting removes some of the magic that comes with the genre: the excitement of discovery is core to the metroidvania experience, so fully knowing there’s a secret in a room when you enter can dampen that excitement. While I don’t disagree with that notion, I found that my fondness for the convenience this feature added outweighed any missed potential.No, my largest sore point with Moonlit Farewell is the missed potential in its writing. I’ve said before that the Momodora games are pleasantly bite-sized, so I’m not exactly expecting Wuthering Heights with regards to the narrative and characters. I would, however, like to actually get some time to bond with my traveling companion. Cereza is your trusty helper and resident Sigil Salescatgirl, and while you do get a small handful of moments to get to know her, they are both very few and very far between. When I’ve maxed my bond with Cereza after sharing exactly one day’s worth of meals, I can’t help but feel hungry for more. Minoria had the exact same problem with Semilla and Fran’s relationship: it’s hard to get attached when our primary cast has only had about fifteen lines of dialogue between them before their Big Dramatic Story Beat. It leaves the world feeling paper-thin, and Moonlit Farewell might even be a step backwards from Minoria in this respect. At least Fran chimed in with the occasional comment on a new area or significant story beat; Cereza will often appear after both with nothing new to say at all. Given that you’re mechanically encouraged to bond with her, it’s astounding to me how little dialogue she has. If I wasn’t fully aware how much time it takes to write and implement, I’d argue she and other characters should have twice as much.That said, it speaks volumes that my largest problem with the game is that I want more optional dialogue. This has been a consistent desire of mine as it relates to the Momodora series - they are lacking only in comparison to my sheer gluttony. Moonlit Farewell is perhaps the most fine-tuned and polished entry in the Momodora series to date, and the improvements it makes on the experimental systems of the games before it are far-and-away full successes. I’ll be praying for the much-deserved success of this game, and eager to see what the minds behind it have in store next.

_childDocuments_.review: rdein and team have done it again. Moonlit Farewell is a gorgeous game with beautiful pixel art, a phenomenal soundtrack, compelling level design, fair and fun boss fights, and an engaging progression system. Only criticisms I'd leverage against it is that it is a bit easier than Reverie Under the Moonlight, and there are no incentives outside of an achievement for doing a zero-damage boss fight (though I personally agree with this change). The game is a fair bit longer than Reverie Under the Moonlight as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful, and quite good for 16 dollars, but I do have some gripes.I found myself disappointed with the exploration, everything being marked out on your map kinda makes it feel more like a checklist, and the world's levels aren't woven together very well. You even get a fast travel around halfway or so through the game. There isn't too much in the way of unmarked secrets, and I had found everything on my first play through, which is quite crippling for a Metroidvania's replay value. Even the money you generally build throughout exploration is mostly useless, since you can easily afford everything in the shop without trying.The combat can feel really button mashy, there isn't much incentive to pay attention to the boss' animations and patterns as you can out DPS them especially by the end. Having just beaten it, I don't actually remember any of the final boss' attacks because I sorta just pushed the attack button until it died. I hope the game gets patched or something down the line. There is a boss rush mode that advertises "nightmare bosses" but really they're the same bosses you fight normally just with red squares added in to the arena that damage you. It really is just a test on if your attention span can hold up for the entire gauntlet so you don't forget to push your healing button periodically.Those are two pretty big gripes for a lot of people, but the game's price makes it a much easier sell. The game does genuinely have a lot of potential which is the only reason I'd be here nitpicking about it's shortcomings to begin with.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: If you played and liked any of the Momodora games you can stop reading here and just buy the game, you'll absolutely enjoy it.If you never played Momodora before, but are interested in Metroidvanias or 2d action games, I also think you'll really like it.This game is the culmination and a love letter to the whole Momodora series. The main plot is standalone, so it's not absolutely necessary to play the previous games to enjoy this one (and there is a handy summary), but I highly recommend you do to get all the little nods and references to the previous games. This game is at the same time true to the classic tropes of the series but it also changes up the momodora formula a bit, but in ways that i ended up really liking.I was unsure at first about the secrets being marked in the map, but in the end it was still challenging to find ways to access them and it didn't bother me.Managing Stamina for dodges and the bow made boss fights really tense and memorable to me.There's also the amazing addition of boss rush mode, that is always a plus in my book.And it has fishing! What more do you want?Speaking of boss fights, bombservice has not lost his edge and delivered amazing boss fights on par with the bests in the series (and one i consider one of my favorite boss fights overall)I would also be remiss not to mention the art and animations of this game. They are absolutely stellar, truly one of the most beautiful pixel metroidvanias that i've seen lately. Not only Momo's animations are amazing but the bosses to, the team managed to craft cinematic experiences that I will not forget anytime soon with their art.I cleared the game 111% and it was a pretty good time overall, my expectations for this game were great, and even then they were exceeded. But I'm a big fan of the series, so your mileage may vary.All in all this is a very messy review, but if you want to take anything from it, is that the game is good, beautiful, polished and I loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The map is a series of bidirectional corridors with the occasional progress check or looping shortcut, the sigil system is a balancing mess, and most bosses—despite their wonderful animation—are bare-bones fights without much incentive to learn. Moonlit Farewell is a straight shot from beginning to end with almost zero friction, just backtracking through disposable and non-threatening enemies; I didn't find traversing the world very interesting, and in a game with this much world traversal, that's rough.I am  in the minority when it comes to this feeling; if you're not looking for tough-as-nails enemy placement or uncompromising, satisfying bosses, this is probably a fun romp, and the presentation is fantastic throughout. But I was hoping for more of Reverie Under the Moonlight, and Moonlit Farewell isn't that.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible farewell to a great series. The game's pretty and goes for a different approach to previous entries; it's slower and wants you to stay close to enemies and dodge well. The tone's also more somber, with Momo just "doing her job" in a way that feels even less personal than that sentence tends to mean.There's a shift halfway through in both the story and your powerset as the game becomes less somber; with enough plucky determination and a little bit of self-sacrifice, nothing can stop Momo.

_childDocuments_.review: An otherwise competent game that's held back by its difficulty, or lack thereof. Enemy attack patterns are simple and trivially easy to dodge due to the over the top signal that precede them. After getting certain upgrades you won't need to dodge at all, simply facetank and mash the attack buttons while occasionally healing is enough to destroy even bosses.I'm giving Momodora: Moonlit Farewell a thumbs up because it's still a nice experience overall (very pretty sprite work, great soundtrack, feels good to control), but the game could have been so much more engaging if it were more willing to challenge the player.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora games are always good, and if you enjoyed Reverie Under the Moonlight you will enjoy this one, Moonlit Farewell is like RUtM but with better movement and visuals.However, this high similarity to RUtM is also this game's worst aspect. See, RUtM was something otherwordly when it launched in 2016. However, 8 years have passed and the Metroidvania genre's quality bar has been pushed way higher in this time, and a game so similar to what was considered the best in 2016 is no longer the best in 2024.You want to play Moonlit Farewell? Go ahead, it's a good game and I enjoyed it. But if you have other Metroidvanias in your wishlist, you may want to consider buying them first to get the best experiences, this game won't make you feel as RUtM did 8 years ago.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a 2D sidescrolling Metroidvania that follows the storyline from the other Momodora games.Those who have played Reverie Under the Moonlight should instantly recognize this, as it is very similar.The pixel art style is well-done, animations are nice and fluid, especially the sprint animation. Bigger enemies, grander bosses, and just more NPCs to talk to in general.Those who are looking for a challenge might be left a bit wanting, though: I found the game to be significantly easier than RutM, though there is a Hardcore mode after you finish the game once, and perhaps that would scratch that itch (I didn't try it myself).There's some nice variety in builds as you have a sigil system where you can equip 1-4 sigils (based upon how many grimoires you've found laying around in the world) and in general, outside of one or two items, most items that show up as a ? on  your map aren't too ridiculous to find/obtain, and the game encourages you to fill in the whole map, as the upgrades you find are quite rewarding, especially the lillies.I love the ability to heal anytime, anywhere for 10MP, though that contributes a lot to the game's lower difficulty compared to previous Momodora games. I personally don't think this is a bad thing, but some players might not like it.If nothing else, you can always equip the sigil that reduces your health to 1, or the one that gives you infinite stamina but makes you take way more damage.The "worst" thing about this game, is its rather short playtime of 6-8 hours (it took me 6.5h to see the end of the story). It can leave a player wanting more.Still, though, at the $15 I paid for it, I'm sure I will eventually come back for more when I'm itching for a good 2D sidescrolling game.All in all, I'd have to give this a solid 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Played through the whole game, and it was the sequel I wanted, for sure. Definitely happy with this product. I will, however, lay out every nitpick I really had with this game: There is no Fullscreen Borderless mode. I tried to "cheat" it in with a window editor, but for once it just added a border around the screen- doesn't usually do that. But whatevs, the reason I wanted this mode was so that audio and gameplay didn't cut off when I alt+tabbed. Would be nice if both of these were added.The difficulty selection doesn't explain itself. Under Light mode, there was "Adaptive Difficulty", which sounds cool. But what is it? It's only under Light mode, so maybe it makes it easier if you die a lot? I played on Normal mode instead, and I think the difficulty was a little easier than past Momo games (Maybe not Minoria?) but was fair at 15-30 deaths first playthrough. The movement felt slower than previous games, but seeing as they midway introduce a sprint mechanic, it sorta makes sense. I don't know how exactly I feel about the three (maybe four?) plants that you have to grow in the game. They are like all the other plant powerups in the game, but you have to wait 10 minutes real time to get the powerup. It's fine, I guess, because the time is short, and you always go back to these spots after a bit, so I never *didn't* get them. Well, I got everything, so I wasn't going to ignore them. This feels like an annoying block for a 100% speedrun playthrough or something. I think it'd be a bit nicer if you could repeatedly give it more and more Lunar Crystals to shorten the timer by 5 minutes, or something. I completed the game, largely with the "luck" sigil equipped, but I have no clue what it does. More Lunar Crystal drops? Higher crit rate? This wasn't the only sigil that I didn't really know or understand. The other I will mention below, in spoilers.A bit into spoiler territory: The White Sorceress' animation feels repetitive and jumpy. Maybe needs more frames of animation, or not to move all the way every cycle? It was a sore thumb in the animations of this game.The "good boy" confused me for a while, because after purchasing his sigil, there was still a "?" in the room. The "?" turns out to disappear after you leave, but I still spent time looking for a drop down or secret that was. And that same sigil, does it remove 1% of your max hp every shot? For equipping? Every time you equip? I guess there is some amount of restarting I could do to test, but I feel like the brief description could use more.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sort of tough to recommend, even though I generally enjoyed it. If you like what you see on the Store page, but are still on the fence, I'd say play Reverie Under the Moonlight first. If what you're looking for is a bite-sized Metroidvania, I'd say definitely give this one a shot.I ended up finishing this game with a lot of caveats. The game is highly stable, polished, feels great to play, and definitely is an artistic achievement, but its design and narrative feel unfinished and are full of nonsequitors which ultimately left me dissatisfied.Notably, the game's short length doesn't seem to support the abundance of gameplay elements present in it. Most abilities you gather will go unused, because there simply isn't enough playtime to experiment with them. The same goes for the companion system. The game also has a system through which you grow stat upgrades in the form of berries, which grow after a ten minute delay and then allow you to pick up the upgrade. There are only three of these growable berries on the map, and the timer is just short enough to not significantly influence the way you traverse the map in any interesting way (especially once fast travel is available), but long enough to be slightly annoying. Contributing to the short length is the game's pretty low difficulty, with the game really not putting any real roadblocks in your way (bosses are a breeze). More challenging difficulty modes are only available after finishing the game once. I don't think the game's length and difficulty are entirely negative, as they at least made for a very swift and low-stress playthrough, but it does leave all these dangling systems which I would have loved to actually... Use and play around with in any meaningful way.As for the narrative, without going into too much detail, the narrative was such a straightforward defeat-evil-and-save-the-world-narrative that towards the end I started hallucinating all the ways a narrative twist would definitely for certain make things more interesting. The twist never came, despite the narrative elements in play absolutely warranting, almost necessitating that something should go wrong, that some tragedy or betrayal should lut everything you've been doing into perspective. The story that's left is fine, but bland and the ending hollow.My general takeaway is that the game has a lot of untapped potential. If its design and narrative had just been pushed a little bit more, if the game had allowed itself to be a bit more daring and complex, even at the cost of its polish, it might have had a much more positive aftertaste. It still was a fun aesthetic and gameplay experience, and it'd feel unfair to give it a negative review. Just be sure you know what you're getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: In the starting town, there is a spot in the ground where you can choose to plant some of your money, wherein a plant then grows after 10 minutes. I found this after having done most of what you can do in the town meaning that after planting I still had a decent bit of time left before it would be ready. In any other game I likely would have ignored it and trucked on with the game, coming back when the game called for it to collect my item. But I didn't. I waited. The town, like most the rest of the environments is beautifully crafted. The pixel art of the Momodora series reaches its apex here and taking in the sights becomes its own reward. Really, the game begs to be appreciated by the player and at times I couldn't help but stop and admire what the game was presenting me with. And really, is there any greater praise for a games visuals than that it tears me away from the gameplay?Speaking of gameplay let me make it clear that this game is certainly not lacking in that department. Just like its predecessor, combat is fast, fun, and fluid. The arsenal of moves is quite concise, mostly filled with the standard affair for metroidvanias but this keeps the gameplay expereince concise. I didn't use half the combat upgrades given to me in Hollow Knight, but I used all the skills I was given constantly in Moonlit Farewell. Sigils (equip-able buffs) provide a decent amount of customisation to the standard move-set. Admittedly there were several sigils that I never ended up using, but there are enough useful ones (and others useful in certain combinations) that I found myself trying new strategies with different sigil combinations whenever faced with a hard boss (for example creating a bow-focused build to make bow-only viable for bosses who were a pain to fight melee). For all challenges the game threw at me, I felt like I had the tools to overcome it.This game also possibly has my favourite map in the genre. While the map does take a step back compared to the previous Momodora in being much less interconnected, I found it to be much more well designed. I naturally got 111% completion during my run (yes, 100% is not full completion) because the game didn't hide secrets in stupid locations, breakable walls etc. The map clearly tells you when you've missed a secret - which I feel doesn't take any of the challenge away because the fun comes in finding out how to get the secret, not realising there's a secret to begin with. For other metroidvanias I've played, looking at guides for 100% ends up being a given. And I never feel like I could have found the items if I had tried harder. The fact that this was never the case in my experience speaks to how nicely laid out the game is.Difficulty is an odd one, with the normal difficulty I imagine not giving a strong challenge to anyone familiar with the genre. Early in the game you can find a sigil called "The Fool" which reduces your HP to 1, effectively making the game a no hit run. For the latter 2/3rds of the game I played with this sigil nearly always on in order to make the game challenging - but this seem extreme to expect others to do. Besides this, upon beating the game you can unlock a "hardcore" mode where dying resets your save file. This again is quite an extreme way to play. The problem then is that there really is no middle ground and can leave many players stuck with either finding the game too easy or too challenging. I would also be remiss to mention that boss difficulty is also all over the place, with many bosses feeling almost unfinished with how simple they were, and quality being a little over the place (though still overall averaging to be quite good).The game is certainly not without its faults mind. As mentioned above, difficulty and bosses are one. A common complaint is with the new controls, which while I personally never had an issue, I am very surprised configuring it to suit your playstyle isn't made into an option for accessibility. Most cut-scenes are not skippable which makes bosses with them, or repeat playthroughs, drag on more than needed. I won't harp on much about these though, because none of the issues I encountered personally brought down the experience for me, so I don't want to similarly drag down my review with them.Overall I'm very happy with this game. As someone who fell in love with the previous Momodora game, played all the previous titles, and played the developer's other metroidvania Minoria, this title really does feel like the culmination of everything they strived to do. It ends up a fitting conclusion to this whole saga and I seriously cannot wait to see what rdien and Bombservice comes out with next in the future. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Having never played a Momodora series before, I'm not sure what to expect, but as someone who likes surprises, thankfully I can say that :  is an enjoyable, pretty decent platformer game after spending hours finishing it.It's worth mentioning that I absolutely love the soundtracks, especially the later part of the game, they're really good!I've heard that Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is the final game in the series, personally I still hope to play more Momodora or any new games from this team in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: The last installment in the Momodora series. This is a sequel to Momodora 3 in the artstyle of RUtM. Needless to say, the game is gorgeous.The story feels like an improvement over the previous games. Same goes for the gameplay. While the main character feels a bit slow to control at first, in the lategame it all feels very fluid thanks to the various upgrades you earn.Difficulty is decent, and it actually gets pretty challenging in late areas. The boss fights are well designed and all feel unique, from classic Momodora style bosses to fights that feel a bit more like a puzzle.The levels are also very well designed. The map shows you when there's a secret in a room, so you don't have to explore every inch of the world to make sure you didn't miss anything. The areas all feel unique and are interconnected, so backtracking isn't boring.Instead of gaining items by defeating bosses without getting hit, you'll instead be collecting them by exploring, which honestly feels better.Expect ~10 hours to complete your first playthrough.All in all, this is a perfect conclusion for the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell is a visually stunning and mechanically succinct celebration of the series as a whole.It's design and gameplay primarily take after RUtM; however, this game is positively brimming with little details and love notes for the earlier games as well, many of which are hidden away as small secrets for the player to discover. The game feels more linear than RUtM, though it still offers a fair share of unorthodox routes, particularly when taking advantage of all the small details in the movement system. I also found that the best time to try out these other routes were during my additional playthroughs on the alternate game modes, which helped keep the game fresh throughout my time completing it. As a whole, playing this game was an extremely pleasant experience, and I'm glad I got the chance to experience it (:The games visuals all look gorgeous (especially the backdrops found throughout each area) and the soundtrack compliments the gameplay and the series as a whole. I loved finding tiny details like how the fated encounter track would switch from and to the area themes. Overall, the arts of the game are a step up from RutM, which I already found very enchanting.Also, it has a fishing minigame, which I am a massive softy for. It's a very simple one, but it still serves as a relaxing yet addictive reprieve from the standard gameplay loop.
