_childDocuments_.review: Blossom Tales 2: The Minotaur Prince is a retro-styled action game that will draw a lot of comparisons to classic Zelda titles. I honestly reviewed this game with a bit of reluctance. It's not that I have an issue as a guy with playing a female character, but a little girl? It seemed a bit much. I'm glad I was able to put my biases aside, however, because this is just an amazingly charming game that I'd happily recommend to even the most jaded or cynical person.The art in the game is all low-res pixels, done to convincingly evoke nostalgia for the classics. This is one of the rare times I'll say that this particular style actually adds to a game's atmosphere. Normally this is either done due to budgetary reasons, or legitimately to cash in some “indie cred”, here it works. Yes, it's deliberately using it to get you to put your rose-colored nostalgia filter on, but it fits with the themes of the game. The music and sound effects are in the same vein, with those simple but emotionally evocative electronic melodies, and bleeps and bloops when you pick something up or talk to an NPC. The controls are immediately intuitive, particularly to anyone who grew up playing on an NES or SNES.The story's framing device is similarly charming, with a nod to the Princess Bride-a grandfather telling his grandchildren a story, and the kids occasionally interjecting commentary about the story's events. Grandpa even bares a passing resemblance to an aging Peter Falk. The plot similarly gives a nod to Labyrinth, with Lily (your character) making a wish that the Minotaur King would take her younger brother away. The gameplay continues the nostalgia trip, with heart pieces and breakable pots and other objects containing coins, and merchants who carry exactly two things that you can buy, along with more than a few wink and nod style quips that reference pop culture. Generally speaking, the puzzles are engaging enough to not feel like a chore, but not so head-scratching that you're going to struggle long to figure out what you need to do. And if you're anything like me, you're going to be absorbed into this story. It's not a world-saving adventure; in the grand scheme of things, it's just a story grandpa is telling to his precocious grandkids to keep them entertained. When you load a save, you'll get a small scene of grandpa recapping where he left off in the story for an extra bit of charm. It's like a comfort food of sorts, digitally weaponized nostalgia designed to scratch an itch you probably didn't realize you'd had. Is it flawless? No. There were points when the controls didn't always work perfectly, like when combat wanted me to grab and throw something. The hesitation that happens when I'd head toward a ledge to jump off of it only to have my character stand there for a moment before the game realized what I was trying to do also annoyed me. In the grand scheme of things though, these are minor. If you even slightly enjoyed classic Legend of Zelda games, you'll probably love this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember A Link to the Past? Remember Link’s Awakening? Blossom Tales hopes you remember them fondly, but not so well that you can spot the blatant cribbing. There’s being inspired by and there’s being a barefaced clone, and outside of the Princess Bride style framing this really is just 2D Zelda with the serial numbers filed off.What works in Blossom Tale’s favour is how rare Zeldalikes are on Steam, despite their stablemate the Metroidvania being absurdly oversaturated. I suspect the main reason for this is that they’re actually very hard to design – puzzles need to be difficult enough that the player feels smart for solving them, but not so obscure that they’re reaching for a guide. That’s in addition to a compelling world, strong environmental design and getting the balance of combat and bosses right.Blossom Tales 2 follows the Zelda blueprint pretty rigorously, making it a solid if over-familiar adventure. Fans of the original Blossom Tales, which I suspect is basically anyone considering this game, might be wondering how much of an improvement it is over the original. Sadly it’s pretty much a level pack, to the point where irritating QoL issues from the original are still present. The inventory still ends up being a mess, you have to switch tools constantly in menus (in spite of having more than enough buttons), and the fact that nothing is marked on the map makes it very irritating to find caves, dungeons and sidequests that you couldn’t complete when you initially stumbled on them. Even allowing you to mark stuff on the map yourself would have improved the game enormously.However, if you still managed to enjoy the first one despite these issues, you’re pretty much guaranteed to enjoy this one as well. It’s a familiar structure – go to three dungeons, collect three thingies (as well as gadgets that open up more of the world), then use the three thingies to open up the final dungeon. Like the first game there’s an enormous amount of side content, and if you want anything more than a token increase in health from the bosses of the main dungeons you’ll want to take on at least some of it. World exploration is generally a lot of fun – the map is nice and compact, and you won’t have to go far to stumble onto something interesting to do.The main dungeon design is also really solid, but suffers from some very boring tools and upgrades. There’s nothing you haven’t seen before in a dozen Zelda games, and while it might be a sincere form of flattery imitation doesn’t make for particularly novel puzzles. Even if they’re overfamiliar they’re tightly designed though, and I still enjoyed my time with them.There’s a good reason why the design worked so well to begin with and honestly there isn’t much in the way of competition. There have been a couple of decent Zeldalikes in the last few years - Death’s Door was fine, if more combat heavy than I’d like, and Tunic really nailed the exploration and atmosphere even if the puzzle design was lacking. Blossom Tales 2 is more low-rent than both of those games, but it’s probably got the strongest core design.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice chill game and a great value! Highly recommend on Steam Deck, played the whole game on it. Excellent battery performance and low hardware temps. Blossom Tales II is similar to BT1 and that is a good thing. Puzzles are creative, satisfying, usually just the right difficulty, and make you feel like a bit of a genius when you get them. Music is good and I looked forward to getting to the next one of each area. The puzzles are the most challenging part of the game, rather than the combat. I love the ways I'm reminded of Zelda: A Link to the Past, yet Blossom Tales is its own game, and it is wonderful! Although I greatly enjoyed it, I will say I  prefer Blossom Tales: The Sleeping King. A couple of criticisms are the animation times for fast travel and horse summoning, and also the reward for too many secrets/puzzles was just coins. Rarely is it rewarding to solve a puzzle and have the chest(s) contain only coins, and it happened too many times. A few of them were downright insulting after a tough block puzzle. Plus in BT2 need space to summon the fast travel... just seems like a downgrade from BT1. The horse mount summon should also be faster. Swimming is excruciatingly slow.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the first one, which was fun but imperfect, I was looking forward to Blossom Tales 2. It turned out to be worth the wait.Once again, Grandpa is telling a bedtime story to his grandrugrats, Lily and Chrys, but this time both children feature: Lily once again as the hero, and Chrys as her sibling rival. The story starts off with an immediately darker tone, and this is the first hint at the greater sophistication of this sequel. Like the first game, Grandpa gives the children choices in the narrative, but this features much more frequently, and in much more salient ways that can even impact gameplay for the entire playthrough. There is also a much fuller assortment of side content, and many secrets hidden all over the world.The dungeon design is significantly tighter. While the basic principle is still to find the key to open the door, there’s less arbitrariness in the way things are laid out and the way puzzles are designed and placed. They feel much more cohesive. There are even puzzle box elements, such as raising and lowering water inside a giant sickly turtle. This demonstrates that the development team learned a lot from the experience of designing the first game and was able to design these levels with much more vision and intention.The enemy design and combat is also significantly improved. The combat is not as over-the-top easy as the first game, and instead of facing screens filled with randomly moving enemies, only a few enemies with trickier movements and characteristics are placed, including enemies which are more or only vulnerable to specific items. The bosses are also way more interesting and compelling. I also actually had to use potions to save myself many times.Blossom Tales 2 is a huge improvement on Blossom Tales, and it’s a great indie Zelda-like for a low price. I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Blossom Tales II: The Minotaur Prince

_childDocuments_.review: I had a blast with this. I haven't played the first game as of now, so I can confirm that this stands perfectly well on its own. The game captures the feeling of the old 2D Zeldas really well. It was fun to explore the overworld and the dungeons and do the many side quests. Really, there's so much optional stuff to explore, which I love. My favourite parts were the first dungeon with the water levels (always love when 2D games feel a bit 3D), the Periwinkle Woods (so mysterious with atmospheric graphics and music) and the haunted mansion (fun item and puzzles).My first playthrough took about 22 hours, taking my time.
_childDocuments_.name: Blossom Tales II: The Minotaur Prince

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.  Probably the best I've played from 2022.  It takes what worked about the first game and refines & polishes it to something better.  The balance for puzzle difficulty is much better.  I never had to play "Guess what the dev was thinking!" like with a couple I did in the first one.  Everything just kinda works.  The combat could be a tad snappier and maybe making the overall game a little more challenging would've been better but really, those are minor quibbles.  I had such a good time wandering the world and going "Huh, wonder what's on this part of the map..."  It's really good and anyone who has a fondness for the SNES and GB Zelda games should enjoy this thoroughly.  I had more fun with this than any of the 3D Zelda games, that's for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Blossom Tales II: The Minotaur Prince

_childDocuments_.review: Do you wanna play a shorter Version of the old Zeldas, then look no further than Blossom Tale 2: Minotaur Prince. The Story is great, the Dungeons are unique and make use of everything you get during your adventure. Some of the Puzzles in the game are challenging, but not too hard. Everything about this game is enjoyable. I wish i had a grandpa that could tell stories so immersive that it feels like im playing them!
_childDocuments_.name: Blossom Tales II: The Minotaur Prince

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a fun game that gives you good nostalgia over classic Zelda games like "Link's Awakening" or "A Link to the Past," then you'll definitely find it with this game. Not as short as the first game, which is cool, and there were some challenging puzzles (a bit too challenging for a few of the later puzzles, given there are no hints... you just have to figure them by yourself). With that being said, I greatly enjoyed this game and felt that it was worth the money I paid for it! And get Blossom Tales 1 while you're at it!As far as cons go... the story isn't there, the characters are okay, graphics are fine, music is forgetable, and the potions were overpowered. I was able to beat the boss with just two potions of bubble orb, one health, and one double damage. If there was a scarcer amount of bottles, scarcer amount of coins (seriously--I think like 99% of the chests in the game have coins) less potion types (or maybe one potion can be activated at a time, instead of being able to use the orb, double damage, AND health all at the same time?), and more use of the harmonica/guitar songs to utilize, then I think it'd be outstanding despite the generic story. If the devs can develop on the characters further and develop an intriguing story with side quests, lore, and also a catchy af soundtrack, that would make this game VERY competitive against the older Zelda games.All in all, a fun game and I recommend it if you're yearning for more 2D Zelda-like games (and, if you haven't, check out Ocean's Heart on Steam - very similar). I'm gonna keep my eye out for future additions to this franchise and I hope the devs introduce more challenge and more elements with future titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game.  Grew up on Link To The Past and this game brings back tons of memories.  Really enjoyed the first and kept refreshing the Steam page release morning to add Blossom Tales II to my collection.  Put in almost 9 hours and loving it so far.  Exploration is awesome, and really loving the graphics, gameplay, etc.  Wouldn't change a thing!  Can't wait for number III!  Also can't wait to play this once my Steam Deck arrives.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awful.I can't even rationalize how they managed to screw everything doing the exact same game but making it tenfold worse.I liked the first Voice of Cards very much, this one is killing me.Everything is worse, the party, the mechanics, the ratio of random encounters, the progress, the story, i can't manage to find something done good here (maybe the strange inside heart segments, maybe).More or less there are the same cards of the first game, i have nothing against re-using assets but when you find the SAME character with a different name it's very lazy, i mean it's ok for monsters not for characters.There are no new mechanics except for the dual attacks which are lazy and half of them are completely useless.Random encounter ratio is increased, i think between 3-5 steps, and this time exp and gold are basically useless, leveling up goes on a snail's pace and stats increments are non-existent. You have very few equipment to purchase, you will drown in gold quickly and the game is so frustratingly easy that you can go without problems with the "free" equipment you find around.But the stats increments are very little so you will go around fighting A LOT of long random encounters, mostly 0 aoe’s to quickly dispatch stuff, doing very few damage, for no exp and useless money. Enemies are of no threat at all, they are just dummy sponges. In 15 hours I had just a single death in the party cause I was too much bored to care about a maiden which was at 2 hp.Even bosses are awful, there is no difficulty at all, no mechanics and absolutely no threat at all.There is a stealth segment. A *stealth* section, which adds more and more boredom, in the only island where the story of the maiden is relatively interesting. That really broke me, not for the difficulty but for the nonsensical idea that a stealth minigame was the correct choice for pacing the story after 15 hours in the game in THAT precise point of the story.The party has zero chemistry, no interesting interactions except the two MC and those are very baseline and rare. All the story you keep switching with temporary party members, which add nothing to the story or the MCs and those are just background lore. You do it continuously, you get a couple of dialogues, drop the party members and go to the next island.The story is boring for the fact that you have absolutely nothing except "go there to find a thing, then go to the other there to go find another thing". There is nothing else, no character development at all, the male MC is a sock puppet worse than the real sock puppet, has no emotion and is extremely far away from the first game MC. Regarding the female MC It's useless to have so much introspection about a character that, except for some few segments, is another wooden dummy and the game gives me nothing of interest on her. The story rotates around her and in 15 hours of game I have NOTHING on her except she had a bad childhood, which was clearly stated around the first minute in game.I can't really salvage anything from this game, it's so awful that I regret every single hour spent on this keeping saying "maybe next chapter it will go better".It doesn't.If you liked the first game stay FAR AWAY from this and forget it even exists.If you really hate yourself and want to engage this torture i give you three suggestions. 1) Always play at high speed, maybe slow down at bosses if you care but it's really an awful experience regarding the random encounters.2) In the stealth section you can click on the card you stay to make the guards pass, nowhere in the game it's explained and you will never solve the puzzle unless looking at guides.3) The final boss requires AT LEAST a firestay +2, it has 4 phases and you can't save between them, you die you have to redo everything. Start with white, it's purely rng since you don't use your character. Don't waste resources, if more than one character dies just restart and stop wasting elixirs. Then go red, equip fire resistance since the boss has a oneshot attack, you will not soak it unless you have firestay 2 or an happenstance card. Then go black, it's the most "fair", just omnipanacea all the debuff and equip protection rings. Then proceed with the last one with the azure maiden. Different strategies may vary, but this is the most safe i found.Good luck. PS: if you are here following some strange internet rumor telling you "there is stuff from drakengard etc." it's a lie. There are, but those are just citations and nothing to contribute to the taroverse. Even if you are deep into the lore of the taro games (like me) just skip this piece of trash.PS2: i platinumed the game just for showing i know what I am talking about in this review and its not pure bias.

_childDocuments_.review: Update 3 after finishing the game! Wrote a full review down below and edited my first impression part a bit, my review contains some very minor spoilers but if you are in between to buy this game or not, really recommend to read it first. My short answer is still same.Would i recommend this game to a friend? Short answer: Not really for this price rangeLong answer: I played the game for a hour right now and finished prologue/played the main game a bit and i must say for this price range, 30 euro/dollar is quite much! (150 TL for me since the regional price) I dont think that this game deserves this price range. While i really liked first game i would still argue it should be around somewhere 15-20 euro and same goes for this game too. I would also like to make a much more detailed review of all things but considering of doing it when i finish the game itself to give it more justice and time.----------------------------------------(First impression, full review down below)Here is why: 1) They copy/pasted nearly all the assets from the first game and gave the same price as first game. By copying i mean in a wide range of it. (villagers/some monsters/combat effects/items/shops are nearly all the same!) (Edit: I would say 50/50 but still too much)2) I really hoped they twisted the open world and combat a bit (since it got really stale in the first game after a while) but as it is i didnt see any change at all which is kinda disappointing in my opinion because game really needed some changes for that, i hope there will be some on later stages of the game (Map and level design is actually better)3) DLC packages i bought and tried in the game -most of the nier automata ones- doesnt fit at all to the setting of the game. While this is more of a minor complaint and an optional one, in first game -nier replicant DLCs- didnt had this problem so really dont know why they decided go this way, however this is more of a personal taste like i also think music is a bit more of a letdown from the first game.- Overall as a first impression i am really in disappointment for this one but i hope that it will change positively the more i play the game in future since i am a big fan of all of the yoko taro's work----------------------------------------Full Review + Comparison to first gameFirstly, positives and negatives:Positives:+ Better map and level design, not completely linear with more interesting places+ More wide range of characters and more interesting ones too+ Story has better premise and more interesting right from start+ Voice actor is better than first one (This one at least give emotions and feels more alive)Negatives:- Game is even more easier, final boss is a joke!- Copy/paste characters/npcs/enemies from first game- Same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UI- Story gets kinda dull in the middle part (gets better at the end again)- Combat is still same ("Partner Attacks" are def. not enough change)- Main trio is a bit weaker character wise- Even less equipment options somehow- Same technical problems from first game they didnt fix any of itThis out of the way, let me tell you this: If you had any problems technical or gameplay wise from the first game do not worry because they are exactly the same here!Some major flags i will explain below shows that devs really doesnt care for fans and do not listen any of us because they really didnt fix any of things they should have already or at least some of them. This is outright a copy/paste game of the first game with new story and world for same price of company greed for money.While combat was okey in the start like first game it gets really boring and dull after a while because game is already too easy! Unless if its some boss fights you never need to think what you should do and just fight with 1 or 2 better cards you have and fight is over. This is exactly why everyone complained about the first game and they made the same thing even easier this time.Or you can use a escape option which also gets boring because of doing same thing over 100x times.Final boss is a total joke compared to first one. At least in the first one final boss was the only thing that was kinda challange but for this one you have 4 separate fight in which you can rest and full up your heal and fights are really not hard.Also in equipment sides of thing you really need to buy much less compared to the first game so you always have ♥♥♥♥ ton of moneyIf you also had any technical problems from the first game you didnt like they are still here and didnt fix any of that stuff, like:- Not having shortcut for equipment, skills, inventory- Not being able to quit to the settings or main game (need to close the game)- Even if escape chance needed is 2 points (from 2 dices) you will get it because minimum you can get is 2And personally for me the most problematic part of copy-paste characters. The Ivory Order (Very important organization from first game) guards are used as the normal guards of some island which also takes big part in the story. (Edit: was wrong it is the Ivory Island as someone commented) And biggest joke is that in this copy-paste problem, one of the most important human villain from the first game is used as an important ally in this game who is also the father of one of the characters from the first game! I thought they were the same characters at start but their names and motives are completely different with age difference. Like why? Can you really not create new characters for that for 30 euro game? Are you really that lazy?All of this major red flags i listed here easily shows that this game is a disguise of a first game which has a new story/characters with a new map for giving the same price of 30 euro! Devs didnt listen any of the problems of the fans from the first game! This explains why 2nd game came out so soon after first one.As you can see from all this problems of this disgusting company practice should not be supported by not buying this game or writing to the game devs about the problems we have here, however i doubt they will listen because they didnt after the first game.I actually enjoyed the game BUT i wish i didnt with all these problems. This game does not deserve 30 euro price tag. And i am pretty sure they are thinking of doing this same thing over and over again as a franchise of "Voice of Cards" to get some easy money.----------------------------------------Thanks for reading my review if you actually came this far! Since my review is fully completed i opened comments to argue with anyone here or help them about any questions in the game.Have a nice day.

_childDocuments_.review: Boy, was I surprised how much I love this game after the middling reviews.Best way to think about the series is Yoko Taro making RPG Maker games, they're really love letters to retro JRPGs. While Isle Dragon was more of a reference to seminal late-80's RPGs like Phantasy Star, FF1 and DQ1, Forsaken Maiden is a nod to early-aughts PS2-era RPGs. There's even a chapter that has  lol. The maiden/attendant set up lends itself to distinctive playstyles in each chapter, which I really liked a lot. It's also a MUCH better difficulty level than Isle Dragon, I feel threatened by bosses and a satisfying sense of victory after battles. It's cool to feel like I almost NEED to work in the 5-jewel attacks.I suppose they might be a difficult recommend for someone who doesn't have a history with classic JRPGs, as they're a bit on the slow side, and the presentation style definitely asks for some investment from the player. They feel aimed at older RPG fans and yokoverse stans anyway.I honestly think the story is pure gold, if "Yoko Taro doing RPG Maker" intrigues you, you'll like these. Also if you're a fan of Drakengard and have a sharp eye for details, you'll be pointing at random objects screaming about connections pretty frequently.Fujisaka's art is also incredible. if you're like me and miss when most Japanese games showed high quality 2D artwork front-and-center, this is a breath of fresh air.I've really loved the first two and can't WAIT for the rest of this series, I've got my Drakengard 3-branded magnifying glass ready. Check 'em out if you like classic RPGs and yoko taro.

_childDocuments_.review: Noticeably worse than the first game in almost every single way that matters.It's hard to put where this game lays for me. Personally I see it as average. I had enough fun with it I guess? Fun is subjective here. It's a slog to get through most of the time, and you can definitely see the cracks, so I can't in good conscience give it above a 5/10 and if I was being completely honest it'd be a 4/10 for me. If there was a way to say you "maybe" recommend a game, this would fall in that category for sure. This is a hard maybe. If you are looking for a tongue-in-cheek laidback experience like in the first game, this ain't it. This one is much more frustrating from boss battles, to general battles, to encounter rates with copious amounts of artificial difficulty. But, if you like the VoC format and don't mind grinding or other JRPG tropes, then yeah... Go for it! It has redeemable moments in it. You shouldn't really review a game in comparison to another in its series, but it's really difficult not to with this series due to how similar the mechanics and other aspects of the game are from the first game, minus the story line which is its own standalone thing, but I suppose I'll get in to some of the pros and cons...Fair warning, some of them are long winded.Cons:--> Assets. The game reuses a bunch of assets from the first game. You're gonna see the same monsters, same "tiles", and the same characters with minimal additions to them. There's not a lot of "new" feeling to it after you're halfway through the game.--> Replayability. Has less "New Game +" potential (You really only need to do a NG+ to get a single achievement)--> Grind. It's WAY worse for grinding to max level than the first game by a WIDE margin. It's pretty bad.--> Encounter Rates. They are extremely high. They are meant to be high because the game WANTS you to grind. No... Want is the wrong word... It NEEDS you to grind otherwise you will be left behind too quickly due to lackluster equipment, stats, and skills.--> Equipment. There's more equipment in this one, but most of it is less useful than before and maxing out with the best equipment you can get feels significantly less impactful than in the first game.--> Equipment Part 2. Your allies, one main character that leaves combat playability, and even one of the other main characters are stuck with their equipment they have when they join. The only exception is your ring usage. You get to control that, but armor and weapons? Nope. Sorry.--> Artificial Difficulty. They make sure that all enemies "scale" with you after each chapter (more health, armor, and damage) and the scaling doesn't match with your stats as much as it does with the chapter. Meaning you spend longer in battles against the same enemies, with marginally better equipment and stats. Your equipment and level-up stats just don't feel powerful at any time. I did a NG+ at max level and by the 3rd "Chapter" I could no longer one shot enemies I was forced to fight even with the best equipment and "max stats". There's 3 more chapters after that. It's a pain in the *ss to spend time healing in every other battle because the enemy is almost guaranteed to get a hit in. --> Artificial Difficulty 2. Boss difficulty. They REALLY want you to spend time on their bosses towards the end of the game (and just in general). The difficulty spikes of these battles makes it feel wrong. The amount of health and status effects they have/use is just... Frustrating. The optional end boss is so stupidly overpowered and has so much health that it genuinely takes around 40 minutes to beat with the game on "fast mode". That is just blatantly asinine. You'll use nearly every item in your item slots (We're talking 50 items) during the battle and it's still not guaranteed you'll win. It has fixed damage moves that can't be decreased by buffs, and all sorts of other annoyances that make you want to quit more than they do make you want to finish it.--> Story. Parts of the story are just dumb as hell. Like irredeemably dumb as hell. Flat out. Like people doing sh*t that is counter-intuitive to them literately staying alive because "muh plot" or some such garbo. When the story is at its worst, it is "high-school shipping fanfiction" levels of contrived and it WILL piss you off at some point.Pros:--> Item Slots. They give you more than the first game... That's kinda cool I guess.--> Artwork. The artwork that aren't reused asset edits/flips is lovely.--> Characters. The main character isn't an edgy little tw*t anymore compared to the first game and you'll find yourself liking the characters more than finding them annoying. They actually feel like they have more than one personality trait! Yay!--> Story! Not to be confused with the story mentioned in the cons, when the story is good, it can really put an interesting idea in your head and make you wonder about your own morality or how you'd treat a certain situation. It can definitely tug at your hearts strings at certain points and you can really get absorbed in to the tale it's trying to offer."Meh"'s:--> Decisions. They still don't actually do anything. There's no "wrong" decisions you can make. It all leads to the same place so you can't really fail anything, just like in the first game.--> No-Encounter Item. It's still locked behind the NG+ wall like in the first game. Also, it still HAS to tell you every time you were about to fight an enemy when you have it equipped. It can't just not give you any messaging and only alert you about events. No. It has to semi-punish you by letting you know an encounter ran away. How dare you not grind anymore you silly bastard.--> Achievements. They aren't as cut and dry for what you need to do to get them done. Especially the "powered up" weapons you have to re-visit locations after a certain point to unlock. I didn't figure out that you didn't have to NG+ those weapons to get the achievements until later on by looking it up, which is crazy annoying. Also the optional final boss achievement doesn't require you to do NG+ either. Just continue your game after you beat the "Big bad", which is also stupid.--> Humor. A lot of the humor elements were taken out in favor of a more "mature" story. Or at least a story that takes itself more seriously. And there it is, there's the review. That's it! You likely won't be like me on this one and take as much time to do everything, but in the event you do, I'm sorry friend. Truly sorry.Call a hotline for help. Or a therapist. I know I almost had to.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty infrequent that I write a negative review, but I cannot recommend this game over the previous one.First issue with the game that I have, the endings are barely different from one another and there is no secret ending to my knowledge; I don't know why the pay off for beating the game is so insubstantial relative the first game when this one is so much harder. _childDocuments_.review: spoiler free summary section:The Forsaken Maiden suffers from to many flaws for me to recommend this game to anyone. Highly frequent random encounters, a clunky menu system, terrible battle system, a generic RPG story that's hamfisted with melodrama, and lack of some basic quality of life things all come together to make TFM a chore to complete. The series has a lot going for it when you take into account the music and visuals but I cant help but feel there was absolutely no risk taken with this game which is sad since the wind is definitely at its back. I bought this game for $30 and I can tell you with all my heart that was not worth the experience. I'd say if you absolutely love turn based RPGS wait till the game is on sale for $10 or $5 and then pick it up, trust me this game isn't going to change your life.full review with spoilers:I want to say right off the back that I have not played the predecessor to this game "Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars" as I was told the two were completely separate from each other and from what I can tell this is true. I am unsure if any of my complaints are also apparent in the previous game but I would assume they are.Gameplay:One of the biggest problems with the gameplay of TFM is the random encounters, TFM is a 7 hour game that took me 14 hours purely because of random encounters. One thing most modern RPGs do to lessen the annoyance of random encounters is adding a fast-forward key into the game, in other games if you get into a repetitive battle you can hold down the ctrl button and the game moves at 3x the speed. In TFM Even if you want to run away you will probably spend about 25 seconds getting into battle and then rolling the dice to see if you get to run away, its like watching an ad on youtube. In TFM half the time you spend in battle will be watching battle animations, which are cool and adds flair to the game but when I'm fighting 2 frogs I don't need to spend 30 seconds watching an animation of my characters doing their epic anime attacks.The other problem with the gameplay is how damage is calculated in TFM, if you have 18 attack and your opponent has 15 defense, you will do around 3 damage with a normal attack. This system really sucks and makes the game heavily gear dependent as leveling up almost always grants you just 1 extra health, at most of the points in the game you are either blasting your opponent or doing no damage. Because of this the game was a breeze and I never saw a game over screen. It would have been better to have opted for a ratio based damage calculation where your attacks deal some damage multiplied by your attack power divided by your targets defense.Story:The story in TFM genuinely feels like it was generated by a computer that was programmed to play every turn based RPG in existence and then create it's own. The way the game presents itself only works to harm the narrative aswell. The entire game is narrated by one person, and while I think he does a good job it sucks all personality out of the characters and events of the game. Characters don't talk to one another, instead the narrator says the characters had a conversation. Characters don't bond, the narrator just passingly mentions that the characters are bonding. What little actual lines the characters have are squandered by the single narrator, especially the female lines. Ideally when a female character has to deliver a sad line a female voice actress would deliver it in a sad tone. Instead in TFM the narrator reads the line in his regular tone and then adds on "she sad sadly" after it. More voice acting would have led to a much more believable and immersive story.You are a parentless teen boy and you embark on a quest with a mute teen girl named Laty to recover four maiden's relics so that you can turn Laty into a maiden who can then preform the maidens ritual and save the island. The game wants you to project yourself onto the the protagonist, It always refers to him as "you" and you are asked to name him at the very beginning. By default the name is entered as Barren but the game suggest you to enter in your own. TFM is very blatantly from the beginning going to be a love story and there's nothing inherently wrong about Barren and Laty falling in love, the problem arises when it's narrated as if Laty and I were falling in love. I played this game alone in my room at 2 A.M. and all the dialogue about how I love Laty and will love her till the end of time makes me feel like a complete goober. This could have been easily sidestepped if the game just checked to see if you left the protagonist name as Barren and if you did it could refer to him as such throughout the game, would have taken some extra work but would have went a long way in letting the player experience the game how they wanted.there's an instance in the beginning where Laty is asleep and you are given the option to go through Laty's diary or not. If you aren't creepy you will probably chose not to go through it as well, you will then be shocked to see Barren go through the diary anyway. This is a cardinal sin when it comes to video games and is repeated multiple times throughout TFM, the diary example even happens twice in the exact same way. There is no decision you make, except for one at the very end, which actually changes the story. My question becomes why present these decisions anyway? All it does is take make the player feel in less control of the game.At one point in the game you get to chose your next destination. if you chose the East you are going to be outleveled and do no damage and the game doesn't tell you this or hint to it. I don't know why the game gives you this option but I got through it by cheesing my companions to do all the work then absolutely blasted my way through the north easily. Again I don't know why the game gives you this option its terrible with how the damage works.None of the maidens or attendants are fleshed out, they die in melodramatic ways, and all the the twist are insanely predictable except for the nonsensical ones. After you beat the Isle eater Laty's father explains that the reason why everyone emotionally tortured Laty was so that she wouldn't become a maiden and thus wouldn't conduct the ritual and sacrifice herself for their sake. This is insanely stupid and preventing Laty from becoming a maiden could have been achieved in ways other than just emotionally abusing her as a little girl to the point where she is to afraid to even speak. Lac being a traitor is just random and contrived aswell, he has extremely limp reasoning which makes him a horrible final villain but visually cool. the part where Laty has to sacrifice her memories to fix her heart makes no sense and is just stupid melodrama, the ending is equally nonsensical.Some Praise:The game is stylistically cool and the music is very good, sadly it suffers from a low amount of tracks but whats there works. The game also handles its music very well in how it plays it, when you are going through a sad instance the sad music will take priority over the battle music when you get into combat. This was a great decision as the random encounters didn't completely ruin the mood.Final Thoughts: There's so much more bit by bit problems this game has that I just cant get to, especially to do with how menus work and a lot of quality of life things. All in all I was disappointed by it and I expect more out of Yoko Taro and his team. To see something bland come out of Yoko Taro is a real shock to me. The game has its moments and has it's charm but poor design choices and weak writing really bring it down to the point where I cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has taken all the feedback about the problems in the previous game and made this game worse in every way.There's still a vast amount of clicking to go through the dialogue and the game over explains everything.Only the main character can be fully equipped. Laty has a weak weapon that cannot be changed, resulting in her attacks barely doing any damage for most of the game. Lac cannot have any equipment and disappears when you recruit a maiden, so he's always under-levelled.The maiden and her attendant cannot change their equipment or level up. As their level matches the player's level when recruited if you recruit them too soon they'd been too weak to be any use. This is very noticeable with the Azure Maiden as you level very rapidly in the early game.Since the number of elemental attacks you have access to has been greatly reduced this means that enemy's elemental weaknesses no longer matter due to how difficult it is to actually be able to use an attack that can do this damage type. Instead attacks that injure multiple enemies are more useful.Due to poor balancing the most difficult enemies are those where you fight four enemies at once, with single more powerful bosses being much easier by comparison. You also can't get to levels 25-30 with a huge amount of grinding.In one chapter combat is broken up by stealth puzzles, where you have to avoid enemies that in every other encounter you can fight without any difficulty. These section are so badly made that the game makes them easier if you fail too many times because even the developers knew how terrible they were.The battle against the final boss is terrible as you have to defeat 3 optional bosses, while not being able to save after beating them. One boss you have to fight without the main characters. This is exceptionally difficult as you can't equip any of the character with any items to make this fight easier.The plot doesn't make any sense. The villagers on Omega Island would rather die than have Laty sacrifice herself to protect the island. Even though one of them, such as the girl who wants to be a maiden, could perform the maiden's ritual and save everyone else. They also don't help Laty leave the island, meaning that she'll die anyway when it sinks.The 4 maiden's you meet don't influence the main story in any way, despite most of them dying due to being maidens.Laty's heart scars should be used to foreshadow why she has these scars, instead of being filled with generic monster. Her diary does what this realm should have done.Finally at the end of the game all the spirits want to live in Laty's heart. After the hero and Laty defeat the leader of the spirits, Laty agrees to let the spirit live in her heart. This made the entire final battle meaningless.Even worse Laty has to choose between sacrificing family, friends, or love but since she ends up in a coma regardless this choice has no effect on anything.

_childDocuments_.review: A must-play if you want a fairly relaxing game, paired with Yoko Taro's dramatic writing. If you don't like turn-based rpgs where gameplay can somehow be repetitive, you might want to refrain but I never felt like I was underleveled at any point in the story or needed grinding. Story-wise, this game is better than its predecessor. Gameplay-wise, it might be slightly easier. The AI seem more intelligent but they hardly offer any big challenge. But really, the jewel of the crown of this game is the story, which will definitely be the main motivation for players to keep playing, especially if you liked the stories of Nier or Nier Automata, or any of Taro's previous games actually.

_childDocuments_.review: These games are very overpriced for what they are. This game reuses a lot of assets from the first one(which is not inherently bad but for the degree to which they reuse stuff you'd expect a cheaper price), all three games came out within a few months of each other so they don't take long to make and there's just very little variety in the NPC's(you'll have 2 or more identical NPC's in the same town). They cost way too much imo but I got them all for about half the price from GMG which is far more reasonable.A lot of my thoughts on the first game are the same here. There is some improvement, there's a lot more challenging fights throughout so far but random encounters can still be too easy and frequent so they become more of an annoyance than a fun fight. Gameplay overall is better though, in the first game you could just use your most powerful attack on each character and easily win most fights. In this it helps to be a little more strategic in what order you play in and how you have your skills setup. I have one main attack character who does most of the damage and another character focused on generating gems and buffing him. You could also do that in the first game but it didn't really matter much and was mostly a waste of time. The story is great, I actually like it more than the first game but I'm not too far into it yet. Soundtrack is godly, very reminiscent of the DrakeNieR series but particularly of Re[in]carnation.I'd say it's an overall improvement of the first game but it could still be a lot better, especially considering the asking price. Like I wish our characters actually had different designs based on your equipped armour. And more variety in NPC designs would be great. I definitely recommend it if you enjoyed the first game but it's probably best to wait for a sale.Minor spoilers after finishing the game:

_childDocuments_.review: Disregard all of the negative reviews on this game! I promise you that this game is nothing but an improvement on Isle Dragon in every way shape or form. This goes for the combat and the story collectively. It also improves on Isle Dragon's story as well by fleshing out the world and giving extra backstory for certain characters.Pros:4 Characters to a party in combatNew itemsWay better difficulty, actually makes you use your brain for most of itArguably better characters than Isle Dragon, Barren and Laty are very goodThe East Isle is the best part of the game, will make your eyes waterMore Yoko Taro-esque feel, i.e. more melancholy and realisticMusic is much more memorable than Isle Dragon, they even have chaos language vocalsCons:Beginning is very slowFirst two isles aren't very interestingThe second-to-last boss is insanely hard for no reason, legit spams thunderstorm every other turnThe last two big areas in the game take forever to get through due encounters being literally every 2 stepsNot a lot of room for equipment builds as Barren is really the only character that you can change his weapon, armor, and ringConclusion: I'd give this game an 8/10 over Isle Dragon's 7/10. It is very fun and even if you don't like the combat that much, the great story and narration will carry you through to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing experience.As someone who fell in love at first sight with the concept of Voice of Cards, I was really excited to discover a new adventure in that series. I can tell that they improved and expanded some elements which contribute to spice things gameplay wise. However, to put it simply, despite all of that, I'd say this adventure blown me away with for its story. Very interesting characters and setpieces. All of that, despite maybe not being as amazing as a AAA game, was totally enough to captivate my interest for this kind of stories and made me went through a lot of emotions. To that I'm now sure I'll get the sequels of that series.If you liked the first game, I can tell you that it's a safe game to get. However if you didn't like it, or expect it to evolve a lot from the first entry, I don't recommend this game despite how much I loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: So...this game is kind of complicated to talk about,so im gonna start saying all the problems I have with it:-Is it better than Isle Dragon Roars? Yea...and no. The thing is that,although I like this story more,I had less fun gameplay wise,and thats because,for some reason,The Forsaken Maiden only lets you FULLY build your main character,the rest of playable characters are: the girl (can't change her weapon),the pet(can't change ♥♥♥♥, besides ring I believe) and your rotating couple of characters (maiden+maiden's knight,you can only change their ring If I remember correctly,and you can't change their skills). So,you have the same type of game as the first one,with a lvl cap of 30,meaning there aren't much skills to learn with each character,you also have a few weapons and armor available in the game,all of this combined with you being able to build 1.75 characters or so (in terms of quantity),forces you to basically get the stronger gear (you will have a lot of gold since you can't spend it in many characters) and use it with your main character,get some rings and thats it,you won't change a ♥♥♥♥ untill the end. -What makes it even more funny is the fact that the gameplay has some improvements: you can now buy party-wide healing,all characters have a "Charge" skill that generates 1 gem (fixing the first game's problem of spamming Melanie's 2-gem skill),now there're 2-person skills,which are stronger skills that need both characters in the party,and give you a great edge in battle (sadly,they are quite similar to any ultimate skill you would imagine with the only downside of needing 2 specific characters in the party). Now there's something similar to a world map so to  the form of an ocean,where you can freely navigate anywhere of this game's world in any given moment,which makes it easier and better overall than the first one.-I actually like that you have 2 people rotate from your party from time to time,but since those people are all the playable characters you are gonna get,gameplay suffers a lot. Just so you know,I've been spamming 2 tactics (1 for bosses 1 for monster parties) for around 90% of the game,with no actual thinking process behind it,just a few tweaks everytime my party members rotate. Oh I just remembered this,the last boss fight before the final fight of the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥,I won't spoil anything,but all I can say is that is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥,I had to burn way too many healing items in that ♥♥♥♥.-Isles are lacking content,every single isle has: main town and secondary place where the majority of the action will happen. That's it,that's all there is to all of them.-Probably the biggest flaw THESE games have is the price. SE always being greedy f***s with their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ prices. I just can't understand how in the world you make people pay 30€ again,for a game that's been developed in months,recycling MANY sprites and animations from the first one. This franchise price should be: 30 the first one and 10-15 for the rest,or just 15-20 all of them,but not this.Now lets talk about some good stuff:-The story is better in my opinion,and I think that due to what I think is Voice of Cards's best character (haven't played burden beasts yet): Laty. This girl's development,backstory,design and personality are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome,I love her.-There's no secret/good/true  the end you have 3 choices (as always) and the differences between them are few,some people may dislike it,but I don't.-Rotating/secondary characters are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome and interesting.-Although I would say that the first one had better OST overall,this game has a few (like 2 or 3) tracks that are a little bit better than the stronger ones in Isle Dragon Roars.-What I've said before about gameplay improvements,they are a welcome addition overall.Final thoughts: I think It is a worthwhile experience,but If I had to recommend 1 Voice of Cards game to a friend,I would recommend the first or the third (heard from many people that the 3rd is the best one),but not this one. I feel like this game is made for people like me,who like to experience Yoko Taro's stories regardless of everything else,or people who are really into this franchise after playing the first one.P.S: I would love a 4th and last game of this franchise,not only improving QoL features and gameplay,but also trying to aim for a much greater story and world,something close to any famous JRPG,with a way bigger world,more weapons and armors,more places to visit,more characters,longer story,etc.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game for the casual player (hence why my review is still positive), but horrendous for completionists. The art style still holds up in my opinion but overall I prefer the first game. Parts of this review will be copy-pasted from my review of the first game. - : Still a classic turn-based RPG, but with the increased difficulty in this title, you really have to factor in buffing, debuffing, and applying status effects instead of just attack and heal like from the first game. - : While most of the NPC cards are reused assets from the first game, it's passable considering this one came out very shortly after the first one. As for the named characters though, the art remains incredible and beautiful, although in my opinion are a little worse than the first one.- : Definitely an interesting plot going on here, as while it's easy to see what's going on in the world, it's a little ruined by how little time you spend in each area with each maiden and attendant pair. There were a few interesting plot twists near the end too though which were a pleasant surprise based on the direction I thought the game was going towards.- : The difficulty ramps up a little bit from the first game, which I enjoy. The overworld encounters are still fairly easy, but the boss fights do pose enough of a challenge where you need to at least prepare a little bit instead of just rushing through and overpowering them. The post-game boss in this game is just extremely stupid though, has 1000 HP total (500 HP * 2 Cards) and can easily deal over half your character's health in one hit. - : Yes, there is in fact a  section in this card-styled RPG. While it's stupid enough to exist, I feel the fact that how this game is presented makes it bearable, as you can easily just look up a guide on how to exactly solve it, which is easily re-creatable. As for a short tip, you can make the guards pass by you by re-clicking on the card you are on, which is never mentioned anywhere, and if you really have trouble,  a guide. - : This game takes about twice as long as the first one to complete, mainly because of the difficulty and money. The optional boss fights such as the one in the arena and the post-game boss are very difficult unless you really prepare for them. And while in a normal playthrough, unless you're excessively spending, you'll have excess amounts of money, but when you take into account the incredible amount of items and equipment you need to buy and how expensive they are, completionists will either have to micro-manage their bank account or grind it out in the last area. - : The $30 price tag is a little steep for the amount of time you get out of the game, I'd recommend either waiting for a sale or buying the Trilogy (which effectively cuts the price of each game in half), or both if you want.- : There's a side activity in every town called the Game Parlor, and beyond the first game mode (Simple), all the other ones are entirely RNG-dependent, and the NPCs don't even try to hide that they're hardcoded to target you except for if another NPC is winning by a large margin. And wouldn't you guess, there's an achievement for winning a game in each of these modes.- : Unlike the first game where you could freely switch between 3 of 5 party members and all their gear, in this game. You only have full control over the protagonist's gear. As the story goes on, instead of you maybe trying out different characters, the game essentially just says "Ok you're partying with these guys now" and then you don't see them again until the end of the game. Even in these characters though, the only thing you can customize is their accessory, their weapon and armor is locked permanently. - : There is in fact a NG+ mode unlocked when you beat the story, but there's really no reason to play it besides unlocking the exclusive NG+ ring for starting it.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: 6/10 (A story worth experiencing, but a game best skipped and definetly not for children 6+)This game is an effective prequel to the first game in the series and plays about 15-18 years prior in an archipelago in a distant ocean. The connections to the first game are shown throughout some overlapping NPC and story-threads, but are so minor they have no impact on the game itself. Unlike the first game, Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden does not attempt to build the illusion of a golden age and hidden decay, the entire game is a cruel march against fate and the acceptance of the inevitable. To achieve that the game uses a lot of dark motifs and storylines many are used to from Final Fantasy games of the 90's and early 2000's in short small story arcs. This game once again is not 6+, it is 13+ PG. You may need to explain to your children why the nice person suffered such an unfair and cruel fate. Beware that this game has heavy motifs.Considering the younger audience this is allegedly intended for, the basic premise and easy to guess storylines for experienced roleplayers can be overlooked. The story itself is still a great adventure even if the ending compared to the first game is lackluster and a slight cope out.Yet, even if the story of the game will keep you entertained and interested, the game tries its hardest to make you quit long before. This game is an unbalanced rushjob and it shows. Beware!Storyline: 8/10 (Needlessly brutal for the age category and filled with stereotype plotlines)The storyline is darker than the age target group and heavily focus on real and psychological horror this time, which once again might imply the testers didn't go past the cutesy facade that this time lasted about only 1.5 chapters. A young navigator and a girl that tugged along with him for a time finally finish their ship to set out to sea. Here they will attempt to heal her scarred heart while trying to avoid the death of the archipelago in the face of destiny and they fight alongside new friends and watch them die... repeatedly. As long as parental guidance and some discussions with the children is involved, the story is fine. Brutal open murder with blood implications and other events might be a bit too much though for a 7 year old. Let alone the psychological horror and identity crisis.The story has several stereotypes and easy to pick out plots. Towards the end it also suffers a very annoying stereotype plotline with an even more stereotypical ending. Both the false age bracket and the stereotypes deduct points from an otherwise decent grim dark fantasy story.I BARELY endorse the game. If it wasn't for the story and art I would not. If you love tyrannical DMs in your pen and paper, this game is one as game incarnate. I have no idea how that sadistic anti-fun and anti-roleplay design slipped in.Gameplay: 3/10 (there is no R in this RPG)The horrible slow and clunky UI with hidden "exit" button in the other category makes its unwanted return for this rushed second installation with litlte balance. Rejoice!The first game was a 5 chapter long tutorial with bosses able to be stunned and many abilities used and learned. You also got team members that at some point did up to 4x damage per skill. Forget about that! The highest damage you'll do is 2x with a crit.This game will use ambush spawn bosses and they come in swarms (often 3+). These bosses are near always immune to freeze (which allows 200% damage combos and next to none of your party has) and even to paralyze, the skill you tend to have available. Meanwhile said enemy swarms can early on spam you with paralyze and freeze like it is candy. The real problem is not the tyrannical monster and boss design which causes people to become save neurotics to not lose progress, it is your "party". The game offers you 2.5 main characters, one of which is a mostly worthless symbolic support to get more gems and emergency heal. The other two are the young navigator and his maiden friend. The maiden friend will be below enemy shield values with her ATK for 75% of the game until she learns Force Impact to ignore armor or until she gets her last weapon. All other party members are temporary and can only equip rings, no armor or weapons. The problem is those characters do not level. They are underleveled in many bossfights and die to two hits. Two hits, especially the water party.A further annoyance is the insistence of the game to use boss gauntlets in which you can not save until all is done. You lose one battle, you lose a lot of progress. The worst offender is the last boss gauntlet in which the hardest boss is the third, comes with a pre-deployed glass cannon party and is actually a battle riddle for you to solve to win. You lose, you lost progress. Fight the doll and kraken first.Even the "open world" experience is a lie and areas open up as railroad in order. There is no free exploration in this game at all aside of some "outer sea" harder areas for loot and some EXP which are tiny and can be challenged when available.Some monster cards are recycled, yes, but those that are near all got new descriptions which is positive. They fill out the lore more. Overall the reuse of assets is a minor thing in this game with several new enemies. It's okay.Art & Sound Design: 7/10Near all sound design is a 1:1 copy from the first game. The music is slightly changed and the English narrator was exchanged. The Japanese narrator is the same from the first game and the preferred option. The English one didn't seem intent on creating an atmosphere this time.It's okay for being mostly copied over, but the new card designs like always are great and flawless. Some map designs were also interesting. An otherwise average score is definetly avoided just by the game's art design alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a mediocre sequel to it's predecessor, The Isle Dragon Roars. This game takes many steps backwards in multiple different aspects of the game.Card art from the first game is re-used everywhere, including for some main characters. The chance of random battles is much higher, causing battles to feel intrusive and annoying. The plot and characters are much less compelling in this game. The story starts to come together near the end, but it's far too late at that point. The first 75% of this game is a slog to get through. In addition, meaningless time wasters are thrown at the player like the Mystic Forest puzzle and the Foundation guards puzzle. The devs also left in lots of dialogue where the English narrator messed up their lines which feels tacky and hurts immersion. Lastly, the NieR Automata outfits and OST do not fit this game well, unlike the NieR Replicant DLC in the first game.If you liked the first game, you may still find some enjoyment with this game. Otherwise, I would not recommend playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review:
Set sail on a voyage to change destiny itself. Voice of Cards: The Forsaken Maiden is set on a remote chain of islands that have been protected by the maidens for generations, but which now face destruction. The hero of the story vows to save the islanders and sets sail for the high seas, together with Laty, a girl who failed to become a maiden.

The second game in the unique Voice of Cards series, where all elements are presented entirely through the medium of cards, in the tradition of tabletop RPGs and gamebooks.

A touching tale set in a world of melancholic beauty, brought to you by YOKO TARO (Creative Director), Keiichi Okabe (Music Director) and Kimihiko Fujisaka (Character Designer).

*This game is not a direct sequel to Voice of Cards: The Isle Dragon Roars. Both stories can be enjoyed as standalone game experiences.
*This product is also included in other bundles sold separately. Please take care not to re-purchase the same content.
* Please be aware that parts of the game which require an internet connection may cease to be supported at any point.

name: Disgaea 6 Complete
detailed_description: Zed is a boastful zombie who wallows on the lowest rung on the Netherworld ladder alongside his sister Bieko. When a God of Destruction threatens their way of (un)life, Zed must harness his unique ability of Super Reincarnation to stand against the approaching menace. Along the way, he will unite with twisted and colorful denizens of the Netherworld, face challenges around and within, and see if even an undying hooligan like himself can defy the odds! Disgaea 6: Defiance of Destiny unites a grim yet touching story with insane tactical combat, while introducing gameplay elements never before seen in previous installments. As a result, new and returning players alike can craft a truly memorable and unique journey through the Netherworld. Bring the pain in battle with special attacks and support from a plethora of ally units. Customizable settings such as Auto, Retry, and Replay allow both hardcore and casual players to fight their own way. And should things take a terrible turn, use Super Reincarnation to rejoin the fight and keep trying until you succeed. This truly is a Netherworld fit for everyone! From Grave to Glory : Join Zed in his quest to rise above his lowly status and challenge a God of Destruction. Along the way, meet zany characters, explore chaotic new worlds, and discover the power of sibling bonds and determination. Undying and Unstoppable : Experience over-the-top tactical combat, complete with insane special attacks and a wide variety of allies to choose from. And when things get too hairy, use Super Reincarnation to keep trying until you succeed! A Netherworld for Everyone : With customizable gameplay features such as Autoplay and Demon Intelligence, both new and returning players can forge a HL-raising experience that fits their lifestyle. Diving into DISGAEA has never been easier! Additionally, Disgaea 6 Complete includes new recolor DLC as well as all previously released character and cosmetic DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: Immediately, the community is right on this one. Since it was on sale, decided "why not" and forked out the money for it, but boy oh boy, has it been massacred. Comparing to Disgaea 5, mechanics have been cut without replacement; The D.I. (Demonic Intellegence) part is nice, but in its existence, streamlines it similar to a idle RPG with the right focus and use of the Dark Assemblies.It seems like the entire game went through an inflation crisis; for in past games, single or double digit HP/SP/Stats was pretty normal. At first, I thought it was an odd bug that Zed's level 1 stats showed in the ten-thousands, but no, every enemy/ally/NPC shows out as inflated. Why would I need large numbers to have any effect? I guess to make it feel the player has an impact?Another takeaway from Disgaea 5; The 3D models are a pretty nice addition, but why in the name of HL was there no animations for the once-existent team attacks/combos? Just enough for the 'team attack' portraits to come on screen, and the initiator to simply punch or swipe with the weapon in hand. That's it. You'll get fairly nice singular Special attack scenes to see for a while, but that's it.All in all, too much hit the cutting room floor for this to be considered at full price. The title might say "Disgaea 6 Complete", but it's 'completely' full of holes regarding prior titles. Play any other Disgaea game, dood.Get it for a better price than it is (even as this is posted for $45.49 USD, 1-30-2023), read the wiki on it, or watch someone else play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Disgaea has been my favorite series ever since playing the original so many years ago. I tried so hard to like this one, but at the end of the day, I just really couldn't. This will be the first in the series that I didn't complete the end game for, I just burned out on it. Lots of people have mentioned the class roster being cut down significantly, but what got me was the cut mechanics, too. No more magi-change, and nothing new to replace it. No more monster weapons, and nothing new to replace it. No more weapon-specific skills, and nothing new to replace it (weapon skills are now tied to class, similar to how monster skills work, which means your characters are drastically limited in what they can do and how they play). If you liked Overload or Revenge or even the Curry Shop from Disgaea 5, they're all gone with nothing new to replace them. The only "new" things D6 adds are:1) Shared exp/mana. You no longer earn exp or mana when you kill a unit, but all units on the map (or that died, just not anyone in the base panel) receive the same exp/mana. I don't hate this feature at face-value, but you quickly wind up following the pattern of "Pull 9 units out, 1-shot the enemy with your strongest attack guy, repeat forever". This balances the "No weapon skills" change, since otherwise characters like Thieves or Clerics have literally no attacks beyond normal attacks. Despite having room for hundreds of units, this "10 units share exp" really locks that in as your maximum. 2) Juice Shop, where you spend Hel and stored stats to level up specific stats per-unit. This replaces the Shards system from D5. This might be useful to add a new character to your roster later in the game, but otherwise at any given point it's prohibitively expensive. When your characters have thousands and thousands in a particular stat, you'll spend every Hel you have to give a static, non-scaling boost to one stat and that's a fraction of a percent of a bonus.3) Auto Battle. The elephant in the corner. With the press of a button, the AI takes over and plays for you. You can even set up some fairly detailed "rules" to make your characters fight as you'd like them to. Honestly, I wonder if this system was the  reason so many other features were cut, simply because so often it's the most efficient route to let the AI handle a fight, and it's easy for the AI to do that with fewer options. It seems a lot of the game's content was designed with this system in mind; grinding has always been a thing in Disgaea, but now that "Have the AI grind for you" is an option, trying to grind manually is just magnitudes slower and feels like a joke. And because so much has been removed from the battles, it doesn't feel rewarding to do it manually, either.** SPOILERS **The storyline by far has been the most uninspired of any Disgaea. The characters that join you have no real motivating reasons to do so, never experience any growth or character change (You get a human king early on that tries to solve all his problems with money; by the end of the game, his "growth" is that he feels bad about it sometimes but still solves all his problems with money). The idea that any of our characters are demons and might act demonly, the fact that it's all set in a series of Netherworlds, are all completely forgotten. One character that joins you has pointy ears, so I believe she's meant to be a demon. The main character has horns, so I believe he's meant to be a demon zombie. As far as actions and emotions and motivations, they're all just humans on a quest to fight the Bad Guy to save the world. They almost have a good thread going with "Despite being a weak zombie, our main character has become powerful through hard work and dedication"... But then at the end tell us "He was born special, he's a rare super demon, this wouldn't be possible for anyone else". Bizarrely, you end every single chapter fighting an "impossible" boss. But as it goes with Disgaea games, the boss is very much fightable, and even without grinding too much to get there. The story handles this by ignoring it and pretending your party got one-shot. Just... Imagine one-shotting a boss, and being greeted by a cutscene of "Argh, I'm so helplessly weak, this thing is a monster, how can we ever fight it?" And then repeating that exact same thing for 10 chapters.** END SPOILERS **If this had been one of the one-off spinoffs, I would have been unimpressed. The fact that this is the next main entry into the series at a staggering $70 is an insult to the fans. With so much cut content, with hand-drawn 2D sprites being traded out for money-saving 3D models, this is just not a game I can recommend. Maybe on sale if it's $20 or less and you want to add it to your collection, but otherwise I'd say reading the Disgaea Wiki about this game is more fun than playing this game, and that's free.
