_childDocuments_.review: To put it simply, I love the Disgaea-series and have had a lot of fun playing through 6 even with it's issues. I've played every Disgaea released on PC so far and 100%ed all but 2 and 4 which I will go back to eventually and overall I don't think of this game as something much worse or disgraceful than the rest of the entries, it doesn't have the polish of 5 or the original novelty of 1, but it's still, well, Disgaea.I was hesitant about the 3D-models and even now I still think they can't compare to how good 5 looked, but in my opinion, the vast majority of them are actually pretty good... Sure, I think the prinnies look hideous in this game, but many of the unique models like Desco or Ivar look great balancing it out.I don't think it was necessary to multiply all the numbers in level caps, stats, damage numbers et cetera and I honestly find them hard to read and look at when they are in the quadrillions and above when for a lot of said stats there isn't really a easy way to read them, but in the end that's a minor complaint.I don't really know how to feel about the auto-battle. On one hand, I found the editing of the D.I. to be fun and when I recalled farming Cave of Ordeals for hours in the first Disgaea or reseting item world for pirates and mystery gates in 2, I found the auto-battle to be a decent solution to that, but... I really like playing Disgaea, and the auto-battle is taking that away from me, there isn't much incentive to play the game manually when the auto-battle will do 32 times faster than me without misclicking tiles or other human mistakes and it's pretty sad. I'm sure there is a way to have the best of both worlds in the future, I just don't know how that could be accomplished.My last note is that I miss a lot of the previous mechanics, classes, characters and so on. Having no Magichange, no Fusions, losing out on so many of the classes like my favorite; the Spirit is heartbreaking, I understand why that is, the change to 3D-models must have meant that they had to cut some things, I simply wish for them to return in future games, preferably with even better looking models than what we have now. I also wish for some more variety in the bosses, Baal is iconic and all, but fighting him three times is a bit much, maybe two of those encounters could have been Pringer X, Zetta or any of the other recurring post-game fights insteadRegardless, even with all these gripes I had, I really enjoyed the game and don't regret buying it but if you are hesitant enough to read such long reviews, maybe you should wait for a sale in a year or two?

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good, alot better then the crappy switch port.PROS:-Fast paced as all hell if you want. Making grinding 10X easier then previous disgaea games, -Auto battle is AMAZING for games like this, meaning you dont have to constantly break your fingers clicking or mashing buttons to beat enemies when you can set it to auto and the match is over almost instantly, saving the players countless minutes and hours dispatching enemies, this in my opinion was the most needed and strongest mechanic for this game if you lack patience like I do. -Beautiful art and cute character models, the 3D change isnt so bad, it just takes time to get used to.-Gameplay is alot more simplified and less complex in comparison to the previous games (although I miss some of the older features the games had but oh well)-Characters from previous games have returned to join you if you wanna play any of the previous protagonists-The level cap being raised to 99,999,999 was a great idea since reaching level 9999 originally was easy but in this game you have to work abit harder for it. Although I think with some exploits you can also reach this easily as well, its more of an approachable thing if you ask me -reincarnation is alot stronger in this game and numbers are off the walls more then ever in terms of growth-Gameplay overall is fantasticCONS:-The story isnt all that good in my opinion, and even though Zed has a good design and abilities hes an unlikable lunatic in the beginning of the game, but I think he gets better as you continue on story wise.-They wiped out soo many of the monster classes and other classes which disappointed me greatly since I loved the male and female versions of classes, this was a huge turn off in itself since monster weapons were really fun despite them not being strong before. -The game is very easy but if you change the difficulty up to the max you can fix this-Way too simplified in my opinion, but I think they had to in order to not break the game.Overall, not a terrible disgaea game by any means, and if you are new to the series you can pick up this one and try it out. Its fun if you are looking for large wacky numbers and crazy leveling with fast mechanics and animations.The gameplay is the games strongest feature, as for the story it kind of bored me and made me dislike the main character, but he is strong to use regardless. But I also wished they didnt removed what made the previous games so fun and likable.Regardless this game has alot to unpack, and you will end up trying to beat it for countless hours. Disgaea 5 was alot better then this one by far in everyway. Just go play that if you want a superior disgaea game, otherwise this one is just kind of a husk of its former disgaea self. Disappointing, and makes me worried that this might be the last disgaea game if it doesnt sell good. Best of luck to Nis if they dont go bankrupt. Also 70$ is abit of an insane price for this if you ask me, so only get it if goes on sale, or if you are a disgaea enthusiast like me. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unpolished even though it's the "complete" version. You'd think they'd fix some things up. Maybe they did though, I never played it until this version, but I see problems. Most notably, the simplification of everything. This is like Disagea's version of Pokemon Sword and Shield. It's otherwise more of the same but now half the classes are missing.I am a HUGE Disgaea fan and have played every one in the series, Phantom Brave and Makai Kingdom too. I loved the level of strategy and the feeling of getting so much stronger. And I loved the characters. I thought Disgaea 5 was the falling point, as it had good gameplay but bad characters. Disgaea 6 is a reverse of that.But for the characters... I like them more than anyone in 5, which is not hard. But they still feel like instead of being a set of characters in a game, it's a tabletop DnD game and everyone's made a character on their own, without consulting the setting at all. It's chaos. Everyone feels very out of place beside each other. This wasn't a good thing, and yet it seems like they went out of their way to do this. The heck were they on?! But as nonsensical as the characters are, they are likable enough. Majolene feels like she gets less screentime and attention compared to the others, which makes me fear she's only here to attract a specific demographic. Though every character is okay, they all feel familiar in the worst of ways. It feels like they have YET AGAIN recycled old characters into these ones. Repeating the same qualities. Basically we have a party made up of Laharl, Gordon, Mid-boss, Seraphina but with her money side split off into an improved Hoggmeiser. And Majolene who is... I'm not sure if they had a character like her before. Whines constantly, sometimes gives exposition, but mostly whining.So moving on from the characters to the gameplay, it feels so weird to have the two versions of each class go from being just a choice of gender, to actual distinct different classes, to just not existing anymore. It makes no sense to remove so much content. Yes there's a couple new ones, but what about my favourite ones? There just isn't any explainable reason for why the 6th game in the series would be so lacking. The way they did monsters seemed to me like they were trying something new, until I realised that they actually weren't trying anything at all. The monsters have NOTHING unique about them anymore. They are just the same as any other demon unit. There was a chance to do something cool here but they didn't even bother. Then there's the evility scrolls. It's so bizarre that every game has given you ways to learn skills from other characters, but evilities took effort to get. Not in this game. Now skills are really tough to share, but you can just train a single character and then make them give out lots of copies of their evilities and pass them around to everyone else. It makes no sense and wrecks the balance. And speaking of balance, and the monsters now using weapons, it feels like there's a massive imbalance to which weapons are most important. Even with the DLC characters it was super obvious that 30% of my team used fists, 45% used staves, and 20% used guns. 5% used the other 4 types. But as weapon type and skills are no longer connected, it really felt like axes stopped being useful. They are just so much worse than spears now that the defense dropping skill is tied to the warrior class.What I did like as a gameplay change is how it distributes XP and such at the end. It finally removed the need to give bows to healers to level them early on, because now they WILL level at the same pace as everyone else. That makes things nicer. And that's the only good thing that comes to mind.So I didn't mention the autobattle system yet. It's a major feature, maybe the main feature. And that's awful. I shamefully do like idle games, but seeing my favourite strategy game turned into an idler is horrifying. I bought this game to PLAY IT. Not for it to play itself. This was such a stupid move to pull. But then part of me thinks this game was meant to be an idler from the start.Let's also talk about the graphics, another major part of this game. And another failure. The game does NOT look better. It looks pretty dang similar, so much so that it makes no sense that they put in the effort to change the graphics, since there are no improvmenets. It even looks a little worse in some cases. But 3D means less effort in making classes and characters. That was the point. So why are there no classes? Why do they use recolored versions of the warrior and Melodia for NPCs? They can make new models, that's the point, but they didn't use the 3D models to their advantage at all. Another benefit of 3D models is that you could have the equipped items make more impact, or a chosen personality not just change voice, but pose too, to have more variants of a model. It would have been easy compared to doing it in 2D. So naturally... They do not even try to do this. They ignore this benefit. It just gets depressing how wasted this is.Sound. This is not an area I usually comment on. I don't consider it too important and I'm tone deaf. But the recording quality makes me think that they made the voice actors also edit their own lines as they sent them in. Some characters have a delay before every line, like Cerberus, which stands out when other characters are talking at the right time. Then there's any time Ivar talks and you can't hear him over the music. Why did no-one ask him to re-record the lines, or why did no-one edit the lines to be louder? It's really awful that they just didn't care. There's also a song in this which is horrible. You Go Girl, a favourite of mine, has a version used in this where it only loops the first part over and over and OVER AND OVER. It's actually gotten me to hate a song I used to enjoy. I don't understand why they butchered the song like this. Or why they used it so often in the DLC stages.So bad content, bad gameplay, bad graphics, bad sound. And most obvious, a really bad price. I paid full price in British pounds, which was 65. Meaning I paid over $77 for this game. Yes, nearly $80. That's how much I had hope that this would be a great new start for the series. And I was an idiot for having such hope.This game is a ripoff no matter how you try to twist logic. Add on that it's got microtransactions and it's just so scummy. They must be making a fortune on this game, and yet they only put in half the effort. And to top it off, all of this after releasing a Gacha game and literally scamming money out of their fanbase! It's not like they're doing bad for money then. This must be their most profitable year. So then why are they barely trying with the games? Does earning money and putting in work really go against each other that much? There are no excuses. This was a low budget game sold off with a price that did not match the work put in.I've not finished the game's story mode yet. I'm still hoping there's some good hidden away. Maybe it gets fun only after you beat it. But so far this has been the worst game in the series for gameplay, worst for graphics, worst for audio issues, and the second worst for characters... Because you just can't beat 5's dreadful cast of annoying boring repetitive tropes. Still I'd suggest anyone play 5 instead of 6 because it was actually fun to play. 5 knew making the game fun was the most important thing. All the other Disgaeas are fun except for 6.

_childDocuments_.review: It's far from their best work, but still worth playing.Disgaea 6 is a bit of a misstep for NIS, but only a minor stumble.  By and large it is a Disgaea game, and fans of previous titles should find it worth playing.  That said, some of the changes they made will put off people, but it's mostly a personal taste situation.  Auto-battling is sort of nice to have, since it cuts down on needing to manually grind the same stages over and over.  On the other hand, it means that you'll be leaving your game running for who knows how long whilst you're not actually playing it.  It would have been better, I think, to make stages a bit more challenging, but also more rewarding to complete directly.The story and characters aren't particularly appealing in this outing.  Again, this is subjective, but I'd place it in the bottom half of the Disgaea games in that regard.The boss of each chapter being the same individual, but stronger, is a bit boring.  The concept behind it is fine, but in practice that means that there are fewer opportunities for humor or interesting drama that facing a boss usually has in a Disgaea game.In summary, long time fans of Disgaea should find it worth playing, but it probably won't be very many people's favourite.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird.If you're here for some good SRPG gameplay, you may want to look elsewhere because using the newly introduced auto-battle system is maybe way too good, especially if you take the time to modify your units' "Demonic Intelligence", and will get you through almost every battle in the game.On the other hand, if the thing you enjoyed from the previous Disgaea games was building up your character(s), then the new Super Reincarnation, D-Merits, and Karma systems are a lot of fun to play around with.As for the story, I was pleasantly surprised: the main character Zed is great and the side characters aren't annoying like in Disgaea 5, although you might think it overstays its welcome because it seems to have the highest amount of chapters out of every game in the series.The presentation, however, is kind of rough. The new 3D character models don't look that good, literally every special attack animation takes place on a flat featureless ground, and the normal attack animations look kind of awkward. The music and art is still great as usual though. Also, there's some technical issues: sometimes the game will just freeze for a solid 4 seconds during combat and if you alt-tab the framerate goes to hell.In conclusion, I would recommend buying this game on a sale if you're a fan of the series or if you want a high rent Cookie Clicker-esque kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: If it's your first Disgaea game then it might be worth getting into, however if you're into the series I don't think I could recommend it in good faith as it eventually becomes an auto-battler that you just leave running while you do stuff on another monitor. The numbers keep increasing and I do like how they got rid of the whole essence system to go over your limits but this one doesn't have long-term replayability in my opinion.Despite all that, I still played roughly 200~ hours on the Nintendo Switch and I was excited to get back into this one but lost the motivation pretty fast when I started to realize all the faults of the game on the 2nd playthrough. Again, if this is your very first Disgaea game then go ahead, there's lots to do and you'll stay entertained for possibly hundreds of hours if you like that infinite grind, but unless you put restrictions on yourself then you'll end up just clearing every stage on auto-battle utilizing the demonic intelligence system and it just becomes a squad simulator game instead of a tactical JRPG.Good news for people who already played this on the Nintendo Switch though: This game runs at a fluid & smooth framerate and isn't terrible performance like it was on the Switch, and it was funny because on Switch there was like no difference between 4x, 8x, 16x or 32x because the game would be lagged out and unable to keep up with anything in the first place until you got the Instant speed.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of Disgaea stories, this is a fun side project to take on if you can catch it for $30 or less.  There are aspects of Disgaea 6 that make it a potential good candidate for a first-timer to start with, but there are a few fundamental pacing/balance issues that keep this from being an awesome gold-star experiment within the series.  85 hours in, over half of that time was at the HQ managing my team, and ~not once~ have I stepped into the Item World.Immediately prior to starting Disgaea 6, I just finished collecting my last treasure map on Disgaea 2 - a process that PHYSICALLY took 120 hours of walking my character, opening menus, running a map, loading a map, resetting a map, etc...  I knew what I was doing, and it took 120 hours just to get that part of the game out of the way, the RNG simply would not allow me to have gotten that ~first half~ of the game finished ANY SOONER.The payoff in Disgaea 2 I feel, is worth it, but I went into Disgaea 6 feeling like the Auto-Battle feature would be a breath of fresh air - automate that 120h process while I work at my desk, and the game could be alt-tabbed in the background.  For a longtime Disgaea fan, this is an awesome feature and it removed the monotony of some of the repetitive actions from the game that are mandatory in Disgaea 2.  The flaw in the system however, is that NIS should have made it so that Auto-Battle is ONLY allowed after finishing a new story map at least once.  As-is, if you have a solid party, the story can quickly become a rush of visual novel scenes rather than a strategy RPG.  I counter-balanced this with making sure to steal items and max out the bonus meter in each story map manually,  but simply requiring 1 initial clear of the map could have balanced the system out nicely.The story and characters are colorful and a ton of fun - Disgaea 6 feels like they took some of the slower elements of the Disgaea 1 and 3's cast and did a great job giving the game's plot a smart twist.  The premise is that Zed initially reads as a trope-ish Gary Stu main character that someone wanted to make as an edgy anime OC, but the story is presented in flashback format - what had to be done to actually ~get~ to that level and what Super Reincarnation actually contributes to that process turns into an interesting enough plot that I could easily see this making for a fun, single-season anime show.  There are spots where it drags however - a few chapters are clearly filler (something that past games have had), but the player is INCREDIBLY limited by the game forcing you to 100% finish the story before they allow your 9999lv cap to break.In addition to requiring 1 clear of a map prior to allowing Auto-Battle, if about halfway through the story, NIS would have allowed us to go up to 99K lv, the balance of some of the fights would have been better.  Disgaea 6 is missing a fair portion of the variety of enemies and character classes previous games have featured (ones added back in for Disgaea 7), and so you NOTICE when there is a filler chapter in the story.  It's unfortunate because even shrinking the story by 3 chapters might have served the pacing a bit better.  Regardless, I made up for this by resolving to make sure that at the start of each chapter, I would reset the party to lv 1 and work back to 9999lv.  Finishing a chapter at 9999lv gives your ENTIRE HQ of characters a ~massive~ Karma boost, and it is a blast making sure to grab this chapter-end bonus each time.So the story can be finished in 60 to 80 hours if you are trying to 100% it like I was.  I have most of the achievements at 85 hours now, and I have never used the Item World once, only the Farm feature.  If you take an evening to set up Mao as Auto-party lead and give him and your other 9 members EXP Evilities, squashing the first post-game tier of lv 9MIL content is pretty smooth but I feel like it's missing its teeth.  In Disgaea 2, if you have no idea what treasure maps are, then you're missing almost a whole half of the game.  Post-game in those older titles can feel like a deep, deep abyss with some wild and exciting things lurking in the depths.  On Disgaea 6, post-game is pretty much a "practical exam" asking you to show off how well you understand the game's systems.  Once the numbers go up enough and I get the last achievements, it's kind of barren, and that's unfortunate because the system otherwise gives you a lot of flexibility to craft a unique party.So in summary, the characters and story made it a fun experience in spite of some pacing issues.  The gameplay asks you to take on a bit more of a team management role rather than a team strategist role due to all of the available Automation, but I actually found this to be a breath of fresh air, coming from Disgaea 2.  If some of the fundamental problems had been addressed by NIS, this would actually be a really great entry for new Disgaea players to start with, but I do caution that once you do finish the story or if you do not fall in love with the characters, then this sort of turns into the EVE Online (spreadsheet management) of the Disgaea series, and unlike Disgaea 2 where new characters and excitement are waiting at the lowest floor, there's not much more here to Disgaea 6 than a quick & fluffy dopamine rush for the folks hunting achievements.  I enjoyed it for what it was, but I went in specifically looking to "relax" and take a break from Disgaea 2.

_childDocuments_.review: For reference I beat the main story as well as one post game story.Overall the game is just fine but a step down from what it has been in the past. My main complaints being...-The 3D models are serviceable but have much less personality than the character sprites in the previous games.-I didn't enjoy the high numbers at the start of the game; in the first few chapters characters would gain hundreds of levels and gain thousands of stats yet still be around the same power as level one characters. It just wound up being confusing.-The auto-battle system wound up being a crutch the whole way through. If I failed a mission, instead of adjusting my strategy or placement on the map I found it way more simple to just afk grind for a few minutes and come back. Totally my own problem but just getting bigger numbers always seemed like the best way to proceed.-The characters and story are at an all time low here. Disgaea obviously isn't the best when it comes to telling complex or interesting stories but this one felt much less engaging as previous entries. The characters are also all very *very* one note. (I did enjoy Misedor ,Majolene, and Bieko but they were still super simple characters)-The extra systems they added were fine but they really didn't catch my interest. I for the most part ignored them.Putting the complaints aside this still is a Disgaea game and it brings what you would expect with it. Its hands down the worst in the series but its still a good time. It really is just a middle of the road game for the Disgaea series. If you like the series I would wait for a sale and grab it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Story : Game plays like the post-game content of the previous games right from the start.Long Story :All the usual jrpg leveling stuff you usually have to deal with is thrown out of the window and you go directly into grinding stats through reincarnation and other methods unique to the serie, some new to this game.Personally I like it since thats what makes disgaea unique.And its nice to see game companies willing to take some risk and change core mecanics to this extent. However you should temper your expectations accordingly and be willing to accept a lot of changes.Some other big changes : - The weapon skills which are now unique to classes. That means the only skills you can transfer between classes when reincarnating are the elemental and healing spells (at least at the moment of writing this, during chapter 2, I dont see it being possible).That also means your weapon choice is now just dependent on the stats they provide and not the skills, which can open up a lot of new possibilities which isnt so bad.- Exp and Mana is given to everyone in the party, not just whoever kills the enemy. Im not saying its equally distributed. Im saying its given to everyone. That means for the first time in the disgaea serie having a full party is way more effective that having one single powerhouse character. _childDocuments_.review: The Disgaea series has always been a mixed bag. The writing can be very hit-and-miss. The gameplay can be either quite satisfying, or tedious - even annoying, in the case of overly contrived puzzle-battles. The myriad of game systems like squads, quests, the item worlds, reincarnations, evilities, scrolls, class ranks, ability proficiency, ability levels, ability ranges, weapon types, character stats and how they relate to different weapons... it could easily overwhelm a beginner just looking for something fun to play. Learn stuff as you go, perhaps, is the best advice there, as Disgaea 6, while including some streamlining features, also piles a bit more complexity on top with, for instance, the option to configure your own auto-combat AI. You can go with the basic AI types pre-provided and be mostly okay, granted, but certain situations call for a bit more nuance.Disgaea 6 is, at the end of the day, a Disgaea game. If you love everything about the series, you'll probably enjoy it. If you're new to the series, I'd sooner recommend Disgaea 5 as an overall superior experience in terms of story and gameplay. The 3D graphics in this one are a fairly faithful recreation of the long-running 2D visuals, and keep to the same visual style, for the most part. The intricate color customization system from Disgaea 5 is unfortunately gone. The music is... eh. A few nice songs, some returning ones, a botched remix or two (You Go Girl comes to mind... an already simple song does not need about half of it cut out).All in all, weakly recommended. It's not bad, but not amazing either.

_childDocuments_.review: As the newest entry in the long running series, Disgaea 6 continues the trend of being the ultimate grinder's paradise. In this turn-based JRPG, you will follow Zed and comrades in a quest to destroy the God of Destruction. The story, while basic, does the job, but the real meat is the gameplay systems that make this game feel endless. With the ability to level up your characters to 99,999,999, enhance skills in multitudes of ways, attach bonuses, and even level up your items, you will be able to go overkill with your heroes and have them doing damage in the quadrillions. There is also reincarnating, as well as autoplay and AI features so you can configure battles to go automatically for easy grinding!This is the Disgaea franchise's first time going into the full 3D space and they took a lot of chances here. I love the increased level cap, creating your own characters, and Demon Intelligence. If you like grinding in RPGs to make the strongest character possible, this is the game for you. Compared to other entries into the series, it does feel a bit stripped down. Compared to Disgaea 5, there are less classes, no team-attack special animations, removed character world, and some assets not looking as great. Overall, this is still a competent and fun experience, and it is even moreso on the Steam Deck!Booting up Disgaea 6 there were absolutely no issues and ran perfectly fine without any changes needed! The game can run at 60 FPS and hold it fairly well, though it isn't perfect. While it will be at 60 FPS 95% of the time, there are a couple of areas that will drop it for a moment. They don't last long, but they are there. Because of how playable it is though, I would consider this a Best on Deck game due to how it can run just fine with no changes, but there are some you can make for optimal play!By changing your framerate and refresh rate to 50, you can not only eliminate any drops and keep a smooth feeling, you will also save a little bit of battery. With this single change, I noticed a 45-60 minute increase to battery life overall, which can help significantly for portable play. Temps don't change as much with this, but it does go down 1c - 2c.I also want to make special mention of the Nintendo Switch version. The Switch has different performance modes due to the hardware, so you can either have 30 FPS with great looking visuals or 60 FPS with blurry ones. On the Steam Deck, you can have 60 FPS with great visuals, which immediately will make this version the better portable one. And with the reduction to 50 FPS, battery life will be even better.The one thing that I would recommend changing is the Display Guide. This is the setting that shows which buttons do what on your screen. When starting the game, it is set to auto, which will show keyboard+mouse keybindings until you use your controller, which will then immediately switch to the controller bindings. To fix this, go to your settings and change the Display Guide option to the colored X, A, B, Y option. Now it will only show the gamepad buttons!There were also reports of Disgaea 6 crashing frequently, but in my playtime with it, I didn't experience a single crash. The game played as intended and I didn't change Proton layers. If you experience any crashes and have updated SteamOS, the Deck Client, and Proton, please let us know so we can investigate!Disgaea is one of the more addicting franchises I have played and number 6 continues that trend. With a bold direction to 3D and auto-battling mechanics, I enjoyed my playthrough all the same. And on Steam Deck, I had 0 issues playing and could easily recommend it as a Best on Deck game. While it has its shortcomings, I had a great time playing and it gives me hope that Nippon Ichi Software will learn and improve for their already announced sequel, Disgaea 7.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, if you're looking for a place to start with this series, I would recommend Disgaea 4 or 5 over this one. I think they are more solid titles overall, and it looks like the Steam reviews agree.That being said: I'm a Disgaea fan, and I enjoyed my time with Disgaea 6. Like the rest of the series, it's a crunchy turn-based strategy game with a lot of character advancement systems to optimize your chosen party. The plot is serviceable trope-y anime fare, about average for this series quality-wise.There were a significant number of mechanical overhauls in 6 -- some that I liked (Demon Intelligence lets you define AI behaviors to automate level clearing) and some not so much (tons of classes were removed; the Juice Bar trivialized a lot of spell and weapon mastery that felt more satisfying in the past.) What remains felt like a "couple steps forward, couple steps back" sidegrade from 5, but at least it's different enough to feel fresh for someone who fully completed previous titles.In summary, I give Disgaea 6 a mixed positive rating. Main story is about 20 hours. 100% achievement completion took me about 56 hours. It sounds like Disgaea 7 took this game and improved on it considerably, so I'm looking forward to trying that one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a bit of a weird one in the series.There are good ideas as well as questionable choices in the changes made.The Auto mode and the configurable AI are a good example of that, and it's the biggest of the changes.On one hand, being able to give each character clear orders based on the situation and let them run the boring grind (exp grind, item world) is nice and you can refine those orders to an extent as well.The issue is that if your orders are not completely messed up you can also use them for the majority of the maps, turning the game into something closer to an idle game.The disgaea series always had that problem to some extent since it allows us to grind levels and become widely over-levelled, making the content extremely easy to beat.In older versions they tried to force you to think a bit with the geo puzzles but those are not really an issue outside of a few specific maps.Even items and item world are in a weird position.Taking a legendary item of the easier ranks and levelling it a lot is incredibly easy (especially on auto) and it makes other items borderline useless.It is especially true since each "difficulty" brings its own set of items, vastly stronger than the levelled high rank of the previous difficulty even unlevelled.Of course you still need to grind stong items and reincarnate a lot for the end game content, that didn't change, but I don't really feel like I achieved much even now that I have 10 characters that mastered all classes and pretty much have the max stats I can get at that point.For people on edge, it's probably best to wait for a sale sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: Based on the game itself, yes, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. This update to the series core mechanics made me nervous going in, but the autobattling and most of the other changes fit in perfectly with the spirit of the franchise. The most unfortunate side effect of the autobattles is just that they've nerfed geopanels to death in the item world. The Item World Research side activity is very useful, but it's lackluster as a side activity in terms of gameplay. By comparison, the map building, invading, and board game activities in past games were much more engaging as a distraction from the core loop. This version looks and feels great, especially compared to the Switch version, with much more attractive graphics and better animation frame rate. Generally, this feels like a great port with a good amount of quality of life improvements built in. The only major criticism I have here is with this anti-consumer price tag. This game can certainly give you $70 worth of fun, but releasing a port of an existing game and then charging more for it than past editions is crummy no matter how you try to package it. The game is recent enough and content-rich enough that full price wouldn't be so bad, but... the DLC included is primarily cosmetics and returning characters from past entries, nothing terribly creative or substantial. We would be better served by a $50 game with an optional $20 DLC bundle.

I don't know If I'm imagining things because It's been a hot minute since I played Disgaea 5, but I feel a lot of similarities. Things such as  as well as a  Oh and of course, we always need a gross Loli character, You'll learn amazing lessons, such as how money Isn't all that matters, what justice Is and appearance Isn't everything! Is this a game for adults or a TV show for toddlers?The ending also felt very abrupt and underwhelming, It really lacked that satisfying feeling after all the time you put In with these "characters".At some point, all the characters In the Disgaea franchise became one dimensional, having a single trait their entire character Is based around, and nothing else. _childDocuments_.review: Disgaea 6 Complete is by far the most accessible entry in the series.No! As the story progresses, you are given more and more menu options and services that allow your party to automatically farm experience points, money, and other resources. This is very good for players who are bored of grinding; now you can skip the process altogether. All you have to do is figure out the process of farming the stage you want, leave the game running, go to sleep, wake up and collect your rewards.Yes! You can customise every inch of your party members thanks to the Super Reincarnation system that lets you change classes and learn new skills. In addition, you can teach anyone any skill (they're called "Evilities"). For example, my Psychic learned "Teleport", my Mecha Girl learned "Three Laws" and my Undead learned "Regeneration". I created Scrolls of these 3 incredibly useful skills, then taught them to my entire party. This feels really good because none of my characters "miss out" by being one class or the other.I love micromanagement, so this game is lots of fun for me! There are literally hundreds of things you have to juggle at any given moment in order to succeed, and it feels amazing when everything comes together successfully. You should give Disgaea 6 Complete a try if you're into that sort of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: To start, I recommend you get this on sale for $45 or less.  This is a good game that if you are willing to put the time in, can hold you for a long time given the amount of progression.  The reason I say wait for a sale is because it is really far less of a tactics game and much more of a game of management, AI, and endless grinds to infinite power.  As such, the difficulty curve is basically non-existent and most people will end up just steam rolling the story with the AI.  Its sad that is the case as there was a lot of care put into the game.  Each unique character and class has a bunch of special moves with animations for them.  There are a decent amount of unique characters especially with the dlc stages each giving you one unique character and unique abilities and animations.  I actually thought they were pretty good before I disabled them in the menu in my quest to speed up the AI grinding and becoming ridiculous overpowered by the 3rd act and subsequently steamrolling the entire game.  In post game, you kinda uncork the bottle and it becomes far easier to break everything as you gain "back to square one" which allows you to play stages as if its the first time and can grind the extremely rewarding boss fights.  Far more interesting than grinding the story though, are the item worlds.  IMO that is the highlight of the game and by going into each item, you can level them up and see weird hidden item towns and make them extremely powerful.  After you can trade the items for item points.  Unfortunately, you can create research teams to do this for you far more efficiently while you autogrind some mindless mission over and over collecting the rewards if 10 different research squads as well as leveling up the items in the process.  TL,DR; Its a good game and it is worth getting on sale, but its more of a management game than a tactical one.Edit:It is really fun to become a power house that can punch gods and instant kill them though.

_childDocuments_.review: The Disgaea series is not something that would be a fit for every player.  One of the gimmicks added to 6 is the ability to auto-battle, and this could be a particular turn-off to some.  The thing is, Disgaea has so much that you can do, so many levels and tactical combat floors beyond the main story, so many things to grind beyond just your characters, that it has always been a massive time-sink for anyone who did not just want to run its quirky story.  With that in mind, the auto-battle and programmable nature synergizes well with the grind, allowing a reprieve when you want to get some items leveled up fast but don't have the time or patience to put full attention into hundreds of battles to achieve it.  You could call this losing gameplay, or you could call it accessibility.Assuming that interest persists with the above, it's a quirky romp through an imaginative netherworld, continuing from the previous world-building in the series.  The story is unique/stand-alone, so you could jump in on this game.  If you're a fan of Disgaea, then this will scratch that itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been seeing a lot of negative reviews centered around the auto-battle, pricing, and a few other unwelcome surprises. Let me break down why all those people are idiots and objectively wrong: 1. If you’re upset about auto-battle trivializing gameplay, welcome to the franchise! This is clearly your first time playing a Disgaea game. Prior games were never difficult and the campaign has always been a tutorial for the endgame/“real” gameplay. Disgaea games are based on time optimization — you’ll get to the finish line one way or another but the way you go about it can end up saving you 5 hours or 50. And trust me, you’ll appreciate auto battle by the time you get to Rakshasa. It saves you from grinding stage 14-5 1000 times, and you can’t cheese the endgame with it because your team is going to hit level cap after 20 minutes or so. It’s a major QoL improvement that some people are (understandably) upset over but ultimately, it doesn’t trivialize anything that wasn’t already broken in the older titles and it lets you focus more on stat optimization. 2. $70 isn’t egregious. Games have stayed at $60 for about a decade now despite inflation through the years, and it would be foolish to think they’d stay at that price forever. The inflation rate this year alone justifies the price bump, let alone the DLC bundled with it. Every upcoming full-price game is now $70. If you don’t like it, just wait, but I don’t think the price bump is nearly as much of a cash grab than other reviewers are treating it as. 3. Cutting down on the available classes is unfortunate, but a ton of resources went towards making the game 3D. You win some you lose some, but it was a bold move to finally make that transition and I think it’s worth financially supporting. Personally I barely noticed because most of my team was comprised of the DLC characters and the remainder were “meta” characters like Zed and witch. 4. NIS killed it with the port. Runs super smoothly, good default button layout for controllers, fixed all the stuttering from the Switch version, and it runs well on both windows and Linux + Proton.5. This game is PACKED with content. I have about 30 hours at the time of review and I just got to Rakshasa mode. I did literally everything in my power to cheese the hell out of this game: exploited DLC character evilities, honed in on farming maps, spammed statistician innocents until every character had a max level one on their gear, used OP characters, you name it. Still took 30 hours to get here and there’s easily another 20-30 left if I want to fully beat the game. Overall I think NIS did a stellar job with this one. It’s a great followup from D5 and scratches that “I want to see insane numbers on the screen” itch. Ignore the haters, buy the game, give NIS your money. Now.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're new to the Disgaea series, this is not the game to play first. The first game is actually a great entry point, even if some of the systems/controls can feel a bit awkward compared to later entries. Disgaea 5 is also great, though the story and characters are meh at best. But this game is an odd creation, with some good steps in the right direction and some major stumbles.Have all the players new to the series left? Okay, so for everyone still reading, I'm going to assume you've played at least one of the previous entries (I haven't played 7 yet, so I can't speak for that one). I'm going to try to quickly go into detail about all the changes from previous games, where things went right, and where they went terribly wrong. I'll try to start each point with a one-sentence summary for those who want the TL;DR version.Story: This is probably in my top three for the series; the characters are all great and funny, they have great chemistry, and they develop and grow well as the story progresses. It never feels too predictable (except for the chapter endings for the first nine chapters) but it does a great job of giving little hints and details so the twists never come out of nowhere. The writing is great with this one, and there were definitely plenty of laugh-out-loud moments.New feature: Karma - Karma improves the reincarnation system, but has big drawbacks because of how they are earned and the cost for certain abilities. Unlike in the old games, reincarnating rewards karma points, one per level (with a multiplier based on quality) that can be spent on stat boosts and other perks, such as breaking the level/stat caps and increasing movement, throw, damage, etc. This works great in theory, but in practice, it has some big issues. Breaking the level caps requires an amount of karma that the player can only get from reincarnating from max (or near max) level at least twice (unless they get bonus karma from D-Merits). Finishing nearly everything in the game can be done without getting base stats above 2k, but for players who want to take on the game's ultimate challenge (not required for getting all achievements), they may need to reincarnate characters from max level over 100 times to reach stats high enough to stand a chance.New feature: Juice Bar - This was a big improvement over the extracts system from Disgaea 5, but because of the scaling with character levels/stats, it only feels relevant when used to super power a character in the early game by abusing the D-Merit quests.New feature: D-Merits - This per-character achievement based system is, IMO, the biggest failure in the game because it is horribly unbalanced, making it easy to create absurdly overpowered characters in the first chapters with little to no effort. Each character has a list of over 100 goals to meet, called D-Merits. Most D-Merits give reasonable rewards, but some of them can be intentionally abused and others are so easy to abuse that you'll reach them by accident. For example, a character who has defeated 50 enemies in the item world is rewarded with 100k karma, the amount they would get for reincarnating a level 100k character. Since this can easily be done within the first few chapters of the story (when the player can't even get a level over 9999) this can be used to superpower a character.New feature(?): Shared EXP/mana - In previous games, characters only received EXP when getting a kill. Now all earned EXP goes into a pool which is split among the party after battle, with characters who performed exceptionally earning bonus EXP/Mana. This works well and makes it easier to ensure that low-level characters aren't a pain to level back up to being relevant.New feature: Auto-battle - early in the game you can unlock auto-battle and the ability to program simple instructions for characters to follow. This is great for breezing through easy battles and late-game grinding but doesn't feel like it breaks the game on its own.Returning features:--Quest shop - Mostly unchanged, though there are a lot more quests to accept now and a much higher limit on how many you can have active at once.--Research - Instead of researching alternate netherworlds, you send characters into the item world. Research expeditions can level up items, though you don't get kill or training bonuses on the items this way. You do, however, get items, extracts, and even innocents.--Dark Assembly, Cheat shop - feels about the same as in Disgaea 5.--Squads - More or less the same as Disgaea 5 but this time you level them up with bonus EXP from the juice bar.--Item world - Item world isn't that much different from Disgaea 5, though instead of growing item level reward bonuses on the bonus grid, stages will frequently have level spheres (the farther you go in the item world, the more levels they tend to reward). One notable change is that leveling up an item in the item world (or through research) will cause all matching shop and bonus/chest copies of that item to be the same level (but without any other bonuses).--Hospital - You are automatically healed when you return to the base, but you'll still get rewards from the hospital like in previous games. You DO still have to pay at the hospital in the item world after boss stages.--Skill shop (and skills in general) - Evilities are largely the same as in Disgaea 5. Skills now go up to level 9999 and you can increase proficiency at the skill shop along with level and, in the case of magic, range. Normal attacks are, for once, not useless in Disgaea 6. In fact, if you don't level up skills in the skill shop, they'll end up being much weaker than normal attacks.--Innocent farm - Seems mostly unchanged, though I feel like once the farm squad was maxed out, it was very easy to farm maxed out innocents. Also, the UI/controls are so much worse than in Disgaea 5. Not sure how/why it ended up with such a noticeable downgrade.--Weapon affinities, mastery, resistances - Unchanged from Disgaea 5--Class mastery/subclasses - Mostly unchanged from Disgaea 5, although generics now cannot subclass until they have mastered their current class and class mastery has no impact on base stats upon reincarnation.Removed features:--The curry shop - Definitely a one-time only thing.--Capture - Capture was always a hit-or-miss mechanic. In Disgaea 5, Interrogation felt a bit too much, even for a Disgaea game, so I'm definitely happy that it didn't make a return.--Equipment affinities - This was probably the removed feature that I missed the most. Considering other steps taken to give characters, especially generics, a bit more of an identity, this served to take that away.--Weapon skills - Characters still gain mastery like in the old games, but they no longer will gain weapon skills based on their mastery with a weapon type. Each character class learns set skills when they reach a certain level. This allows them to be more distinctive, especially after the evility changes introduced in Disgaea 5, but with the ability to level up mastery at the juice bar, it makes it so any character can be good with any weapon with little effort.--A lot of classes - This is one thing that really upset a lot of the fandom. Disgaea 6 removed a lot of classes, especially in cases where two classes fulfilled very similar functions (Lady warrior and warrior, Skull and witch). I think this does improve efficiency and make it easier to give each character useful and meaningful evilities to learn, but I can understand why some were disappointed in the reduced character diversity.On the whole, Disgaea 6 isn't a terrible entry in the series, but it is one of the weaker ones. It falters most noticeably when it comes to balance and a low level of relevant post-game content, but makes up for it with a great story. If you're a fan of the series (and chances are that you are if you've read this far) I'd recommend picking it up, but on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Zed is a boastful zombie who wallows on the lowest rung on the Netherworld ladder alongside his sister Bieko. When a God of Destruction threatens their way of (un)life, Zed must harness his unique ability of Super Reincarnation to stand against the approaching menace. Along the way, he will unite with twisted and colorful denizens of the Netherworld, face challenges around and within, and see if even an undying hooligan like himself can defy the odds! Disgaea 6: Defiance of Destiny unites a grim yet touching story with insane tactical combat, while introducing gameplay elements never before seen in previous installments. As a result, new and returning players alike can craft a truly memorable and unique journey through the Netherworld. Bring the pain in battle with special attacks and support from a plethora of ally units. Customizable settings such as Auto, Retry, and Replay allow both hardcore and casual players to fight their own way. And should things take a terrible turn, use Super Reincarnation to rejoin the fight and keep trying until you succeed. This truly is a Netherworld fit for everyone! From Grave to Glory: Join Zed in his quest to rise above his lowly status and challenge a God of Destruction. Along the way, meet zany characters, explore chaotic new worlds, and discover the power of sibling bonds and determination. Undying and Unstoppable: Experience over-the-top tactical combat, complete with insane special attacks and a wide variety of allies to choose from. And when things get too hairy, use Super Reincarnation to keep trying until you succeed! A Netherworld for Everyone: With customizable gameplay features such as Autoplay and Demon Intelligence, both new and returning players can forge a HL-raising experience that fits their lifestyle. Diving into DISGAEA has never been easier! Additionally, Disgaea 6 Complete includes new recolor DLC as well as all previously released character and cosmetic DLC.

name: Mothmen 1966
detailed_description: More Pixel Pulps! More Pixel Pulps! Buzz About the Game At the edge of reality, where nightmare creatures lurk... November, 1966. The Leonid Meteor Shower. A young couple, a gas station owner, and a paranormal investigator get caught up in a terrifying conspiracy taking place at the edge of their reality, where nightmare creatures lurk, and the mysterious men in black lie in wait... Mothmen 1966 is the first in a new series of interactive adventures: Pixel Pulps. Created by novelist Nico Saraintaris and artist Fernando Martinez Ruppel, Pixel Pulps are a fusion of exceptional writing and stunning illustration, inspired by mid-20th century pulp fiction and 80s home computer graphics. The first volume comprises three games: Mothmen 1966, Varney Lake, and Bahnsen Knights. Mothmen 1966 , like all the Pixel Pulps, is made to be played by anyone who enjoys fine storytelling: Unfurl the dark wings of the rich, branching narrative Immerse yourself in the story with its rich, evocative illustrations Decide the fate of Mothmen 1966’s characters in ‘Choose Your Own Adventure’ style gameplay Solve accessible brain-tickling puzzles throughout the story

_childDocuments_.review: The art was what caught my interest and then it said Mothman in the title and I was hooked. Gameplay is decent. You know it's a visual novel, so there's limited interaction, but you do get to make choices albeit mostly for flavour instead of outcome and there are a few puzzlelike minigames, so there is enough variety.Story isn't as B-movie as the, well, marketing suggests, because I thought the texts and characters were pretty well written and interesting. Wasn't too happy about what they did with the Mothman and the overall horror aspects, but it was okay and had an eerie vibe paired with more action than I expected. (To be precise, the Mothman comes across as just some monster, even though the writers do try to link it to some greater lore or mystery, but that aspect of it isn't explored enough to have an impact.)While I did like this visual novel, I also thought it was too short and the ending felt abrupt. While it tries to leave you with ominosity, I honestly didn't think it was interesting and disappointed after the otherwise good story.Still, it is nice gaming has room for weird little titles like this. Try it, if you have two hours to spare. If you think it looks interesting, you will probably like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: I came for the art style and stayed for the story. It reminded me of when I was a kid playing on an Amstrad CPC 464 because of the artistic choices and the UI.I appreciated that despite the possibility of death, you do not have to start the whole game over, just the part where you made the wrong choice.Oh, and I played it on Linux, using Proton. It worked perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, but it ended up feeling very short. It's a VN but with a lot of retro-game vibes. The graphics are great and I really loved the art style. The music and sounds were also really good. The story was nice and I liked the whole twist on Mothmen with all the other additions that was thrown in. The ending was very good but it felt like a cliffhanger and made me want more. I loved that the game offers different deaths. I really appreciated the solitaire minigame. I haven't heard of a solitaire using "betting" to play, which made the usual tripeaks/pyramid solitaire a bit more interesting. I didn't experience any bugs while playing the game. I also didn't notice many grammar issues while playing the game, though the more obvious one was in the brain teaser. It is nice that the menu offers the ability to play the solitaire game once you unlock it. However, when you exit to the game, it goes right into the point after the solitaire in the storyline. I'm not sure if it's on purpose, but it would be nice if it would go back to the menu instead.  Overall, I really loved the story. I definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves spooky or sci-fi/cryptid related stories. Just be aware that it is short, though I do believe the art and story make up for the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible art style with an interesting concept, this game/vn features 2 very annoying things that make it almost not worth playing. 1. Being able to accidentally go to the main menu from the death screen and wiping out all your progress from your last save point. I understand implementing an auto-save feature might be a big ask, but like maybe just save whenever the player enters one of the possible death scenarios first? Having to fast forward through dialogue to get back to where I was, is mostly just annoying but still. 2. The instant death mechanic based on failing a scenario is incredibly annoying. Some of these situations, the solution presents it's self rather naturally, but there's been a couple where I feel like I'm just banging my head against a wall until some new prompt appears. For a game of this style, it feels weirdly cruel and unusual. The characters are kind of all over the place, and sometimes the dialogue comes across as unnecessary exposition. The story goes off the rails at the end in way that betrays the first half of game. It's ultimately not worth the 2 or so hour experience tbh.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: + Pixel art is superb. Some crazy good dithering technique here.+ Story is well written. Although tone of it relies heavily on aphorisms, general characterizations, pacing and that 80s half 'twilight zone' half 'weird sci-fi tale' vibe is brilliant. Never bores and constantly throws something surprising from start to finish.+ Price is spot on for the content. (Took me 2 hours to finish, just mind that i savored pixel art of it for a long time while playing).+ Even they are few, there were puzzles to let you feel playing a game, unlike any other generic visual novel out there.- Even the sound design is in sync with the general design. Some sound loops in particular scenes distracts the atmosphere and reading. It would be better to throw some SID tunes or alike in it. A great execution to mesh a well written story and pixel art into an interactive story. Loved the system and design they achieved here and will be on watch for more stories from the devs.

Absolutely worth your money and a few hours of your time to admire all this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a negative review with a couple of caveats: the concept and style are great, there are some terrific visuals, and I hope to see a lot more from this studio. _childDocuments_.review: Short and stylish visual horror novel with light puzzles.  Cool experience that could have been fleshed out just a bit more but still ended up being satisfying, enjoyable trip.Here are the main takeaways:-	To get the most obvious out of the way – the graphics here are brilliant. The artists that managed to put together this incredible picture out of pixels, making it simultaneously retro-inspired and visually pleasing to the modern player are beyond talented and deserve all the accolades. Every scene could be snapped as a screenshot and posted for the world to admire. Absolute eye-candy, this one.-	The story (which is the core of the game) is very much a-la old Stephen King (or rather a somewhat rushed take on those novels), nostalgic in the best possible way. It has a base of solid writing, well-developed (at least for such short piece) characters and exciting, all kinds of crazy, plot. It does seem to be running a bit wild towards the end, and I’m assuming natural limitations of budget/time came into play here, but this slight jumble aside – this is a well-written work that shows potential of the writers behind it.-	The puzzles here are few and easy and mostly built on trial-and-error approach that you can attempt to re-try immediately upon failure. They play well into the narration and serve as a side dish to the events unfolding rather than a challenge on its own. There’s a built-in solitaire in game which you don’t have to engage with at all or engage with for hours, to your heart’s content. I like the player’s agency over this plot-related mini-game.-	Speaking of player’s agency – even though there’s a tag for Interactive Fiction on the main page, this is very much a visual novel with puzzles and choices (the wrong ones will simply lead to quick death, so the ending will stay the same) without any interactivity a-la Zork that I, personally, associate with the IF tag. That’s not a slight on the game, by the way – it totally works as a visual novel, just an observation.-	There’s a pleasant soundtrack here that is, yes, also retro-themed and could be described as unobtrusive, the kind that you’ll notice while t’s playing but will promptly forget when the game’s over. It wasn’t trying to be anything other than that, though, so it worked well. I noticed a few odd fluctuations of volume (the menu music was too quiet, while the settings slider showed it all the way to the right. Naturally, I turned it up on my computer just to be blasted with sound when the chapter started) – but it’s a minor gripe, nothing serious.I’d call “Mothmen 1966” a worthy debut, where you can simultaneously see the quality of the job done, the artistry and the potential, while still seeing little kinks that could be worked out with more practice and confidence. I, for one, already got the developer’s next game – Varney Lake - and I’m not really into VN genre at all. If you fell under the charm of the visual element (and I think that’s how majority of people will find themselves drawn to this one), there are only two more questions you’d need to ask yourself – do you like horror stories and do you enjoy visual novels? If that’s a yes on both – this game is a no-brainer. Of course, it’ll also be a good choice for fans of interesting indie adventures (hi!), where small talented developers explore whatever it is they want in whatever sub-genre they choose. This was a nice little gem. Now I’m off to take a few more screenshots…

_childDocuments_.review: There is no shortage of revivalism in today's gaming scene. In fact, the desire to attract players by referencing the classics has only intensified in recent years as opposed to the pursuit of originality. Mothmen 1966 may very well be an admitted exercise in nostalgia, tapping into the great tradition of visual novels and graphical adventures from the mid-eighties, the age of the ephemeral reign of the EGA display standard in personal computing. Instead of directing its efforts towards the reinvention of the celebrated genre and its time-honored interface functionality, the developers at LCB were at pains to introduce an original piece of written fiction, one breathing new and inventive life onto the Mothman creature lore that both draws on core elements of the original myth and blends it with a host of other provocative references. The writing is steeped in elements of pure pulp literature, with all the hallmarks of what constitutes a fine horror piece in short story format. More than a mere complement to the text, the daring and often grotesque artwork is the indispensable companion in setting the game's dark and foreboding tone. Playing Mothmen 1966 has been the chilling antidote to the torrid nights of July 2022's heatwave.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: Despite high hopes, I did not enjoy this game... Truthfully, I wanted to refund my purchase of this - but it took me too long to play so I was unable to do so.  The art is spectacular. The story of this game was all over the place, none of the characters are particularly likable, and I found myself (at multiple points of the story) begging them to shut up. Mothman is also portrayed as an antagonist - in ways which don't necessarily jive well with his mythos.  This game has deeply uncomfortable themes around  that included jarring and unnecessary story beats around . Animals exist in this game simply to be . The only cool character is a .TLDR: I do not recommend this game to most audiences... It generally has the feel of a Delta Green homebrew campaign gone horribly wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly disappointing. The writing is good and the art is incredible which makes it sad that there's not very much meat to this visual novel. No branching paths, no alternate endings, and all your choices result in just a couple of lines of different dialogue or death. The game is short enough that I managed to get all of the achievements within the 2 hour refund window without really rushing.I'd recommend to grab this game on sale or look into other more substantial VNs for the same price.There's also some UX issues. With no auto save and no warning to go back to the main menu without saving it's very easy to lose all of your progress from the death screen. You also can't save or access the menu during puzzles and dialogue options so seeing alternate dialogue is a pain unless you constantly interrupt yourself to save just in case.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: If you like retro games, mystery novels, solving puzzles, The X-files and Stranger Things, this is the game for you. The pacing of the story is great, and the art style is beautiful. The fact that it isn't a long game adds to the charm and the whole concept of translating pulp novels into a videogame works really well.This game is an awesome ride for all the narrative videogames lovers out there. Can't wait for the next game from these guys.

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't find this too good at all.Story-wise it was kind of boiler plate and there were some brilliant illustrations during the playtime.However the choices are binary with one of the two being fatal, but immediately reloading you to a checkpoint, meaning that the choices are a facade and the story is genuinely linear.There's a occasional mini-games but they're groan-inducing activities like stacking shelves or throwing stones at a coyote.Linearity wouldn't matter if the story was more interesting, but it...isn't
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Untold Stories and other low graphics games…Mothmen 66 was an interesting concept. As soon as I saw the game, I wanted it, and I’m thankful the devs granted my request to play.It took a while to get to the story, though, and unfortunately by then I was annoyed at the characters. This game is a good framework for a better game. Bring different characters together for an event, terrific! But we didn’t care about them. We didn’t know who they were, their interactions didn’t make a lot of sense. I wish there were more puzzles in the game, and choices mattered. If I’m given choices, the story needs to follow said choices instead of just automatically jumping to the dialogue I didn’t want. If you put solitaire replay in the menu, don’t make us scroll through story/instructions every time.Did the resolution leave us open to a sequel? I wouldn’t mind that, but I hope they put more into the story. There were a lot of questions left unanswered, a lot of story needs filling in. The graphics are awesome! Even viewers complimented the color choices, and it felt great to go back to that time. It did actually jump scare me a few times, and the old-style DOS interface was nice with great sound even without a lot of modern options. I recommend the game if you can get it on sale, but I cannot recommend it at $9. I see they’re developing another game, and I look forward to trying that one.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, that was quite the story. The visuals are very clear pixel art and the way the change from one dialog to the other adds up to the storytelling. The soundtrack is good but I would have preferred something less SNES-esque. All in all, it was a nice experience.Now, if you don't mind, I will keep playing Impossible Poker until I beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: This kind of game isn't for everyone, but if you like short visual novel experiences with an interesting art style and theme, I'd definitely recommend it. It captures the essence of both the pulp fiction and 80s style computer graphics that inspired it. That being said, the story obviously isn't going to blow your mind, but it's a fun, creepy, and sometimes humorous ride. It also contains an interesting take on solitaire that I really enjoyed. So much that I spent time trying to get the related achievements. The most notable negative in my experience was the puzzle/minigame design. At times it can feel a bit too trial and error based, and the menu system you use to make your selections is the same as the dialogue options menu, which means it can feel a bit clunky. Though you could argue that they were going for that as a part of the retro inspired experience.If you're into the theme, like visual novels, and don't mind the short length, it's definitely worth your time, though you may want to wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: A neat little short story that manages to somehow out-weird its namesake as it goes on. The story is engaging enough and the art is pretty good too, $13AUD is a somewhat steep asking price but not the worst if you're a fan of these kind of bite-size horror shorts (and you can always wait for a sale). Looking forward to Varney Lake when it comes out
_childDocuments_.name: Mothmen 1966

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very strange game. I don't think it will be to the taste of many but I found the mystery compelling and surreal. I do think there's some elements of the interactivity that could be improved. Fiddling with menus can get tedious at times but otherwise it's a very interesting experience.I think that's the way to describe it. It's an experience. You either find it compelling or you don't. It's short enough to not overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite what may feel like physical limitations during the 80s and 90s, the Choose Your Own Adventure genre flourished despite the technological advances of the current day.  Whether through low-bit graphical DOS titles or the tried and true “flip to page 38 to see what that decision did to your boys” method, it’s hard to put down a CYOA with a delectable plot and the urge to see what path to take.  With my ever present love for the retro-indie and my initial inquiry for “why Mothmen?” and “why 1966?” I took a trip down memory lane with LCB Game Studio and their title, Mothmen 1966.Nothing like a special date under shooting stars, right?  What if it was the Leonid meteor shower on a picturesque night in 1966?  Being the history major you are, you would be keen to those details.  As one of our main three protagonists, Lee, drives his long-time but internally contrite girlfriend Victoria to a surprise date under the stars.  Finding the best spot to witness a historic event brings the two to an agreement with an off-the-road gas station owner, Holt, to use his spot for their potentially romantic getaway.  But the shooting stars bring more than history to the small station, as large cryptid figures have been spotted as the date rapidly approaches and a few people around have had their interest piqued by more than the stars…Taking their new interactive adventures into a newly minted genre: Pixel Pulps, Mothmen plays like you took your favorite B-Movie Sci-Fi/Slasher and slapped it on a fresh 32KB Floppy Disk.  Mixing Visual Novel tendencies with small brain teasers to break up the clicks, Mothmen was right up my alley and was an easy one-sit experience.  The characters provided a good amount of depth given the screen time and no characters really overstayed their welcome or became obnoxious by the end of the story.  I really enjoyed the prologue as it really gave off No Country for Old Men vibes and really set the stage for the mystery of what was coming.The biggest love for 1966 has got to be the artstyle.  The green and teal tones supplement a mysterious yet intriguing hue to the outside world while creating piercing images of mysterious figures half-shrouded in darkness yet almost straining when illuminated.  I love the simplicity on the surface but the ability to convey striking and emotional scenes with such a small amount of graphical power shows a real care for the product and a small but noticeable flexing of the muscles.But no date is completely perfect.  While Mothmen does carry multiple choices in dialogue which can then branch to different reactions from other characters, all points lead back to the straight line.  There are points where a wrong decision can prove fatal, but a quick restart at forgiving checkpoints make it less of a stressful situation and more of a gentle tap on the wrist.  For all the ramping up the story does to really press the unhinged nature of the supernatural, especially with a rather busy third act, Mothmen ends rather abruptly and haphazardly.  There was so much momentum being built with the scene at hand, and then the text reads, “THE END,” and you’re a little taken back.  Some after-credits bits play up the possibility for more down the road, but we were just getting to the good parts!But I did enjoy what I got to play.  Mothmen 1966 gracefully plays into the nostalgia of the DOS-era while providing a fun twisting tale of the supernatural and all the shenanigans that come with it, even if it is cut off a little too short.  Now, if you’ll excuse me…I have a game of Impossible Solitaire to win.  Maybe.Red or black…red or black…
