_childDocuments_.review: I liked the upgrading aspects of making your train better and better, and the different paints were nice. _childDocuments_.review: Choo-Choo Charles is the kind of game you would pass off as just simply being Youtube material. But this game surprisingly had more depth and gameplay variety than I thought.The whole premise revolves around you navigating the island, completing side missions to unlock weapons and scrap to upgrade your train. While doing this, you must find the three eggs scattered around the island hidden in enemy camps/mines to summon Charles for a final showdown and ultimately defeat him. Very simple concept, but very fun to play through. The tensity when you're just a lowly weak train trying to fend off Charles in the beginning was the best part. While the fear subsides once you're able to quickly shoo him away after getting enough upgrades and weapons midway through the game, traveling on foot still remained very dangerous and you'll be doing it quite often.Overall, I highly recommend it. Game length is perfect and doesn't overstay it's welcome. While I would say the $20 price tag is a bit hefty for the two and a half hours I spent beating and 100%ing it, I still think it's worth picking up if it goes on sale for roughly $15 in the future.

When the train starts chasing you and the andrelin filled music kicks in, just begs me to start shaking. You help out several NPC with fairly lackluster fetch side quests and a cult subplot that though basic is quite fun to play around with. However the stealth sections in the game is terrible. With no real stealth mechanic outside of not being seen and having no weapons at your disposable i found myself stopping the game to get myself seen then running back to my train to use the mounted gun to shoot them before finally exploring the cave. The length is too short for the price as well with the main quest being around two hours and the side quest only adding an extra hour of content. And without much replayabilty apart from trying to max you your upgrades then the price of £16.75 just isn't worth the money. If you can buy a copy for less than a tenner then abousutly spend a couple of hours trying to defeat choo choo charles. But until then, wait for a sale

_childDocuments_.review: With the right expectations this game delivers what you expect.It's not without its flaws, but again, if you know what to expect, none of those flaws take away from enjoying the game.The game is pretty straightforward, you arrive to an island with the mission of getting rid of Charles, a spider-train hybrid monster that's terrorizing the people in the island. You'll be driving your own train which is equipped with a machine-gun and you'll visit people in the town that'll help you progress in your mission.You'll also have optional missions to help people with some errands in exchange of the game's currency which is scraps that'll help you upgrade your train.As you progress in your mission you'll have to defend yourself from Charles, who'll show up every now and then and from some kind of cultists who protect specific places you'll need to go in your mission.The game is short, enjoyable, has it's scary moments and plays well which is amazing considering it was mostly done by one guy.I found no real technical errors, like bugs or glitches (maybe I saw Charles get stuck in some trees once but that's it and then there's parts of Charles clipping inside houses and other places, but that's it).The only flaws I could list are: - The obvious lack of character animation (mainly facial animations, the characters do move).- Some of the voice acting was so over the top it was more comical than anything (the pickle lady being the best example of this).- The stealth mechanics were lacking (there are some attempts at stealth with even controls to peak to the sides, but that's it, no crouching or something to distract enemies).- I was never able to find how to remove a marker from the map (don't know if it's even possible).That's very much all I can come up with for flaws. There are things I can think that in my mind would make the game "better", but I can't list them as flaws of the game. For example, I wouldn't have minded the game being a little longer, not necessarily 100 hours of content, but even with the mechanics already introduced, I could see how some missions could have been extended a little and different types of missions could have been introduced, that said, that falls more on the territory of personal preference than problems with the game.All in all, like I said, if you know what to expect, none of the flaws I mentioned are game-breaking and the game is more than enjoyable even with those flaws, so I recommend it to anyone who likes horror games and/or is curious about the game and wants to support the developer(s).

_childDocuments_.review: So I'll start with the good - Charles is really well designed. That's about the only really good thing about the game. _childDocuments_.review: At this time, I already beat it, with only two hours played. But those two hours were fantastic. This game is a fantastic, if short, horror game. It has funny characters, a simple story, stuff to do to gain lots of resources quickly, and Charles himself actually makes the game scary with his random points of attack. name: The Kids We Were
detailed_description: Set in the late Japanese Showa era (the 1980s), it's a nostalgic journey through a unique time in Japan's recent history. Take on the role of Minato, a young boy who sets out on an unexpected and incredible summer adventure. This game is an award-winning adventure game originally released worldwide for smartphones in February, 2020. Selected as one of the top 3 titles at the Google Play Indie Games Festival 2020, it has also won the Special Award, and been chosen for the Best Indies category of Google Play's Best Games of 2020. To celebrate the release of The Kids We Were on Steam, we've added a bunch of brand-new content. If you want the full experience, look no further than this, the Complete Edition! The Complete Edition includes the full story available in the app, in addition to a new bonus episode set after the events of the main game. There are also brand-new collection items to find! [Game Details] ・Unravel the secrets of the Seven Mysteries notebook to save your family and fix a broken future ・Collect over 90 retro items hidden in the nooks and crannies of a Japanese town in the 1980s ・Unlock over 20 original Steam achievements ・Play through a bonus epilogue episode that takes place after the events of the main game! [Story] Our story begins with Minato arriving in the small town of Kagami, an exceptionally ordinary sort of place in a sleepy suburb of Tokyo. But there's more to this simple trip than meets the eye. Minato has a secret objective: he intends to find his missing father, who is supposedly living somewhere in the area. Our young sleuth Minato wastes no time getting started, and soon finds a puzzling clue to his father's whereabouts. A mysterious notebook left for him with the portentous title 'The Seven Mysteries.' With this notebook as his guide, Minato sets out on a long and difficult journey, not through space, but through time. For his destination is none other than 33 years in the past—the day his father and mother first met!

_childDocuments_.review: is an adventure game focused on storytelling. There’s little to no gameplay; instead, it’s like a visual novel with exploration mechanics.Visually, it looks like 3D pixel art. Everything is blocky, yet more detailed than something like Minecraft. It gives off a retro vibe that fits well with the 1980s setting. The collectibles have especially beautiful models that show off the game’s cute aesthetic. It’s far from a technical marvel, but it’s great for an indie title like this.There’s no voice acting, so the only audio comes from the soundtrack and occasional sound effects. The score features quite a bit of music, definitely more than I expected, I thought the story would be shorter than it was, so the soundtrack wound up being the perfect length and never felt stale. The songs are typically slow and simple, often featuring minimal instrumentation. They are mood setters, not attention grabbers, and they do their job well.As I mentioned in the intro, the gameplay doesn’t play a major role. You walk around town talking to people and searching for both coins and collectibles. That’s all there is to it. The items you find have little snippets of info, usually pertaining to their relevance in 1980s Japanese culture, but it doesn’t serve a purpose outside of these fun tidbits. Coins are used to buy more collectibles, so they’re essentially the same thing as finding items directly. Walking around is mostly unnecessary because it’s a linear narrative. You can talk to other residents, but it’s only killing time until you go to the next story section. Granted, the dialogue is usually interesting, but it typically isn’t relevant to the plot.This is where all the meat is. Without the story, there would be no reason to ever play this game. Thankfully,  delivers a meaningful tale with a solid blend of humor, nostalgia, and sadness. It’s balanced well, so nothing feels tacked on or unnatural. It begins with you playing as a young Japanese child in the year 2020. Your family has assorted health issues, but you aren’t given any specific details. This part of the narrative is setting up the main plotline, but I didn’t read the store page before playing, so I was blindsided by the transition to a time travel story. Once it did though, I was pleasantly surprised by how much I liked the writing. Outside of a couple of typos or mistranslations, and some very telegraphed twists, it was excellent. It overstayed its welcome near the end, but only slightly. A few of the later chapters could have been trimmed down and combined into one big chapter, but it didn’t ruin the game or anything like that.I loved some of the story’s themes, specifically with regards to childhood experiences shaping your adulthood. There were some thought-provoking moments that stuck with me, something that rarely happens to me when I play games. I didn’t love the ending, but it was only a slight step down in quality compared to the strong middle. isn’t much of a game in the traditional sense, but it was good as a purely narrative experience. Because of that, it’s going to be fairly hit-or-miss for a lot of players. The heavy, emotional story beats are fantastic, but there are still a few missteps that didn’t go over well. Even though it’s technically an adventure game, visual novel fans are probably the most likely audience to enjoy it. Overall, a solid indie game that might be priced a bit too high, but definitely an enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Kids We Were

_childDocuments_.review: The Kids We Were is a charming title with a retro asthetic and a lot of heart. It's also exceedingly linear, and pads its length via backtracking and collection mechanics. While I enjoyed my time with it, I very much feel like it's not a good deal at full price. ($15.99 USD at the time of this review.) It's worth noting that this originally was a mobile title that was available for free. At the time of this review, while it is no longer on Android, it's still available for iPhone. While they did add an extra epilogue, I kind of question their pricing structure on this re-release.Now for the good: the voxel-based graphics are sharp, and lack the sometimes-blurry resolution of pixel graphics. The soundtrack is pleasant. The story, despite having children as the primary characters is surprisingly dark at points. It's designed to be played by Gen-X and Millennial adults and really push those nostalgic feelings in them, and it works incredibly well in that regard. The older you are, the more this game is likely to resonate with you.It's all not sunshine and roses, however. This game is extremely linear, and you'll spend your time walking to and from key locations. The map is small, so it's pretty hard to get lost once you've gotten the lay of the land, but you'll wish for fast travel. Why? Because any NPC unimportant to the plot will never say anything of value. They're just window dressing. You can search for coins or hidden items in every area, but unless you're chasing an easy achievement, there's no point to doing that either, outside of a small number of quests. On the bright side, with the push of a button, you can normally see if there's anything hidden for you to find in the immediate area, preventing you from going on too long of a fruitless hunt. There's also a mechanic to allow you to fill up your collection without having to hunt for those last few elusive items. It feels like they're trying to respect your time, but I'm not entirely sure why the backtracking and collection elements exist at all other than as a way to pad playtime. Given how short the game is overall, I feel like that's probably the case.There's no fail state in the game (you immediately retry if you do anything disastrous), so this one's definitely very new-gamer friendly. (Or for those of you with accessibility issues.) The story is unique and creative, but once you've played it, there's no real replay factor at all. I heartily recommend this game, but would definitely suggest waiting for it to go on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Kids We Were

_childDocuments_.review: The Kids We Were is a simple, medium-length (~9 hours) adventure game with a focus on story. It's a game about children, but - like the title suggests - not made for children, but for those who once were children. And, like the original title suggests (忘れないでおとなになっても。- "Don't forget, even when you become an adult."), it just may remind you of some things you've long forgotten.The main character, Minato (11) goes back in time from 2020 to 1987, where he has to solve some mysteries to change the future - his present. Aside from time-travel, the game is rather realistic, and the problems he encounters are mostly down-to-earth, even if at first they may seem to be of a supernatural... nature. During his adventures he meets people, makes friends, finds more about his parents and - optionally - collects 91 items from the era (all with 3d models and descriptions).At times the game is funny, sometimes emotional, often nostalgic - even if you happen to not have grown up in a 1980s Japan. It also touches a lot of serious subjects that not many games pick up, and it's very subtle about it too.I'm not really a fan of voxel graphics, but The Kids We Were is quite pretty, the music sparse but fitting the atmosphere.Overall, I think anyone who likes a good story should be able to enjoy this little gem. 8.7/10

You can find some stuff from that time, including short descriptions, and I have to say: My youth in the 80s/90s in Germany wasn't that different from what see in the game, especially stuff like candy etc.Because of the voxel/3d pixel art look, it's probably not a game for everyone, but if you like anime/manga with emotional and nostalgic stories or games like To The Moon or visual novels, this might be a game for you.

name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter
detailed_description: Gerda: A Flame in Winter Modstand Bundle The Gerda: A Flame in Winter Modstand Bundle contains: Gerda: A Flame in Winter (main game) Gerda: A Flame in Winter Liva’s Story (DLC) Save your husband in the original Gerda's Story and lead a daring mission in the additional content Liva’s Story. About the Game February 1945. The war is almost over but your fight is about to begin. You play Gerda Larsen, a young nurse who is torn between her community and her desperate quest to save her husband, Anders. Many other lives will come to depend on your decisions.  Gerda’s journey will involve moral dilemmas, difficult conversations, and sticky situations. It’s a dangerous world and you must help her adapt to it with the choices you make, which always have both short- and long-term consequences.   If you give away precious resources to somebody who needs them now, will you come to regret it later? Will there be consequences if you, as a nurse, help a person who is suffering even though they may later cause suffering to others?   Make the most of what you have: your personality points, your allegiances, and your resources. Your relationship with people and factions will determine how your story unfolds. Level up Gerda’s mental skills by reflecting on her experiences in her diary to gain personality skill points. Use these skills during events and conversations to unlock special actions, gain others’ trust, or keep them from suspecting you.      You can choose where to explore and when – but do so wisely, as people move around and events can be time sensitive. As you investigate and make progress, your choices will send you down many different narrative paths. Will you do whatever it takes to save Anders, or will you cling fiercely to your morals? Your actions will lead to several poignant conclusions and change the fate of your community in Gerda: A Flame in Winter.

short_description: You have five days to save your husband, who has just been arrested by the Gestapo. Investigate, explore and form allegiances in this story-rich RPG-lite. Who will you trust?

_childDocuments_.review: Nowadays, numerous titles focusing on World War II put you in the boots of valiant soldiers or sharp commanders, throwing you into the chaos of a battlefield. However, their presentation is often unnecessarily idealised, purposefully omitting countless hardships these people faced and how it all impacted the civilians. Thus, I always appreciate when a different take on this conflict appears, especially in this medium.Luckily,  is such a take, sharing a tale full of courageous and desperate acts. Because despite not witnessing the brutality of the front, many still had to fight their own battles to ensure a relatively peaceful life or worse—mere survival. Where games like  or  portray such themes in a more educational style, focusing on the memories of contemporary witnesses, this title deviates from this approach, and instead, it delivers a fully fleshed-out narrative that you can influence.That one, as the name suggests, follows the story of Gerda, a half-Danish and half-German nurse living in a small town in Denmark; due to her profession, she naturally gets in surprising situations and meets various kinds of people. Moreover, her mixed origin gives her the advantage of flawlessly understanding both languages. Unfortunately, it comes at a cost, as her interactions with others make her feel like she does not belong to either nationality.Yet, she has to endure—not only for herself but also for her loved ones. However, the more Gerda tries to help, the more poor souls in need she encounters, and since she is in desperate need of help, she can only do so much. With that comes the natural problem: whom can you trust? The Nazis are powerful, but it is hard to believe they would be keen to help out; the same goes for the resistance whilst having admirable goals, but achieving them might come at a regretful price.And that is where  shines, as it delivers a tense atmosphere with a focus on the fate of ordinary folks that are far too irrelevant to the ongoing war theatre, albeit them still being under its harsh influence. Even though it pushes pressure on you often, it knows when to relieve the tension a bit from time to time, to bring those small yet crucial lights of hope and happiness amidst the darkness.While the narrative undoubtedly is a dominant aspect, it is perhaps even more admirable how well it portrays the behaviour of people during these dark times and how it reflects on their actions and relationships, pushing them further from the principles they sought to abide by for the rest of their lives before the war unleashed. Thus, the fear of what could happen or whose loved ones might suffer crawls on all characters, not only Gerda. It leads everyone to various paths: some moral, some immoral.Such an approach allows you to understand their situation and sympathise or – in the case of Gerda – even empathise with them. That is up to you, however, as your choices do not only affect dialogues and relations but even what kind of places you visit during the day. Witnessing two playthroughs, I can confirm that my journey towards the finale differed significantly at times, but at the very end, it all comes to the same spot, albeit with slightly varied escalations. Thus, the plot still pushes you in one direction, only giving you numerous means of how to get there. Nevertheless, it mostly makes sense, and I never had a feeling that the game would suddenly force its way by illogically twisting my actions. Thus, the horrendous design of  titles is not present, do not worry!However, there are still a few shortcomings. Like, I would not mind if it would punish players for some choices a tad bit more or had paths that would lead to Gerda’s inevitable doom. There is nothing like that, so you will effortlessly observe her story from start to finish, even if it will not have a favourable outcome. Even though a reputation system is present – influencing how both characters and groups view you – it only serves as a helpful tool for gaining a higher chance for persons’ cooperation rather than having an impact on the plot as a whole. It might be for the better, however, as you both gain and lose sympathy points based on actions that others have not even witnessed. While the game tries to convince you that this is purely Gerda’s view, it does not explain why other people react based on her score. Luckily, it is simple enough to get a lot of points, so exploring various paths should not be an issue.That would be all about the gameplay, as you will not do much else otherwise. Well, apart from galavanting around from time to time, I guess. I do not mind that there is no more to it, though; there is simply no need for any action or puzzles to bloat and prolong this captivating narrative, as that would hurt the experience anyway in my eyes.Even the said walking might be enjoyable, as you can admire all the different environments. What is so interesting about them? They are visually present in an impressionistic form. Thus, if you stay still, it might look like one of those charming paintings. However, I do not have much knowledge in this field, so I can hardly say whether it accurately represents its techniques. Nevertheless, it looks extraordinary, and that is what matters. Unfortunately, though, there are no voice actors—you can only hear Gerda’s voice when she reads her diary. It is a bit saddening, as its omission removes a bit of an emotional aspect, but I got used to it quickly.Still, some of these shortcomings do not make a subpar title from ; in fact, it is superb! With its length of about eight hours, it delivers a thrilling and haunting journey in quite a unique setting that does not overstay its welcome. Thus, I can safely recommend it to the fans of narratively-driven adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda: A Flame in Winter is a riveting narrative that explores a fascinating civilian perspective during World War 2. The choices are bleak and have severe consequences which adds to the realism of war. It demonstrates that despite not being on the frontlines, the impacts of this conflict were truly felt by everyone, with many having to make sacrifices to survive. This educational game taught me more about this period than my history lessons at school ever could, and the adjoining narrative was just as memorable.You play as Gerda Larsen, a half Danish, half German woman in a small town in Denmark. It is 1945, she is a nurse, is married to a nice man, lives in a modest house, and is the daughter of a respected German officer. There are murmurs about the war, but it all seemed too far away to impact her ordinary life. Until… it was right at her doorstep and things begin to turn awry. Her husband, Anders, is taken by the Gestapo and is questioned for being involved in the Resistance. Gerda is desperate to have her normality back and worries for the safety of her husband. She decides to take matters into her own hands to try and get him released. Will she work alongside the Resistance, cozy up with the German authority, or seek the assistance of a somewhat deranged German guard? Who will she help along the way? There is limited time to help everyone, and astringent decisions must be made. These decisions will directly lead to the survival, or death of those around her.I found the setting for this game rather enlightening. Whilst I am far from an expert on history, I had never seen a movie or game touch on Denmark during WW2. This setting combined with a civilian perspective was fascinating to me. Despite knowing almost nothing prior, I was able to play the game without issue, and learn along the way.Gerda: A Flame in Winter is described by the on the store page as “A story-driven RPG lite,” but I feel it more closely resembles narrative, choice-based games such as the Telltale franchise, just with much heavier themes. The main gameplay is making decisions during dialogue, or choosing what actions to spend your time on. Players control Gerda typically from a top down perspective and click on interactive spots around the scene. Through exploration, different useful items can be found which may prove useful or even life-saving in later situations. Most areas cannot be searched extensively, as there is a timer on the top-right of the screen. For example, there may be limited time before dinner is served, and every action you take, or object you inspect will take up time. Once you have interacted with enough items, effectively progressing the time, dinner will be served, and you will be locked out of further exploration. Similarly, this also happens with other scenarios such as when you need to be quiet. Make too much noise, and you will be locked out from searching. Players must be careful to make thoughtful decisions, as there is not enough time to visit all locations, and many different people will request Gerda’s help. Similar to games such as  there are small optional articles of text to read that explain specific concepts or terms in relation to the war. They are always first mentioned in the game, and then can be further explained by reading the article. I really enjoyed this, as it allowed me to gain a full understanding of all topics covered and learn about history in an interactive manner. Interactions with characters will impact Gerda’s relationship with not only them, but whole factions. Having a good relationship with someone is key to gaining their trust, and this will be important in the future if Gerda needs their help. Navigating this social and political minefield can be tough, and it is impossible to appease everyone. Help a German soldier to improve your character relations with them, and perhaps some German officials, but this will impact negatively with the Danish. Words must be carefully chosen, but sometimes, it may be better to say nothing at all. Gerda also earns personality skill points by reflecting in her diary on her thoughts. These skill points can be used to improve outcomes and sway characters to your will. Whilst I enjoyed this approach, it felt odd wrongly choosing descriptive thoughts in the diary, only to be granted a useful point that I am lacking.Due to the sheer number of decisions to be made, it felt like any choices I made did have weight to them. Characters which I did not indulge, suffered or died. Others were not so simply categorised and were impacted by numerous decisions. Despite the severity of Gerda’s actions, it never felt like she was in danger, only everyone else around her was. Despite her going behind the Nazis’ backs, having a husband accused of being in the Resistance, smuggling and stealing goods etc etc. Only those around her seemed to suffer, which I understand is the point of the game, but it did make her character feel a bit superior or untouchable. The game has a rather unique visual style and reminded me of water colour art, but very muddy and muted.  Admittedly, I do not personally like this style, but I did get used to it. Whilst it may not be my personal preference, its dreary, undetailed strokes do mimic the lifeless, controlled setting well.Perhaps the most lacking department of the game is the audio, particularly void of voice actors. Understandably, I can only assume there may not have been a big enough budget for them, but they would prove beneficial to help express the many emotions prevalent throughout the game, particularly the turmoil and passion that comes with war. Even so, reading the speech bubbles did suffice perfectly fine, but does not help the story reach its full potential. I did have to restart twice after finishing conversations as I was unable to move. Approx. 8 hours. No Yes – plenty of choices to make that influence the game as a whole.Gerda: A Flame in Winter is an interesting narrative game that lets players shape the outcome of events whilst simultaneously providing an educational experience and insight into WW2. The unique choice of Denmark as the setting and Gerda as the protagonist help make it both a unique and memorable adventure. The choices are harsh, and the entire game is melancholic, but its rational decision-based gameplay kept me engrossed from beginning to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda: A Flame in Winter is the story of how normal lives are turned upside down when German forces occupy a small Danish village in World War II.I loved everything about this game. This will mostly appeal to narrative lovers, with its branching dialogues and storylines, determined by your actions and decisions. I was hooked from the start and got heavily absorbed into events. I can’t remember playing a game that was so spellbinding as this. It plants you firmly into the action, and makes you agonize over decisions. The tension in some of the scenes is almost unbearable. A good sign that this game had me captivated. There are numerous routes the story can take depending on your decisions. Almost every decision or action you take will have a consequence down the road, and it almost always comes as a surprise. The plot is brilliant at throwing curve balls at you, so you have to backtrack and use your skills to get out of tricky situations. It is incredibly uncomfortable and uneasy at times. The game is based on real life events, and the inclusion of historical facts, in the form of documents you collected or events you witnessed, was a lovely touch. As the story develops, you will naturally start forming opinions on people, and events and decisions steer you down certain plotlines. Siding with one faction may put you at a disadvantage with other groups, and keeping a middle ground may not influence the right people when they are needed the most. There seems to be a lot of scope for playing the game in different ways. For example, in one playthrough you could take the side of the Occupation and The German characters, whilst in another you could favour the resistance. There are places you won’t have visited or situations you wouldn’t have seen in your first playthrough, as events are based on schedules and times of the day, and sometimes they clash, forcing you to make tough decisions on who to see, and potentially who to save.These decisions, sometimes going against your own belief system, help to keep yourself or your loved ones alive. The narrative was excellent at showing how normal people had become heroes in times of troubles, and the most unexpected people stood up for their beliefs. It was quite an emotional and harrowing story.There are ten main characters for you to interact with, and they can live or die by your decisions. These characters you will get to know quite well so losing any of them is quite upsetting. There are peripheral characters too, but they’re just included to bulk out situations and make events look more believable, but they can still have a profound effect on affairs.Dialogues between characters are always very brief, but yet the game manages to lay down thick layers of lore and relations between them. There is a diary which details more information about each character but the gameplay is forever moving you around different places, introducing you to new characters, and potential story plots, that you feel you are juggling many decisions at once. Conversations are over quite quickly, but they happen often and build layers of intrigue. There is not much to read at all, and these meetings are interspersed with Gerda’s own thoughts and what I would call interactive sequences to keep things fresh and varied. There is no voice acting apart from Gerda’s diary entries, which are narrated beautifully, but emotion is still injected into proceedings by the use of text, with punctuation marks, fonts and colours giving a surprisingly effective outcome. Animation also plays a part, with characters shaking fists to show anger, or playing out action scenes with dramatic effect.  The game looks incredibly beautiful and quite unique. Somehow, it fitted into the subject matter perfectly and added a somber ambience. The graphics are actually based on Nordic impressionist paintings and look stunning. The title tune sounds very poignant and memorable, and sound effects are cleverly used to enhance tension and drama when required.Playing as Gerda in a third person view, you walk around scenes interacting with objects marked for examination, or talk to characters. Certain objects can be stored in you inventory and used when the situation arises, but you have the choice whether to take these or not. Sometimes, taking objects will aid you later, but they may also hinder someone else. There is no way of knowing for sure. Gerda often has a choice to make, up to four different answers are displayed, and she must choose one to continue the conversation. Some of these choices may be greyed out because they require an item, like feeding someone or providing a bribe, and others may cost you attribute points. You have three attributes in wit, compassion, and insight. There are also four factions namely The Occupation, The Germans, The Danish, and The Resistance.Choosing certain dialogue options may appear to favour one of these factions, and if it does a point is placed against that group. If you upset a faction, a negative mark will be issued. It is not always clear which answers will be negative or positive and I was surprised a few times how my answers were interpreted. I think a hint as to what your answers will achieve would have been helpful. This is also the case for every character you meet, and they can have a positive or negative score depending on how you interact with them. This can have a huge affect on how they treat you. During the day, and often due to the previous day’s events, you are presented with choices on which destination you would like to visit. A brief synopsis gives you a clue as to what to expect. Some are time sensitive, and some clash, so you may need to make choices as to where to go and who to see, influencing faction scores. These points build up over time, and can be spent on one of the dialogue choices, if the situation presents itself. For example, you might want to try and influence a German officer and it might use up a wit point to do so. Your attributes sometimes combine in very dangerous situations and all three attributes are needed. If this is the case you can roll your dice to try and influence events. Depending on your scores for each attribute, you are presented with a likely outcome, between easy and challenging. If this throw goes wrong, it can have devastating consequences, and plenty of times I lost on an easy outcome! It is a real shame that you can’t see the dice rolls or know what score you need to beat. A green or red text box is the only indication.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Well, it is a far smaller and more focused game compared to Life is Strange. It is a an adventure taking place during WW II. Not in one of the war's hotspots, but in a small rural village of a country that, although occupied, was mostly spared from the extreme violence of the warfare. It takes place in Denmark, in the southern part which has German minority that actually welcomed the German army in 1940. The Danish majority was not so happy, but for the most part the situation in Denmark during the war was calm. After a short prologue, the game starts in February 1945. German troops are retreating on all fronts, it is just a matter of time until WW II will be over. The story is based on historical events and gives you a lot of information about the situation in the region during the time. I found this quite interesting, but I am a WW II buff and love to read about what happened in smaller countries during the war. During those final months of German occupation, Gerda, a nurse from the German speaking minority, but married to a Danish man, will soon have to take sides in a conflict tearing the country apart. Whom to support, whom to trust?The game is an adventure, but not with many puzzles. You mostly have to explore the sourroundings and make a lot of (multiple-choice) decisions. You will also soon have to decide where to go, because you cannot be at all possible locations before the day is over. Based on your decisions, other people or factions (Danish and German population, German Army and Danish Resistance) will react to you. It is more of a social simulation than a classic point and click adventure, although there are quite a few rather tense (mini-)chapters with life or death situations and hard decisions to make.Gerda writes a diary but it also contains information about her relationship with the factions, her mental energy and her possessions. It also contains info about the characters of the game, some clues and some historical facts. The game is saved only when you enter the map, which happens only when you complete a (short) chapter. The visuals are amazing, I haven't seen such a watercolor graphic style for a long time. Conversations are not voiced, with the exception of Gerda's enties in her diary.A historic adventure taking place in Denmark during the last months of German occupation in WW II.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: This is mostly a choices matter type of visual novel. It's broken up by clicking on hotspots, which are unmissable in a scene (apart from one instance.) These hotspots are usually on people giving the visual novel part of the game but sometimes it's just info or items. You can move and interact by only using keyboard but you can also play this purely as a point n click with no keyboard. There is a voiceover but only at the end of day summary.There is a journal with all the important info. Under your character there is a list of what you have in your inventory. But there isn't really an interactive inventory, these items are only used by choices given to you in conversation. So gameplay is very simple, it's impossible for you to get lost, not know what to click on, or even what to do (click on Gerda for your current objective which is usually just to speak someone in the scene.) This game is all about the story. The 'big picture' story is mostly told through information you pick up and is in your journal. I love when games do that, as you get to pick how much or what you want to read about. Here it's a small village in occupied Denmark at the end of the war. The 'smaller' story with its characters I thought were excellently done - each type (dirty officer out for himself, smuggler, resistance etc) I thought was well done and no one was made to be squeaky clean. I felt it was probably true to life, grimy dirt on everyone just different type of dirt and how much was the only difference.There are a couple of 'chance encounters' but the main events in the game won't change, you are at them but how you are viewing them does, depending on your choices of who you have built up trust with. You do this through choosing normal dialogue with them, using up your 'compassion/wit/insight' points or a chance dialogue which can be either easy or hard to get depending on the factors shown.There is no manual save but at the end of the game your 'days' of the playthrough you've just done are now open to replay from that day onward. It's one of those game that achievements help show you everything that you've missed, could've played like. I read in a review you can play as anything you want. This isn't true (thankfully) you can try and be a 'good citizen' to get your occupation points up but you can't play as someone in the occupation or even a friend.  but that's it and all your dialogue choices will show this. You have 'relation' points with factions and this will vary greatly depending on your choices - annoy everyone, go it alone, try using the dirty officer (which doesn't affect your points with the occupation) or the resistance.This is my game of the year, purely how they've done the characters as well as the story. Although this had some warnings, due to the type of graphics I recommend this for you to play with young teenagers. The bad language is only a smattering and not really bad, the violence isn't gratuitous at all and it's more a wiki style of info in your journal. I would have loved something like this game when I was at school.See link for more info regarding achievements (sort of mini guide for those that want to work it out). The following is for main game achs, do need the paid DLC to 100% game.Regarding the type of story (not the point system) if you like this you should check out Attentat 1942, Svobada 1945 Liberation. So if you want a great story, lite on the gameplay or just want more information about the history of Denmark at this time but done in a fun way then I recommend this. Nominated for game of the year.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Hell of a game. The absolute example of a ''Choice Matters'' genre.It's depressing, fulfilling, gruesome and everything you can imagine. A beautiful and hard WWII tale that throws ''Humanity" in your face, when all the thematic "2nd World War" games just rely on the Tanks / Nazis / Military factors. 'Gerda: A Flame in Winter' reminds you what should really matters the most: the people living this era, perfectly displayed wither the ''Danes / Germans / Occupation / Resistance" relationship meters.And the best of all: your choices. really. matters. And there are no easy ones. This game is going to test your empathy on several levels. With a good dose of 're-playability' as well, to check how everything would end up taking other paths.10/10. Period. One of the Best Narrative-Adventures game I've ever played. F***ing round of applause.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about ordinary people trying to navigate the German occupation of Denmark in late World War 2. Everyone knows that the war is winding down, but the situation is still tense and characters can die.Other games claim that your choices matter. In this game, your choices are what the entire game is about. Your choices determine where the story goes and which characters will make it to the end.I found the game to be an incredibly tense experience that I became very invested in. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: You are going to like this game if you like any other story-oriented games such as Life is Strange or Oxenfree. It is a point-and-click adventure where choices really do matter whether someone lives or dies.It is also quite replayable since most of the time you can visit only about 1/2 to 2/3 locations that are available in each chapter which does make a difference in the long run.It is a shame it gets only a fraction of attention of the games mentioned since it definitely is as good as them.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Serious deep mature story about nazis occupation of ex-German territories in Denmark. Oppressor vs oppressed is not the same as saints vs sinners. Reality is more complex than this. Expect a lot of meaningful moral dilemmas and compelling drama, very good texts and multiple choice dialogues. I really appreciate this kind of production. Nevertheless we are far from the richness of AAA productions. Such beautiful story would deserve the best technical support and the biggest investment. But videogames are children of a lesser god. Still in 2023 the gaming industry prefer to identify itself with immature, childish mainstream titles where shooting, fighting, killing, violence, muscles, weapons, blood is what matters more, A waste of billions dollars, most of which invested in hammering marketing. On the contrary, great stories like this or Pentiment have to do with really low budgets and are still a niche. Still in 2023 mainstream gaming has very low cultural profile, promoting ignorance, violence, anti-social behavior. Puah!
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Anything Don't Nod really never disappoints. Gerda: A Flame in Winter isn't much of a game but more of a visual point and click novel where your choices really matter. The story is intriguing and I find the whole game educational as it has a lot of 1945 Denmark facts that I've never read before. Aside from the game is based on facts, the character's moral dilemmas and situations are on point that it makes it too hard to make any choices. The Nazis and Resistance is never just black and white and the game shows that well even tho it is a bit short. The art style is beautiful, Gerda's VA adds more feels to the game, and the dialogues aren't cringe. I have yet to play the dlc but im sure that'll be good too.As a fan of story heavy choices matter games, for me this game is just too good. Saved the one I care the most but at what cost? My Gerda is a compassionate nurse the whole game. A good friend, a decent citizen but also a rebel, smugglers' assistant, playing on both sides of the fence. Game lets you decide which faction you wanna side on and I mostly remained neutral, or a fake, as I only went through situations that will benefit Anders the most.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda: A Flame in Winter is a game with an incredible atmosphere. The story is really beautiful and catchy.Gerda will meet a lot of people and there are difficult choices to make. Sometimes you need to work together with the enemy or lie to reach something you want/need.After each episode you earn skill points: Compassion, Insight, wit. When earned enough points you could use one of those skills in a conversation.After each episode you return to a city map where you will see the place and description of the next episode. Sometimes there is only 1 episode, but sometimes there are multiple episodes where you need to choose between. But when chosen 1 episode the other choices will desappeare.The game will also make a save when you return to the city map.Also the music is appropriate with the atmosphere with the game. The game is also a good representation of the life in times of World War 2.Here is my gameplay video:

_childDocuments_.review: As a Dane this is really interesting and cool! Especially that old Danish songs were used throughout, even though some of them are sad. Jens Vejmand for instance, which played here, is about an old guy working in stone. He passed away in December working and the final verse is about how he, despite working hard in stone his whole life, never got a gravestone of his own. the attention to detail is really cool!
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot fathom why the developers figured it was a good idea to make you unable to save. If I want to explore different options at the end of a scene I have to replay it from the start every time? Add random rolls to the mix and you have a recipe for tedium. It really shouldn't take 5 minutes to see the difference between option 1 and 2 for a game like this. Surely if you want to play some kind of "iron man" style people can limit themselves without the developer forcing a tedious play style on everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game.  It's not the best time for humanity during these times but it's great that we have this game to remind us that this was once a reality.  I worked at a retirement home where most of my residents are holocaust survivors, some were even experimented under Dr. Mengele.  They would ask us to ask them questions about it so they can tell their stories over and over, how they were separated after getting dropped off in camps and how they would never see their families again.  It's a devastating and horrific experience to have as little kids.  Great game DONTNOD, appreciate this.Update with some spoilers ahead: After numerous plays, I finally was able to get Esther & Sophia to safety, Anders, Liv and Peter are all safe, Wolfgang is safe, Harald was alive, Dieter was alive.  Everyone with me is safe! Good lord, took a while.  There is a little glitch, I couldn't at all give Sophia a cough drop when I have one in the backpack this whole time smh!
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: It is very difficult to give a negative review to this game. In no way did I regret the money and time I spent. The whole inspiration and execution is very original. The gameplay keeps the interest and does not become tedious at any point, the music fits the theme, the graphics are sufficient (it is not a game that needs something better on this aspect). Maybe the autosave feature is a problem, but if it wasn't there I'd be tempted to keep trying different options all the time, which, from what I understand, is not in the spirit of the game. Dlc, Liva’s Story, is very good, and recommended to be played before the main part.The only reason for the negative review is the scenario. I have read several books about WW2 and especially about the living conditions in the occupied countries of the Balkans and the East. There the occupation was particularly inhumane and brutal. I know that in some countries, like Denmark, where the people were considered more fraternal or at least not “subhuman”, the occupation was milder, there was no widespread starvation, indiscriminate executions, rationing, destruction of communities, etc.In the game now, even within this above context of a "soft" occupation, the actions and behavior of both the occupying forces and the occupied population seem out of place. The resistance appears as an act of whim or ideology and not as an act of necessity. Also, the methods and actions of the occupying forces are not the ones that sufficiently explain or cause the acts of resistance. In general, the whole scene of the conflict seems pretentious, set up, forced, and not as a natural continuation of a situation of oppression, lack of freedom and need for survival. Nowhere does the survival of anyone who does not come into direct conflict with the occupying forces appears to be threatened.My grandmother, who lived through the occupation in a Greek town, conveyed to me, with her description in a few minutes, the terror they felt when they heard the German boots from kilometers away, before they even saw the soldiers, while in the game you visit the Gestapo headquarters without the game successfully managing to create a sense of fear, desperation, terror, or even particular anxiety. The whole scenario would seem more natural or realistic if it were about living in a country with a local, somewhat authoritarian regime, rather than an occupied country.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: I really appreciated the story in Gerda. The writers were very sensitive to the perspectives of war and the consequences that left everyone a victim in the end, even survivors. It is a beautiful, well-developed game with a unique game-playing technique with multiple endings. I really love what the developers did here. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game. It teaches a lot about life in southern Denmark in the last months of the second world war, from a very personal perspective, unlike history books. There are a lot of tough choices to make and there's not always a perfect outcome. But that makes it a somewhat realistic experience. What the people in this game experience happened to real people in one way or another. Games like this are capable of providing an empathetic understanding of the past and its people instead of merely stating facts.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: This game masterfully merges RPG mechanics with a compelling story of Danish resistance against the Nazis. It adeptly explores the blurred lines of loyalty and the harrowing choices made for survival. Remarkably, it humanizes each character, offering insight into the complexities of even the most morally ambiguous individuals. It's a raw portrayal of a tumultuous period, presenting all characters in a nuanced light, and captures the era's tension in a way that continues to fascinate. I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda is a great game where choices you make actually matter and impact the story. It’s very refreshing that it offers a completely different perspective to a ‘war game’. And the way Mental Energies work is great gameplay element that I have never seen before, which I would love to see in more games.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Not as simple as it looks at first glance, the charming and deliberately "muddy" graphics hide a rather complex series of choices which may or may not be meaningful to the story in the long run. Every choice seems to change relations and what item interactions/context menus become available later. It's also very nice to be able to play a historical game in the proper language.I would love to play more and certainly will, but at the moment the game still needs some post-launch optimization as it makes the fans of my old GTX980 spin up like it's trying to run Forza Horizon 5 with ray tracing on.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, despite anything I may mention below. I have not played the DLCThe art style is suitable, the music is beautiful and perfectly matched, the voice acting is excellent, and the writing is evocative.There is some minor gamification with the journal, where you end up picking what you think is the most mechanically sound option, but that's a minor nit-pick. Gamification in a game? It is an extremely taxing game. Not in a negative connotation, but in five hours of gameplay, I broke for the night and had three or four breaks for 10 - 30 minutes just to clear my head. If you want to go in blind, I'm going to discuss some non-spoiler things now.The game understands the complexity of the situation. People judge you based on what they think you are, not what your intent is. They judge based sometimes on your actions, but other times they hate you because you're not a "true German/Dane." It places you in a bad situation you had no knowledge of, and you play the hand you're dealt. And it makes it easy to be complicit. I'm not talking the wider situation, but each person has a little flag, denoting their affiliation. As the devs mention elsewhere, this is not a political tag, it's a language and culture indicator. You, the player, can make decisions based on that flag, if you'd like. Only Gerda has a flag consisting of both icons. It's up to the player if these flags mean something, nothing, or everything.People are, generally, written as real people. They have motivations, make both good and bad decisions, and generally believe no matter how hard their decision, it's in the right.I've seen enough of this kind of thing to truly appreciate what the devs did for a nuanced story.And I'm happy my decisions were rewarded. The events unfolded in a way I could at least tolerate, if not be happy with. (not a dev problem, simply the scenario was so bad, there was no "happy ending"). Given the prompting about repeated playthroughs, it appears it could've gone to much worse places had I made different choices. Anything too radical, I'll tag:There's something ominous about the end telling me the violence didn't escalate. And when I was confronted with  at the end of the game and I had to decide  well, that's a decision I'm glad I won't have to defend.There's certainly a story being told, and any decisions just change the events on that line, but the consequences of actions, and the limited resources available, make for a fascinating game. I very strongly recommend it, so long as you can take a step back and not assume there is a "good" and "bad" answer to every question. Gerda is doing the best she can with a bad situation, and making the trip with her can help us all be a little more compassionate to the desperate.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a bit of a shame that story-driven adventure titles, and I mean the ones that are almost purely story driven like Telltale titles or Life is Strange, became almost a separate thing, very disconnected from the “classic” adventure games, even the ones that were also heavily story-driven. But at least we’re seeing more of them trying to experiment with the boundaries of the genre more. Gerda: A Flame in Winter is one such title – it’s not about puzzles and free exploration of locations or even really inventory usage in a classic sense, instead it’s all about choices and consequences and the storytelling. But it has a few very cool tricks to achieve its goals, even if it ends up being somewhat rough around the edges.The game is set during the events of World War 2, specifically the final months of it (apart from the prologue-tutorial) and it presents an interesting perspective on that time being set in a small Danish village of Tinglev that has both German and Danish population and how people, who weren’t directly affected by the war, still felt the effects it had on the economy, the community and the relationships between people. I was afraid, at times, that it would try to ponder to blindly humanist ideals about “divided people who just need to understand one another” (a sentiment that is especially toxic now with the genocidal Russian invasion of Ukraine happening). But luckily, the title doesn’t try to infantilize the players and just leaves tough questions lingering, letting the players answer them for themselves most of the time. And I have to say – the storytelling here is solid and really well done.As for the gameplay, despite looking and working like a point and click adventure, this title really works far closer to the already mentioned Telltale-style games. Once a scene or an episode (or whatever you’d want to call this) starts, you’re locked in the location, that is usually rather small, and there are some optional actions that you can do, and some obligatory ones that will move the story forward one way or the other, often locking you in a series of events where you must make choices. And then it’s time for another such scene to happen and your previous actions will affect what happens in those next scenes.However, there’s a twist to this structure. While the overarching story is linear, the way you go through it depends on your choice. The main game’s events happen over the course of several days and they all follow a similar structure. You’re presented with the map of the town and several locations you can visit. Every visit moves the time of the day forward. And while early in the day you usually have all of the options available to you with no issues, as you get to evening, whatever events you have not visited yet become mutually exclusive – you can only select one of the remaining ones, the rest are no longer possible. And then the day ends with some big event, that is usually preceded with a random encounter event, and the situation and options available to you in that last event are, of course, dependent on what you did throughout this day and the previous days.What’s more, there are many stats and variables – essentially resources – that are constantly used for choice making. Your actions may increase or decrease the trust people have for you, what reputation you have with certain groups of people. Which affects what you can or cannot select in dialogues or the chance of some rolls being successful or not. And yes – rolls. Sometimes the choice you have to or can make is a random chance roll and whenever it succeeds or fails, the story moves forward, but your resources are affected. Items you can find are also used in this system so you can, essentially, bribe people or trade something, or reveal information to someone only if you have it. And after each scene you also have a little summary that let’s you pick an option, each of which give you one point in yet another system of stats that can be used in dialogues. It’s a really cool system which works to create tough decision making a lot of the time.At times these random elements and forced story events do get in the way. Whenever you get a chance roll that says that the check is Easy and it has several additional checks that you all successfully pass you just expect it to work. But it’s a random chance, so it can fail. And in real life you expect a random roll to miss, but in a story-driven title, where you put far more emphasis on your choice, rather than some random element, when that happens it feels unfair and frustrating. And of course, while the resource managing is a really cool idea, the developers couldn’t cover all bases, so only preset elements are accepted in specific dialogues, even when it makes sense that an item, that you might be carrying from the start of the game, would fit too. It’s extremely rare that this happens, the developers really tried to polish this experience, but it can happen.The biggest issues, though, are on the technical side. I’ve had the game softlock once, as it got stuck in a dialogue state with no way to do anything. The way animations play out and how pathfinding works can look and feel extremely rough. Not helped by how incredibly limited the field of view always is. The game saves only when you return to the map screen, so if you need to exit in the middle of a 20-minute segment (especially if it’s the last segment of the day and you had a random encounter before it) – you’ll have to replay all of it from before you entered the location.Overall, though, this is a wonderful title. It looks nice, the music is fitting, the story and characters are well-done and choices feel meaningful and genuinely tough. The resource management for problem solving is a really cool idea, even if it doesn’t always feel right. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re interested in a story-driven adventure title. And I do hope that more adventure games experiment with using such resource-based systems to enhance the choices and problem solving.

_childDocuments_.review: Point and click adventure with some very interesting mechanics making every resource and choice feel important. The story feels real and hits home because it is about what regular people experience during a war. The divide between neighbors with different cultural backgrounds is painful and interesting. The game feels insightful, beautiful and painful all at once.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game during winter season with the snow falling outside your window with a cup of coffee by your side only added more immersion to this already highly immersive RPG!   As others have already pointed out, Gerda does feel somewhat invincible at times; like no matter what comes along she'll always be out of harms way. It also would've been a big plus if you got to know the characters on a bit more deeper level. This, however, was greatly improved in the DLC!   Other than that, Gerda: A Flame in Winter is a thrilling and thought provoking experience that every RPG lover out there should get their hands on immediately! The very definition of a hidden gem. Hatts off to the devs!9.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: To call this a visual novel wouldn't be close to doing it justice. Sure it had strong elements of choose your own, with multiple paths, different results and endings - but on a MASSIVE SCALE! The characters were amazing, all with their own stories, paths, relationships and motives. There were tons of locations. The war element was interesting, historically informative and at times heavy. But the story here, the characters, the gameplay and the feeling of free choice made this game pretty darn incredible. I like all kinds of games, from adventure, to P&C, to hidden object, to shooters, etc and I still thoroughly enjoyed this game very very much. The authors obviously put ABSOLUTELY TONS of love, creativity, research and probably thousands of hours into the conversations, interactions, relationships between multiple characters and how it all plays out as the story goes along, at certain branch paths and ultimately the end results. You truly get different experiences upon subsequent play-throughs. Bravo. Can't wait to play this again soon. LOTS of love went into this gem of a game/story/novel (could be a movie) and it shows!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda: A Flame in Winter offers a deeply sensitive exploration of the Holocaust, set in a small town in Denmark during the Second World War. It delves into the harrowing realities of Jewish persecution and the horrors of the SS with a level of sensitivity and nuance rarely seen in the gaming world.As players navigate the streets of the town, they are confronted with the stark realities of life under Nazi occupation. From the arbitrary violence of the SS to the clandestine efforts of resistance fighters, every interaction serves as a stark reminder of the brutality and inhumanity of war. And yet, amidst the darkness, there are moments of courage, compassion, and hope that shine like beacons in the night.One of the most striking aspects of Gerda is its portrayal of moral choices in the face of unimaginable adversity. Players are forced to grapple with questions of right and wrong, courage and cowardice, as they navigate the treacherous landscape of wartime Denmark. And it's these moral dilemmas that lie at the heart of the game, challenging players to confront their own values and beliefs in the most difficult of circumstances.But what sets Gerda apart is its unwavering commitment to sensitivity and respect in its portrayal of such sensitive subject matter. From the meticulously researched historical details to the nuanced portrayal of characters and events, every aspect of the game feels carefully crafted and thoughtfully executed. And it's this attention to detail that allows Gerda to explore themes of persecution and resilience with the depth and complexity they deserve.As someone deeply moved by the experience of playing Gerda, I can attest to the profound emotional impact of the game. It's a testament to the resilience of the human spirit, the power of compassion, and the enduring nature of hope in the face of unspeakable darkness. And while the journey may be difficult, it's ultimately a journey worth taking, offering players a chance to bear witness to history and honor the memory of those who lived and died in the shadow of tyranny.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! No trailer or description can do justice to the complex decisions I had to make playing Gerda. It felt like going on a joruney though sth familiar and yet so new. So many angles to consider.The art is so pretty and I was impressed by how fluid the gameplay expetience was. _childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Gerda: A Flame in Winter is a narrative-driven RPG-lite game that’s about the life of a small Danish town that’s living through World War 2 through the eyes and actions of the protagonist, Gerda.As World War 2 that’s waged on most parts of the world begins to wane, the small town of Tinglev starts to feel the grasps of the Third Reich begin to strengthen on them. The small and initially invisible resistant group begin to show its head and start to act as a way to rebel and hoping to take back their village from the Third Reich.Things aren’t as simple as that as the village of Tinglev’s minorities welcomed the German forces due to the fact that they were once part of the German Empire till shortly after the end of World War I. Resulting in the village having two sides, one supporting Germany, the other supporting Denmark. And in turn leaves Gerda torn into two, as her father is German and her Mother, Danish. Balancing Gerda’s opinions of the different factions and characters and their opinions of Gerda is not an easy task. Siding one side will no doubt open the pathway and choices for situations to help them when circumstance warrants it, however it’ll be at the risk of blocking off other possible routes that could help Gerda if she were to try to side the other end. Gaining the trust of the people you encounter is paramount whether or not the trade off means sacrificing your humanity, as Hell is full of good meanings, so let your deeds decide that heaven will be full of good actions. At the end of major scenes, Gerda will write in her journal on how a situation happened and from there the player can decide on what she learns and picks up on from that situation which will grant her a point for Compassion or Wit or Insight which she can spend in certain dialogue situations which will assist her given she has enough opinions on a faction/person that can sway it to her benefit.In terms of the gameplay aspect to GAFIW, it solely relies on player choices in dictating where the story goes, be it in dialogues or making the choice on where to be in. This is where the difficult nature of the game comes from. Rarely does a choice have a clear cut answer as there’s a level of risk and reward on your decisions and trade offs. You can interact with some items in the environment which would give you an item which you can use for certain dialogue options or scenes.The aesthetics of GAFIW is like a well made watercolor painting being animated and coming to life, in terms of characters and the environments excluding the assets. Colours have that soft look to it with pleasing and gradual tones. The highlights of the style is emphasized in some scenes such as sunsets or at the start of a scene.The main strength of GAFIW is the story. Rarely do we get the chance to learn about countries that are affected by the World Wars outside of the usual general coverage, especially if you aren’t from the area. And with tackling such a heavy topic in human history, it is hard not to be affected by it. The manner GAFIW tells the story of how life was like back then together with its story telling of the game simply immerse you into the world as though you are going through it.If you are a fan of history or want to know more about it or are into narrative driven games then Gerda A Flame in Winter would certainly be one you shouldn’t miss. A highlight for a narrative driven story for 2022, that is a flame that reminds us of the dark period in our history that won’t go out no matter how long time has passed until we’ve learnt from it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: The plot is well written but the subject matter is hard so it's not for everyone. The voice acting is quite good but it only appears as sporadic voice over. Getting any good endings are pretty hard which only makes the difficult subject matter more stressful. The art style is like a water colour painting which some might find lacking detail but I liked it. The music is nice as well. Overall, I recommend it, just don't go into it expecting warm and happy feelings by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with an incredibly heart-wrenching story. One of those games where you really have to think about what you're saying instead of just choosing an option to advance the plot.There are some who can criticize that you can't easily save-scum in this game, but I think it justifies a more conscious play style. There is finality to your decisions and the game wants you to feel the weight of your actions. In order to really take in this game, you should be ready to do that. It makes the highs higher and lows hit harder than if it allowed you to save when you felt a hard decision.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really solid game with a unique take on WWII. The choices feel meaningful, and I found myself thinking about the consequences of each decision. The story is engaging, and the way it blends narrative with strategy kept me hooked. It’s not a fast-paced action game, but if you like slower, more thoughtful experiences, this one’s definitely worth a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: A well told story, good acting, and beautiful art. While there is black and white, the right path ahead is never obvious and in that respect the game feels educational but in the best possible sense.  Gerda is a bold attempt at merging world history with local  sensibilities and grounding  - and it succeeds. We need more games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game! So much so that as soon as I finished playing it I restarted it.It's a game for narrative novels and you can complete it in 6-8 hours (but there's multiple replay value). It's interactive in the sense that it's a multiple choice puzzle, those choices have consequences running throughout the game. It's impossible to be everywhere, help everyone and keep everyone happy.A lot of it's down to luck with chance roles and points. It's really interactive, a captivating story and such a cozy game. Imo the best thing since life is strange albeit a much smaller game.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: I can only say omg this is a great game! Historically, the mood and everything is very authentic, every decision you make feels wrong, but that's exactly how you imagine it in war. An addictive adventure that you can play multiple times as there are different perspectives depending on the choices you make.The soundtrack is very simple but very appropriate and atmospheric. Historically, the game also has various facts built in for reference, which you can even look at and read offset with a photo each. All in all, very important work that is done here, since there are also fewer and fewer contemporary witnesses who can tell of the horrors of war.Thank you for this game - Absolute recommendation not only for people who have historical interest.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. I was completly immersed in the story and its impeccable writing. I also recommend picking up the dlc "The Liva's Story". It provides you with a deeper understanding and appreciation of Liva - the leader of a resistance group, while also including interactions with Anders expanding on his reasons for joining the cause. If you are new to the game, play the DLC first.This game will force you to make tough choices where there is not always a right answer. There are references (historically accurate) to the Second World War in Denmark, which is woven into a compelling story with relatable characters and scences busting with suspense and tension.The writing is my favorite part of the game. It made the characters, their interactions and the story believable and engaging. Even when branching out into different dialogue options and choices, it always seemed to make sense. There was never a point where I went "huh, would she/he really say this?" or "that came out of nowhere!". I was invested and immersed in the story from the burnt porridge to the action-packed finish.In conclusion:The most gripping stories are about regular people doing what they can to protect the ones they love and fight for what they believe in. Sometimes you can't do both, and choosing to do one jeopardises the other; this dilemma is captured to a tee in Gerda - A Flame In Winter.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: A short, engaging experience w light RPG-Elements where your decisions impact the story in a meaningful way, leading (at least in my playthrough) to a satisfying conclusion. The small-town setting is beautifully realized with a lot of care for detail.I recommend it, even though I sometimes felt worried by the "Both sides" rhetoric the game applies when dealing with literal N*zis commiting atrocities against civilians but the main-character wags the finger at armed resistance-fighters for being too extreme in their response...The way my story ended didn't pull too many punches though, which made me feel more positive about the story overall in hindsight.
_childDocuments_.name: Gerda: A Flame in Winter

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the story that was told here and look forward to exploring other choices and paths not taken. I am glad they recommended this game.
