short_description: Using the power of virtual reality, Song in the Smoke puts your survival directly in your own hands. Enter this dangerous world outside of time, where you must craft weapons, make clothes, build fires, and brew healing elixirs to steel yourself against its vicious predators.

_childDocuments_.review: Saw this game had no review so decided to just try it out. Wow, great little survival game! You have to craft your own stuff, so creating arrows, knives, spears etc. You can hunt animals, eat berries, upgrade your clothing, gear and more. Only played an hour but it seems like a fun game! It can also definitely be a bit scary, so keep that in mindI had most settings on high, with AA turned off, and the game looks great and ran pretty much smoothly (the tutorial had some very minor stutters when explaining things). During the actual gameplay, there was pretty much no stuttering at all. Ran on an index @80hz, 100%SS, RTX 2080ti, i9 9900k.edit: Okay this game is genuinely scary at times, but so good!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without a doubt, the most fun VR survival game I have played. When I saw the trailer, I thought it was a simple survival game that looked awesome but the more I play the more intricacies I discover. I keep finding new things that change how I interact with the world.Do yourself a favor and grab this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the smoke is an unpolished gem. There are some glitches and fallbacks - I can't deny that. That said, however, this game is a one-of-a-kind. You will not find a survival crafting game of this caliber in VR. They exist, sure; but all are unfinished with game-breaking glitches.My first playthrough was on easy difficulty. It took about 15 hours to complete. Future playthroughs on higher difficulties may introduce more mechanics that I have not yet seen, either way, I'm aching to get back in and try a harder difficulty; perhaps even unlock those pesky hidden achievements.Song in the Smoke offers something no VR game has truly given me to date -- a survival crafting experience with a story to squeeze your heart and titillating game play that chaulk up to a phenomal VR experience. There are bugs. The occasional wood flying across the screen due to some strange collision mechanics, or items on the ground disappearing after you've slept off a night. None of these bugs are game breaking though and the game play and story make up for the cons of this game 10 fold. It's worth the price tag.It's not hard to see why UploadVR nominated SitS for PCVR game of the year.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a few hours to get the hang of some of the finer game dynamics (best to do a quick check on youtube), but once you have the hang it is fantastic!It is suited to people who like exploring levels and taking the time to level up their gear - you could rush just to the objectives but i imagine it would quickly become very hard to kill anything you meet if you did!I find it lots of fun hunting around for good items and exploring the world anyway - so may as well take your time and get your money's worth from the game is my view!Great game.Tips it would be good to know from the start i have found:As you are searching around always look out for items with 3 teeth (stars) - they make significantly better weapons and armour so always try to have everything 2 or 3 teeth gradeFires - you need to build big fires to last the night while you sleep (or things will get you after the first couple of levels) - the trick to building fires is watching the circle that goes around the side of the fire pit - start your fire with bark and 3-4 small sticks - you will notice the circle goes around and goes past a point labelled M - this means the fire is big enough to take medium sticks, once you throw a few of those on it gets to a level to take large logs and a few of those should max out the ring and get you a good night's sleep! Also the extra long sticks can be grabbed at each end and snapped into a small and medium stick.You can also collect arrows you shoot that miss their target so definitely easier to go looking for them than making new ones all the timeLast one - you can leave liquids in your mortar and pestle so if you make a health potion and dont need to drink the whole thing then sip it and just keep the rest in the vessel for laterHave fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: While it isn't without its flaws, Song in the Smoke is criminally under reported and underappreciated. At the time of writing, there are only 23 other Steam reviews. Oomph. The development team deserves better. This game is a well produced, functioning full length product with plenty of features. For these reasons along, it is a positive rating and well worth trying. Everything that follows may sounds negative, but Song in the Smoke is still an enjoyable VR experience of which there are far too few. Fighting the animals is a ton of fun. Being chased by the dinosaur sized animals is a ton of fun. Taking in the large forests in the twilight light, firefiles scattering through the air, is a ton of fun. If you liked the art of S&S, you should be at home here. It runs fantastic on a 4790k and 2080 Super. It has some of the largest environments that I've encountered in a VR game. Boneworks had giant street and building interiors, but they were mostly empty rectangular spaces. Subnautica has large waterways but, when I tried it, they were plagued with assets popping in once close enough to the player. Here, there are giant forest areas with many nooks and crannies to explore. The colors are vibrant and lush. Ok, it isn't super detailed, but I assume, like S&S, the developers were balancing style with VR performance. Both S&S and Song in the Smoke are masterclasses in the ethos of doing more with less. It felt like a mix of Turok and open world Zelda. There are lite, lite story elements. Personally a weak point. Dropped immediately into a caveman doing his thing. Your mission is collecting hidden orbs per zone and then fighting progressively harder animals. After you collect orbs, you're treated to a brief cinematic. There are also hidden power ups. The biggest flaw is its clunkiness, which is likely the result of being ported from the PSVR. Inventory management is more smooth and intuitive in PCVR first games like HL:A or Walking Dead: S&S. For example, there are two quick slots for inventory, but they're seemingly bound to specifically the left or right hand versus shoulder location. While you'll access them by reaching over your shoulder, if you reach your right hand over your left shoulder, you'll pull out the right hand item. It can be confusing until you realize what is happening. There are other nagging object and inventory interactions. New instructions are floating tool tips that can be easily missed, such as if you are in active pursuit of an animal. Between tracking down the orbs, you'll have to survive. Frankly, I liked S&S's or the Forest's survival balance better. There is no stamina meter. Instead, you'll progressively become hungrier and sleepier. The survival elements were on the tip of being overbearing. For example, you basically need to eat a couple pieces of meat or fruit each day. However, most of the animals only drop one piece of meat per kill, and the act of harvesting the single meat usually takes half the day cycle (it fast forwards). Unlike S&S or the Forest, where I could stockpile plenty of food materials during the day and then prepare meals to last several days, I basically just kept my head above water each day. It ended up being faster to skip harvesting meat and grab berries or mushrooms on the fly. Physically crafting each item, like knives, arrows and campfires, is really neat. Still, like the one to one meat experience noted above, crafting is one to one also. While quick, you will be hand crafting each and every arrow you use (unless you take time to find the hidden caches). After building your 10th campfire (which has to be rebuilt at least once or twice in the night), the experience starts to drift from game to chore. Plus, items tend to wear out really fast. The starting bow broke on the second or third hunting trip. Each item has an independent quality level, but you would be forgiven for overlooking that detail while scavenging. There is simply a lot of upkeep.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: The initial impressions of the game are very favorable. The crafting is satisfying and discovering new crafting recipes while exploring is great. You search for the required three items while trying to gear up and getting pumped to face your strongest foe yet.Then the game keeps repeating the same thing. Location after location  you're doing the same thing. Create camp, hunt local wildlife and gather local resources to upgrade yourself to next tier. Move to next area and repeat. Creating a storage sack is often very important but each storage is it's own thing. You're always starting with stuff on your back when moving between areas and all your previous work becomes moot. Having a Resident Evil style universal storage sack would be incredibly welcome and cut back on the repetitive tedium of the game.The last areas are very disappointing. Boss of the second to last area is nothing but a walking target, offering no resistance.  Last area is very arduous and frustrating.You need to feed yourself, keep warm and for some reason keep away the dark. Hunger is great and easy to handle. Staying warm doesn't seem to come into play until closer to the end of the game which feels like a missed opportunity. Cold snaps could have been a great thing.Keeping away the dark... it's not about the darkness. A magical floating goat that people usually call Wendigo will haunt you at night. It causes massive damage, clips through walls and can't be fought off without light. Game wants you to explore at night for upgrades but the Wendigo actively encourages you to hug your bonfire at night.I would recommend not building a bonfire at all but to simply have a torch in your inventory at all times. When the menace wakes you up at night, simply smack your torch against the wall to light it and it will go away. You have to do this twice a night to keep him away but you will save a lot of time fetching firewood each day.Repetitive and stretched out nature of the gameplay combined with the awful Wendigo mechanic is the reason why I'm giving this negative review.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game so far, gives off a Monster Hunter/Valheim vibe. The best VR survival I've played to date. All the systems/mechanics have some depth and feel meaningful, the creatures so far are varied and unique. The crafting feels very "VR" and less clicking buttons to make things appear, without being tedious. I find myself truly immersed, trying to plan out tomorrow's hunt/forage while I stack the night's campfire. I've only made it to the second area but can definitely recommend at this time.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like in the beginning the way bow and club activation works (pressing left or right triggers, instead of grabbing the bow from behind the shoulder etc) and teleporting instead of jumping. But I got used to it the longer I played, so it wasn't a problem. Overall I really enjoyed the whole playthrough (I played the hardest difficulty). Some mechanics are not explained in written form, so you have to be aware of visual hints, which I liked, though I didn't pay enough attention sometimes and learned about stuff from videos. The overall feeling of loneliness and adverse world was fantastic. Gameplay loop of traveling into new territory and finding optimal camp sites and exploring the land for hunting places and materials was very satisfying. Especially the feeling of visually remembering and getting to know the place and creating your own paths etc, stuff that I am longing for in todays gaming industry where you are guided by gps from point to point and dont really see the world. The progression felt meaningful, because it wasn't just the stats of equipment. I was forced to try different approaches to my daily survival and learn, which led to becoming better at hunting, traversing the land, foraging etc. Fun game!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a bit less than 17 hours on a single play through.  I started on hard and I was dying too quick while still learning controls and mechanics of the game play.  Restarting on regular difficulty it was a breeze difficulty wise.  There is only the main story to play and it is an excellent experience, but hardly any replay value.  It wasn't spectacular enough to play through on the hardest difficultly, though I probably should have switched to hard after the the first stage/learning how to play.Quite an underrated game by review count.  There were also a few unpleasant bugs.  I have a KatWalk and had to re-calibrate often.  I am not sure if the treadmill was at fault and couldn't pinpoint what exactly caused it.  It often had something to do with holding something in each hand.  There was also a bug that caused my bow to disappear twice.  It was in hand and I was putting a new bowstring on it... and gone.  Poof.  Not in inventory quick spot. Not on the ground.  Nothing.  Just had to reload a save to get it back.The troubles were worth it and I recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the Smoke is an excellent game, and well priced for $30.It may soon list here that I've refunded the game. That is because I'm counting pennies and decided I can't justify spending the money right now. My situation is anomalous (compared to most PCVR users). You should buy it for $30. I very literally only drink tap water and never ever buy prepared meals, so I'm allowed to say that!!! I thoroughly enjoyed my first 1.5 hours with the game, even despite some controller binding issues with the G2 (this is a solved issue - it's expected these will be fixed in a patch soon, but also I've made a public binding for other G2 users that fixes the problem, so just select my public binding if the patch hasn't come yet).The game looks beautiful on the G2. It runs well. The crafting was engaging, the world was immersive, and felt like a world I wanted to spend more time with and learn more about.I only got a small abstract introduction to the story. So I can't comment much about what I feel about the story.The devs have been adding patches regularly since the game released on PSVR a couple months ago.Song in the Smoke seems like a polished, immersive, lengthy & replayable (from everything I've heard), interesting adventure survival story game made for VR. It got some stellar reviews on PSVR and it seems to me this is for good reason.I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I'm playing a different game than everyone else.  I really want to like it but the core game play is absolutely awful.  It is way too hard to aim the bow which I guess makes it more realistic.  That'd be fine if the resources to make arrows was easier to come by.  The hunting is awful.  Even after watching one of the developers tutorial videos I still have no idea what I'm doing wrong.  I just wasted the last 4 hours alone trying to finish the terrible hunting tutorial. (my steam playtime is off because it launches better from the oculus app).  The one time I did manage to finish it I was not able to save before dying.  That was after hunting the phantom deer for 2 hours.  My second attempt ended up in me hitting the phantom deer with countless arrows but ultimately dying form starvation because there is not enough food to forage and the hunting is awful.Part of the fun of these games is figuring out some of the mechanics on you own but tutorials are necessary for core game play mechanics.  I don't know if my game is glitching or what but "hints" pop up at the weirdest times and are confusing because they have nothing to do with what I'm doing or was information I could have used hours ago. They also only seem to pop up when I'm crouching ie in the middle of something.The controls are usually fine and actually fun for the crafting but they are terrible in combat.  It took me a very long time to figure out that you can equip items to RT and LT but that just causes me to whip out a club when I'm trying to nock an arrow.I rage quit earlier and then watched some of their tutorial videos.  Definitely watch those since the game does such an awful job at explain the actual game (seriously, how in the F are you supposed to know that there is a campfire "gauge" around it?).  I thought I'd enjoy it more but ended up rage quitting again.  Even knowing how to play more didn't make the game any more enjoyable because the hunting experience is so bad.  I hope they patch the game because I really liked it up until the hunting part. I can't see myself wasting any more time with it in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE BEST representation of the early VR Survival genera! Crafting is intuitive, making good use of motion controls to keep immersion high. Status effects such as cold, tired, hungry or bleeding, are shown subtly as a few floating HUD icons like ice-crystals, sleepy-eyes, or blood-drops. The fear can get pretty real as there are many dangers and encounters to avoid or conquer. The upgrades feel useful and rewarding by covering areas like larger-packs and higher armor/weapon stats. Keeping all your "meters happy" includes managing hunger, fatigue, temperature, and light-sources. Item management includes having enough firewood or light, with deadly consequences if neglected. Campfire system is unique that it requires a "pyramid" mix of timber using sticks, medium-Sticks, and logs.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Fun exploration, survival and combat. The crafting is well-done.Gorgeous environments with a nice art style.Not really an open world, but rather a series of medium sized to large levels.Runs great on minimum system requirements.My only gripe would be the inventory management, but hey, it's a survival game after all!"The ultimate caveman simulator" pretty much sums it up accurately.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: All around great VR survival game: cool setting and atmosphere, good looking stylized visuals, smooth difficulty curve and addictive gameplay loop. The only weak parts are awkward melee and teleportation climbing, but even that is tolerable.In my opinion, it is one of the best games that came out in the last 2 years.You play as a lone hunter in beautiful prehistoric environments that get more a more hostile as you progress. Stylized visuals look almost as good as Saints and Sinners, and later levels have those breathtaking vantage points where you can see almost whole map from high above. Forest sounds and realistic lighting with pitch black nights create thick atmosphere of wild nature and sometimes primal horror.All interactions are designed for VR with intuitive item crafting and building. Gameplay loop is addictive, you constantly have something to do as you hunt and gather to get better equipment or explore the land to progress in the story. Song in the Smoke never leaves survival phase for base building like many similar titles do. You are a hunter, not an industrial builder: food will always be scarce and nights - dangerous if you do not prepare enough wood for bonfire before dusk.Archery is deliberately slow: bowstring draw speed is limited, stopping you from becoming an arrow minigun like you usually do in VR archery titles:) And there is huge difference in damage between hitting a heart and anything else, further encouraging accurate shots. Melee is weightless and not very enjoyable, but it's usually only used to finish wounded animal with 1-2 hits to the head or block enemy charge.The campaign is quite long for VR and will take about 10-20 hours to finish depending on chosen difficulty and your playstyle.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an underrated gem. You are a cave-person / native trying to survive and level up your equipment as you face increasingly dangerous animals in the prehistoric wild. It's exciting (& creepy at night), challenging (with a good difficulty ramp), uses VR mechanics (vs. simply being a survival port), great sounds (crank it up), and has a unique art style. I hope more serious players give it a chance as it is completely worth the journey. I'm probably 1/3 the way in at 9hrs. The survival aspects of the game have not been too consuming/distracting thus far. For me, hunting and exploring during the day are the most fun, and crafting / surviving are the means to that end. The game has no words (great) and the few dreams/hallucinations serve as hints. I am thoroughly enjoying the well-designed maps and heart-pumping moments.Areas for improvement: the grabbing/placement is imperfect and in key moments can feel like I am bumbling around for a key item. Example: In the day I use the bow and club, but at night, I find myself clamoring into the inventory to pull out a torch. I discovered couple rendering errors with objects hovering high in the air. Hearing gripes about auto-save and would generally agree that if you get back safe to a fire, the game should not require you to manually go save (immersion breaking).A gripe with my fellow Steam community - this game is well reviewed and popular on PSVR and Oculus (500+ positive reviews), yet has very few reviews (and I assume purchases) on Steam. Why? From reviews/chatter it feels like the bar is much higher here (and I can partly see why - better equipment, other platforms are lower res, often much younger...), but seriously this game deserves much more love...spread the good word!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the Smoke is a full fledged, open world survival game that guides you further and furhter through various open maps.I find it strange and funny that this game is so low radar here on steam. You really wanna feel like grown up Mowgli without his pack to protect him? You really wanna feel like a caveman, 10000 bc surrounded by predators that rival you?You really wanna feel like a prey animal that, through bow and club, rises above the food chain?Then this game will give you exactly all of the above.There are not many games that can draq you outside of your comfort zone while being in your own room at the same time.The mechanics get intuitive quick, the graphics are good on the valve index and i enjoy sometimes not enjoying this ride, especially when night is drawing near starting at the thrid map onwards.A really good survival game, in VR, the best there currently is IMO.Its August 2022 now and there is, in my humble opinion, still no other VR-Prehistoric-Survival Game to rival this raw gem deeply hidden underneath the layer of sameish VR-Titels. Its kinda sad that this does not shine more.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: What a cool game! I don't play alot of survival games, but this one was alot of fun. I really liked the mechanics and the story. Really got a Breath of the Wild vibe from the graphics which isn't a bad thing. I wish you could use your hands for climbing and/or grabbing items instead of trigger press, but that hardly takes away from the fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review:
Song in the Smoke immerses players in a mysterious prehistoric world full of strange beasts where they must craft, forage, hunt, and fight to survive. Featuring art by famed illustrator Katsuya Terada (The Legend of Zelda, Blood: The Last Vampire, The Monkey King), Song in the Smoke has atmosphere and adventure in spades, with fantastical creatures and stylized scenery that pack an eerie, otherworldly punch.

Awoken by a three-headed crow at the edge of the woods, players will travel through eight stages including forests, valleys, and frozen terrain. You'll battle the elements and strange beasts alike, crafting tools, weapons, medicine, and more to stay alive. In true VR fashion, you'll identify threats by sound as well as sight. Intuitive controls mean you can line up the perfect shot with your bow, but you may not be the only one stalking its prey, so keep your wits about you.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

ZERO • Season Pass - 3 Packs including Dragon Ball SUPER: SUPER HERO and Dragon Ball DAIMA content that contains more than 20 playable characters • Season Pass Bonus - Summon Shenron and 3 Days Early Access to the 3 DLC Packs DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO Ultimate Edition The Ultimate Edition includes: • DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO • Season Pass - 3 Packs including Dragon Ball SUPER: SUPER HERO and Dragon Ball DAIMA content • Season Pass Bonus - Summon Shenron and 3 Days Early Access to 3 DLC Packs • Ultimate Upgrade Pack • Ultimate Edition Bonus - Summon Super Shenron About the Game DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO takes the legendary gameplay of the Budokai Tenkaichi series and raises it to whole new levels. Become a super warrior and experience the earth-shaking, limit-breaking power of Dragon Ball battles! Unleash the strength of over 180 fighters from Dragon Ball Z, Dragon Ball Super, Dragon Ball GT, and selected Dragon Ball movies, all in the base game! Each character comes with their own signature abilities, transformations, and techniques. Make the destructive power of the strongest fighters ever to appear in Dragon Ball yours! Engage in heart-pounding, high-speed 3D battles that stay true to the anime and video game series, with breathtaking visuals and authentic combat moves like beam clashes, rush attacks, movements too quick for the eyes to see, and planet-razing ultimate attacks. Challenge other players online to test your skills, or sit down with friends offline to hone your skills exclusively in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber! Fight your way to become a champion across various tournament modes and victory conditions. Conquer the action-packed battles from the beloved original story, or discover and unlock new encounters for your favorite Z-Fighters and more. Relive your favorite moments from the series through cutscenes you can experience from the perspectives of eight characters! Recreate your favorite battles from throughout the Dragon Ball story, or set up your dream story battle with your favorite characters! Share your creations with other fans and experience the battles brought to life by imaginations around the world. *In addition to this edition, Deluxe Edition and Ultimate Edition are also available. Please be careful not to purchase the same content twice.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Xenoverse. I loved Xenoverse 2, but im sorry guys, the controls and difficulty are not the same.I like the difficulty personally, but i can see how this is not a fun experience for more "casual" players. Be prepared to sometimes win battles without a sweat and other times the CPU not allowing you to breathe or think for even a second.A big negative (that should honestly be explained before you buy the game) is that you HAVE to run the game above 30 fps, due to the frames being connected to the game logic. There are a few fixes for this but youll have to do your own research. Im also not a fan of there being 4 different ways to counter all attacks and you being able to do them practically whenever, granted I still need a little more training so this could change. In terms of training, the game tells you next to nothing. Youll have to figure it out on your own or in the training room.Besides those things, the game feels great. Ive enjoyed the "what-if" scenarios, the combat, the difficulty, the graphics, and amount of characters put into the game. It feels like there was effort put in, which is refreshing for gaming these days. Overall id put this game at about the same level as Xenoverse 2. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Long ago, Dragon Ball Z aired on TV in my country and me and my brother were hooked, we would play together and act out battles of our own. Then, Dragon Ball Z Budokai came out and we were hooked, ever since then, we played every part of that series, and then moved to Tenkaichi as it came out and we played that through together, playing 3 -a lot-. Then life sent us in separate directions and we don't even talk anymore... But yeah, so the series is very important to me considering the role it played in my life for the duration it was in it. I believe that Sparking Zero is a faithful sequel to that series and that it is a great game worth anyone's time, despite what the online community may be like, despite how unbalanced or unfun it may be to others. The graphics are improved, we get to see characters that never existed before, though some old timers didn't make it- mostly everyone DID make it. The only negative is the Communication Error business, which bothers me because I cannot play online, I can only play with my friends through off-line splitscreen.. so that is a big negative... But as it is, otherwise? Definitely recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stellar. For someone who's only experience with DB fighting games was Xenoverse 1 and 2 this was a well welcomed surprise. It's engaging and honestly a very stunning and cinematic game, albeit with a steep difficulty curve.The amount of content in this game is crazy, and I've only touched the surface of things to find in the game, and I 100% recommend this for anyone. I've been having a grand time with the stories. Although an issue I have is the fact that scenes feel a little incompete, like Goku going super saiyan isn't it's unique  fully animated cutscene, but it's mostly nit picks.Character dialog interactions when starting fights is kinda limited? Unlike FighterZ or Xenoverse, it's far more limited in what is said.There's not too many stages either, there's enough but looking at Budokai and other games, it's quite limited.There's also the fact they gloss over entire parts of the story, like the Universe 6 tourney because they didn't want to make chars for it, or the fact that Piccolo's story ends so... drastically. He basically goes Cell Sega and then NEVER again, and his story just straight up ends.Overall, this game is probably a 9.3/10. 100% recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: The core fundamental foundation of the game is very solid, but a plethora of individually small issues ends up resulting in a death by a thousand cuts for me with regards to playing this game.In its current state I honestly don't recommend this game. Its foundation is there and it has a lot of potential to be absolutely excellent, but as it stands it has a few notable issues that detract from the overall experience to the point of complete frustration. The biggest issues to me personally, at least at the time of writing are super counters, vanish wars, and the overall lack of quality of life in the menus. There are other smaller issues I have with the game as well, which I'll bring up over time. First and foremost, the main menu screen for the game is gorgeous and filled with so much charm and detail it's hard not to love it, at first glance. But when you actually play the game, scrolling through the options on the menu mwill result in noticeable lag which makes the actual experience of going through the menus more tedious. Ontop of that, there are various points in the selection of modes where, when you back out, you will be taken directly back to the main menu as opposed to 1 step back in the overall process, the biggest example being shop and customization.For some reason, despite using a controller, my mouse is still "active". This has, on numerous occasions, caused my menuing inputs to be incorrect because my mouse just happened to be hovering over a certain selection, which results in a misinput I was never intending.Character selection also sucks. It's bland and boring, especially compared to previous games in the series.Custom battle was legitimately the one feature I was looking forward to most. As a kid I would constantly just do random battles and make up storylines in my head, and now that it's an actual feature in the game directly?! That's awesome. However, the experience of making battles is sullied by the overall lack of QOL within the menu itself. I understand why the game won't let you just write your own dialogue, but digging through the over 5k options available is tedious at best, frustrating at worst. All we need is a search function to find phrases and words that we want to use.Now onto the actual combat side of the game. It has a very strong baseline foundation that makes playing the game feel very fun and pretty rewarding but there are a number of things I personally take issue with that detract from it being the best experience it could be. For reference, I'm playing on standard controls.I'll start with the lack of customization in the controls settings. Despite playing on standard, I have swapped around my inputs via in game menus a little. However, the amount of freedom you have with changing and remapping your controls is very limiting, to the point of confusion. I personally never would, but if someone wanted to bind their basic attack button to say R1, why can't they?Despite not being in my initial paragraph, my absolute biggest issue is with the current state of inputs. They just don't work. There will be various times where I will say vanish a beam attack right next to my opponent, and then even when I'm no longer pressing the guard button, I'll grab. But since I'm not *quite* close enough to grab, it whiffs and I take a punish, despite said grab not being my intention in any way. Also, the moments when I'm doing a combo and I want to finish with a super attack, but instead of doing said super, my character either vanish follow ups or spams ki blasts or something. The last big thing in this regard is either transforming or swapping characters, for some reason when I bring up the menu half of the time I either can't transform or swap characters out despite the menu being open. Or the menu will open but kinda close shortly after, without doing what I want anyways?I don't know what the fixes to these problems could potentially be but as it stands it makes the actual combat of the game, the explicitly best part, into a grueling grog that is just very tedious to work around with. I've never had these issues with the previous tenkaichi games, so I'm not sure why they're an issue now.Now onto super counters and vanish wars: I'll preface this by saying I like that, as mechanics, they exist. I like that they're in the game. Just not in the current state they're in. Super counters are a very strong "get off me" tool that is useable in so many situations it's crazy, however the fact it costs no resources and isn't even that strict of an input is crazy. It's a fundamental defensive tool that is definitely necessary but they either need to make the input more difficult like in BT3 or add some sort of resource cost to it.Vanish wars on the other hand are just really boring. At a high enough level of play, EVERYONE is consistent enough with the vanish inputs that it boils down to just "more ki wins". And when both players are like 4+ bars of ki, it takes so long to finish said vanish war. There have been a ton of suggestions online as to how to fix it, be it either just costing more with each subsequent vanish, clashing after 4 or so vanishes or making them faster, thus harder inputs, with each subsequent vanish. I don't know which would be the ideal fix, but personally I think something needs to be done because as it stands vanish wars just completely ruin the flow and pacing of the fights in such a negative and boring way.There are of course other common complaints people have about Sparking Zero's combat, such as instant spark, unblockable ults, afterimage strike, senzu bean (which did get nerfed), giant characters, etc etc etc. But honestly, while they are frustrating, there is counter play to basically everything here. Frustrating to deal with, for sure, but you can work around them. But, saying that, I understand if some people dont want to work around them. I don't expect ranked to be the most balanced game mode in the world, on the contrary I expect it to be full of shenanigans and cheese. But I do think there is a distinct lack of non ranked quick play for online matchmaking. It can be fun, and even very rewarding, to beat up the meta characters in the game with someone like Babidi, but it can get really grueling after a while. Having a casual option where more people are more likely to explore more of the cast would go a long way to making the online experience more enjoyable, especially long term.Playing offline is an option of course, and it can be fun, but after reaching a certain point in skill level (which I will admit isn't even that high of a skill level), the CPUs even on the hardest difficult aren't really that challenging, at least not challenging enough to justify just spamming cpu matches over and over with no other goal in mind.Offline also has its own fair share of issues. I already mentioned my issues with custom battles. Story mode is fine, and while I can take it or leave it at the presentation, some of the choices made are just baffling. Some characters story modes are just super short when they really shouldn't be, and while some of the what ifs present are good, I feel they also dropped the ball on them to some extent.Honestly we need more offline game modes. Let us expand the roster size of tournaments to 16 or 32 people, give us 100 man battle where the fights get harder and harder with each subsequent fight. Give us more developer made custom battles. Just something *more*, because the offline options are leaving me wanting.Ultimately, this is an amazing game with a lot to offer and acts as a good love letter to fans, myself included. I do genuinely like this game, but all of the things mentioned made the game a very frustrating experience to enjoy. So many small things that add up to a death by a thousand cuts situation. Each of these problems individually aren't that bad, but when stacked ontop of one another it becomes a very frustrating experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to play PVP this game will be right up your alley.The graphics are amazing compared to where DBZ games started from. I was super excited for this game however, it did not meet my expectations. I was hoping for content akin to Tenkaichi 2. However, this pales in comparison. Key pieces of the story in episode gameplay were turned into slide shows.And I know these scenes can be seen by watching the anime. However, I would have preferred it in this format and graphics to see them again. How the ♥♥♥♥ can you turn Vegetas death in the Frieza saga into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slideshow. And then Goku turning super saiyan the first time is also a slide show. WTF.What gets my blood boiling is the fact that they animated some things but these pivotal moments turned into slideshows. Either do one or the other, otherwise it looks like you are cutting corners. And that's exactly why they chose the slide show format for certain scenes.Additionally, one key piece about Tenkaichi that I enjoyed was hunting for dragon balls. It made the replay value that much better. However, in this game you unlock all of the dragon balls by completing certain challenges and you get to make your wishes. They did keep the rewards for wishes somewhat the same.Long story short: this is a watered down experience compared to it's predecessors.Combat is great. This one focuses more on timing and other nuances to provide skill based combat.Like I said at the start if you are looking for combat/PVP this is right up your alley but I was hoping for a Tenkaichi experience beyond the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Sparking Zero is a fun dragon ball game overall, with fast engaging combat and some pretty faithful recreations of characters. There are a couple gripes I have though. THE STORY MODEA pretty standard story mode for this type of game but I found it kind of lacking and half baked, all of the show including big moments like SSJ are reduced to slideshows trying to rush through the plot as fast as possible. The only redeeming quality of the story is that there are a total of 8 characters to play as. There are also choices you can make along the way where you can change how certain events play out. _childDocuments_.review: Dragon Ball: Sparking! Zero is an exhilarating love letter to the franchise, blending explosive visuals with a colossal roster and chaotic, high-octane action that is both fun and strategically nuanced. While the campaign lacks depth and the limited map pool may disappoint, Sparking Zero’s true strength lies in its raw 3D arena-fighter appeal and its execution of it, firmly establishing it as a worthy successor to Budokai Tenkaichi 3. Sparking Zero condenses the DBZ storyline and beyond, focusing primarily on key moments from the perspectives of seven prominent characters. Each narrative unfolds through iconic battles and light character dialogues, intertwined with in-game stills and static interactions outside battle. Unfortunately, this is why the campaign falls short: it relies too much on superficial, static screenshots and brief exchanges to propel the story, failing to capture the depth and intensity each moment deserves. This leads to erratic pacing, iconic scenes come and go with little buildup or emotional payoff, making the story feel more like a checklist of fights throughout a slide-show presentation than an immersive journey with cinematic cutscenes befitting of DB.While additional What-If scenarios add unique twists and explore sick alternative outcomes, they still face the same issues as the campaign. Ultimately, the campaign does deliver thrilling battles and fresh takes on classic showdowns that fans of the series would love, but its shallow storytelling dilutes pivotal moments, leaving the experience feeling flat, especially for newcomers to the franchise. Dragon Ball: Sparking Zero delivers precisely what fans crave: a spectacular, high-speed, chaotic, but fun experience that builds upon the beloved formula of Budokai Tenkaichi 3. The combat may seem simplistic, but it is deceptively layered, with diverse and intricate mechanics. You can scrape by with button mashing in solo play, but fall into that trap, and you will be easy prey online. The combat revolves around high-octane action throughout the free-form stages, where every clash feels like a scene from the anime. Characters zip through the air, dash, and teleport across the massive stages. The combat flows seamlessly from incredibly satisfying melee combat to explosive ki blasts, letting you pivot between close-quarters brawls and long-range assaults instantly. But it's not just about offense; you have plenty of defensive options such as guards, vanishes, counters, bounce-back mechanics, and more to keep you engaged, demanding constant adaptation with a high-skill ceiling. The character roster has a staggering size of 182, from anime and movies to various transformations and eras, each with unique moves and abilities. As for stages, there are 12 different stages, each packed with destructible elements and vibrant, detailed visuals. The diverse roster keeps every match fresh and exciting and allows for experimentation with characters, strategies, and matchups. However, I can't help but wish for a few more maps.First off, the absence of crossplay is a disappointing oversight that could hinder the long-term viability of multiplayer on PC, compounded by the fact that there are no penalties for rage quitters. Multiplayer offers normal and ranked matches and four modes: singles, teams, DP battles, and tournaments with local play also available.DP battles are particularly notable and enjoyable due to its unique system that allocates 15 DP points to build your team. Stronger, canonically powerful characters cost more DP, while weaker ones require less. Due to the cap of DP, it fosters varied playstyles, challenging you to balance your squad without relying solely on powerhouses, effectively reflecting the series' established power levels without being overly unbalanced.With custom battles, you can create fully customized fights with options to change intros, voice lines, conditions, mid-cutscenes, and more, then share them with the world, which is a sick feature and helps alleviate skipped encounters. Sure, there are some limitations, and the UI can be a bit clunky, but having the ability to build showdowns beyond just pitting two characters against each other is incredibly fun and unique.As for character customization, in the shop, you can buy ability items that, when equipped, boost stats, and these carry over into multiplayer. Beyond that, you can grab costumes, music tracks, voice lines, and more. Outside of the shop, Shenron allows you to wish for additional stuff once you have all the dragon balls. The level of customization here is impressive, giving you tons of things to unlock.The visuals are nothing short of explosive, capturing the dynamic, high-energy feel of the anime. The character models and environments are polished and faithful to the source material. Each era of characters is beautifully represented and rendered with meticulous attention to detail, particularly in their animations, transformations, and ultimate moves. Each clash fills the screen with vibrant colors and dramatic effects, while crisp sound effects and a powerful OST heighten the impact of every ki blast and melee attack.

_childDocuments_.review: Return to the Budokai Tenkaichi series! Sparking Zero is a blast! 182 characters on launch with each character feeling fleshed out and different to one another. Even the giant characters are fun to play. This game has a variety of single player content: Episode Battle: Which is essentially story mode with a twist. Certain missions have alternate objectives which give you an alternate side path to go down which unlocks a new "what if" story. There are many different perspectives of the Dragon Ball iconic story to play from, it's not just Goku! There is Piccolo, Gohan, Vegeta and many more! World Tournament Mode:This is a staple in the classic BT games back in the day with having the option to disable flying and enable ring out. Its even more fun online with a whole tounrament flled with friends.Custom Battles:You get to create your own Dragon Ball episodes! Having an episode title screen that pops up at the beginning, being able to pick what characters say to each other. Being able to choose how the cutscenes plays out. Also, being able to change the actual battle with buffs or certain events that trigger in the midst of fighting. There's endless possibilities. (I do wish there was a search feature when choosing dialogue for your scene as there are over 5000 pieces of pre-made dialogue and it takes a long time to find the most fitting dialogue for your dream scene.) Another thing to add about Custom Battles is you can upload your completed battle to the network so that other people can play them and try and beat them. You can also download others too and you can search by difficulty or how popular a Custom Battle is and so on.Of course there is online mode that has Player and Ranked mode but what is brilliant about ranked team battles is there is a "DP" or  Destruction Point feature. Stronger characters have more DP, i.e. SS4 Gogeta, Beerus, Whis etc who have 10 DP. And the max DP for ranked is 15.  So, it's up to you if you want to have 5 man team of mid tier characters or 1 OP character with a mid tier tagging along. Its very interesting to see other peoples teams (Although every man and their dog runs fusion characters as they have more health and hit like a freight train being thrown at you by The Incredible Hulk)I cannot recommend this game enough if you are a Dragon Ball fan.Things i want in the future:Characters i would love to see as DLC in my opinion are:Fit Buu (DB Super)Chi-Chi (World Tournament and DB Super as optional skins)Bulma (Could be in some form of mech or have some form of weapon like her early DB days)Tambourine (OG DB)All the Shadow Dragons (DBGT)Towa (DB Xenoverse) and her many forms from DB HeroesEven Bonyu (DB Kakarot) as i really enjoy her design and how she fought. The list could go on and on...I hope they continue to support this game for years to come and continue to expand the roster, i want every niche, random, filler , unimportant character playable too. EVERYONE!Raid battles:Raid battles would be fun too. Similar to Xenoverse 2 where you have multiple people working together to take out one super powered enemy. Or, even like FighterZ raids too.More Episode Battles:I would like more from other perspectives as well as having the OG Dragon Ball as a story arc as well as GT.If you made it this far down my review then thank you so much for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Sparking:Zero offers a nostalgic, long-awaited reboot to the budokai tenkaichi series stocked with an impressive roster and fleshed out, vibrant landscapes. -This is a game I have been waiting for forever, it reminds me of battling with my brother on  BT:3 when we were kids. But sadly it is not the same, which is okay for the most part, and overall I love this game with all my heart and recommend it to anyone with interest in Dragon Ball or Budokai Tenkaichi type games. I still one specific personal gripe.The shift to a more competitive scene leaves a sour taste in my mouth and leaves room for unnecessary toxicity from the community, I personally play these games for fun and not an arbitrary ranking that takes away the games 'spark'. It would be a great ranked system if it wasn't the ONLY way to play the game seeing as the unranked portions of content do NOT have a "matchmaking" system like ranked does and instead uses 'rooms' akin to guilty gear or fighterz. This would be okay if the rooms weren't poorly designed. Allowing players over 8 slots for each room, which sounds amazing but the game pots for a 'king of the hill' method, knocking losers down to the final place in queue meaning that they need to wait potentially 30-50 minutes depending on game type to battle again. Again, this would be tolerable if not for the added effect of the games lack of activity within these rooms. Taking up to an hour just to find active players in unranked in every single mode. (Not to mention the ghost-town that is world tournament). This overall creates a dependence on the ranked portion of the game, as it is the only accessible content to me if I want to engage with the community. With that being said, and personal bias aside this doesn't have to be a bad thing. If you love ranked systems in games then this is a perfect game for you, I personally believe that ranked systems create a negative environment that serves to punish players for playing causing them to always need to be better than the next person. And yes, this is the essence of ranked systems and Gokus whole character inspiration. But this doesn't need to be your interpretation of the game as it is an incredible celebration of Dragon Balls lifespan and Akira Toriyamas (RIP) story. If you are a fan of Dragon Ball then this game is perfect, allowing you to re-create stories from your favourite dragon ball episodes in fast paced combat with stellar animation. Whilst allowing you to peer into alternate 'what-if' scenarios for the classic story. Overall, I recommend this game highly to anyone. I just went through the content too quick and do NOT enjoy the online portion in its current state.

Sure they wont use the funimation dub but other Bandai games let you add a library of custom mp3's into the game or replace existing tracks. Very poor show here and limits the ability to enjoy the sound track.- Combat!? Super weird in the sense your counters have to be nano second perfect to pull of, it takes the fun out of the game for me. I have no plans to ever play this online and will only ever play offline. Recreating cool moments owning characters are too hard to recreate.- Story. Yes we've seen it many times but weird things like key moments being very short cut scenes (Goku's SSJ transformation vs Freiza), slide show presentations of other story parts and no narrator talking at times, just having to read text are a let down.========Summary========A great DBZ game for fans with some faults but it is the best DBZ game since Legend of the Super Saiyan on the SNES. It gets a solid 8/10. I am interested to see what sort of DLC will come in the long term and if quality of life features will be added and issues fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is super fun and engaging. It manages to bring the intensity and "Anime" moments of Dragonball to your fingertips. That being said, I cannot shake the feeling of the Devs being very new to their Jobs. The game absolutely LOVES to waste your time for nothing. Starting with the main Menu. (Tested on a Gen 5 NVME SSD)Then in the Story Modes, loading into Character Selection, Loading into Level Selection, then, AGAIN, noticable delay between selecting the individual episodes, even those your selected char cannot currently play in (which is slightly circumvented by a quick select option, none the less) and then loading into the Cutscene. The cutscene then is only skippable after around 3-4 Seconds, which can feel like forever if you want to unlock a particularly hard alternative route and have to rewatch all that over and over because there is no quick retry button once you already lost the fight.Making your own Custom Battle is probably AS INFURIATING AS CAN BE. As everytime you want even as little as a Text box to appear you have to search the list MANUALLY for the Character Names, without search function. You can Filter the list for "Characters". I get why they chose to have it so you cannot input your own Text, but with all due respect. This is a bit much to ask for. It feels really amaturishly put together in a lot of places, made by people who never played a game or at least thought about why things are the way they are.All these things (of which there are many more examples to chose from) are no "total-joy-killers" for me personally, however, as much as I like this game, I have to admit, they do add up... And add up they shouldn't considering the AAAA price tag for this software. Which is something to keep in mind when you buy this game, hopefully this helps you make your decision, whether to buy now, on a key website or wait for a discount. I guess it's worth the wait though.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I want to go more in depth as to why I don't recommend this game.When I heard about Sparking Zero, I was hyped to finally play a modern version of many other's people childhoods. However, once it's release settled in, I've realized that this game isn't all it's hyped up to be. Rather, it feels like a half baked product that came out to thrive on the Dragon Ball hype.1. AnimationsThis was a problem I noticed when the Master and Disciple trailer dropped within Piccolo's sparking attack. When Piccolo does this mouth beam, you can see the momentum of the camera immediately switch from going down fast to going down slowly. This is what started to decrease my hype of the game, and the issue still persist within the final game. Within the majority of Super Attack animations, it feels as if your watching key frames transition from one place to another. This makes the game feel as if it's a 60 frames per seconds version of a storyboard animation.Not only that, but the Story Mode animation feels as if they were did body tracking with no clean up afterwards. Sometimes you can even notice when the motion tracking stops.  2. CostumesThe costumes in this game feel like they were only added to make the characters look different within the story mode and so they could say Original Dragon Ball got more content then Goku (Teen). Where's the Goku Black in Zamasu's outfit costume? What about Goku (Teen) in his blue suit. There are plenty of costumes that could've been added yet aren't for unknown reasons,Now these two points are okay. Had it only been these two reasons, I would still give this game a recommendation to play. However, the problem with this next issue is so astronomically high, it genuinely makes me wonder how $70 was considered to be a great price for the base game. 3. NetplayIf anyone has seen the dreaded error code 2E795EC5, then they know how much this completely tarnishes the game. As soon as the intro plays out within a ranked match, I immediately get disconnected. At least with Nintendo Online, I'm able to play the game. Is it because of the kernel writings wine detects? Is it because of the pipeline library? I wish I knew, but I unfortunately don't. This game had my expectations high when it was announced. However, I now feel as if the development should've taken at least one more year rather than being released in the rushed state it is in now.Original Review: As much as I love this game, the majority of enjoyment I'd get out of the game can't be experienced by me due to the kernel-level anti-cheat within the game. Due to the anti-cheat not being able to activate on Linux-based operating systems, I can't play online; therefore, I can't play with my friends. I wish the anti-cheat is either changed to not be kernel-related or for a Linux version of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately no, I do not recommend this game. I would like to, as I want the Sparking! (BT2&3) style of game to continue. However, there is just so much that immediately catches my attention as far as things that simply do not work or need to be fixed. Pros.  0 Graphics - The graphics are decent. Not great, but pretty okay. The effects especially are good but there is a lot of the time, too much going on. It starts to seem like a departure from the actual style of the show.  0 Music - The music is great! No complaints here, though I do wish there was some tracks leftover from BT2&3. 0 The character selection - There are a healthy selection of characters and outfits with hopefully more to come.  0 Not a huge departure from the BT series combat wise - If youre a BT veteran, you will be able to jump in with relative ease. Cons. Starting from the top.  X Menus - They're awful. Completely atrocious. Slow to navigate, uninteresting, basic and glitchy. This means the main menue, the pause menus, the sub menus, literally everything. Its all bad. Even online menus are awful.  X Episode mode - Episode mode is the excuse for a story. There is almost not a single thing I like about it, besides the music. The story is told in a series of snapshots. Still frames, then still 3d models, then the occasional painfully half effort cut scenes. The addition of a first person mode on occasion is kind of cool but it doesn't make up for the sheer lack of creativity and effort. In episode mode you follow a single character, not one contiguous story. Interesting idea but it ends up feeling like Goodwill Kakarot. They added a 'custom story' mode as well where you set up a simple scenario. Its interesting and works fine, but like most everything else pretty basic.      Part of the reason I say its a sad excuse for a story mode, is that there is no story. Yes they make some effort, but not nearly enough. The whole thing is a very pale and uninteresting recap. I'll explain what I mean.      Skipping fights. A. You only get to fight Raditz with Goku. Not Piccolo or Gohan. One person per opponent, per scenario. This is important as you (as stated above) follow a single character. Whereas you might argue this makes sense in this single context, there is no argument to be made for the sheer amount of times this happens. The whole thing feel rushed and last minute.      Skipping fights B. Literally just, not putting in the fights that should be there. No Tien vs Nappa. No Vegeta vs Dodaria. Vegeta only fights Zarbon once and he never transforms. The list goes on, and on, and on, and on.      Skipping fights C. Not so much skipping, as adding in fights that shouldn't be there. I don't mean the 'what if's which i will get to. Example being you have a full Piccolo vs Gohan fight, but no Gohan vs piccolo and no Piccolo vs Gaint Ape Gohan. For whatever reason, Ape Gohan is largely excluded from Episode mode entirely. The fights they chose to add, or keep out make almost no sense whatsoever. It feels like they were just trying to be different. Which in a long awaited Dragon Ball game with the best combat and maybe graphics to date is possibly the worst decision they could make.      The 'What if' scenarios described above are almost a plus. Some are genuinely interesting and you can tell a lot of work went into them. They would be a plus, if it wasn't so aggressively frustrating to get to them. Some have massive super fun and lengthy payoffs, and others are a waste of space. A bit of a grab bag where there's a few fresh turds in the mix.  X Episode mode gameplay - This must be its own category due to how awful it is. In other BT games, you had a lot of 'what if' missions. In Sparking! the bulk of them are told in episode mode. You access these by, in a VERY general sense, beating opponents the character you're playing as wouldn't normally. However the issue with this, is everything. It rarely works. At all. The game in a completely arbitrary and seemingly random fashion pick and choose when to allow you to complete a mission in the intended way.      One example. You can hit an opponent with an ultimate attack that should absolutely be overkill and KO them, and not only will it not do that, you can then go into sparking mode AGAIN and rush them with a 30 hit combo and they will still have 1 hp. Then the game proceeds to not give you the win and carry on as normal. While the opponent is invincible and fighting back and doing dialogue relative to the normal episode route. In short, the game runs out the timer for beating the opponent under a certain time, by making the opponent invincible thus not allowing you to get the special win condition. The game does this, CONSTANTLY. This has happened to me repeatedly. On the flip side, there are missions where to progress the actual story you have to run out the timer and it is actually easier to ko the opponent and you have to go to great lengths to NOT ko them.      The episode mode map, is also awful. Its slow, unintuitive, uninformative and confusing.     All in all, Episode mode seems like a last minute edition, rushed, incomplete and not well put together. I hope they add an actual story mode later or I may never recommend this game.  X Controls - There's a classic mode, and an updated standard mode. All good, except there's little customization beyond that and when you go online, as of right now it changes your controls to standard. Except it didn't even do that with me, it literally just changed how I did super attacks and had no idea what was happening. Which was as you might imagine a frustrating experience.  I don't see much excuse for this. It actually seems like no one tested the online features. Its lazy and annoying.  X The Combat - The combat is passable. They definitely dumbed it down and "balanced" it for online gameplay, but its 'okay'. The things that make a con as opposed to a pro (which is an issue for a fighting game if the fighting of the game counts as a Con) are the delay, and the targeting.      Delay. In Dark Souls it makes some sense that your inputs carry over and cant be cancelled. The whole game is built around careful planning and timing. Not a Dragon Ball game where everything is lightening fast and you have to adjust on the fly to new situations. Its difficult to quantify. The combat just feels delayed and floaty. Every other thing you do comes with a weird cool down where your character is just standing there or the game tries to play for you (even with all the auto assists turned off). Like the controls themselves are on ice. Feels bad man.      Targeting. I hope this doesn't need a lengthy explanation. When the GAME misses, that's an issue. When you're opponent isn't even moving and you teleport, dash or fire a projectile in the completely wrong direction, that's an issue. Holding down a directional input, or not, if you get random results as far as how often your character decides to aim in the right direction it gets old REALLY quick. Its nearly as bad as Xenoverse when it first came out. I DO mean, by the way, that characters will without any input from you, just turn and fire in the wrong direction and not hit the target that wasn't even moving in the first place.      My favorite example. Rush specials. When you activate them, you charge forward to make physical contact with your opponent to activate the attack. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottom.This game was fun for the first week, but I had to uninstall because people online prefer to cheese instead of just have fun. The game is deliberately unbalanced, which on paper, sounds fun - Until you understand that the playerbase can and will optimize the fun out of online play in favor of quick cheap wins with low skill ceiling fighters - And they have already done so at the time of this review. It goes to show how much gaming has changed since the last Budokai Tenkaichi, and how everyone has grown to prioritize virtual points over fun.You'd think that with a roster this enormous, there would be a huge diversity in the different fighters you'll be tackling. But if you buy this game with the intent to play online, you will go up against the same 12 characters, and your skilled plays will be punished with unskilled cheese (unblockable attacks, hyper armor, auto-dodge, stalling until the timer runs out and the person with the most health across their entire team wins by default).Oh, and I've never gotten a beam clash in Ranked. It's not meta to hit a beam attack with your own, apparently. It's fun to do with friends, it's extremely hype, but it's not optimal for quick and easy wins.  Okay, so some clarification since a lot of the comments on Reddit referring to this review gave me some ideas of what to talk about--1. The AI is a mixed bag. You'll either find it too easy or too hard, I can't comment on it because everyone's mileage does vary and so will yours.2. The online multiplayer is a direct influence on this review because I am reviewing the game based on my enjoyment of it, and everyone is obviously going to explore their PvP options at some point while playing this. I'm not gonna gloss over technical details like netcode or matchmaking, you can find other reviews for that from people with actual wrinkles in their brain.3. "Just play offline", no, I don't want to fight the CPU, I don't find that fun. That's like going to a movie theater by yourself, it's highkey miserable, don't do that.4. I am not harping on the "difficulty" of the game, and I am not having a "skill issue" - I am making commentary on whether or not I enjoyed it, and I simply did not enjoy Recoome popping Instant Sparking, dashing behind me, and triggering his unblockable AoE. Of course I could cheese it by popping Afterimage Strike or something, but frankly, I don't always run characters with auto-dodge skills, so 9 times out of 10 I have to eat poo.5. The dorks saying "online is easy", cool, I never asked though but I'm glad you're enjoying it, still kinda hate playing online.6. "You only play Ranked", no, I mentioned it exactly Once (1) in passing. Apparently some people think that because I wrote 'Ranked' exactly once, it's all I play, you're missing the point entirely, please focus on the bigger picture.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fighting game, it almost excels. You can do mixups, callouts and counters. You can land combos, and then your opponent gets a few options to counter. They can block high and low, they can sidestep out of the way, and if they correctly call you out, you get stunned and they can combo you. Or you can grab them, or jump behind them, all of these have callouts that can punish you. There's also a resource you can spend to stop their attacks via revenge counters, mid combo, but even that can be called out if you counter it properly.So yeah, great game... At least... almost.Sadly, there's a game mechanic that literally ruins the entire competitive aspect of the game. It's called a super counter. Hit up and punch within some frames of the attack landing, and you do a super counter. These counters can be done at any time, regardless of position, regardless of attack, and regardless of resources. It costs nothing and gives you a follow up attack. To simplify it: There is literally no such thing as a combo. You literally cannot combo off of anything, because anything can be super countered at any time. All those mechanics I mentioned before? The high low mix? The timing counters? The resource counters? None of it matters. You have a free, perfect counter to everything that can't be punished. It breaks your opponent's combo even if they catch you with a huge whiff punish.There's no such thing as a punish.No such thing as a combo. No such thing as a whiff. You can just super counter out of it.It makes bots extremely frustrating to fight, as well. All in all, the game would be absolutely amazing if not for a single mechanic. The cutscenes are horrible, too. If you're not a Dragon Ball fan, you won't enjoy this. I know not everything HAS to be competitive, but the super counter also makes the fights look less like cool dragon ball fights. This, at the very least, ruins it for me, personally.I'd recommend it, if you either like Dragon Ball, or if it cost less than $40. At $70, this game is not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Since this released 23 hours ago for early access I have played 21.4 hours of it and feel quite qualified to give a review. Here are my thoughts:The Excellent: The Graphics and the Animations. They are stellar and I don't think I could get tired of how good they look. Also huge props for all the "what-if" scenarios you can get. A couple that I wont spoil made me flip out with joy. Basically if you perform fights differently the world will give you a cool story on what would have happened if the fight ended that way.The OK: The combat for me is a mixed bag. I love the Sparkling mechanic and feel like its really easy to make yourself feel like a Z fighter and get off a bunch of really cool moves, but the blocking/evading to me could use work. It doesn't feel very responsive and honestly I think it may be bugged somewhat. If someones coming up to hit me I feel pretty helpless about the 20+ hit chain combo they could do to me without me being able to stop it. It feels 50/50 to me. Also the AI could be a little less perfect. Like if you dodge and blink around behind them they immediately blink behind you again almost 100% of the time.If I had one main wish it would be a team battle mode where you could team up with another fighter and take on a team.Well that's it. So do I regret my $110 dollar purchase? Absolutely not. If you're a Dragon Ball mega fan there's almost no way you'll regret this IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best Dragon Ball game I've ever played. It's not perfect, Vegeta's campaign is like 5 missions compared to everyone else who gets at least double that. The What If scenarios are awesome for fans of the story, but it's not likely to suck in anyone new with it's telling of the story. The cutscenes and dialogue are super simple, and are done better in other games, especially Kakarot. What this game does well is the actual fights. It's hard to compare this game to anything other than Sekiro. It's not as unforgiving as that game, but the timing windows for parries, super-counters, vanishes, perceptions, and other techniques are very tight. Each fight is very cinematic and sees you crashing through buildings and mountainsides in huge arenas. You can go incredibly fast and blitz almost anyone in seconds if you are really good at the game, but I found some of the episode battles to be pretty hard. The bonus battles have some of the most challenging content in any game I've ever played... Still can't touch Beerus in his bonus battle...There is a ton of offline content to grind through, but that is all basically training for the online PVP modes. These are so much fun it's stupid. The custom battles have essentially infinite permutations and there is always a ton of tournaments to hop into. The roster of characters is somewhere near 200, which is insane and I'm sure they will be adding DLC for whatever characters they missed. Highly, highly recommend for any fan of fighting games. Basically a must-have for any fan of DB.

_childDocuments_.review: Noticeable FPS drops, shader compilation stutter (pair that with egregious texture pop-in even on an NVME), a 60FPS lock (paired with slowdown below that), and no ultrawide support on a game that the publisher (Bandai Namco) is charging $100+ for. If you buy it on a key-site (like Humble or GreenManGaming) then it's around $90 but you forfeit your right to a refund.The only positive thing I can say about the PC version is that it has some graphics options (DBZK was barebones in comparison), PlayStation button prompts, and actually lets you play the single-player mode on Proton/Steam Deck.The game is seemingly using Unreal Engine's Fixed Framerate settings which is bad news because if you raise the framerate with INI tweaks, it will slow the actual game speed down if you can't hit that target, and even with the default settings if you can't hit 60FPS it will slow down. Just use delta time normally like every other Unreal Engine game does.Alt-tabbing is completely busted as it won't hide the window when you focus another one.The HDR display mode looks incredibly washed out and dull (Probably poorly configured defaults in Unreal Engine striking yet again). At least on Linux (through Gamescope) it is, on Windows, it looks fine. Some people report it looks washed out for them on Windows, so your mileage may vary.This also isn't using the Unreal Engine 5 version that has built in PSO caching (This uses 5.1.1 if the exif metadata is anything to go by). Turning down the graphics options does squat to help improve performance or to fix the physical slowdowns.The online multiplayer doesn't work on Proton and the Steam Deck due to the anti-cheat shenanigans.Played a few matches, the game itself is fun, but they learned nothing from the DBZ Kakarot PC port. _childDocuments_.review: The game DRAGON BALL: Sparking! Zero is a game that can trigger nostalgia for you if you have previously played the previous Budokai games. That's it.Characters locked- Now, I understand that in some games they had this as well, but, why even lock characters to this day? If I want to play as a character, I don't want to GRIND LEVELS just to be able to BUY them. Not unlock, but BUY with the in-game currency. It makes it more of a drag.Now, as the time of me writing this, I only have 22 hours of playtime, so my review can be slightly less intriguing than from someone that invested 100+ hours into the game. However, I only speak from the viewpoint of someone who works, and does not have enough time to play the game all day.Verdict: It's a good game for nostalgic reasons, however, it can burn itself out really quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation for this game is totally based on where you play it. Sparking Zero on console? Yes. 100%. If I was reviewing this for PS5, I would give it a solid 8/10. Sparking Zero on PC or Steam Deck? Absolutely not. 3/10For PC and Steam Deck, it runs, frankly, like absolute ass. Even with my 4080. Steam Deck can get an "okay" amount of performance, but is locked out of online play and has to run on the lowest settings, while barely hitting a solid 30fps. PC is still a mess. It's rough, regardless of how powerful your rig is. All that being said, the game itself is great. As a long time player, and fan of the Tenkaichi games, all the way from the very beginning, I adore this series and this game is the entry and BT4 we always wanted. The game gets almost everything right. My only criticisms is in the performance of the PC/Deck ports .... well that, and the elephant in the room. The online. This game, well this series rather, has always been a fun casual party game you play with friends. The meta and competitive side of it isn't by design of the developers, but by the community. I used to play BT3 competitively pretty hardcore back in the day, and even back then, the same issues of character spamming existed. SS4 Gogeta and MUI Goku are the new thing, and if you are playing ranked, expect to see a lot of sweaty players with zero technical skill spam the use of them. Good thing is, if you are good, and you understand the fundamentals of neutral, blocking, parrying, etc, you can send them home crying with pretty much any character. The only major problem with this, from the actual side of the functionality of the game is the lack of punishment for rage quitters. So, even if you end up flooring that SS4 Gogeta with Tien and Kid Gohan, just know that you still won't get that win if the player gets mad and rage quits. I hope Bandai fixes that soon. Overall, 8/10 - but on console. Skip the PC/Steam Deck port - Perfect Cell, Roshi, Teen Gohan, and Future Trunks are the secret meta best characters - go make SS4 Gogeta cry.

Another thing, which serves nothing but to annoy, is that if you do not manage to get the outcome you had wished for in a certain battle, the story simply continues, and there is no fast way for you to retry that particular stage. You have to menu around for at least 30 seconds through a story mission selection screen that feels stiff. And now for the absolute worst thing of them all. When playing BT3, all those years ago, that game made you feel powerful. The sounds were crisp and had a certain amount of weight behind them. The effects and animation undermined this. When I throw a Genkidama in this game, it feels like throwing a massive water balloon at someone. I feel absolutely nothing. The one thing we as kids loved about DBZ back then is missing from this game. And that is why I cannot recommend it. I will continue playing it as a means to play BT3 on PC, but boy am I disappointed after an initial "Honeymoon Phase".Wish they had just ported BT3, even with the same graphics.
