_childDocuments_.review: Rating: 4/5Laika: Aged Through Blood is a haunting and emotionally charged experience that delves deep into themes of sacrifice, survival, and the bonds that tie us together. Set in a dystopian world where humanity teeters on the brink of extinction, this narrative-driven adventure captivates players with its gripping story and atmospheric gameplay.- Compelling Narrative: Laika's story is a masterclass in emotional storytelling, drawing players into a world ravaged by despair and clinging to hope. The journey of Laika, a canine protagonist, as she navigates the horrors of a post-apocalyptic landscape is both heart-wrenching and poignant, leaving a lasting impact on players long after the credits roll.- Atmospheric World-Building: The game's atmospheric world is brought to life through stunning visuals and evocative sound design. From the desolate ruins of civilization to the eerie landscapes of a world reclaimed by nature, every environment feels rich with history and atmosphere, immersing players in its haunting beauty.- Emotional Depth: Laika: Aged Through Blood tackles weighty themes with a depth and maturity rarely seen in video games. Through its exploration of sacrifice, loyalty, and the enduring power of love, the game resonates on a deeply emotional level, prompting players to reflect on their own humanity and values.- Engaging Gameplay: While primarily a narrative-driven experience, Laika also offers engaging gameplay mechanics that complement its storytelling. From tense stealth sequences to heart-pounding action set-pieces, the game keeps players on their toes with a variety of gameplay challenges that enhance the overall experience.- Pacing Issues: Despite its many strengths, Laika occasionally suffers from pacing issues, with certain sections of the game feeling rushed or underdeveloped. This uneven pacing can detract from the immersion and impact of the story, leaving players wishing for more time to explore its richly realized world.- Limited Replay Value: Once players have experienced Laika's story to its conclusion, there is little incentive to revisit the game. While multiple endings and branching paths could have added replayability, the linear nature of the narrative limits its long-term appeal for some players.Overall, Laika: Aged Through Blood is a dark and gripping tale that stands as a testament to the power of storytelling in video games. With its compelling narrative, atmospheric world-building, and emotional depth, it's a must-play for fans of narrative-driven experiences and a worthy addition to any gamer's library.Check out my Laika walkthrough here:

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking about Laika: Aged Through Blood because that game gives me some Feelings, and I'm usually very positive when a game does that. And it's true: I am, in general, positive on the game--mastering the mechanics is fun and the story hits hard despite being so larger-than-life. If that's all you wanna know, yes it gets a hearty recommendation with a small asterisk. Asterisk to follow, Both the gameplay and the story leave  on the table. First, it's a metroidvania, but you only ever get two abilities that impact traversal. Second, the story always pokes at the deeper implications of Laika's actions, but never quite confronts them.Story: Laika *gets people killed*, both directly and indirectly. But we never actually see the impact it has on her, besides making her more angry. *Does* Laika experience guilt? Or does Laika experience no guilt? The story implies that Laika experiences no guilt, but absolves her anyway. This is an okay direction to go. The implication is that the bad guys are so bad they need to be mowed down by the hundreds, and guilt is a useless feeling to have.So why does the story try to inject nuance there? Or actually, inject nuance and do nothing with it? The best scene in the game is (BIGGER spoilers)  It's a POWERFUL scene. This is the sort of scene where you EXPLICITLY lay out whether there is guilt over the action, or no guilt over the action, because either one is  with implications.Story doesn't do anything further with it.Gameplay: Once you master the controls, which ARE inherently interesting and are a requirement to get to the halfway mark, there really isn't much else to it. There's one new traversal method near the end which practically obsoletes the first, PLUS if you figure out how to abuse it, trivializes the reload mechanic the game insists upon.In a way, "figuring out how to abuse the new mechanic" does add one more complexity, but it comes at the cost of removing several others. But also... I'm not sure the other complexities added enough for a 16-20 hour game. There's a lot of repetition. By the time I got to the final area I was a bit tired of it all. The game's combat escalates, but not by as much as you'd think. The most interesting setpieces were the boss encounters, and there's only like five? of those.There were also a handful of design issues. One of the enemies jumps out of a box, but their hitbox does not activate when they appear. It's sometime during the height of their jump. But also sometimes bullets just miss the hitboxes of enemies despite passing right through their sprite.Still, I think it's worthwhile. For what they had, it feels like the game is a bit overly long, and if they had a little more story or more gameplay it might have justified the length. But it doesn't run SO much longer that it hurts the overall Feelings.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to choose the best indie game this year, I can't recall so many wonderful original high quality ones on just 1 year! And yet, Laika still shines among all them with its super polished gameplay, wonderful storytelling, beautiful soundtrack so characteristic in Brainwash Gang's games, original boss fights.And the riding... I have the same feeling I got playing the first Spiderman, when it didn't really matter what was the fastest route or the next mission to achieve, just wondering around was fantastic. And going across the incredible world of Laika on your motorbike is, by itself, incredibly satisfying. Then you manage to perfectly time an acrobatic jump with a shot-recharge-parry-shot combo and feel the king of the world. A game worth experiencing, a Top 3 (at the very least) indie game of the year, and an absolute steal for its price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the  metroidvania with bullet time.While it does have a sprawling map, it only has 3 ability-gating upgrades, and just the general feel of the game causes me to want to call it metroidvania-like at best.This game will not be for everyone, even I was frustrated in the first few hours as I acclimated to the controls.  The controls are actually great, there is just a bit of learning curve to master them. The gameplay itself is working out how to approach each segment and is a bit trial & error (rotate my bike this way, shoot this enemy up top, then reflect the projectile of this enemy, then shoot the two down there). On a screen you'll probably fail at the execution a few times tweaking exactly how you want to approach the segment. Once you get past it, you'll immediately undergo the same situation again with the next segment, with different mob and track placement. As you master the controls, it can get a bit more free-flowing, but most of the gameplay is stop-start like that.  I think this game is at its best in sections like the boss in the mines where you are constantly moving one way, it feels faster paced when its like that, it would definitely be a more.. 'comfortable' experience if it were a straight up 2D sidescroller in this style.You'll die quite a bit from enemies that appear on screen too late to realistically react to them in time unless you already know that they're there.Backtracking in this game was a little more tiresome to me than a typical metroidvania.  Teleport points were spread out, and so i would have to repeat a lot of sections.  What made it worse was that the quest would suggest an area (and sometimes this was unclear too), but not tell you where in that area to be looking.  You may have explored that entire area already, and all you can do is go over the whole thing again.  It's tedious.  NPCs that you find on the map should also be marked for you to easily return to them.  The game does give you the ability to mark your map, so you can get around that at least.The music has had a lot of effort put into it, and works for the most part.  Rather than have specific tracks for areas, you have a looping playlist which expands as you find more cassette tapes.  I dislike this system and prefer biomes/areas to each have their own track, which gives an area a bit more character.  I would prefer the playlist as an additional feature where if i really want to hear a track, i can go into my tape player and mess with it.  As for the music itself, it isn't my style, but sounds quite modern and the sort of thing that might play in a t.v. shows emotional montage.  Tracks are vocalised, and have a 'jilted woman' and sometimes a 'travelling' vibe, which does fit biking around the gritty world as the female protagonist.  Not my cup of tea, but it works and on some level i do like and appreciate it.Laika was fairly enjoyable, sometimes tedious but quite impressive. _childDocuments_.review: This was a sleeper hit for me, I'd heard about it's praises and played the demo but was still not hyped or anything. After one more round of praises I decided to take the plunge and man am I glad I did. Laika is a beautiful game about motherhood, about sacrifice, it's filled to the brim with passion and is honestly just amazing. The OST is one of the better ones I've heard in a while, plus points for it also being diegetic and a collectible. The story while quite simple does tug at the heartstrings and the complicated relationship of Laika with both her mother Maya and her daughter Puppy is expressed very well. The worldbuilding is also great, it's simple things like the simplified naming scheme that are very to the point because it's a post nuclear world just adds so much. Honestly if people can get over the controls and get them to click then they should play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Metal Slug games used to be one of my favorite genres that set the stage for my expectations of side scrolling shoot-em-ups.  I fear that Laika may have now have overshadowed my love of the classic genre by far and exceeding any expectations I had for this game.The story is gritty and doesnt hold back. It doesnt let you explore the Overworld without first unlocking the next area through story progression but this limitation is understandable due to needing to keep the narrative moderately linear while giving the player limited choice.Though I'm only 4 hours into the game, I expect that it will keep surprising me with more heart wrenching plot twists and turns. _childDocuments_.review: I give up. I've spent an hour driving through the first section of the game waiting for it to get good and it never has. It's just been more of that indie game trend of "difficulty via bad game design = good" that seems all too pervasive. The gameplay is supposed to consist of you riding around in a motorcycle and shooting the bad guys with a gun that has bullet time and reloads by backflipping. Sounds great on paper, but in practice balancing not being shot with actually shooting feels super awkward and I usually ended up overfixating on one or the other. Combine this with the fact that your  for some inexplicable reason only has TWO rounds in it, and it means in practice the game is encouraging you to stay back and farm for more bullets. Oh yeah, also why in Christ's name is PARRYING tied to a consumable? Does that not get rid of the entire skill factor in parrying? Awful design decision.The enemies aren't very good either. They stand in one area and fire a bullet that basically immediately flies towards you, with 100% precision, every time. Since your bike blocks bullets, you're intended to use that to block them as you take aim. So how does this work when there's multiple enemies at different heights? Simple; it doesn't. You once again are forced to take it slow. Take out enemies from a distance, because you can't realistically be expected to take them out normally due to the game's poorly thought-out mechanics.While the artstyle was fantastic, I also found the story lacking. I enjoyed the post-apocalyptic scenery, but I found a lot of the actual story beats were too much. At a certain point it just started feeling like a torture porn that was being needlessly edgy just for the sake of it. Also, and maybe this would have been addressed later in the game (God knows I'm not playing the game any longer to find out), but I can't help that the birds feel like extremely plain villains. I'm not asking for you to make us feel sympathy for the Nazis of course, but for God's sake we don't get even the slightest hint of even a single bird not being a bad person in the entire first section of the game. Keep in mind by the way that in-universe birds ARE just a race of people, not some hivemind species of hate and anguish that you'd think they are with how they seem to act. Again, maybe this is addressed later, but it almost feels like they flanderized the main villains, and that is not a good impression to make.And the artstyle almost makes it worse. I LOVE the artstyle, and I LOVE the animation within. But unfortunately, I have to live with the knowledge that this beautiful artstyle was wasted on a game without good game mechanics. I would LOVE to have seen this in a game with well thought-out gameplay and combat, but instead all of that hard work and effort is relegated to this and nothing else. It's a shame.All and all, for $20 I would recommend this if the game wasn't just SO unfun. This is not a cheap game, and I went in expecting much, much more out of it than I got. Sadly, I'll be refunding this game because it's not every day I get $20 of spending money, and I know I could spend it in much better ways than this game. Maybe next time.

_childDocuments_.review: I wholeheartedly recommend Laika: Aged Through Blood. It is a metroidvania set in the post-apocalypse. It took me about 17 hours to finish and another 4 to 100%. You play as the titular character Laika trying to raise your daughter and not die while fighting against The Birds. Everything is done on a motorcycle. Combat, traversal, ability usage, all is tied to Laika's interaction with her motorcycle. I'm not usually a fan of metroidvanias, I always worry I'm going to miss an area, but I very much liked the gameplay.The game is very visceral, lots of blood and gore, which is interesting given its almost cutesy artstyle. Games like Darktide or Doom that involve a lot of viscera are more photorealistic, whereas Laika: Aged Through Blood is not. This doesn't detract from what it's trying to do. Backflipping in bullet time onto a group of unsuspecting birds, screen shading redder and redder with each subsequent kill feels more brutal than tearing the heart out of a Cacodemon or decapitating 7 Poxwalkers in a single swing. I do recommend the game based on its artstyle, and is HEAVILY boosted by the fact that you play as an anthro coyote.The story is fine, but what really shined was emotional impact. The game features several mature topics, death and torture of children, suicide, suicidal ideation, loss of innocence, alcoholism, etc. This is one of the very few games I have written reviews for and for good reason. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if it didn’t make me cry.In conclusion, Laika: Aged Through Blood deserves my wholehearted recommendation based on gameplay, visuals, and emotional experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes.  Teared up for sure. Absolutely. One of the best games I've played this year. Some, but the overall game play helps mask the small nitpicks you might have.There needs to be more furry post-apocalyptic stories and worlds. It combines cute animals with grim settings as the perfect yin and yang, grim and gritty with likeable character designs.10/10 - I may be a  but I'm not biased.

_childDocuments_.review: The biking and gunplay feel really good together. Juggling bodies and blocking/reflecting shots by hurtling through the air makes Laika (and by extension you) feel like a serious badass. The cooking and upgrading doesn't feel out of place, as gathering what you need comes with the same loop as dealing with your foes. The monster designs are amazing and lead you to really wonder about the lore of the game's world, but that leads me to what I think is the game's weakest part: the story.The game's music, environment, and circumstances get you to the edge of intrigue and emotion but don't have that final push to leave an impact on your mind. We get bits of background information on the enemy Laika is dealing with, but it leaves more to be desired and can be missed very easily. At many critical story points, things go by so fast that you don't really attach to the events and characters in front of you. The game's story is very comparable to LISA: The Painful, if LISA was watered down a ton. Worst of all, things happen quicker and quicker the later into the story you get. While there is still plenty of side content, it's unfortunate the parts everyone will experience feel like a second thought.Ultimately, really interesting and fun game that I think could've done more with what it had. Very much worth buying and playing despite the story's pacing. Also feels like a perfect game to have a level editor system where you can share your creations with people.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika is not for everybody.It's grim, gory, vulgar and difficult. Try out the demo first and make sure you can get to grips with the unusual controls, and be ready for your death counter to reach the hundreds before the end of the game. If you've played either of them, the gameplay is essentially an open world Trials meets Katana Zero, with a demand for consistent acrobatic precision that brings back memories of Super Meat Boy's single-screen gauntlets.It's also the most motherly game I've ever played. I don't think I've even played any other game that brought the word "motherly" to mind but Laika sure did. So if you, like me, value new experiences above most else, then motorcycle platforming with guns and post-apocalypse dog motherhood will probably swing Laika over to being a worthwhile time. As long as you don't mind spending half an hour fighting a crab and repeatedly being called words I can't spell out in this review. (You can yell those words at the crab if it makes you feel better!)Huge bonus points for a wonderful soundtrack that, much like the rest of the game, feels unexpectedly fresh. Loads of acoustic guitars and vocals coat the otherwise brutal and dark scenery with gentle, somber, sometimes bittersweet vibes. I've been listening to it almost every day since I finished the game a couple of weeks back.In summary, if you're good with wastelands, swearwords, viscera and the desire to slap yourself in the face for perfectly executing a lengthy encounter with Keanu Reeves-like precision only to accelerate too hard, flip your bike, bump your head and get reset to the last checkpoint, then I can very much recommend Laika. It's not the sharpest game, but I genuinely love it for what it's going for.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to review. I did enjoy it, but I had to use a mod to make it consistently enjoyable. Without the mod, it was difficult to the point of being frustrating and frustrating to the point of not being fun. You shouldn't have to mod a game to make it enjoyable. I don't suck at the game, it's just really hard and I don't have the time or patience to get good enough that I'm not dying over and over. Also, early in the game you are such a huge disadvantage that it feels unfair. This game desperately needs a difficulty setting and some tweaks of the mechanics. First the good. It is an interesting and original game. It is very polished and beautiful. The music isn't for me, but it's not bad and adds to the atmosphere of the game which is dark, but good. The controls feel tight and responsive. There are some great cutscenes. The story and dialog are pretty good and substantial for a video game, especially an indie game. There's a few rough translations, but nothing too bad. The combat is fun and engaging. When it works, it makes you feel a bad ass, flipping around blasting everyone. There's a lot to like.Now for the bad. Aside from the difficulty, there are a lot of really weird design decisions that contributed a lot of frustration for me:-The pacing is off. You won't fully unlock everything until just before the end of the game. And the later weapon upgrades are really expensive are require extensive backtracking, so you may not unlock all of them.-At least one of the abilities you unlock is completely useless other than to unlock part of the map. Actually two similar abilities, but they are used in slightly different ways in different parts of the map. This bugs me as not only is it a wasted opportunity, it makes me feel like the effort I put into unlocking the abilities was wasted.-In many cases, the upgrades aren't worth the hassle. Most of the weapons are designed in such a way that they're more trouble than they're worth. In particular, one weapon uses all its ammo regardless of how many bullets you fire. Another weapon is powerful, but it is really a pain to reload. In a game where reloading can be difficult or in some cases impossible, that's a big problem. I found myself just using the default pistol the vast majority of the time.-Level design is creative and interesting and maddening at the same time. Let me tell you, if you're a fan a backtracking, you're going to love this game. I can tolerate some backtracking, but this game really pushed me to my limits. Many of the levels are mazes, which I'm not a fan of. Not puzzles, but literal mazes where if you take the wrong turn you have to navigate the entire level all over again.-Unlocking music as a reward sounds like a good idea, but it means that in the first part of the game you're listening to the same three or four songs over and over and it gets old real fast. -The game has fast travel, but it's spaced out in a really weird way that severely limits its usefulness. In this game, it can be extra annoying because enemies respawn every time a new map loads (or you die), so if your path requires getting through a difficult cluster of enemies, fast travel often doesn't help. In any case, I'm glad there's something there, but it really doesn't save you much time. And with the amount of backtracking involved, it gets...you guessed it...irritating.Otherwise, the game's main mechanics are interesting and they can be fun, but they also contribute to the difficulty and frustration of the game. Reloading requires you to do a flip, but there's not always a ramp available and this puts you at risk of landing on your head, which kills you instantly. This bugged me probably the most. More on that later. The game isn't as cruel in its death mechanic as other games. You can usually find a respawn point not too far away and you lose about half your resources, but it's usually not too painful to get them back. That is, unless you lost them in an area with a million enemies. All in all I found it tolerable, though death punishment mechanics do grate on my nerves. So, the mechanic where you die if you flip your bike, I found really exasperating. I used to ride a motorcycle IRL and dropped it plenty of times and I'm not dead. In this game, if your head touches the ground, you're dead. What's more, your bike randomly backfires, giving you a little speed boost, but also causing your balance to go haywire. You'll die a lot just going straight. You get used to it kind of, but it's just another thing to add to the list. There is a setting that I think was added in the latest patch which gives you a little bit of a break on that front, but I didn't notice it until I was halfway through the game.If you're like me, you won't enjoy this game unless you mod the difficulty. If you're not lot me and have a lot of free time and patience to master a game's mechanics (and cat like reflexes), and/or enjoy dying 50 times in a row, you will probably enjoy this game without a mod. In any case, I still recommend you give it a shot. If it's too frustrating, try a mod. If it's still too frustrating, either refund it or be okay with a loss of at max $20.I'm only giving this a thumbs down because:a) The Steam hive mind overwhelmingly likes this game, so it doesn't need my endorsement andb) The average player who isn't a Dark Souls enthusiast type will most likely not enjoy this game without modding the difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika is a motorbike riding mother that takes out facist bird soldiers with revolver and other firearms. All weapons that Laika uses are reloaded by doing a back flip. While this mechanic fits well to the Elastomania like gameplay it can get frustrating to be doing back flips all the time, especially before upgrading magazine size of your weapons. This game has plenty of small things that had me frustrating me with the experience, but their weight got smaller and smaller as I got to unlock better guns and traversal options.- World navigation * This part of the game is what's most important of metroidvania, yet the game won't get grade A as navigating the game world is not easy. What makes this hard is how map system works. Only way you can acquire parts of map is by finding a certain npc hanging in that area and then buying a copy of map from him, meaning you can't see what all areas you have visited or not as map don't update upon visiting areas. What game also misses is some kind of travel log similar to Zelda:BOTW Hero's path system, meaning you can only rely on your memory what parts of each area you have visited.- Part of sidequest and rewards for completion * As world navigation ain't the best, tracking the route for completing part of the side quests is also a hassle, as part of them objective is located in one area but in reality you have to access it from another area. * For vast majority of side quests the rewards for completion are laughably small amounts of resources. I wish there would have been some money rewards, cosmetic unlocks or food recipes also as a reward. * At least one side quest is mandatory to complete, but it's not marked as main quest .-  feels like wasted potentialI wish that  would have been available for expanding moving mechanics and toss away flying enemy corpses. Right now it only ended up being used couple of times in main quest line and tore down few statues, making it very useless otherwise.Despite my review focuses mostly on few nitpicks that game could have improved upon, Laika: Aged through blood is a good metroidvania game filled with great storytelling, soundtrack and visuals. While I 100% agree with game's deloper Brainwash gang that game doesn't need dlc/ expansion, I partly wish we see a sequel for this great and grim experience on the future.Unless Elastomania like gameplay, extensive violence and/ or themes around leadership pressured pregnancy program, violence towards animals depicted as child, suicide and innuendo of rape are too hard for you, Laika: Aged through blood is great game I highly recommend to experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely in my top 3 for 2023. Absolute gem. Difficult (frustratingly sometimes), but (mostly) fair. I think there are some late game pacing issues around some of the unlocks, but don't want to get into spoiler territory. Have already recommended to a few friends. Enjoy your time in the wastelands!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I think the best recommendation I can give on this game is that it's the first one I've bothered to get all the achievements for in over ten years - because I was so engrossed by the gameplay, artwork and writing that I was already 90% of the way there by the time I hit credits. There are pain points here or there. You'll get fed up when you're trying to traverse the map and, half paying attention, wheelie so hard you slam your head into the ground. You learn pretty fast that the reward for most sidequests is a handful of crafting materials you could have gotten faster farming yourself. There is a *lot* of trekking back and forth to your fast travel points.But it's worth it. You really feel like you are mastering your bike, and within an hour or two you'll be doing frontflips with an inch of clearance off the ground while shooting across the screen. You'll find yourself picking up every sidequest so you can squeeze a few more sentences of lore out of NPCs and your journal. This game has collectible cassette tapes for background music and you will treasure each and every one of them as your faithful companions on those long drives through the lonely desert. This is not just a game with a fun motorcycle gimmick, this is a world that wants to pull you in, wants you to experience this beautiful nightmare of a setting. If you like metroidvanias, motorcycles, or world-building you can sink your teeth into, trust that this is best-in-class for all of the above and give Laika: Aged Through Blood a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing. There are some frustrating spots, but overall the greatest feeling I've had pulling off combos. Wheelieing to block a machine gunner, and shooting him in the back as you blow past him, to then hit a small lip and back flip while shooting 3/4 birds, reversing direction, landing and just continuing on. I had to pause a few times after pulling off some combos....such a cool ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea, shooting platforming while controlling a bike. Can't wait to see the next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: One of the rare games that I would call "Insanely good." It has a unique gameplay premise which doesn't get stale and introduces new mechanics, the boss fights are distinct from normal encounters, there's plenty of puzzles, collectibles, and sidequests, and the music and story mesh BEAUTIFULLY with the theme and each other. Every aspect of this game you can tell was handcrafted and polished. The only real criticisms you can make are 2 minor ones: Slight clarity issues, and slightly annoying fast travel system. However every other aspect of the game is near a 10/10 and it makes me wonder why this game isn't talked about more. Worth full price, solid 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game about 15 minutes ago, and I am currently in a completely incoherent state fueled by adrenaline and sadness. It has fun and satisfying gameplay, a captivating story, beautiful art, music and animation as well as art/music direction, great characters, bosses that are challenging (but not to the point where it isn't fun), and genuinely interesting and creative worldbuilding, which is all tied off with an absolutely top-notch soundtrack.Oh, and whatever the ♥♥♥♥ the writers for this game were on, I want some. NOW. They absolutely cooked with this ♥♥♥♥. Experiencing this game is basically like that scene in Ratatouille with Anton Ego eating the food and having a flashback to his childhood. The setting is a mix of post-apocalyptic with a bit of fantasy, and not only do the writers make great use of various writing techniques, they actually managed to turn the game mechanics into plot points. And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that ending.Its enough to leave the manliest of men broken down on the floor crying. Even just looking at the icon on my monitor makes that whole ending sequence along with the music replay again in my head. It was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful.This game is a true work of art. If anyone comes to me saying "games aren't art" I'm going to show them this and their head will explode.If you still have doubts about it, play the demo. It is absolutely worth your time.TL;DR: This game left me crying like a little ♥♥♥♥♥ for the first time in years, and I will never emotionally recover. 10/10.Also, the banner art for this game goes hard as ♥♥♥♥. Just felt like I had to say that.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. The art style is fantastic. The animated cutscenes sprinkled throughout are such a treat. Absolutely beautiful soundtrack.  NPCs are fun and entertaining. The writing is wonderful, funny, and heartbreaking. There's a good variety in weapons, though keeping the pistol and shotgun in rotation feels almost necessary. Boss fights were always unique and interesting in concept (though not always in execution).Now, the things that I did not like. -The dash comes FAR too late in the game. For this to be a metroidvania that requires you to constantly backtrack, it takes FOREVER to go from area to area, especially when you aren't 100% sure where you need to be looking for whatever quest item is necessary. -The game desperately needs a better fast travel system. The fast travel points are oddly inconveniently placed. There are large parts of the map that are without them (especially central of the map) and you seem to have to go to those areas frequently. Not to mention the fast travel points ALSO cost a unique currency for much of the game. A currency that you have to gather in the world, and then make at the fast travel point, to use the fast travel point (stupid, STUPID).-The turn around function is not perfect. I don't know if it needed to be a shorter duration held but MANY of my deaths were because of thinking I had turned around only to ride in the same direction to my death.-The hook function is dicey at best and extremely difficult to use at its worst and made that whole boat area of the map feel like a pain to get through. It got so frustrating that I considered quitting the game. I'm glad I didn't, but that level of annoyance does not make for FUN. Having the dash there would have made it significantly easier to get through, but that was still 2/3 of the game away.-Upgrades cost FAR too much. Max upgrade costing 3000 of the currency when you typically get 5 (FIVE) for killing enemies is insane. Especially considering there's like 6 weapons and multiple bag upgrades. I didn't have it in me to grind it out just for achievement sake.-Nearly all the side quests were ridiculous fetch quests forcing you to go from corner to corner (again, the terrible fast travel does not help this) only to receive basic upgrade material you can easily get from respawnable chests. Make the side quests feel like they're worth doing. I don't care how interesting the NPCs are (and they are all quite varied) if I'm getting useless rewards in return for the quests.-I initially started this game on a controller, because that's how I expect to play a platformer, but I VERY quickly switched to mouse and keyboard. Godspeed to anyone that persevered with a controller, because having to move, aim, reload with the flips, use the hook, etc all on a controller feels absolutely awful (lol at console players).I really wish there had been another boss or area like the mines. That was one of the only times that the fact that you're on a motorbike felt fluid and fast. I understand that really isn't the crux of the game, but I still feel like it should have had a greater impact, rather than the start stop start stop precision gameplay.I know this is a review mostly focused on negatives, but the entire 30-35 hours I spent on this game (a bit of afk) I loved. But there is truly a laundry list of caveats. The game itself was never too difficult, but as I said above, I nearly quit from frustration over a poorly implemented core mechanic. Buy it full price, buy it on sale, just play this game. It really is beautiful. Just mind the bird ♥♥♥♥ that you will step in while playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Explaining this game to my friends is hard. It's a Post-Apocalyptic Metroidvania Acrobatic Bike-em-up shooter.  It's got exploring, it's got gunplay, it's got intricate level design. It has a beautiful soundtrack, memorable characters, GORGEOUS artwork, and a heartbreakingly good story.  It was as if this game was designed for me specifically and everything I love in a game.  EMPHATICALLY Recommended.  A+ to you Brainwash Gang.  You knocked it out of the park.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Great music, but the game somehow feels too padded. Could be because of too much backtracking, could be because of limited-feeling moveset leading to repetitive platforming, could be because of not enough oomph to the weapons + the reload mechanics, could be because of not enough oomph to the bike (when it's your primary mode of movement, it starts to feel too slow too quickly).
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika's a 6 or 7/10. A good idea executed in a way that sucks a lot of the fun out of said idea.The story is engaging, depressing, and bloody as hell. I enjoyed that a lot, as well as some of the gorgeous locations, amazing animation especially after boss fights, and awesome soundtrack. If this game didn't look and sound as great as it does, I'd have refunded it.Exploring the world is tedious as hell. More interesting gameplay with weapon variety is locked behind that world exploration and a ton of side-questing. Combat difficulty comes down to boring, precise execution rather than exciting improvisation, as enemies will likely kill you and then you'll just pre-fire at where you know they will be. What could be exciting upgrades like the ability to deflect more shots is made inconvenient to use via the cooking system. The only fun upgrade you get comes very near the end of the game.Looks great on the Steam Deck though.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Just a really good, incredibly solid game. Do yourself a favor and pick this up. There is someone in this games story team that truly understands the tenants of telling a satisfying story. From the gameplay to the sidequests, everything about this game informs the arch of the story, incredibly strong.I will say the backtracking can get a bit tedious, but the quests that require it are so satisfying storywise, it didn't really bother me.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This is the coolest metroidvania I have ever seen. Visuals are gorgeous, music is amazing. The story is painfully brutal and nihilistic, in a  great way. Its all very fitting with the feel of the world, being that life sucks ass a lot of the time. The gameplay is badass as hell, you backflip to reload and you can parry bullets back at the shooters, and there is a lot to explore that feel worthwhile.Some flaws with the game is that some parts of the main story feels like they go over too quickly, and should have been expanded on. It can also feel a little bit pointless to do sidequests since they don't really give you anything, but I found them enjoyable still if you just try to act as the character you are playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, look me at the eyes, devs. You did not playtest the game past the lighthouse checkpoint, did you?EDIT:This would be probably my hidden gems of the year contender, but the game ultimately overstayed it's welcome. It should be ultimately cut off right after the Giant Tree on some ambiguous ending.There more I played it the more I got tired of it, of it's boss fights that are shoehorned to the game not suitable for them, of all emotional notes that grew progressively hollow, of the edgy forced writing that only 12 years old would take seriously, of endless backtracking on the map with zero markers, of the quests that require wiki to figure them out, and of the game in general that stops bringing anything new.Less is more, folks. Appreciate the originality, but I can't recommend this to any of my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot put into words how much i recommend everyone to play this game! It has been one of the best gaming expiriences recently for me, a fantastic piece of art that is criminally underrated! Especially at the asking price of 15 bucks there is no reason for you not to play it! Now for me personally it was a bit rough, i got some trouble dealing with emotions and this game will hit you in the feels every damn chance it gets so if you have trouble getting sad easily this is gonna be a hard journey. There are also a lot of very heavy topics this game touches on that can be shocking to people so do be aware of that.Gameplay wise i had a lot of fun as well! It runs very smoothly and the controls are easy to learn, yes there are a few frustrating portions but it was never to the point i had to put the game down from it, it always kept me hooked and wanting more even after it was over i kept wanting more! _childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I have ever played, which took me on a emotional journey, which I was not ready to take. The Story is really dark and depressing but is also quite beautiful at the same time and even got me crying once I got to the end. The gameplay was a bit hard at the beginning but once I mastered the bike movement and gunplay it was really fun to just cruise around the wastelands and shoot birds.There are plenty of missions and side quests, which offer rewards and some lore, which helped me to immerse myself into this game's world even more.And the music is just so beautiful, it really fits the game. _childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game with a few flaws.This game has a super neat concept and amazing presentation, with a story that kept me interested for the whole runtime. However, the game does have some flaws. I experienced several bugs; dialogue repeating, bullets disappearing, etc. Although none of them were too game-breaking or difficult to deal with.My biggest issues with the game are some of the boss fights and level design.The first couple bosses were really good and fun to fight, but I found the rest of the bosses (except for the final boss) to be not as great. I found there is a lot of downtime where you are just slowly riding the motorcycle through the arena, waiting for the next phase of the boss so you can continue the fight. These sections aren't too big of a deal, but if you die on the final phase of the boss, you really realize how long they take to get through, they aren't difficult, just monotonous.As for the level design, I think the game excels in open areas with lots of ramps, or areas with lots of loops and jumps. However, I found the closed in areas where you are fighting lots of enemies in cramped spaces to be way less fun to play. You don't get the fun excitement of doing cool tricks and actions with the bike in a stage designed for it, it feels more like you're playing an area designed for a regular metroidvania, but you have to also worry about the bike.I still loved this game, it was super fun and unique, if a bit flawed. Definitely try the demo, I think it's more than enough to determine if you like the game, and the save data carries over to the main game, so there is really no reason to not start with the demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: TRY THE DEMO FIRST BEFORE PLAYING!!!Wonderful music, beautiful graphics, fun combat (if you can learn it) and a heavy story line; all things that make a great game and all things that Laika has. The first thing I'll say is that this game is not for the faint of heart. It gives you a brief warning about its contents upon startup, which I greatly appreciated. The motorcycle combat take a lot of getting used to, and that can throw a lot of people off, but once you understand how it works and start practicing, it gets much easier and actually begins to flow with the other aspects of gameplay very nicely. Again, this takes a lot of practice, but the better you get, the smoother it flows. It feels really rewarding when you manage to pull of a x6 kill streak without touching the ground. The art is stunning, and the music is as well. It is implemented in a very unique way, in the form of cassette tapes you can find around the world. Most are easy to come across. The story pulls no punches, which I appreciate.I have three main critiques.1) The bike upgrades are not very well implemented into the overall gameplay. One of them in particular you will only use in extremely specific circumstances and then never think of again.2) One specific story event felt disconnected from player choice and from the world itself, as your character apparently has the ability to travel to this place (that is only relevant for this event) but you yourself can't find it on the map and can never go back. Most of the event is like watching a cutscene, and I feel as though it could have been something better seeing as how it was a very important plot point.3) One major plot point surrounds you destroying something, and despite the characters acting like it is destroyed after you finish the quest, it's actually not????Overall, I absolutely loved this game despite the issues I have with it. Play the demo and see if you like it, too! It's a pretty good representation of what the rest of the game will be like.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to describe just how good this game is.  It's a work of art, a journey, and I am so glad to have been along for the ride.  The art style is amazing, it gives you just enough info, but leaves room for wonder and speculation as to the world and it's background.  It is certainly one of the most pleasing games to look at, far better than the ultra realistic direction everything has been moving in.  The gameplay is challenging but rewarding, and there is an option to make it more forgiving if you need that kind of thing.  I have been playing games for 20 years, and nothing has come close to this story for me.  This has left me in a different state of mind, for the better, than when I started the game for the first time.     Even if you aren't into indie games of this kind (I wasn't either) it is worth while at least picking up the Demo to try it out.  It transfers your progress if you end up purchasing it later.10/10 - What's my Destiny?

The controls felt a bit wonky at first (I swapped from a controller to keyboard and mouse and that helped), but you get used to them. It's a great game that honestly needs more love! _childDocuments_.review: At my first couple hours playing I wasn't gonna recommend because of how frustrating the bike controls are but the game won me over by the end. The soundtrack is very nice both on the vocal and non vocal sides, with a mad max esque setting having a more softer soundtrack over something like heavy metal was a nice change of pace. The back tracking can be annoying at times until the dash ability is unlocked late game which alleviates a lot of the pain the bike controls cause, just wish was added more earlier on or something. Some mechanics should have been cut, the wheelie for the tightrope section sucks hard because you never build enough speed for it and the hook is only really useful for one main quest and the statue side quest. The story is very touching on how Laika cares for her child throughout the game and still pushes on despite the odds and past traumas. Really hoping the devs make a sequel and make some improvements to gameplay specifically. Buy on full price if you played happy wheels a lot or light (10-15%) discount for newcomer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty rough. The flip to reload slows gameplay to a crawl -- permanently losing currency in a trial and error style game is too punishing. The story is amazing but is hampered by awful gameplay that is incredibly punishing. I found myself forcing myself to play the gameplay segments and hating them to get to the story I enjoyed.story = 10/10gameplay = 4/10controls = 2/10music = 9/10overall = 5/10Edit: To further clarify, this game is also incredibly inaccessible.I am colour blind -- I can scarcely tell where my character is pointing when the camera zooms and when covered in blood? GOOD LUCK, me! With one-touch death mechanics, lack of early game upgrades, and a learning curb more steep than Gungrave: Gore (which introduces 8 mechanics back to back, some of which don't work at all due to hitbox issues), this game has few mechanics, fails to communicate them, and then punishes you for failing to understand said mechanics.Two hours in and I am just getting this cooking things that is important? Backflips in different directions do different things?The backflip is perhaps the most annoying -- I have more often than not exhausted my ammo and died trying to flip on a smaller obstacle because I didn't want to go into a battle without ammo.Also, I have no currency due to trial and error learning, I can't even afford the guitar strings (I had to farm the single enemy outisde the gas station to do it). I am told having more viscera bags alleviates this but the thing is -- The game doesn't explain this or anything, really."You just want your hand held" -- No, I just want the game to communicate and introduce me to mechanics and give me a place to practice them. A "Death arena" where death wasn't punished but offered no award so I could practice would be great.A colour blind mode or palette change would be nice.More variety to approaching an obstacle would be nice -- I have no real options early game and towards mid-game I still have few options because I can't afford anything due to the Viscera bag death mechanic.All this, I discovered in two hours. I want to like this game, I want to have fun...But it's not rewarding and only punishes you for failure.Some changes -- A reload button Out of Combat.Backflip or front flip reloading and recharging your parry -- Or better yet, parry not having a cost mechanic associated but a very tight window to execute. Perhaps the bike's bottom should reflect projectiles in the direction its facing like a pong paddle, rewarding precise blocking? Maybe I should be able to plow into my enemy on my bike or drift slide into them to kill them comboing into a parry and killing two others with my loaded gun?There's just not a lot of interplay with mechanics other than "Move fast, read the screen that fails to communicate up/down/character facing when they're blood soaked and somehow juggle all these mechanics flawlessly or die instantly".I kinda wish I could ram into someone at speed with my bike and ramp off their body, do a flip reload while firing at a full screen of enemies, timing my flip to block projectiles. If the Viscera bag dropping was altered, a colour blind mode added, and a little bit of clarity on the screen were given I think this game might actually have some less irritating gameplay.Oh, and the worst part? The "Git Gud" fans that don't want me to be able to play.Piss off. I can't read the screen because everything smears together blandly when I kill something -- I want slightly less punishing gameplay so I can enjoy what you take for granted. If keeping the gate closed to other people is what makes you feel special than sod off.I've played games that are challenging. Dark Souls 2 was a lot of fun. It communicated mechanics, rewarded clever builds and strategies, and had more ways to approach problems than...Whatever this is trying to be. Oh and you drop currency on death! It adds tension. However the key difference is you have more tools and build upon what you've learned.This game? I can't even tell what's going on sometimes! I've died to invisible geometry! I died at spawn because an enemy just off-screen shot me and I lost a viscera bag! I once got stuck in a death loop and lost ALL my viscera and I couldn't figure out how to deal with more than 5+ enemies.The answer? I memorized their spawns and shot them from out of aggro range. Then proceeded to shoot the next checkpoint instead of activating it because I thought they were an enemy, overshot it, then died to an unknown enemy in the next screen and had to start over.What did I learn? I can't really tell because EVERYTHING BLURS TOGETHER BECAUSE I AM COLOUR BLIND. Every encounter is trial and error. EVERY ENCOUNTER.Also the bosses, especially the first boss, are really boring.Edit:For the love of god play this with a keyboard/mouse. It's night and day.Still not recommending it due to the colour-blind thing but it's more manageable. I am no longer dying due to control flailing.

_childDocuments_.review: Having 100%-ed the game, here's my two cents. The game wasn't perfect; as others have said, the boss fights are probably the worst part of the game, and there are bits of backtracking you have to do for quests or items that just isn't fun if you don't photographically remember the map.On the other hand, the art style and music rock! The story, while a little edgy at points, never crossed that line too far and I was consistently intrigued the entire way. I empathized a lot with Laika the whole way through, and enjoyed the worldbuilding a lot. The gameplay was generally pretty clean and enjoyable, and I didn't experience any glitches. The achievements aren't too hard to get, either.I definitely recommend this game, especially if you can catch it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: "Laika: Aged through Blood" is pretty darn unique, and it's hard to slot it neatly into any comparison. But, if I had to draw a parallel, it's like "Katana Zero" in an open-world setting with some quirky motorcycle combat.The connection to "Katana Zero" comes from the whole 'dying over and over, grinding through encounters' vibe. You'll face plenty of deaths, taking another shot at a challenge until you finally reach the next checkpoint. Now, let's talk about the combat; it's got its quirks. Reloading means doing a backflip, and a frontflip refreshes your parry, all while dodging and trying not to fall onto your face, as that is an instakill. It can get pretty annoying when you're dodging bullets, parrying like a champ, and then eat dirt because you couldn't nail a flip.However, when everything clicks, and you're parrying perfectly, sniping enemies, and blocking their shots, it's a satisfying rush.What really stands out in "Laika" are the cutscenes and the music. They're top-notch and add a ton of value. The combat is decent but can be a bit unwieldy.Now, here's the curveball – there are these moments where you have to do some platforming on a motorbike. To be honest, it feels out of place and doesn't jive well with the rest of the game.All things considered, Laika is an enjoyable ride. It's not a game-changer, but it's a load of fun, quirks and all.Upon completing Laika, my initial impressions have undergone some adjustments ( after all they were limited to the first 4 hours of gameplay). While I still recommend Laika, my overall experience is not without its criticisms.Laika undeniably excels in its storytelling, artistic presentation, and music. However, other aspects of the game are ranging from decent to problematic.Combat:The combat closely resembles Katana Zero, requiring the player to repeat stage sections until they are successful by chance. This repetitive nature can be frustrating, especially when a missed shot results in death and having to restart an annoying section. Notably, the probably best upgrade in the game only gets unlocked near the game's conclusion with the introduction of an ability that enhances both combat and traversal.Bosses:Boss fights, excluding the initial two, tend to be tedious and somewhat irritating. For instance, one boss battle involves a vertical sidescrolling format with combat sections interspersed. The challenge arises from dodging projectiles and waiting for the boss's vulnerable point to appear. Some boss fights become particularly frustrating due to issues with motorbike controls, adding an unwelcome layer of difficulty.Quests:Side quests are mixed in design, ranging from decent to poorly thought out. While some quests offer engaging challenges in specific areas, others involve mundane tasks like buying quest items from wandering merchants. The "Wastelanders" quests, in particular, lack inspiration, requiring players to reunite scattered musicians with nearly identical quest structures.Each on of these Wastelanders quest, 6 overall, have the EXACT SAME structure.-Encounter Wastelander-Receive their Quest-Buy their Item from a Wandering merchant-Return to the Wastelander-Give them the item and finish the questExploration:The game features numerous areas but offers few fast travel locations, resulting in extensive travel to reach quest locations and resources. This repetitive travel becomes tedious and may deter players from fully enjoying the exploration aspect, even more so, considering you will be forced to do it for quests. The excessive backtracking, especially for resource gathering, at some point made me groan when I had to enter an area for the fifth time and go there the long route because it lacks fast travel locations.Side Content:The limited side content consists of Blackjack and cooking. While Blackjack proves mundane, cooking lacks meaningful impact due to the scarcity of cooking spots. You will never have a boss encounter or a section in which you say that "X"-Buff would help here, simply because the cooking spots are so rare. A different approach to cooking would have made way more sense. Have it like in Bloodstained, whereas cooking a dish for the first time provides the player with a small permanent buff.Laika is still mostly a fun ride, primarily attributed to its outstanding soundtrack, captivating art, and compelling narrative. The game's strengths are for the most part in the initial and concluding hours, with a challenging and engaging experience despite occasional frustrations. It would have made way more sense for the developers to cut down the needed resources and tedious quests. Even if it makes the game shorter, it will leave the player with mostly good afterthoughts.The positive aspects, particularly the story, music, and challenge, make Laika a worthwhile experience nonetheless, although I recommend to wait for a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: A Metroidvania mixed with something like the Trials games? Certainly not a combination you would think could work but boy does it and does it well at this point! For a first of it's kind done right Laika really did manage to stand out to me alongside it's competition just cause of how fluid it feels to play once you get the hang of it since everything really is packed in with the whole idea of being stuck exploring a ruined land on a bike.Everything really does revolve around you and your bike at this point, tilting it to block anything trying to attack you, doing a flip to reload your gun or gain a parry back, working with that momentum to get to places that just seem out of reach with the help of a trusty shotgun later on and when you get the dash near the end of the game? Boy can you just weave everything together into a real dance even when a single hits all it takes to put you in the grave for the moment!I will admit though i do have some gripes with things when it comes to the gameplay though since some stuff feels a bit undercooked in all honesty, the parry kinda just feels like an after thought since once you get your pistol and even just an upgrade for it the parry just doesn't really keep up especially since there's no upgrades for it outside of food buffs and thats for only 15 minutes. I got really excited when i saw there was a hook in the game! I thought there would be some really neat physics puzzles that relied on you hooking on to something and flinging yourself with some built up momentum but sadly it's only used for its tutorial section, some optional achievement deals and then just one boss... Seriously thats all you ever need the hook for, cause even in the final area of the game it gets no use whatsoever and it's honestly a shame! The camera does get to be a bit of a pain to manage since a lot of the time when it zooms out for larger encounters it get's a bit hard to orient yourself outside of your reticent giving you an idea of how your oriented and i could only imagine the pain it would be on smaller screens and then theres the issue of getting around. The worlds a fairly big one and though moving isn't a problem thanks to the tight controls, getting farther distances or to out of the way areas is a bit of a pain since though there is a fast travel system it doesn't feel like there's enough points scattered across the map to make that bit of backtracking less tedious since some area's lack one of those points entirely compared to others that have one at the start and another halfway through the place and when some of the objectives for both main and side quests can be a little obtuse on what it wants it can wear on your nerves a bit...Then come the bosses... Sadly the majority of them are just underwhelming on the gameplay side of things even if very well designed on the artistic side of things and really just turn out one note or otherwise incredibly easy, you'd think the final boss could put up more of a fight but you just upgrade the machine gun to it's 3rd level and it just makes the fight trivial once the first opportunity for damage shows up and that fight just takes place in a basic box rather than anything extravagant! There's only really two bosses that give an interesting course to fight them on and one of them you have to fight on four occasions only with a differing attack set, i really wish there could have been more of a focus on the movement around the arena...The story is a bit of a wild card here. It starts off incredibly strong with just painting a picture of how life is in this wasteland and just how cruel it and the people who live in it can be when you see a child hung up by their own innards! I will say a part of the story really depends on how much you engage with it and the world and some parts sadly fall a little flat, for example later in the story there's a bit of a betrayal and though i can understand the rage Laika felt in the moment it's more directed towards a bit of a nothingburger of a character you who might not even know exists unless you explore your home base a bit and it even leads to an area you don't really get to explore outside of a story bit that at most lasts about 10-20 minutes. But the moments it hits, it can definitely pluck at your heart even in the side missions. Finding a last meal for someone terminally ill that happen to be lethal on consumption just for an easy way out of things, coming across a troubled father who was looking for his daughter who ran off... Only to find out she had VERY good reason to though subtext. And then there's the relationship between Laika and her daughter Puppy which i won't go into for the sake of the experience but stuff like this really wants to make me see more mother and daughter dynamics in worlds like these! And for those versed in other games by the creators here you might just have a little extra insight to the world that others might not, though it's far from required to enjoy it!I can't help but want to recommend this to people even with the flaws it has since in the end they don't really detract from the experience enough to put me off of it! I'll just warn that you've got to have a bit of patience with the game at points and if it really comes to it don't be afraid to look up a path! The world on offer is something wonderful that i wouldn't want people to miss out on it even if it's just through watching someone else play it!

_childDocuments_.review: *A one-of-a-kind take on the genre, it mixes 2D action metroidvania with dirtbike stunts and fast-paced gunplay. Beautiful hand-drawn art style with great music and a compelling story. I highly recommend this, my only complaint was that I wanted more. Also, demo progress was immediately carried over to the full version without any issues.** Do be aware of very mature themes in story, presentation, and gameplay. It does not shy way from the brutality of survival in a post-apocalyptic world, despite a colorful cartoon style.Without spoilers, you play an anthropomorphic wolf riding a dirt bike and firing various firearms through a Mad Max style wasteland. You'll take on quests, trade items, and acquire weapons and equipment that will further your exploration. I'll try to give some explanation of the unique controls, but honestly it's best to jsut give the demo a go.I played with a gamepad, so I can't speak for other controls. They are very different from what I first expected, but it didn't take long to get the hang of it.Movement consists of controlling your bike through various 2D environments using hills and ramps to gain speed and launch yourself from platform to platform. The left stick is used to control the radial orientation of your bike, not the direction of movement (for example: hold right while in the air and moving to the right does a front flip, while doing it on the ground while facing right and stationary will balance you on your front tire). The right stick controls your aiming , while the triggers control your acceleration and firing your weapon. It might sound like a mess of a control scheme, but it really comes together in a fun way. You are fragile. If you take a direct shot from an enemy or land your bike upside-down, you're dead. There is however a very generous checkpoint system, but you mainly will use your speed and the bike itself to avoid or block enemy fire. Gunplay feels fast and rewarding, as you are always able to fire in any direction around you. The only gimmick here is that reloading is done by doing flips on your bike. Trust me, when you get in down, it feels incredible.It's wild, it's gory, it's sweet, it's heartbreaking. I can't recommend this enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This game suffers from serious visibility issues, which make otherwise great mechanics feel extremely underwhelming and frustrating. I'm honestly not sure how these issues could've slipped past anyone, and they unfortunately render the game borderline unplayable.Why am I still recommending the game then? Because the soundtrack absolutely slaps, and the game is almost worth playing just to experience it. I also hope that the previously mentioned issues will be patched. Please, I beg of the developer, it's not too late. A simple post-processing filter to highlight important information (namely the player and the ground) might be all the game needs, along with zooming the camera out a bit. It pains me to see a otherwise wonderful game be run down by an issue which has a clear path to amelioration.In conclusion, this game is great, but it feels like a bit of a prototype. If you're alright with some visual clutter and the ensuing confusion, it's worth a try, but in its current state, it needs some work before I can call it "good".P.S. Y'all know the connotation with the word "wanker", yes? I fear it may be misplaced, and if not, eek.

_childDocuments_.review: Mad Max: Furry RoadThat joke out of the way: Laika is one of the most fascinating titles I've played in recent years, a game that makes up in soul what it lacks in perfection.Everywhere you look, you can see the love and passion that went into its making. Gameplay, visuals, story and music echo each other, and the brutality of the action finds itself woven into a narrative about desperate survival, itself framed inside the hand-drawn beauty of a desolate wasteland, all carried by the soft melody of an absolutely haunting soundtrack.And what a soundtrack it is. The composer and singer's name is Beícoli, and I think she's earned her place among indie game giants like Darren Korb (Hades) or Andrew Prahlow (Outer Wilds). I hope we'll get to hear more of her work in the future.All in all, Laika isn't without flaws: the final confrontation is a bit underwhelming, and I think overall the game would have benefited from a more linear and focused storyline, rather than a quest-based design that lets players choose their own path also but hampers the sense of general progression. Thankfully, it only takes a few lines of well-written dialogue to make you instantly invested into Laika's world, characters, and story.Laika is not a perfect game, but it's a game I'll remember.

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions;Laika is very fun. It's got all the best (and worst) aspects of the metroidvania genre when it comes to progression and map design, the movement and the combat are fluid and responsive. Easy to learn, hard to master, all that jazz. I  the art direction, even if the environments can be a little difficult to read at times, and a special commendation goes to the soundtrack, it fits the tone of the game perfectly. Playing In The Sun has burrowed its way into my brain, and I'm sure the rest of the cassette tape collection will follow suit.One flaw that I find rather critical and worth pointing out is that the game doesn't feel that well-optimised. Now, I haven't got the best rig out there, but I have been able to hit 60+ fps just fine for most of the game, even during hectic combat, but depending on the location and the scenario, the game can dip all the way to 20-30 fps seemingly at random (no stutters, at least). Some screens ran fine except for very specific parts even when nothing was happening in them, it all feels... uneven.I'm hoping future patches will include more framerate improvements, but even at the moment it's not unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game captured the feel of a metroidvania perfectly. The music combined with the style and look of the world makes this world have the exact feeling that the developers were going for when designing the game. After beating this game and taking a couple months of hindsight I have seen some issues.The character development of the game is extremely lacklustre where you will often meet a character and in the next 15 mins they die, I am not even kidding it became an expected thing I kept noticing after the second area, whether this was intentional or not, it makes it feel like the people you meet are just bullets in a firing range, they are shot and introduced but after that you dont worry about them. Even worse is that your character will mention something once then have a short talk and then they are never mentioned again no sign of remembrance or care for the lose off life she just continues like nothing had changed. My other gripe with the game is that it felt way to structured and the mechanics of each areas was often never repeated anywhere else. I am going to use an example of a game like little big  planet three even with all its problems it gave one big show down at the end that allowed you to show off everything you had learned in previous areas of the game. Laika fails to do that having in my own opinion one of the most lacking final boss areas and fights of the entire game. youve met characters with better motives then this final boss throughout that game.one last final thing, this is not a game about being cool and riding a motorcycle its about going through puberty and having a period. thats it the whole game stems from something that girls go through every month. thats literally it, yes you fight in a war to save a village and yes you fight the big bad but if you didnt have a perioid you would be dead

_childDocuments_.review: I hesitate to refer to Laika: Aged Through Blood as a metroidvania, at least, not in the traditional sense; the game offers you very clear quests marked through a journal, and only contains, if I remember correctly, three items which change the way you progress throughout the world.This does not mean, however, that Laika is a bad game; my first blind playthrough lasted a little under 13 hours, which consisted of doing all the side quests I ran into (Though I do not think I did all of them) and exploring liberally; which, while not a supremely long amount of time, was thoroughly enjoyable all the way throughout.Laika isn't going to change your life, its not a genre defining game; neither the story nor the game play do anything all that extraordinary; what Laika is, however, is a polished game with an enjoyable story and world, that doesn't waste your time, which, at least to me, makes it worth every penny I spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a bittersweet tale from start to finish. It is a bleak, brutal and desolate world and you can see and feel it in everything you come across. From your own small tribe clinging desperately to life, to the bone-dry wastes, to the bullet-blasted ruins of yesteryears' wars, to even the chief antagonists' lot in life.Laika offers a heart-wrenching story with its gameplay that is heavily weighed towards precision in movement and in combat. You have no health, but neither do your enemies: everything except bosses die in one hit, so make every single shot count. You have a small arsenal of weapons, up to six if you find every single blueprint, though the game only really requires the revolver you begin the game with, and the shotgun you must unlock to progress. Notice, however, that your weapons generally have 1-4 shots loaded, depending on their upgrade level.Every weapon has four levels, with two-through-four giving small but important bonuses, such as increasing the magazine capacity of your weapon by 1, or giving you a more generous reload angle for faster and easier reloading. Though you will have to look around for materials to upgrade these items with, do not sleep on them. Naturally, you can carry between two and four weapons at a time, depending on how many times you upgrade your weapon bandolier.When it comes to the movement, if you have played any 2D game where you ride a motorbike, the movement should feel very familiar. You have acceleration, and you tilt your bike backwards and forwards to wheelie, or if in midair, flip the bike around. Flipping is extremely important for this game: backflipping is the only way for you to reload your active weapon, and front flipping refills your parry. Parry is your only active defense against a bullet careening towards Laika, though the timing can be very tight and sometimes frustratingly difficult to get right.The art and the music are some of the best Laika has to offer. You will be accompanied by a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack throughout the entire game as you ride through a wasteland that feels hand painted. In the bone-dry wastes, there is very little color: mostly the bleached white of dry bones, ashen grey of dead trees and the deep red of the blood you spill. Weapons sound punchy, the bike roars pleasantly and the wind howls to accompany the wistful soundtrack that accompanies you. There are a number of songs, though at first you only have a few cassette tapes and the same songs loop over and over. Later, as you explore and find cassette tapes, the repertoire of songs naturally expands. Also, back at your village, should you find musicians to play, you will hear them play at nights.Laika is an excellent showing, though it is not entirely without flaws. The most frustrating part is how finicky the bike occasionally feels to control. If you do not make a perfect landing and your attention wanders for a split second, you may find yourself unexpectedly dying because Laika's back briefly touches the ground, or because a pixel touched a surface that is considered ground.At times there are sudden difficulty spikes that force you to retry a sequence over and over again until you eventually master it and clear the stage. Thankfully Laika is very generous with checkpoints scattered everywhere so you never lose much progress, but at times it is aggravating to die in the same spot a dozen times or so. When I finished the game, I had 328 deaths total.The pacing of the game feels a little wonky. Though I ended up spending 20 hours playing the game, I did just about everything there was to do in the game, save for getting every single weapon upgrade. There are only three or four main story quests and they are over sooner than you might expect. That leaves the side content to fill the rest of the runtime, and while that is not a bad thing necessarily, it left the main story feeling a little short and bare-bones. Likewise for the animated cutscenes that are sparingly sprinkled here and there during the game; they are short and sweet and carry the emotion of the scene excellently, but they feel a little rushed, as though they were sped up or otherwise in a hurry.Finally, the weapons that you unlock feel largely superfluous. The crossbow is a shotgun that takes far too long to reload without investing tons of resources into it. The machine gun blasts its entire magazine in one go, so long as you hold down the trigger; if you stop, you might fire a single round at the cost of 5 or more, yet it does not excel better than the starting revolver. The sniper is effectively a second revolver that seemingly offers a slightly stronger bullet time effect, but not sure if anything else beyond that. And lastly, the rocket launcher arrives far too late in the game to be of much use, though you can use it to blow up the shielded machinegunners risk-free. It is a shame that most of the weapons are not very good at their jobs, so you can easily get through the game with just the revolver and the shotgun.Finally, what happened to all the men? There are only a small handful of men anywhere and most of them are either crazy or crippled. My only explanation is that most of them have died in the fighting of the past, but that leaves the game feeling strangely packed with almost exclusively women who never really even reference them. While this doesn't really impact the game much, it was something I couldn't stop noticing. Especially in a world as harsh as Laika's, you would expect to see fathers, brothers and husbands trying their damnedest to help their tribe and their family survive.Laika is a beautiful game that is close to perfection in many aspects. The story holds no punches and many of the stories end in the only way they could end in a world as harsh and brutal as Laika's. It is a story well worth experiencing, even if the gameplay can feel like a real struggle at times. It holds a similar place in my recommendations as Dust: An Elysian Tail, which is exceptionally high praise.
