_childDocuments_.review: How to "git gud": Visually, it's a lot more "realistic" than the first game. The soundtrack is not for me (I prefer Redout 1's music). The base game has 24(?) race tracks. From Mars, to .There are 5 new ships, and all 12 ships have their own good/bad base stats. You also have components: Some increase top speed, others increase handling or boost power. Saving this into a "loadout", you can build the perfect ship for every situation!Racing has a lot more "grip" than in Redout 1 but this also depends on the race track. Unlike the first game, you must rotate and pitch your ship in jumps (Though in both games, you can't play properly with JUST steering alone!). It can be very overwhelming at first, because of how much controls you get. This game takes away powerups, but gives you a turbo and a rechargable super boost. You can overheat from boosting, which then burns down health. The career mode lasted a bit too long for me. The gradual progression of stats DOES help you get used to the tracks and the increasingly high speeds as you play. However, there are so many items to unlock through >100 career missions that it can feel sluggish for some players.When this game came out, there was a  issue with the difficulty being too high and the Thrust stat being broken Luckily, the game's overall difficulty and some jumps are now easier. Thrust is working, too! The goal in RO2 speed events is to get as much score as possible in 3 minutes. You need to boost a lot. Score increases exponentially (Example: 2 points a second on 800km/h becomes 6 a second on 1000km/h or 12 at 1200), so you'll want to go fast and stack both boosts.Newcomers might find this game challenging. It has a high skill ceiling, with several layers to its controls. Because there are no powerups, making a mistake is very punishing. It's almost unavoidable that some players will be far ahead of you. Still, if you want a super fast modern antigrav racing experience where skill means victory, this is for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'll literally just copy & paste my Redout 1 review here, since everything I said there is relevant here (notable changes listed at the end):By far the best track racing game I've ever played.What makes Redout's gameplay and control feel different from your normal racing game is that you also need to rotate your ship up and down to follow the road - so it's not just a road that happens to sometimes have vertical turns or loops, but you need to manually react to those turns too. The ship will still follow the road through vertical turns automatically (you can't fly off the road), but turning it manually has a big impact on your speed so you'll want to do it.It's a really simple but effective change to the gameplay and control feeling, which helps make it feel more like a special levitating/flying ship rather than just a car on a magnetic road.The first ships might feel kind of slow compared to what you see in the trailer, but you'll quickly unlock faster and faster ships.PS. The OST is great, and it fits well in the game.---Then for the changes from Redout 1:- As you progress in the game, you'll unlock parts for your ship, and you build it up from 6 different categories. Each piece affects one or more of the following stats: Durability, Thrust, Top Speed, Stability, Steer, Strafe. So instead of picking from preset ships, you'll basically build your own from multiple parts.- Boosting has some changes: you have a basic boost meter that you use to boost. But if you keep boosting even after the boost meter is used, you'll "overheat" and start losing Health - so you can take risks and boost for longer, but it will require not hitting anything for a while so your health can regenerate back.- There's also a Hyperboost, which locks you into a fast boosting mode for a couple of seconds - using almost all of the boost meter. You can pair this with normal boost and go *really* fast, but it's really risky as you'll quickly end up losing almost all of your health. Really need to know the tracks.- Abilities (magnet etc) have been removed, probably to focus more on this boost/hp resource balancing minigame - personally I like this change.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first game a lot and as far as first impressions this looks great. The new boost system of eating through your health was intimidating at first but was a nice and intuitive change. As well as getting rid of different power ups and combat gimmicks the first game had. And now there isn't classes, now you progress getting better parts. And you can even customize each individual ship. And it is pretty indepth you can change most parts as well as the livery and color palette. Honestly this is such a step up from the original game. I was surprised at how they made everything look soo much better but still feel similar. Honestly still love the first game but this is already has surpassed it and feels great to play. I have lots of content to look forward to, and many completionist things to do. edit: After playing longer and getting through the first league in career mode I understand why most people said it was repetitive. And that is because it is. There could have been so many events condensed down, considering some don't even give an reward for getting the 4 stars. Not really a big problem for me considering I played to almost the end of the first game/s career mode. But still a fundamental issue that carried over into this game that they had years to correct. I don't agree with it but still enjoy playing it if that makes sense. I enjoy just playing the game. And mainly the gameplay is the real selling point for me. Getting more and more chances to play and get shiny new things is fun. But it is a bit extreme the amount that actually is there in front of you and how many times different tracks are reused. I didn't get to experience over half of the tracks the game has to offer in the first league.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun but difficult, a lot of people compare it to wipEout but i feel its more similar to speed racer. No air brakes but a dual joystick steering system adds depth and makes it very satisfying to chain turns together. This is not a game like Forza where you can pick up and just play, you really have to spend time to learn the courses if you want to get good times.Maps and ships look fantastic and the visuals are bright and flashy but not overwhelming.The customization is quite good. I do think the paint scheme unlock is a little jank, maybe something where you unlock the colors/paint material over time would be cooler.Multiplayer is good but a server browser + some more map selection/game mode options would be nice. There are plans to add ranked but im not sure that will be that for a while as the player base is quite small still. I believe the best way for this game to grow would be an added replay option to review recent races and a custom map editor.Overall great game and im excited to see what comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best AG racer i've played ever. Love the sence of speed and quick decision making. The different locations all feel very unique and have their own quirks. This game is not trying to recreate the Anti Gravity Racing genre (f.e. Wipeout), its doing its own thing. No vehicle combat or item pickups other than boost pads. Just pure speed with a regular and a superboost that are combineable. If you dislike its features like the flight system, you can enable automated control assists for it and many other controls.Only downside are somewhat frequent framerate stutters when playing certain tracks for the first time of a session.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I gave it a positive review, BUT this game is inferior to the first Redout in every way except graphical, still a good pick if you know what you’re getting. The racetrack progression is weird at best, so is the AI. In terms of difficulty progression this game has none really, it is difficult from the first race on, but not in a fun way. You have no time / space to learn the fundamental mechanics of the game, but are expected to instantly know tracks etc. The AI is a beast, with perfect boost control, great lines and insane rubber banding it is just not fun to race against if you are new and still learning and ok if you know what you’re doing. So how can you resolve that issue? Easily! Just lower the difficulty from Redout to a lower setting that makes you feel like a complete fool, who can’t even play the game on the “normal” difficulty setting. All in all, if you are looking for the best, most fun anti-gravity racer nowadays just pick up Redout 1 enhanced edition. Sure, it may look less impressive, but it has its own stylized look I am quite fond of, also the races and progression are just way more fun in the first iteration. Redout 2  the savior of the genre that many hoped it would be.Here are a few pros and cons.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like Redout 2. But it is a challenging game. Don't be afraid to use the drive assists when starting out. They really help to make the game more enjoyable when you don't know how to strafe efficiently. (Also it's OK to skip the early speed challenges until you get a better ship.) I bumped up the steer, strafe, and break assists up to like 20% or 30%. But I started to tone them back after I got the hang of piloting my ship.There's a lot of content in the career mode. I'm trying to go through the events in order, but after nearly 24 hours, I haven't finished the first league. (Although, I've had the rank up event available for a while now.) It can feel like a grind, especially since the early career only uses the first 3 or so locations. But man, it's so much fun to just fly the ships that I keep powering through.The ships are very fast, but are still feel very responsive. I especially like the little animations on the wings and fins. Strafing is an awesome mechanic that adds a lot of depth to every corner. It can kinda feel like drifting in other racers, but with more control. The two stage boost bars is also a clever way to make a traditionally simple mechanic way more interesting.The tracks are long, and each one feels unique. My main complaint is that every track at a location shares a starting line, so it's hard to immediately distinguish which track is which during the countdown. The long length also makes each a bit more difficult to memorize, but career does a fair of getting you familiar to previous tracks before introducing a new one. TLDR: Redout 2 is a challenging racing game. The ships are fast, the controls are tight, and over all it's a blast.Oh. Also the OST, and the situational audio effects are a delight.Edit: Since this review, the -dx11 workaround is no longer needed and it's a great experience on desktop Linux. (Still stutters and eventually crashes randomly on Deck tho.) Still not done with the career mode tho. I'm like 80 hours in and I'm a little stuck at the end of class S.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of Anti-grav racers. I've played everything from F-Zero, Wipeout, and the original Redout. I've had a blast with them and would consider myself someone who enjoys this genre of games. When I say that Redout 2 is fast, I mean that it's . I don't think I've reached speeds like this since playing GX on my Gamecube. The controls are easy to learn but difficult to master. The tracks are well designed and are technical enough to require real effort to navigate but still feel satisfying to complete. The air roll mechanics, while a bit clunky at first, are extremely satisfying to pull off. This game looks and feels far better than its predecessor. _childDocuments_.review: IT is brutal. Its not an easy game, reminds me of the stories of how hard F-Zero GX is and I would call it in par with Xenon Racer in terms of mastery and difficulty, but both are fun for a lot of people and I love Xezon racer and even Quantum Rush Champions which is another anti gravity racer with is brutal!Redout is all about being a twin stick racer with breakneck speeds with a high risk high reward with boosting that one mistake can cost you. You need to know how to play chicken with your health, when to break off a boost before you destroy yourself.The controls are simple to learn and hard to master. The one thing you need to know is when to break and let off the gas, took me a bit. To put it simple, ever drive a racing game where your car is clipping into the ground dragging on the track slowing you down? You try in vain to tilt your control stick to tilt the car, but it won’t?  Its why the dual stick is important as you can tilt your ship to match the curves of your ship.It's also to avoid gets red outs or black outs like a real fighter jet pilot has to do. Hence why they named the game Redout. Now the only hard thing about it is the tilting controls. To barrel roll your ship left to right when in mid air you need to use the D-Pad. If you got an elite control or one like it map the back paddles to left D-Pad or right D-Pad. This is easier to race with and its just harder to move down to the D-pad so fast or not.Luckily if you want the Mario kart controls of auto tilting it comes with assists. Think like in Forza Horizon. Each assist is for breaking, tilting and everything to help you learn and get better at it. I barely use any but Boost Safety. For me I wish they handled Boost risk like in Quantum Rush Champions with how by default ships will not explode due to you using boost for too long and eating up all your health. They did have a ship line that did ignore that and select modes that had it disabled but for Redout 2 it has no safety system unless you use the assist.Lastly the music is good! Now its is not like the Redout 1 music that each track felt like a different environment or remain in your mind when you are not playing. But they due all fit in and work great for the tracks you are racing on. Just not always memorable in the I want to listen to them out of the game. Granted if I sit down that might change.All in all, if you like hard racers and ones that are fast and breakneck speeds you should get it. IT is hard at the start, but you are not suppose to get 1st on each race, just not last. It’s how the tutorials don’t teach you everything but over time goes over more and more advance tricks on its mechanics. It’s about going back and mastering the tracks and challenges. It’s the classic;  So when you get it, just keep at it. It’s a rewarding game and a high skill ceiling.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is different to the first one in some ways, but the formula is still there. The tracks are tough the first few times until you memorize the layouts. It's then that you can take full advantage of the straights. The sense of speed is incredible when you get that double boost going at the right time.I see many people complain about boosters right before a corner. Keep in mind that all tracks have a reversed version in which those boosters will become useful. Also, you get 3 rewinds in case you fall off the track. Another thing that may put off some fans of the first game is that many of the tracks can't be completed with full throttle throughout the whole track. However, it does make the brake button more useful now. Lastly, the only issue I've come across is some hardcore lag on tracks from 2 different worlds. I am certain it isn't my connection, just a bug from these worlds that will get fixed in time.Other then that my experience thus far with this game has been fun. 4/5 StarsUpdate:Now that I'm at the final boss races of the career I can say that the game is super fun and challenging. About what I said previously, the lag in two of the worlds has been fixed. And the part where I said you can't full throttle every track was just lack of experience on my side. If you steer into a turn and strafe away from the turn at the same time you can basically drift sharp turns. All ships are viable with the right build. Tons of variety in terms of tracks. Knowing that the chance of DLC is high, I am very excited to see the future of this game.Keep it up devs! You're doing an amazing job with game! New rating: 4.5/5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: A racing game that ins't "boring"! Now hear me out. I like racing games. It is just they get a little predictable and repetitive. Skill only helps so much. Get the fastest car and power-slide around corners. One direction is to add chaos with items and such (Mario Kart). This game takes a more interesting route and makes the racing require much more skill. While the vehicles are on a track, they control much more like aircraft. Pitch and strafe come into play making you think about many more dimensions while speeding down the track and super sonic speeds.  There is a nice upgrade system so you can tweak each vehicle to your liking. Add in some strategic boosting and now you are having to actually think will racing.10/10 hyper boost, will boost again.

_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is a major improvement over the first game. Graphics have improved, but are still simple enough to run at higher settings and achieve high fps.The controls remain largely the same, and I vastly prefer the new loadout system over the module system in the first game. The addition of assists also help a lot if you are new to the game or need to get back into the groove; a very much welcome feature. I also really like the rewind feature, which is very similar to Forza's but actually better. Gameplay has actually been improved a solid amount and the tutorial levels are very helpful. If you don't have Redout but are interested in getting into the series, I would honestly just start with Redout 2; unless of course you are an anti-grav racer nerd, the first game still has lots to love. I really don't have anything bad to say about the game. Any gripes I have could easily be rebutted with "git gud." At it's core, this is a very hard game. Even on the easier difficulties it manages to have a high difficulty curve thanks to the complex controls and wicked speed; and when you crank up the AI difficulty, it becomes even harder. Even on the easiest AI setting where you can breeze through races with little effort, some other game modes require a lot of skill and mastery of the game mechanics. Time trial levels are very difficult to take gold medals in, and I have yet to even get bronze in any of the Speed trials. Personally, I am not a huge fan of the soundtrack this time around. Don't get me wrong, the soundtrack is great and very fitting for the pace and style; but something about it feels off compared to Redout 1's soundtrack. I also find it somewhat comical and disappointing that they use Dance with the Dead in the marketing, but only have one of their songs on the soundtrack...I'd probably like the soundtrack more if there was more Dance with the Dead, lol. Overall I highly recommend the Redout series to fans of Wipeout, Ballistic NG, F-Zero, and other anti-grav racers. It is absolutely worth the price, and if the first game is anything to go by, the DLC will keep coming for a while and always be top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long-time fan of AGR games and have several hundred hours across the F-Zero franchise and Redout. I have waited patiently for this game to be released while 34 Big Things continued to put out garbage like Space Assault and for the money I spent, I am a very happy customer.I am very much in love with the meat of the game. It FEELS fast, smooth, and real. It looks beautiful on my medium graphics setup and doesn't lag much if at all. The soundtrack, though less listenable as standalone songs compared to this game, works better with the active mixing system and is very immersive. Several changes from the first game, including the reworked boost system, removal of power-ups, and vehicles that are more similar stat-wise have removed uselsss mechanics and put emphasis on the inherent high-risk/high-reward concept of AGR. The skill floor has been increases albeit a bit too much at the beginning of the game. The skill ceiling seems so high that no one can reach it (this is a good thing unless you are a casual gamer). This may be the greatest AGR game of all time after some fine-tuning.That said, currently I believe that the goals of nearly half of the events in the campaign I have played so far are unrealistic and generally not possible without making over a dozen attempts at each individual event. The gold-level goals for speed trials, time attacks, and qualifying rounds are just too much to ask for. Some events want you to qualify in at least first place so that you can unlock a cosmetic item, but give you a time that not even the AI can come close to when they actually race you on the same track. I'm just wondering where they came up with the numbers. In races, the AI you play against seems to inconsistently play much better than you or allow you to win. They clearly rubber-band if you start to accumulate a nice lead in most instances. There is even one track where they crash at a specific spot seemingly on purpose then respawn several KM ahead of you. They are also not subject to the same rules you are. If they crash on an arena race, they respawn. You don't. The campaign feels grindy so unless you are in love with the game like I am, it may feel like a slog.In short, the game succeeds at what it needs to, and has its work cut out for it in order for it to be optimized and more accessible not just to new players but veterans such as myself. I am getting my ass kicked in good ways and bad ways. I would have payed way more than 30 bucks for this game. I will buy the OSTs and any DLCs as soon as they become available. 34 Big Things can go far picking up where Nintendo left off if they stay on track (please make another attempt at Space Assault and don't make it a mobile game, that is not what your fans want).Go fast.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to Redout 1 this game is lacking in every single department except graphics (it looks gorgeous).Music is forgettable. _childDocuments_.review: First 2 hours gameplay impressions in brief:The game is incredible. Coming from a huge AGR fan and one who placed Redout 1 at the top of the AGR list (yes even on top of WipeOut Fury and F-Zero GX etc), I think Redout 2 is worthy of stealing the no.1 place from Redout 1, but I'm going to give it time to see how progression goes in the game. Otherwise everything feels much better than R1.It starts off a lot faster, tracks are a lot better, sounds are better, a few more ship classes which are nice, some classes like Conqueror/Koeniggsworth feel very flexible to use now, Lunare is not longer the go-to noob ship, new boosting system is based on heat, and then when heat it maxed it takes away from your hull health, but you don't have to wait to keep boosting, you just have to keep your ship cool, there's a LOT of career events, you can play with all the ships without customisation in Arcade mode, but you start with only ESA-AGR on the Career and have to build it up slowly as you go.Responding to the negative reviews about difficulty: if you learn to control the ship properly and manage your boosts, you wouldn't have 'rubber-banding' issues. There is not rubber banding, it's that the ships behind you will boost to get in front of you, and you can do the exact same... just outplay them, otherwise there's no shame in putting the difficulty down, unless you're going to publicly complain about rubber-banding which doesn't exist in the game. Higher difficulty = better AI management of boosts.In proper criticism of the game, Tartarus Tantulus and Ixion need reworks. These levels prevent the players from performing at their peaks due to some misplaced boost pads which throw the race instead of helping it, and ridiculous jumps on Ixion which are severely affected by sidewards gravity, but the player must somehow fly straight. I've died trying that jump about 90% of the tries. Otherwise, the tracks are amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a confusing, frustrating mess that punishes you for mistakes, and also has technical issues.The first problem I ran into is that at the default settings the game constantly stutters and hitches. This was resolved by setting the quality to low, and I suspect it has to do with asset streaming but stuttering should never happen in a high-speed racer.The second major issue is with track design, which is that the jumps are terrible. As the tracks get harder, there are more frequent and harder to land jumps. Often it is difficult to even figure out which piece of track you are supposed to land on, and air control of the vehicle is somewhat tricky. Often the hardest jumps happen near the end of the track, so it is hard to practice them, and they just kill you.The third major issue is that the controls are too complicated. You have to use both joysticks and the d-pad to steer the ship. For some reason there are two boost buttons (small and big boost). For the most part to turn a direction you push both joysticks in that direction. Does this add anything beyond pushing one joystick?

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is great, and I'm having fun. If you watch the late, great Totalbiscuit's video on the first game, most of it still applies here.BUTI have a two minor gripes and one major gripe.1. The soundtrack isn't as good as the OST from the first Redout. I'm no music critic, so I can't quite put my finger on it. I just prefer Aram Shahbiazians' work.2. The original Redout gave you a better feeling of speed. I'm fairly certain it's an issue of track design and decoration. Redout 1 had lots of repeating objects at regular intervals next to the track. Redout 2 has those as well, but I find them less noticeable.My major gripe a rare but severe camera glitch. I can't quite replicate it, but, under the right circumstances, my camera will start cycling through the different points of view. You don't need to be a Lewis Hamilton if you want to overcome this glitch, but it definitely raises the skill threshold for a good race. This is especially bad if you're trying to learn a new track.Don't let my review scare you if you're interested in picking up Redout 2. If you're new to the franchise or AG racing itself, you may get more enjoyment out of the first game. If you've already played the first game, or you're looking for a challenge, I can't recommend Redout 2 highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually exciting, audibly visceral, mentally taxing, and a great challenge. Unlike the first Redout, which demanded a focus on planning your cornering and pitching to keep your careering craft from smashing into a wall or flying off the track, this game focuses on playing chicken with your ship's health by constantly pushing your boost to its max, mainly due to what feels like a kind of wind drag effect that requires you to constantly boost to keep from slowing to terminal velocity in a way that reminds me of the one thing that bugged me in Wipeout Omega Collection when you were maxing out your speed down the vertical drop on Empire Climb. This makes the game feel completely different to the first one, leaving me exhausted after a session as though I've been riding a motorcycle with an open-face helmet all day, unlike the first game, which left me exhausted in a more adrenaline-dump kind of way, like after getting off a rollercoaster, or how I imagine one would feel after careering down an ice tube in a bobsled. Steering feels more forgiving in this one, while jumps are more difficult, with some requiring you to use boost just to make it. Blind corners are as frequent as before, so memorization is key. The learning curve can be steep for non AG racers, or non-Redout players, but once you master the controls, and realize that some events will need revisiting later with upgraded ships to be fully completed, it's a super-satisfying challenge. The campaign is looooooooooooong, and upgrades, liveries, and ships get drip-fed to you one event at a time.  Sound is bigger in this one, there's so much going on, and the effects are really satisfying, with engine and boost sounds whining and whooshing convincingly. Music serves its purpose well, with some great thumpers and aggressive tunes that keep you on edge, which fits in with the general theme of the game. However, it's taken more of a back seat this time, and doesn't reach the epic and memorable heights of the first, which, let's face it, would be really hard to pull of a second time in a row. In summary, the game's an absolute blast. If you go in expecting the same experience as Redout, you could be initially disappointed, but keep at it and it'll keep growing on you.

_childDocuments_.review: After having put 200 some hours into the first Redout game, and already having put a bunch of hours into Redout 2 (65 hours at time of Review), I can say with certainty that Redout 2 is the greatest AG Racer ever made, and lives up to the series tagline, going FASTER THAN EVER! The controls feel fantastic, the environments are diverse and beautiful, and the original's sense of speed has truly been topped. I'm currently playing on an outdated PC that struggles to run the game (and technically doesn't meet minimum requirements) and I'm STILL having fun with it! (I'll update this review once my computer is upgraded and I get to see the game in its full glory!)UPDATE: After upgrading my PC, the game is even better than before. It's beautiful, and runs spectacularly well. I would recommend it even more now!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel many of the complaints about this game are a bit overstated because there is definitely more good than bad.  Easily the best antigrav racer on the market with it's fair share of bugs and annoyances.pros: - controls, streamlined mechanics, and increased variety in ship performance and upgrades make this game wonderful if you want your ship your way.  However they take some time to unlock.  Campaign is tough-tracks have ditched the portal system and instead opted for branching circuits similar to Extreme G 2.  each track has 3 circuits + a boss mode which combines all three circuits into one gigantic lap.  this allows for more focused and crazy sections of racing, which is aided by direct callouts for incoming elements.  - the campaign mode is hard, but incredibly lengthy, allowing for varied events with unlocks aplenty.  cons:-few bugs, some really bad, but sure to be addressed in a future patch (few bad colliders)-some track elements are almost too crazy, meaning you'll need some memorization, practice, and plenty of rewinds to get though them safely.- music is pretty forgettable minus a handful of licensed tracks.  Wish there were more inspiration for music based on the fun of the first game.- ♥♥♥♥ SPEED EVENTS.  in their current state they are nigh impossible to place.  they need an entire rework.- unlock progression a bit too slow, with many ships hidden behind multiple racing speed classes.  10 hours in and only four ships have been unlocked for me so far.overall mostly recommended.  thing to remember is with this type of antigrav racer, it's niche because it's less approachable than many other games.  It's hard and gnarly by design so prepare for a fight.  That said, if antigrav racing is your thing, it's hard to find anything else that comes close.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: While the criticisms of my original text below still apply, honestly, I'm changing this to a positive review after seeing the post about wresting the rights away from the publisher. Good for 34bigthings. Explains a lot about the game.Man, the more I play this game the more it makes me want to just play the original Redout. There's a lot done right here: controls are generally better, game runs better, game balance isn't Lunare City. However the new music is awful, the career mode's a slog even more than Redout, and most of the tracks are just boring. The latter is a clear consequence of having to make every track reversible for padding purposes...sigh. Also, what the hell is wrong with the flight controls? I don't want to necessarily put that in the negative bin because I might be missing something, but boy howdy does it not feel intuitive or responsive...like, it's based on setting up the jump in advance instead of having air control like the previous game.I don't entirely dislike the game--it does feel good in the moment here and there--but I'm struggling to recommend something that I can't say much good about. Moving away from Aram Jean Shahbazians and Nils Iver Holtar was a mistake. This trance music is about as appealing as eating paste.[EDIT: fixed a typo]

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say this AG-Racer is absolutely ballerI love how challenging the track itself is within Redout 2. A lot of people with negative reviews bring up how the game has a lot of blind turns and turns with no borders which makes you spin off the track. But I'll let you in on a little secret... you're not supposed to be hitting track borders in the first place as it makes you loose speed. You'll usually hit a blind turn once or twice and then you'll instantly know how to turn. That and the game actively notifies you on which bends or turns are coming up next, so I wouldn't quite say they're completely blind turns. This comes with almost everything in Redout 2, like the jumps people complain about. And if people are so hell-bent on completing it first-try, then there's a VERY generous rewind system.The game has an emphasis on boosting, as with Redout 1 (but to more of a degree than the first). A lot of people take displeasure in it since it's the meta. But for me, this only contributes to the sheer amount of speed I feel on straightaways and other spaces on the track where I can fit my turbo in. Next is the difficulty. A lot of people say the game has no chill when it comes to the difficulty. And all I gotta say is... what? I do not get people's issues with the difficulties with the game as I'm often finishing at 1st with either over a kilometer (it seems much bigger than it actually is) or finishing with a good few seconds. All I gotta say with this one is skill issue, especially since it's a twin stick racer (steer and strafe) that can be complex to control sometimes.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal game and damn near almost flawless. If you've been waiting for another game like F-Zero this is it. Every course is brilliantly crafted and every car looks exceptional. I don't have enough adjectives to throw at this game, it really is that good.  The only aspect of this game that I don't like are the speed challenges. You're supposed to drive as cleanly and as fast as possible to rack up as many points as you can. The issue is that the threshold for success is far too high and the ramp up in difficulty is jarring especially when you absolutely demolish the competition in a previous race of the same skill level. It's quite disheartening too as some of these speed challenges house either valuable rewards or act as a barrier to progress. If you have the patience, you just have to "git gud", but I do hope that the devs reevaluate these speed challenges. The curve in difficulty, especially in early in the game, is far too steep. Other than that this game is the best racing experience I ever had. The sense of speed and the rush you get hitting those well timed boosts and jumps is unparalleled. The fact that a small team can achieve something like this speaks volumes for 34BigThings. All of my praise goes towards this studio.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, Redout 2 unapologetically demands that you git gud.  There is a lot of nuance in moment to moment gameplay.  Track knowledge and understanding how best to leverage your chosen vehicle are critical to success.You will almost certainly be running the same event a couple times as you learn the racing lines and best places to boost.  If that doesn't appeal to you, probably stay away.If that does appeal to you, I can't think of another racing game that will give you the same sense of speed or satisfaction when you're in the groove and performing well.  Blasting through a section at full speed that was previously giving you trouble is extremely satisfying.  It is a game where a primary source of fun is seeing yourself improve and pushing your limits to perform a little bit better the next time.There's a few bugs (some of which are major) and some features yet to be implemented so it wouldn't hurt to hold off for some additional updates.  Even its current state though, the game warrants your attention if it sounds like a style of game you would enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get this out of the way, this game is both the most accessible and the least accessible game in the Redout series. How so? There's tutorials for each aspect of the game... but most of it is stuff you'll be exposed to before the tutorial is unlocked. You'll encounter things like how the temperature of each location affects the heat buildup and heat dissipation of your boost meter. Furthermore, you'll run into how different terrain types and gravity affects your vehicle's handling. You'll get familiar with these before the game ever explains them to you and, for the record, I've yet to unlock these tutorials myself at the time of writing this. I thankfully already knew about that stuff, and more, going into the game because of the videos that I watched.So, yeah, that's why I say the game is both fairly accessible but also not very accessible to new players. How many games have you honestly played that explained important to know mechanics far after they came into use? Typically, at the latest, they'll do so when you first encounter them... if they do so at all. Figuring things out on your own is a great feeling I'll admit but when a game has a tutorial system and fails to utilize it well then that's a big problem.Other than that, this is a legitimately challenging racing game even if some parts I'd say the developers went too far in that regard but that's a 'me' problem right there. If you want to grab the game anyways then go right ahead. Just be mindful that not everything you need to know, outside of the basics, are explained when they need to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Note: They've already patched the difficulty in the tutorial that many users mentioned. I don't like racing games because I suck at them. I love this game though and I think the reason why is based on how the vehicles control. See, I play flight simulators, space simulators, arcade flight games, etc. And with a few changes to the control scheme they control like a fighter jet in Ace Combat. Cars are hard to control with a controller I have found but not jets, while I don't use a HOTAS (I don't think you can or would want to) it still follows the same logic that I have mastered throughout these games. Pitch, Yaw, Roll, left and right rudders (game calls it strafing) etc. Thought the game holds you to the track except in some instances where you fly (think mario kart where the glider initiates). Once I realized that they control this way I fell in love.Oh, also the graphics are great, the music is amazing and the tracks are beautiful. The track introductions are so relaxing and this really is a "sit back and enjoy the ride" kind of experience. Fun races and fun trial modes. I am hooked.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the original Redout, Redout 2 is an excellent antigrav racer. It's different from the wipeout series in that you don't aggressively turn with air-breaks, rather you can turn and strafe.Comparing to the first game it has a way more fleshed out career mode, it might seem slow at first, but it definitely gives you a lot of building variety as you keep playing. The difficulty can be mitigated a lot by skipping events and coming back later with a more specialized build.The jumps and tracks have gotten a bit harder but the difficulty, assist mode settings and tutorials are excellent.Visuals are different to the average antigrav racer, less grounded in reality but instead everything dialed up to 11.Colours are vibrant and the soundtrack absolute bangers throughout, just like the first game.Lastly, you can gamble your health to boost more, absolutely amazing mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Overall very good racing game. I didn't have a issue with the beginning trials as other people said they had, I just played the trials and completed them on the first go. My only dislike with the game is the time attack and speed game modes in career; THE TIME TO BEAT IS INSANE FOR TIME ATTACK to me at least 1:35:997. And you never know what the time to beat before hand, it only shows after you finish the race. That 1:35:997 is all i ever saw for time attack and of course its always on the most annoying type of map to race on, odd turns, boost near sharp turns that you'll wall bang on etc. Speed is nearly the same thing, as far as the map selected goes. Now the racing is where this game feels most rewarding, aside from a few maps that have jumps ( too short of a jump you'll crash, too long of a jump hmmm you'll crash, you think you landed the jump...nope just missed it...good thing for that rewind feature) or no railings which lead off the map for you to crash and burn. Not every race level is like that from my time playing, but they are there. Ah yes the racing, it is pure fun. Everything just flows right, the level design, the speed, it all blends very nicely. I wish i could praise the other modes in the career mode like this but they are annoying to say the least. This isn't my go to type of racing game ( I mainly play console for racing) but this is really good, if they can update the time attack and maybe the speed modes in career to favor better maps more suited for the cause i believe it will be even more enjoyable experience ( or remove those crazy 1:35:997 run times, I have always came in at 1:40 and some ) The bots for the most part aren't a problem, but they seem to be rocking upgrades before you even earn 1. And some of the early goodies to upgrade or customize your ship are locked behind ( you guessed it) the time attack or speed modes in career Yayyyy. If you like this type of racing, it's a really good choice to select and add to your collection. I don't know what PC specs you're rocking but if you don't meet the requirements maybe pass on this game until you can upgrade for a more enjoyable experience. <MSI GS76 Stealth, 2070, I9>

_childDocuments_.review: ANOTHER EDIT: THIS GAME HAS BEEN UPDATED SINCE I POSTED THIS REVIEW, AND IT IS A LOT BETTER NOW. Still not recommended for those who are easily frustrated, but a lot of the issues i mentioned in this review has been solved.I can't give a complete recommendation, it's fun to play once you get used to the controls and how fast the game actually is, however, i can't give a full recommendation until something is done about the difficulty of the Time Attack challenges and the Speed challenges. They're way too high and too difficult to achieve, even at the very start of the game. Sometimes landing on the wrong track or too far on the right one as intended will have you fall right through the track. It's good when preventing cuts, but it's very frustrating when trying to land normally.Edit: Okay, i played through the game a bit more. Again, it's not that bad, but it can be better.First off, the campaign is LONG. About 1,449 stars are there to collect over 5 chapters. For reference, each race can earn you 4 stars. 3 stars for finishing first, and one additional star for completing a certain objective like reaching a certain speed. As i write this now, i have finally unlocked the 5th and final chapter, AKA the SRRL Invitational. If you want to receive every part in the game, every ship part and livery, good luck. All of that is locked behind super long campaign, and you will have to 4 star everything to unlock everything. Currently, i don't think anyone has done that, and i wouldn't be surprised if i was right, because there is a HUGE difficulty spike right at the beginning of the game with the Speed challenges and the Time Attack challenges, which do not scale with difficulty and is extremely hard when you encounter them for the first time.I guess a part of me is still waiting for a patch to fix those challenges, but until then, i still can't give a complete recommendation.Some of the positive things about this game are: the handling, which is hell of a lot easier to control over the first Redout, and the music, which is actually really good. Redout 2 is a mixture between F-Zero and Motorstorm with an extreme sense of speed and a huge difficulty spike and is a hella well made game for an indie game. If you like anti-gravity racing at a really high speed, this game would be for you. But it's not for those who are easily frustrated.EDIT: THIS GAME HAS BEEN UPDATED SINCE I POSTED THIS REVIEW, AND IT IS A LOT BETTER NOW.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a negative review, but I wanna start by saying that I really enjoy this game. This is a style of game I love and it checks almost every box exceptionally well. I mean c'mon, why is capitalism still alive in a future with such boundless resources? It's so cartoon-ish that I can't help but laugh. But on to the negatives. The multiplayer is unfinished. 1v1 random matchmaking is un-fun. It leads to players leaving the race as soon as they think they'll lose. Ranked is not yet implemented over a year later. The career mode is extremely tedious and required to unlock parts--parts which only can be used in career mode and have no other purpose. It makes the career mode seem like a waste of time in the grand scheme of things. That's all. The game is great but without solid, completed multiplayer this game is doomed. I hope if they have a ranked mode or multiplayer update coming that they implement it sooner rather than later. Until then I'd suggest you wishlist and follow this and wait for a sale or maybe a big update--fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is fun.I loved the original, and jumping into the sequel feels new and exciting while still being familiar.Only first impression gripes I have are the annoying tutorials, and having the game's assists locked to 'on' before completing the trials and having the reigns handed to you.Plus, many will complain about the boost tutorial..Your health bar is basically an extended boost bar; boosting past full overheat drains your health, but it's encouraged; balancing risk and reward. You can also boost  a hyper boost; which is what the tutorial wants to teach you to do.If you want the old feel of the original Redout, you'll need to turn off the assists (which come automatically enabled) and do some control remapping. The ships will feel grippy and sluggish with the assists pushing and pulling you toward the racing line; but without them, it's the same chaotic energy as the first game.The starting (un-upgraded) ships don't feel slow, but they  handle like crap. You won't be winning many races starting out, since you have no upgrades and your opponents will be better.Too many people have been goaded into this false sense of 'every event must be winnable right off the bat.'Wrong.Racing drivers don't win every single one of their races, it just doesn't work like that.In Redout 2, you have to  advance, upgrade, and return to older races to beat them. This makes winning more satisfying, since it isn't just handed to you on a silver platter.Even on difficult settings in Redout 1, beating the AI always felt stupidly simple (at least to a half-decent player).If anyone is unhappy with the difficulty curve of this new game, just turn the difficulty down to 'chill' and enable all of the assists. I don't understand why adding difficulty to a game is a bad thing, when there are lower options available right off the bat...Personally, and so far, I love the game. It gives you speed, new toys to play with, an interesting boost mechanic that rewards taking risks, and beautiful track designs and environments.Any fans of the original can use the settings to tweak this game to their liking; otherwise, if it's 'too hard' go find something easier to play...

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: If you are new to Redout 2, do not listen to the negative reviews.  Most of the negative reviews are from people who put many hours in to the first Redout.  While that isn't a huge problem, it doesn't give Redout 2 a proper unbias assessment.That being said, I am new to AG and Redout 2 and this game is PHENOMENAL!  As oppose to just Gas, Brake, Steering, and turbo, the game adds more "depth" to racing.  That leads to more engagement when you are racing, which I truly appreciate.  You have to focus when playing Redout 2.Speed This game is very fast and you honestly need to pay attention more so than any other racing game.Career Mode: A lot of people complain about the career mode and I can't understand why.  The career mode is LONG, but that is a good thing.  There is so much to this game, that you shouldn't just jump in to arcade or online mode immediately. _childDocuments_.review: The soundtrack is a straight downgrade from the first game and no amount of balance patches can fix that. Legend of Anxanum was one of the weakest tracks in the prequel and i can tell you that the majority of the soundtrack in Redout 2 actually undercuts it by a long shot. It's mostly just inoffensive, lukewarm, limp wristed drivel that only ever gets you hyped when you pause the game because THEN the game decides to turn up the bass boost to 11, which makes you momentarily believe theres some actual banger going on until you accidentally unpause and its just the same uninspired elevator music as before.Also, so far career mode has been a letdown in terms of player agency (on top of dragging on way too long with same-y events). You get upgrades to your vehicles when you have headroom in terms of class limitations and if you play all events in a row you'll never be in a situation where you wouldn't just slap that new upgrade on your vehicle the literal moment you acquired it.Track design is ... different from the prequel, to say the least. Jump sections don't rotate your AGR towards the landing spot (of which there can be multiple now, anyways) so the whole flying part is not just strafing and pitching anymore but also rotating your vehicle to align yourself properly to the track to get a speed boost. In general, the track design now involves the player way more with the more complex jumps as well as more tight corners that force you to use the brake more, and thats good.Whats not good about track design is that overall, tracks feel less inspired. While playing them is generally way more involved I can't help but notice that there are several sections in every biome that just feel like they needed to add more "stuff" so they just slapped a bunch of random winding curves down and called it a day. This design choice isnt helped by the fact that each biome has 3 courses that all reuse several parts of the whole circuit, because the starting location is always in the same spot.The tracks have also been designed to be driveable in reverse. Reverse tracks are honestly one of the better ideas the devs had here, since they actually feel less same-y than having 3 tracks that share a lot of their design with each other.There are driving aids to help the player with the on screen route notes similar to what you'd expect in a rally game, for instance. But in my opinion those are relatively useless in more situations than not, since they dont take the player's speed into account. On a course that i don't know yet like the back of my hand (which is hampered by the repetitive nature of each biomes 3 courses), boosting makes it so that by the time i actually processed what is showing up at the top of my screen i have probably already rammed myself straight into a wall. So a QoL change that I would welcome is to be given more than just one or two notes based on how fast i am going.I'm not even going to touch on the difficulty of each event because let's be honest, people need to get good and from what ive seen on Redout difficulty (the one before the AI starts to get genuinely stupid, probably with the help of cheating), everything is doable and people just need to focus more.That all being said, there is a lot of things to unpack about this game, but i'll also try to summarize it: The sequel is definitely a continuation of the prequel, that much is for sure. But it is no successor because the word "successor" implies "success", and this game does not succeed redout 1.

_childDocuments_.review: Now, you may notice the developer actually says in the warning they present to let you know they're going to be harvesting data about you, and that if you're under 13 that means they'll be breaking the law when they gather all this information about you (so, if you're under 13 they want you to not play the game to help them avoid doing their law-breaking pastime of spying on children), that there's an opt-out mechanism.   There's no way to opt out of the game and you can't start playing unless you agree to surrender your legal protections over your privacy to Saber Interactive... I'm not even sure about the legality of that, but it's not okay. Redout 2 is a console ported "anti-grav" racer which just means it's an arcade racing game that has loops and other generally non-gravity obeying jumps and stunt sections in it.  Despite being a shallow arcade racer they tried to add some needless convoluted mechanisms like heat management to the game, which comes across as a little schizophrenic as the game doesn't know if it wants to be a dumbed down shallow racer or if it wants to compete with the latest F1 game on the highest difficulty... and neither of these two conflicting states of mind results in a game that's going to appeal to a lot of gamers.  Console peasants won't enjoy anything that involves pressing more than 2 buttons on their console peasant childrens toy controllers, and PC gamers will be annoyed by more console crap polluting the place. Having said that the visuals are pretty good (if needlessly noisy, I guess the console gamers need bright flashing lights to maintain their attention) and the game is optimised okay for a console port, so you could, if you really wanted to, play this while the developer harvests all kinds of interesting, personally identifiable information about you for sale to third parties.  Of course they'll say they don't intend to sell your private data for profit, or profile you, but can you trust them?  If they were trustworthy, They also ask if you would like to link your game to Epic Games (backed by Tencent/CCP) to increase the amount of spying and profiling they can do to you.  They might as well have asked me if I'd like to have bowel cancer.  You don't have to do this, but it makes you wonder what kind of agreement they have with Epic and how much of your data flows to them anyway. As always with console ports, because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.I know a significant portion of my review has been about warning gamers about the privacy risks and concerns associated with this game than the game itself, but those are important considerations.  Developers must not treat gamers like cattle or property as Saber Interactive are doing here. The final reason to avoid this console game is the almost comically insulting pricing.  Redout 2 is the kind of game that would go almost direct to the bargain bins outside the games store in the brick and mortar days, but they've given this pretty much full AAA pricing for what is, at best, a B- game.   Redout 2 has the ridiculous price of $30 USD, plus another $46 in DLC.  That's right, an eye watering $76 if you want to own this complete set of spyware with a simplistic console game wrapped around it.  Jesus wept.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated and incredibly fun racing game.They absolutely nailed the sensation of crazy speed that you want out of an antigrav racer. The tracks are complex and visually impressive. The gameplay is incredibly engaging.However, the skill floor is quite high - you will probably struggle to navigate the tracks at the beginning. Luckily, the game comes with a bunch of ways to make picking it up easier: Playing through the campaign introduces you to the tracks and gradually raises the speed of your ship, letting you work your way up to top speed. There are rally-style turn indicators. There are also highly customizable assists, which are in the game for a good reason. You should not be too proud to use them at the start unless you're prepared to mess up a lot, and some of them always remain useful. You can turn them down as you get used to the game, but if you simply disable all assists and jump straight into arcade mode, you will have a bad time and probably crash every corner/jump. The same goes for your use of the rewind feature, which will save you restarts and frustration from crashing out horribly on the final stretch of a race. The developers clearly put a lot of thought into ways to make the game more approachable and easier to pick up without compromising the skill ceiling.And once you get into it even a little bit, it's incredibly fun. Blasting down a straight, burning up your entire hull in the process and navigating the following turns with your ship integrity at a sliver is an absolute blast. With 10 environments each containing 3 tracks for a total of 30 (without the DLC), plus the combined boss tracks and a reverse version of everything just listed, there is plenty of variety as well.I personally also greatly enjoy the absolutely absurd tidbits of background lore casually delivered to the player through the context of racing, but maybe that's just me.If you like the idea of going very very fast in a videogame, then I highly recommend Redout 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is an amazing experience, more polished than the first Redout, but not necessarily better, rather a different flavor.After playing for a few hours:Music: RedoutTracks: RedoutAtmosphere: RedoutDifficulty: RedoutHandling: Redout 2Races: Redout 2Customization: Redout 2SFX: Redout 2I feel the skill ceiling has been lowered quite a bit, ships have much more grip and durability, tracks are bigger, turns longer, it has been dumbed down, this makes the game generally easier, less frustrating and more accessible (with the exception of jumps, which suck now), which is fine given the first one was hardcore.There are some performance issues, games freezes for a tiny bit quite often and given the Mach 2 fighter jet speeds there would be a lot to gain from higher fps. It doesn't look that much better to justify the big performance cost.Maybe it's just bias but the first one felt more authentic and cohesive, this one feels more commercial, more candy crush.It seems like I'm trashing the game, I love it, I hope they keep working on it. I wish they will go back to a more serious tone for the next one. Keep the gameplay and make the rest grittier, more ships (there are more ship makers now, but less ships), more customization, more tracks, less cringeworthy stuff like the narration.Maan the experience of piloting these things is incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun, feels very much like Redout 1 which was great. Music and sound design are great, game looks nice, feels really fast. Love what they did with the boost system, instead of a boost meter that fills over time that you can spend on little taps or dump the entire bar for a huge boost, they now have a Heat system, where both the standard boost and the mega-boost generate heat. Go over the heat cap and you'll take damage. This is awesome, because now it gives you an incentive to avoid pinging off every wall like in Redout 1, since you can trade health for raw speed. It's now more important to avoid the little chip damage that resets your ship regeneration since it'll cut into your effective boost capacity if you can't heal up. Minor nitpicks though:- The AI feels like it will straight-up stat-check you at several turns. Their ships are rarely maxed out for the rating that you're racing at, but they'll often be sporting upgrades to engine or boost that you don't have access to yet, so they'll just be flat-out faster than you at all times.- Bonus trophy challenges are wildly inconsistent in difficulty. Every 'Time Attack' that requires you to win with a 1-second lead is basically a freebie, as is any 'Race' that requires the fastest lap time; if you win 1st in either of these, you're practically guaranteed the bonus trophy. Any 'Race' that requires a win by 500-1000 meters is a toss-up depending on how badly the rubber-band AI wants to cheat, and which track you're racing on. The 'Finish at x speed' challenges are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though. If I have to do ONE MORE 'Finish at 1250 kph' on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rainbow Forest where they put an S-curve 100 meters before the finish line, I am going to lose my mind. This barely matters for progression but if you're a completionist this is going to piss you off.Overall, very good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This so far is probably one the most challenging AG games I've ever played.That's not to say it isn't merciful either. It's more merciful than Redout 1 IMO with the combination of it's difficulty slider and tools to help control the ship if you don't want to control the roll, strafing, pitch and whatnot. Very considerate!But I'm playing on Redout difficulty and controlling with no help. I want the full experience! That said. The game's got a high learning curve. Moreso than the first one from what I can tell.Not only that, the game wants a lot of your time.... and that's what I've come to love the first game for.The second? To me, is a large improvement.No items. No annoying EMP to disrupt the action. Just tuning up the vehicle with modules you earn, far more style customization, and a beautiful three-tier boost system. Outside of the tuning up, the only way forward is basically just get better at the game, and I love it. It's boost system is a very intense risk versus reward mechanism as well that can simply eat through your health fast if you're not careful.I think my only complaint about this game so far, I'm about 60 hours in, halfway through A-class. Feels like I'm only racing Sulha, Ahkal-tech and Conqueror here. All the others just seem left behind, but I'm hoping that changes over time! It doesn't go against my bias though, I'm a Sulha fan. I like rockets on my rockets, simple as that. (Edit: Good news, almost 100 hours in now, seeing other companies again. That was fast!)And to end on a higher note- The OST. Not everyone seems to agree, and that's fine. I regularly listen to both Redout 1 and 2's soundtrack back to back, but I am a little more biased to 2. To me, it's got more variety. While still maintaining a mostly trance focus like the first game, but when it does diverge from that... it's all Zardonic EMD from there. Literally. And this game is the reason I'm a Zardonic fan now.I'm hoping the DLC's ost will be released on steam sometime though. Gods I love those songs just as much as the main game.It's definitely different from the first game, that's for certain. It's easy to see why some decisions are even a bit divisive. But fortunately, I exist on the end of the player base that considers this an improvement instead of the opposite.I hope this isn't the end of support for this game! I'd love to be taking for a ride through DLC like I was through Redout 1! Because as it stands, Redout 1 would be my favorite AG racing game and racing game in GENERAL, if they didn't make this one!Don't leave us, 34bigthings! You've created a beautiful piece of work here! I only hope it's sales numbers go up like it deserves!
