_childDocuments_.review: Rode its way to one of my favorite games in the series. Instead of Kazuma Kiryu and modern yakuza this game follows the story of Sakamoto Ryoma and the shinsengumi during the bakumatsu era. You can still expect everything from this game you would find in a mainline title, from the many weird but funny moments to an actually good story which puts its own twist onto the story of Sakamoto Ryoma. Although the characters share the appearance and some character traits from the characters we know and love they are still different people with their own goals and motivations, which I all found to be interesting and entertaining. I also recommend reading about Sakamoto Ryoma, the actual person, a little after finishing the game. It makes the story and some major moments hit much more and really adds to the experience. The game uses the “four style” system again already known from 0 and kiwami. They all feel unique to one another, swordsman giving a well-rounded and heavy hitting kit, gunman offering spammy distance fighting and wild dancer a very fast mix of both with a wild set of moves. The only style feeling very lackluster is brawler. I basically only used that style for the tiger drop, but other styles offer similar moves with better damage because the damage in brawler is not affected by the gear system which makes the other styles much stronger. The gear system allows crafting of swords, guns, armor and other special weapons. Some of these weapons bring special abilities like elemental damage or life steal with them, which made experimenting with different weapons and armors fun. I really wish there were gloves or something like that to make the brawler style stronger and usable. The only negative of this system and for me in the entire game is the grinding. I basically save scummed to farm money because the higher tier gear would have taken hours of farming to get otherwise. And that still requires farming the necessary materials from the battle dungeons which aren’t guaranteed, meaning you must play the same missions over and over again just to get these materials.       The game also offers a ton of side content again ranging from small things like the karaoke (search for “ishin truehearted samurai”, thank me later) or fishing to bigger things like the farm management and the battle dungeons. The card system was fun to use too, offering a lot of abilities to mess around with but also some really strong ones like the time slow.All in all, I hope they remaster kenzan too if it gets the same quality treatment as this.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin is definitely one of the more controversial titles within the Yakuza series with the weird transition into the unreal engine which is a first in the series (and probably last), along with adding the Trooper Cards system into the rest of the game which a lot of fans were skeptical with that decision to say the least. However, what do I think? I think that this game is a new personal favorite in the franchise for me.Gameplay - Now if the idea of a samurai wild west gunslinger strikes as exciting for you, it pretty much is. The whole concept of it is exciting but it plays so damn well. You get introduced to the 4 combat styles of the game being fists (for parrying/defense), swordsman (burst dps), gunslinger (ranged dps/heat generator), and wild dancer which is the best style in the game and even upon its nerf its still so damn good. Now using these styles in unison was confusing at first, especially when a style is just both the 2 styles mixed together (sword and gun = wild dancer), but each style has its own situational use, and when you finally get the flow and muscle memory of the styles down you glide and navigate through combat like a trained killer. All the styles felt fleshed out and useful, even if the unarmed fist style did feel super weak on damage even fully maxed. You are also able to equip additional weapons from the skill tree of the styles like spears, odachis, and a cannon. They aren't as fleshed out as the main styles but they were still fun to mess around with in random street fights.Trooper System - After a few chapters of getting used to your stock styles, you will get access to the trooper system. Basically you will be able to activate different cards in fights that give you abilities. This system before was only usable in the dungeons side content of the game, but has been expanded upon and made available throughout the entire story, in fact even bosses can use these insane powers. Now, understandably a lot of players don't like the inclusion of this system in the rest of the game, but for players who have played the original this is definitely some much needed spice to the gameplay. For many this is their first experience of Ishin, and I think the game would of benefited from having the trooper card inclusion be accessible in new game + or the Ishin difficulty or just an option to toggle on or off. It didn't ruin my enjoyment, mainly because I have the original game so that could definitely give me a bias here so take that with a grain of salt.Setting - It's great taking a break from Kamurocho and the modern setting of the Yakuza games, and the new location for this game being Kyo is definitely hitting for me. I have to place Kyo as one of my my personal favorite locations in the series next to Okinawa from Yakuza 3 and of course the iconic Tokyo streets of Kamurocho. Kyo for me is a totally fresh take on what we have seen in the series thus far. Its a completely different Japan set at the end of the Edo period in the 1860s. The environment changes in different sections of the map, whether you are in the bustling streets of Rakunai, the markets and riverbay of Fushimi, or my personal favorite location, the bandit city of Mukurogai. Everything just looks so damn nice, especially in the Unreal Engine. The shadows and lighting is the best in this game compared to the other releases and honestly I wouldn't mind another game in the unreal engine. Don't get me wrong, the dragon engine is probably my most favorite engine in gaming period, however to see the devs go back from time to time into their old game design to recapture the original game is a nice and much needed breath of fresh air. Minigames - My favorite part of these games are the side content to lose yourself in, and where to start? Karaoke is rebranded as the "singing bar" since karaoke didnt exist yet time wise and Ishin's line up of songs are another reason to just give this game an install. I love me my dancing mini games since they never seem to miss and Ishin even has that with Buyo dancing (fan dancing). Sounds lame but trust me you will need to be on your toes on the higher difficulties. You have chicken racing which was my favorite way to make money in this game, and really is going to be your bread and butter for the grinding sections of the game and oh boy I have section on that, that's how bad it is. Then the hostess mini game is replaced with the courtesan games. You basically play 3 different mini games with a courtesan, one being sake showdown (a drinking game), rock paper scissors, and then finally sensual healing which is a sex bullet heal mini game and my god is it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard. I would definitely have to say the asura mode on the sex mini game gave me the most trouble in my completion like what the hell I was not expecting that much trouble and bottlenecking from the sex mini game of all side content.Another Life - The big mini game of Ishin is titled "Another Life". Its Yakuza's take on a slice of life where you farm, take car of your house/pets, cook, and even sell the before mentioned items off like the stuff you cook or your produce. The money you can make accumulates over time with the more and more orders you put out, but honestly I just had myself coming here to take off stress from the grinding and just relaxing because they definitely nailed that aesthetic. Really for the money you are just better off with the Chicken Racing mini game but i'm still happy for this whole mode's inclusion, was super fun.The Grind - Now this had to be a whole section of its own. Yakuza games can be a little grindy here and there. Especially if you focus on crafting or completion, but its usually not THIS GRINDY. In this game you grind for everything. Need troopers? Gotta spin the gacha mechanic case opening that can drop 1 of 400 troopers. Need materials for grinding? Perfect, which material because there are 4 other sub categories of which supply you are looking for (seafood, produce, etc.).  Need materials for another life? Go grind the 4 different fishing spots for the unique fish, aswell as wait on the farming timer for your crops.  Need a specific high grade material? Its either random world drop, or farm the specific dungeon for a chance at it dropping, and of course the worst part had to be crafting weapons and gear. Which I say with a heavy heart because that was what peaked my interest in the combat of the game to begin with. All these cool different pieces of gear, fully modeled, performing different things, whole seals giving you a chance to socket a bunch of neat stats to optimize the gear. Like, that all sounded so sick. Until you actually start trying to gear up and you realize the big problem which is the resource sink. Even fully upgrading your blacksmith (which gets you a reduced rate of money/materials spent on gear), you are still sinking tons and tons of money and materials into these weapons. There is a whole section, and mechanic for the gun style that has you swapping out different ammunition types that play super fun like flash bullets that daze the enemy, lightning bullets that stun, poison that adds a DoT to the target, etc. But, these cost so much just to fire 30 OF THEM (which is as much as you can craft in a max stack), like that goes away quick on a maxed out gun. So I couldn't really get experimental without having to shave away hours grinding for more mats and money just for all of that to be spent on merely an hour of shooting off the thing. It just was not worth it. Its true that you can completely ignore the crafting section of the game since story missions give you upgrades on items nonetheless, but this is still a big part of the game, and a big part that could help you not struggle as much in fights.Other from those gripes, the story, the gameplay, the world of Ishin is phenomenal and even know this remake hiccups here and there I do still think this is worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking for a while about how to review this game because I think it's not that easy. It's a good game and a good Yakuza game, but there's some things that bothered me during my playthrough. If I had to answer "should you buy this game", I'd say yes, but wait for a sale, and if not, only if you like the era it's set in or if you're a Yakuza fan as is. I'll let just give a list of things that I think it did well and it didn't do well.The good:- The atmosphere is great as is always the case with Yakuza and Judgment games, the map is pretty good and exploring is rewarded with finding substories or content in general- The game runs well, I know I've read that others have had issues with the port but it ran flawlessly on my computer- A lot of the characters are from previous Yakuza games, I think it's a cool nod to fans of the series but new players also won't feel like they're out of place- The cinematics look great as usual, they felt like a reward sometimes for how well they're madeThe meh:- The combat didn't feel nearly as good as in most other Yakuza or Judgment titles. For reference, I played on hard. The styles didn't feel cohesive at all in my opinion. There's four styles which are Wild Dancer, Swordsman, Gunman (I think it was called?), and Brawler. Wild Dancer is your "AoE" style, but honestly once I made it past the early game it felt a bit underwhelming, I just found myself using the same simple move set in it. Gunman felt, outside of it being used for special ammunition, like it was just a cheese style to shoot enemies from far away, but I also didn't put many points in it so I don't know if it gets better late on. Swordsman felt like the most fleshed out of the four and was a fun style to play in, but it also got meh towards the end because again, it just felt like I was using the same move set and the same two heat actions. Brawler felt underwhelming the entire game long and was overall just weak and not fun. I put more points into it towards the end of the game and I still didn't feel like it was fun. Everything I could do in brawler, other styles could go better. Generally I also think switching between styles wasn't fluid and they didn't feel cohesive. It felt like there's little heat action variety. Besides that, I also felt like I spent a lot of time in combat on the floor because everything knocks you down in this game.- The soundtrack wasn't very memorable apart from some iconic ones, the absolute bangers that I am used to from Yakuza games were far and between. I didn't even notice each style had a separate soundtrack because it felt so same-ish to me.- The story felt like it dragged on, towards the end of the game I kind of just wanted it to be over already and be done with the game.- The side content ranges from great to awful. There's some fun side content like the second home feature, but most of it and the heart "side content" (to me at least), the substories, were mostly boring. Most of the side content I tried wasn't very engaging or fun, usually I tried it and left it at that, or if I did it more often, it wasn't very long. I think it's because the combat hindered a lot of enjoyment, for example there's a scarecrow maze thing where you have to destroy scarecrows in a specific style (usually) within a certain amount of time, and I didn't complete too much of it because it felt very clunky.- On the topic of substories, felt like every other substory was turned into a bond (which there's so many of). If I think back to Y0 for example, there's so many memorable substories, but in this game most of them boil down to "give me this item", and then they turn into a bond, which means to finish it, you have to give them an item (sometimes a specific item) five times or something like that. That's just flat out boring and feels like filler content. I mean why are there at least three bonds related to you giving vegetables to someone?- Trooper cards. I'm not sure how I feel about them, I think at first they were pretty fun but they became a thing I didn't even think about much outside of "just using them" fast. They are OK.The bad:- This might just be me being lazy, but this game needed more taxi spots, I had to walk a lot and maybe I'm spoiled from the other games having much easier means of travel- Everything in this game is so clunky and slow. Opening menus, picking things up and so on. It feels so non-responsive and it just wasn't fun to "navigate" the game sometimes, I don't recall it being like this in past gamesI don't think I've ever written such an elaborate review for any Yakuza game, usually I just feel like "yeah, it's more Yakuza but improved from the last game" and I am happy with that, but I didn't feel like that with Ishin, but I do recognise that this game is a port and remake/remaster (?) from a game that's been out for a while. All in all I enjoyed the game, but it's not their best work.

_childDocuments_.review: "Like a Dragon: Ishin!"? More like "Like a Snail: Ishin!" because that's about how fast the game progresses. They should have called it "Like a Dragon: Yawn Edition." This game is a masterclass in how to bore players to tears.The graphics look like they were dragged out of the early 2000s. I half expected to see my old CRT monitor make a comeback just to handle the pixelated horror. And the gameplay – oh, the gameplay – is a sluggish, unresponsive mess that makes you wonder if the developers ever played a video game in their lives.As for the storyline, it’s as if they hired a team of monkeys to bang on typewriters until something resembling a plot emerged. The characters are so wooden they make Pinocchio look lifelike. And the dialogue? I've seen more compelling scripts in infomercials.Combat feels like trying to swim through molasses. The controls are laughably bad, and the camera has a mind of its own, often deciding that walls are more interesting than the actual action. And the bugs – oh boy, the bugs! It's like they programmed them in on purpose for some added comic relief.In short, "Like a Dragon: Ishin!" is a disaster of epic proportions. If you enjoy wasting your time and money, then by all means, dive right in. Otherwise, do yourself a favor and steer clear of this catastrophe.

_childDocuments_.review: I believe this is an incredibly rushed, buggy and (in my opinion) boring game from RGG Studio. If you’ve never played a Yakuza game before, go look at Yakuza 0, Yakuza: Like a Dragon or Judgment, all three of these will scratch a similar gameplay/storytelling itch minus the Edo Japan setting, and are not only great starting points but are also just amazing games. They all have their unique pros and between the three there’s something for everyone. For RGG veterans who absolutely must experience this long anticipated game, I'd recommend you either watch it on YouTube or wait for it to get patched so at least the bugs listed are fixed, then buy the game on sale without the comically useless and scummy DLC in the Digital Deluxe Edition. Otherwise I think you're wasting your money.Review:I'm going to be as objective as possible here, and I really hope you spare a few minutes to this read review before you consider buying the game in its current state. This review is not only , but also a little long.Firstly, this game is incredibly buggy, not unplayable by any means, but I was fed up with it by the end. Multiple times character models would disappear during cutscenes, the cutscene camera would start flashing intensely or go into walls, obscuring what’s on screen. I once had the water textures bug out and obscure the game in all directions and had a boss’s theme play twice simultaneously with delay. This is just the tip of the iceberg for strange occurrences, and I've even had friends whose games crashed on them, which I’ve never heard of happening with any other game by RGG Studio.The game also suffers from many frame drops when displaying blood, when some bosses use their "superpowers" for the first time and in action sequences, which made timing QTEs especially difficult since not a single one of these sequences in the game didn’t have a frame drop or freeze. Another thing I took issue with is the new cast changes leading to very off-putting face movements from characters. The main example I point to is Yamazaki Susumu, whose counterpart is Joon-gi Han. They cast his face over a character who had very unique facial movements. However despite the model change his animations were not adjusted, making his facial animations unnatural and uncanny. This applies to all the new characters who were cast over old faces to a lesser extent as well.Denuvo usage and the scummy DLC practices are very disappointing to see. Many DLC packs are one time purchase, meaning if you lose your save, you must buy the DLC again to use it only one more time. It’s not worth it, and despite buying the Digital Deluxe edition for the Early Access I never once had to use it. Denuvo means you need to play an offline game online, which is questionable at best.Finally, while this is a more objective point than the rest, I found the game to be incredibly tedious. The enemies in this game feel like they have way too much HP, especially if you opt not to play with the Trooper Cards. RGG Studio went on record saying you didn't need to play with the card "superpowers," to enjoy the game since many community members didn't think they fit into the game, but that could not be further from the truth.It also felt difficult to maintain any momentum in this game. A lot of the fun of RGG's combat is about trying to experiment and come up with your own style of gameplay. In Lost Judgment, you had style switching juggle combos, in Yakuza K1 you had to try maximise heat gain while also maintaining max speed with well timed moves and style switches. In comparison, Ishin's styles are all very unbalanced. Brawler does way too little damage, Swordsman is slow even with speed upgrades, Gunman is barely interactive at all and while Wild Dancer hits a decent balance it's limiting to only use this style. Heat actions also lose their impact as they do minimal damage and the more you them the less damage they’ll do. It's a mechanic in most of the other games but it’s especially harsh here. All of these factors lead to an overall underwhelming combat system which makes the game difficult to get through.A lot of these issues are things patches could fix, and I think this game has many positives too. The story is incredible, one of the best by this studio, and that says a lot. Your usual offering of side activities and distractions is here. It’s the blueprint for a solid Yakuza game but held down by horrid performance, weak combat, disgusting DLC practices and a frankly sloppy job from RGG Studio. Their move to Unreal Engine 4 is mostly to blame for poor optimisation and bugs; and the kinks of the original Ishin are still here unimproved because this game is a port from it's original engine to Unreal 4, rather than a ground-up remake like Kiwami 1 and 2.For now, I recommend taking the advice in the TL;DR. I adore RGG Studio, and this review is harsh because I don’t want this to be the future of their games. I still really want to see the other Japanese-only Yakuza games like Kenzan or Black Panther (Kurohyou) get localised through remakes, ports or otherwise. I believe this studio should absolutely be supported; this just isn’t the quality standard I think warrants your support.

_childDocuments_.review: What is there not to like.Its our favorite characters from the Yakuza series put into a feudal japan setting while u slash and beat people to pulp again as Kiryu (Ryoma). Im sure people missed the brawler beat-em up / slasher em up style from the good old Yakuza 1 - 6 games. (i love the rpg style too from LAD dont get me wrong)Seeing Kiryu being a bada** again and still being kind as f*k always make me smile. The game as always starts with the main story build up where u have to follow it to a certain point, but its pretty good and the VA's are top-notch (not dubbed but i feel like playing in English would take away from the experience tbh) .Once u get free reign, u will most likely skip story stuff because in every cram and nooky there is a side-quest. Some are kinda meh, others are surprisingly fun and other times they just make u cry. (yea the game can definitely play with ur heartstrings) The story so far is pretty good, already seen a lot of the familiar faces from the yakuza games and theyre still doing an amazing job. I don't know if its a story everyone will like, i certainly do, but i love the feudal Japan type of thing and there's a glossary for explaining some of the stuff that u might not know what it is/was. The mini-games so far are pretty fun. (Singing, dancing, Udon Chef, chicken races, shogi, chopping wood just to name a few with still a lot more! ) There are 4 different fighting styles each with their own grid, but u will get orbs that u can use on any of the paths. I'm sure eventually if u grind enough u are able to max out all of the grids but obviously its not necessary. I personally enjoy the wild dancer stance (the one with a gun and sword) but u could just play brawler style and never touch a weapon.All in all, i will recommend this game if u are a LAD fan or if u want to play a Feudal Japan setting game with amazing cast and great story.

_childDocuments_.review: Intro starts off with Majima and several others recast characters you know you'll be in a crazy ride from beginning up until the end and there's no exceptions here. If you wish to experience Yakuza series but in a medieval setting with lots of crazy encounters, fighting & non sense situations then hop on in. I'm sure many fans wanted the 4 style system from pre-modern Dragon Engine to be back and they certainly kept its diversity offering us a Yakuza 0 type assortment. There's a clear sight of high effort put into animations and combat as everything is visually pleasing when you cut, shoot or simply rampage through everything that stands in your way. Beautiful environments enveloping medieval looking Kyoto with realistic lighting & shading especially during sunny mornings. Katanas, guns and all the weaponry available are superbly designed with attention to detail to the tiniest component part. Facial animations & textures of characters are massively improved coming back from the original with life-like graphics vastly enhancing the immersion during cutscenes. The choreography is designed like a true masterpiece; every start of a boss fight is pure raw hype that blends near perfect into the in-game combat itself. OST is as always a banger with some comebacks meant for the respective character in their original appearance. Lore itself is displayed purposely to fit 1860s Kyoto and Japan in general, narrative choice is one of true honor or simply dirty deeds and backstabbing just to obtain more power and a higher title in these harsh feudal transitioning times. Don't expect the more contemporary worldliness you have previously encountered in the series, it's vastly meant to be authentic notably for those unfamiliar outside of Japan. The minigames are back and in full force offering everyone something to their preference, be it wildly hilarious or more serious toned. Additionally the trooper card system is welcoming addition for those wishing to bring third party elements stylishly to the table.- character cast quality- extremely diverse combat- feudal japan immersion- voice acting - OST & ambience- ee ja nai ka- bond system overused

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played all the Yakuza games including the original Ishin, it's more than safe to say this is a dreadful remaster. Somehow they thought this game should have the same price as Lost Judgment which is hideous and makes me think they just used a random number generator to generate the price. Just like Y7, this game has a bunch of scammy DLCs which just include half-assed retextures, weapon materials, and finally the god-awful, poorly edited guest cards without even mentioning the cringe fanservice. This is essentially a 9-year-old game repacked on UE (which was its final nail in the coffin) with added microtransactions and it somehow manages to be worse than the original in every single way. Like a Dragon: Ishin! took an absolute nose dive when it comes to quality. Frankly, I refuse to believe some aspects of this game were even quality checked. The only good things about the game I can think of are probably Fly and Affected fight remixes and the fact that the dog follows you now, while when it comes to bad aspects:-Awful AI-The engine itself-Price-DLCs-Laughable lighting (or the lack of it honestly...)-Localization (As someone who knows Japanese I can safely say the Judgments localization teams did a pretty bad job but this is on another level)-Cards-Bosses and their special abilities (Most are just reused card effects)-Brawler absolutely sucks-Spear enemies-Blacksmithing system-Addition of those huge enemies for whatever reason-Fanservice -Hanpeita's recastI'd unironically rather pay the same price for the original Ishin localized on PC than for this. _childDocuments_.review: I'm about 33% through and this is a top tier game in a series full of fantastic games.Fully recommend to newcomers as well as Yakuza fans.Pros:- The combat styles are a ton of fun and once you get the hang of switching between them mid-fight you'll steamroll enemies.- Substories are hilarious and always a highlight of these games. Fantastic comedic writing.- The plot is pretty simple and engaging! I usually lose track of the plot but this one is great.- The minigames (Dancing, serving food) are challenging but fair. - There's a side story (Another Life) where you work on a farm and upgrade the farm. This can be overwhelming at first but once you get into it, its a ton of fun fulfilling orders.- The environment is a lot more entertaining to move through than Yakuza 7's , which I found boring. It's easy to memorize: not too big, not too small.Cons:- The combat system and level ups seem to want you to use the "Heat" mechanic, but it's really hard to generate a lot of Heat, even against the most basic enemies. Previous Yakuza games didn't seem to have this issue.- The weapon crafting/upgrade system is too tedious. It costs a ton of in-game currency and materials for seemingly very little rewards.- Some of the minigames are so much fun that I wish there were MORE of them!- I simply do not understand Mahjong. I've tried to learn it in every Yakuza game and it doesn't click with me.- You can press "Pet the dog" but it doesn't SHOW you petting the dog

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin is a Yakuza spin-off set in a   version of 19th century Japan. I especially like that part of Japanese history where the Shogun one-shots Ryoma with a kamehameha.Ishin has all of the classic Yakuza stuff like the amazing story, the incredibly wacky side content, and the dozens of minigames. It even has karaoke xD! The combat is in the old style and not like the dragon engine games, so that took me some time to get used to again after playing the newer games. It definitely isn't bad though. If you're a fan of the Yakuza series, you obviously gotta play this one too. And even for newcomers, it can be a good entry point because it's unconnected to the main series plot.A tiny negative though is that since all the main characters share likenesses with characters of the main series, you can guess who the bad guys are pretty easily. It's not a major issue by any means though.And another, much bigger negative is that if you buy the deluxe version, the upgrade materials are tied to a single save file. So if you wanna replay the game or more than one person shares the game, you gotta buy the DLC again, which is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid and I dunno wtf Sega and RGG Studio were thinking. This didn't bother me too much but consider it before buying the deluxe edition.

_childDocuments_.review: as a big fan of the yakuza/like a dragon games, this game was alright.1. story was fine. i enjoy a good mystery, but rgg should probably just leave mysteries to judgment and LJ. none of the boss fights really felt that interesting, not even the final boss. 2. gameplay is fun, nothing really too good or bad about it. leveling up and getting upgrades feels slow and can get grindy. the mastery system encourages you to just stick with one or two styles since getting the masteries for all four would take forever. kiryu punches as hard as my (dead) grandma in brawler (only use is the parry), swordsman does a lot of damage but is simply too slow to be effective, gunman is good against normal enemies and completely useless in boss fights, and wild dancer is just broken and the only really useful style. i like how you can master the style but it really just encourages even more grinding.3. another life is cool and what rgg should've done for yakuza 3. it's the only real way to make money in the game so it's kind of mandatory. 4. one thing i actually really liked was the cinematics (dynamic intros and qtes). to be fair, rgg tends to not disappoint in this department, but they were definitely really good in this game in particular. SPOILERS SECTION:overall, its ok. play if you want but you really dont have to.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommendation, if you have put up with the problems of past RGG games or Yakuza titles and don't mind experiencing the same jank again and again then you'll be right at home. The problem I have with this game is more of a long standing issue with RGG and not really the game itself, I'll go more into detail.  Normally I'd give a pass to developers who aren't used to the way western audiences perceive quality, (look to Kagura games library of copy/past JRPGs) but if I can hold lazy western Developers like Rockstar and Bethesda accountable then I can do the same to RGG. Speaking of which, Atlas includes all the DLC as a one package deal for Persona 5, so that you won't have to purchase it seperate or have a "digital deluxe" edition. Food for thought as to where your money should really be going. So why can a Japanese developer who puts out regular bangers get their collective ♥♥♥♥ together for a re-release of their content on a new platform, but RGG doesn't and or can't? (Lets not talk about Persona 3's port lmao)The game itself is pretty good, the performance on older systems is untested and bad, constant stutters when blood is shown or spurted over the ground or surrounding area, makes the game a living hell with combat. The voice acting, while good, starts and ends at cinematics and in game cutscenes, no side-substory voice lines like in Y7. For those who liked Yakuza 7's ENG VO, (not me), say sayonara to that because it's only the JP VO.  The newest update allows for you to reaquire "lost" DLC weapons, no idea if this covers all the DLC weapons and if lost how many times you can reaquire.It's nice to see subtle improvements to the AI but its lost when the AI barrel roll straight through your attacks like you didn't just slash them 1 second ago. I can get stun locked for 5 seconds but for them they shrug it off, very infuriating. Major disappointment in the settings that the cutscenes cannot be set to 60fps, every single Yakuza game that's on Steam at this moment has the option to set cutscenes to be 60fps, why is it different for Ishin? Nobody will ever know but RGG. The 60fps issue extends to the Minimap as well, it stutters when rotating because that's locked to 30fps or lower, extremely weird design choice. Texture loading on a M.2 SSD takes longer than it should, idk if its the way the developers stacked priority within the application itself but Yakuza 7 and Judgements do not have this issue, and those games are using the more newer version of the Dragon Engine. (This actually makes sense because Ishin is running on UE4/UE5 and Unreal Engine games like Fortnite run like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unless you force DirectX11 on the launch settings, which by the way fixes the majority of the stutters, not all unfortunately).Honestly if you're on the fence, just wait until you hear that the game has been updated with fixes. If not, jump on it with a sale because while its fun in the short term, there's a lot of problems with it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this was done on Unreal engine for the remake, but the framework of the game is basically still that early Yakuza 0/Kiwami engine.  Because of this, the Steam port is a bit funny (some of the others have problems as well, like Kiwami and 0's inventory glitches). Switching between the styles to really punch up the flare and flash, and achieve the highest possible performance rating is really fun. _childDocuments_.review: Have you ever considered how a “shot-for-shot” videogame remake would look and play like? Well, now we have the answer – Like a Dragon: Ishin! is, for all intents and purposes, a remake of the 2014 Japanese-only title Ryū ga Gotoku Ishin! (and to avoid confusion the Japanese title of this remake just added Kiwami, just like with previous remakes). But unlike the Yakuza 1 and 2 remakes, this one feels, looks and plays almost exactly the same as the original game did. Is it good? Is it bad? Probably neither, but the result is a pretty cool entry in the Like a Dragon franchise that, however, does feel like it’s from the past in more ways than the setting.Just as with the majority of Like a Dragon titles, this is an open world action adventure title with beat ’em up combat and a cinematic story, where the open world part is not that big but rather dense with events and stories. However, being set in the Bakumatsu era of history of Japan, presumably in 1867 if we align it with real world history it… let’s say “takes inspiration from”, it also prominently features usage of weapons and not just fists or feet. In fact, for the most part this is more of a hack and slash than a beat ’em up title, even though those familiar with combat of the series will quickly adapt to the tweaks and changes.As the original title was made in the period between Yakuza 5 and Yakuza 0, a lot of the design decisions were and still are very close to that period of the franchise. So going from Lost Judgment into Ishin! might not be the smoothest transition. Thankfully, the auto-save and ability to save anytime are here and even though most of the mechanics and concepts are more or less the same as they were in the original version, they were updated to be smoother, more responsive and just easier to enjoy. Although, again, it’s a far cry from just how comfortable and user friendly the latest entries were, with very limited fast travel points, limited inventory and the need to drop items off in the storage, no auto-pickup for items that drop from enemies, slower in and out transition for combat, no way of seeing substories (side content) on the map without a special item… Lots of great quality of life features that the later game added are just not here and you will feel the absence. And also, in my personal opinion, the mini-games for some activities in this entry are pretty bad. Then again, even in newer titles there can be stinkers.I wasn’t joking about “shot-for-shot” remake nature of the game otherwise, however, as despite being completely remade from ground up on Unreal Engine 4, despite changing some of the character looks and voices, despite tweaking the music here and there the presentation and storytelling of the game is exactly the same as in the original. To the point where I have to wonder if the RGG Studio somehow managed to reuse all of their capture work and camera movement from the original game in UE. The only notable change I know about is the absence of one post-credits segment which looked at the events of the game from the modern time perspective, but everything apart from that looks exactly the same, just prettier.Luckily, the lack of story changes doesn’t feel bad as the tale was interesting enough as is. In general, it is a reimagining of the historical events that directly led up to what is now known as the Meiji Restoration and it features fictionalized takes on real historic figures and moments, but all told with the usual Like a Dragon melodramatic flair. If you’re not used to it, some moments can be very frustrating as the characters often make decisions that in real life would feel really dumb, like this game’s Kiryu – Sakamoto Ryōma, who survives through the story just because he’s so honest and idealistic that people can’t help but admire him, even when they should probably kill him instead.And also there are moments, especially the whole ending bit, that are very patriotic in their message to the future people of Japan to keep fighting for the better future, from the perspective of the characters of the era when Japan was on the verge of being colonized by western powers. It’s a bit awkward for me, but at the same time – this is a tale about an extremely important moment in Japanese history so I get where it’s coming from. Especially as a Ukrainian who at times caught myself thinking of direct historic parallels with our history and how we could probably make the game with at least a few similar messages that would feel important today.Nonetheless, the story is good, the characters are fun, most of the gameplay is very good and is both fresh for the series and also pleasantly familiar. The way the leveling up works is really nice and feels surprisingly natural and not grindy. In fact, apart from a lot of the side content, most of the game is far less grindy than what Like a Dragon games from that period of the franchise were and the game is overall less tiring than Lost Judgment even. Plus, since it doesn’t have any connections to the other titles in the franchise, it’s easy to just go in with no extra knowledge and enjoy the game as is.I liked Like a Dragon: Ishin! quite a bit, even if I did feel at times that maybe more things could’ve been remade to fit better with the quality of life features of more recent titles in the series. If you’re going in just for the main story, you’re going to have fun (unless, of course, you somehow hate Japanese history entirely). If you like to 100% these titles, it’s going to get a bit frustrating, but it’s not among the worst entries in that regard either. Honestly, though, I wish to see more Like a Dragon titles from older times, but no need to tie them so directly to real world events, they can happen in the background.

_childDocuments_.review: ~FINISHED THE GAME UPDATE, 02/24/2023~I may very well be in the minority, but my disappointment in this game carried the entire 30 hours and the game is less than the sum of its parts. I honestly didn't enjoy myself as much as I thought I would and this will end up as my least favorite RGG game I've played--yes, even the laughed-at Yakuza 3, which I think had a lot of heart and great points. I didn't hate all of it, and the highs are extremely high, but the lows were far, far too low for me personally. I walked away more annoyed than anything, and that hasn't happened before in this series.I don't have much else to say, so I'll sum it up very quickly: the combat didn't work for me; the gearing system took up too much time, and the reliance on gear didn't gel with me; the story was slow at first, got really interesting, and then completely lost me at the last 1/4. Those are basically the main sticking points (not including my complaint below about this being a so-so remaster).I still recommend this game cuz it did a lot of great things, but maybe wait for a sale. Don't let the cool samurai aesthetic fool you, the crime drama modern era games are far superior in my eyes. ~ORIGINAL 02/21/2023 REVIEW~This is the exact game fans have been clamoring for since 2014 and we finally got... basically the same game from 2 generation ago with a nice coat of paint. I'm enjoying this game just as I expected as Yakuza/Like A Dragon fan and fully expect to beat this game and see a decent chunk of the side stuff. The world is fully realized and fun to explore, side quests can be entertaining, the combat is cathartic and bloody, and the story--while it takes a couple hours to get going--is captivating and well written. This series is one of the few where cutscenes feels like the reward itself, I'm always excited when the frame rate goes to 30 and the mo-cap is in full swing. The graphics are impressive, as usual, especially with the Unreal Engine 4 powering everyone's pores to the max; lighting and texture work are a major highlight, especially the detailed haoris and weapons. But I can't help but feel a pang of disappointment around the whole thing. For starters, as I mentioned earlier, this is same game that was released in 2014, almost literally. Kiwami 2 this is not--this is more in line with Kiwami 1, complete with all the stiffness the series had before the Dragon Engine, for better or worse. I'm in the camp that loves the Dragon Engine despite some combat downgrades, so having an Unreal Engine 4 skin over a PS3 game feels dated off rip. The lack of voice acting for 80% of the game (read: anything not main story) is particularly heart breaking since you know they have the budget and a top class cast. I find myself skipping side quests now thanks to games like The Witcher 3 spoiling me, and I find myself only stopping occasionally when something seems extremely goofy or especially thoughtful or emotional seems to occur. You really start to feel how awkward and cheap it is to not here music nor sound effects during most of this, just the typewriter sound of the text appearing on screen and the occasional grunt. I also find myself missing the seamless exploration of the Dragon Engine games that had no loading screens when entering buildings, getting into fights, etc. Kiryu may've controlled like a bus, but the immersion, for me, more than made up for it. I never fast traveled in those games, but I look for the nearest palanquin in this one. I miss Bus Kiryu. The pacing, too, is disorienting. Realizing what this game is and not what I wanted it to be, I decided to just focus on the story and do the side stuff in a later Yakuza game, like Yakuza 7 that I have yet to finish. But in the first 10 hours or so, be prepared to stop at every alley while Ryouma does his best Kiryu impression and tends to the needs of every man, woman, child, and whimpering animal that stands immobile until approached. As a whole, it's a familiar and mostly exciting formula, but again, it's 2023 and they've already done better. To regress (or rather, choose not to enhance) in so many ways technologically and mechanically effects me a lot more than I thought it would. I typically love older games and their jank, but Yakuza series is huge, storied, and has a LOT of titles. There's a lot I love about this game--the combat, the world, the story, the performances, the exploration, the fact that it feels like a movie cuz all the faces are the same--but the stuff that bothers me really sticks with me, like a splinter under my fingernail.I recommend this game, I really enjoy this game, but I am disappointed. I'm just glad we finally got Ishin in the west, and it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! Follows the same structure as the rest of the Yakuza games, there’s a lot of story and narrative, most of which you can skip if that’s your thing, and there’s an open world to explore as well, in this open world there’s a ton of different activities to complete, from interesting side quests that range from generic to some being pretty interesting in their stories, to other activities involving a set of challenges to complete, like dungeons filled with enemies to defeat, or target practices.There are restaurants, karaoke games, and a sort of different neighbourhoods all with their own unique styles and people; there’s the marginalized areas that are mostly riddled with crime, whilst there are others that are filled with dojos and temples in which to train and interact with a multitude of characters from the main narrative.Overall, it’s a pretty darn good game, but there are issues when it comes to the pacing of the game, and some of the combat, which in a lot of aspects is a step back from other Yakuza games, but I wouldn’t personally say I found it to be bad; the combat here is much more focused, it asks you to choose from four different styles, some that prioritize melee unarmed combat, others that combine your swordsmanship and gunplay, and even one unique one that makes you a master gunman. Generally, these are all fun to use, but you’ll have to make a choice as to what interests you the most to level up and focus on. There are also a ton of different dojos and trainers that are specific to your abilities, so you’ll want to progress their stories in order to get better and better combat skills. In the end you get a new game plus mode which is a staple of the franchise -thankfully-, and there’s even the option to respect your points to prestige them and get better buffs to your core abilities. Definitely recommend this game, but know that it can be quite slow at times, specially at the beginning and with its narrative presentation, but the world, activities, and combat make for it more than enough.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe I'm leaving a negative review on a Like a Dragon game, but what it all comes down to is, after years of goodwill, years of excitement for this story in particular to be localized, too, I went through 40 hours of this game repeatedly saying to myself "okay. Alright. Just hold on, it's gonna pay off eventually". And now I have finished it. And it absolutely didn't! People definitely worked hard on this but a few terrible design decisions likely forced in at a board meeting now very clearly rip open and destroy the gameplay balance in every feasible way.Let's start with the good, the REAL good. Combat animations and impacts are really, really satisfying; the upgrades you get for them make them feel better and better as you learn them, and there just isn't anything like swinging your sword and sweeping around to reach for your gun mid-slash, fire off a shot, slice through your opponents, and sheath your blade just to get right up close and personal and deck that last guy.The music, while strangely missing some of the original tunes in some spots, is superb fanservice with lovely new mixes of classic series tunes, as well as just some lovely atmospheric music overall. I listened to a lot of it before playing this version and I'll sure as heck be listening to it after.Translating a story like this was no easy feat, and they do a wonderful job of immersing you in the setting while also keeping terms that truly don't have any direct translation. It trusts you to understand without just sort of leaving you on your own on that front; many of the cast are returning from other games, and they do a great job. This has an enormous cast to keep track of and yet, though I'll admit I lost track of some names, it's one of the more follow-able bizarre conspiracy plots of this series, and they really do try to wedge in an irreverent take on actual history whenever they can. It's educational in the sense it gets you to go read a book on the things that happened because it very intentionally isn't getting much right, and I think that's fine when you're having fun with it.So why would I come away from this disappointed if it's a tight story, interesting setting, great music, and fantastic combat flow?Because every single facet of that's been kind of broken to bits in the remake. Which it isn't labeled as such, but this IS a remake.The Trooper Card system. Play the Combat Demo and if you aren't sold on it, you won't be. This was formerly for a small portion of Ishin before, but now it's the whole game. I would be lying if I said I wasn't excited to equip Kenny Omega the whole game and hit bosses with the One-Winged Angel, that's very funny, I try to take it in the spirit it's meant, but the problem is twofold.A. These cards were designed for some bonus dungeons. These are still in the game, bearing most of the game's loot drops (more on that later) and they are fantastically boring, bland empty locales bereft of much but enemies and crates.B. The rest of the game is rebalanced for their addition, and by rebalanced I mean all foes are now overpowered until you spam these or start grinding for really OP weapons (which requires the above aimless tunnel wandering). This in particular ruins the tone and flow of the boss battles, where they all now have instant stunlock elemental attacks with... man I don't even care about no explanation, sure, you get magical powers, they might as well, too, but it's just not fun when a fantastic final boss meant to be an exam of every single fighting style you've learned just KO's you again and again not from superior fighting technique, but from becoming Emperor Palpatine and blasting you with unblockable inexplicable Force Lightning dozens of times. It isn't fun. It makes the great big payoffs of each chapter a miserable slog until you press the "let somebody else do it" button and demolish their health bar, undermining *all* the fantastic combat mechanics in the game.Weapons require smithing. Smithing requires resources you find in the empty sad dungeons, and also grinding to increase the level of the Smith. Or just buy something OP on Steam, sure, whatever.The recastings are... notable. Heads sometimes seem clearly stuck on to a different body, particularly during the emergency meetings. A trend in the recastings kind of instantly blows the majority of the plot points and allegiances which is not great.Substories typically involve all manner of wacky bizarro things that make you believe this world you're living in is, well, lived in, by all manner of lovely strange characters. Nine out of ten of them in this game are requests for vegetables that you have to grow in your farming sim which by the way you also get a farm here. Most people in the town will ask you for vegetables. There is a boy next to one of the key locations you'll be returning to whose mom won't let him eat veggies. You can click on him, and then offer him a vegetable. However, due to each line being animated, you cannot actually skip ahead once you do this, so if you'd like to complete the game thoroughly, be prepared for"Oh boy!""Veggie time!"*eating noises**gauge slowly increases*and multiply that by many times for the lady that lost her wallet and the woman that's definitely not using them for the intended purposes and the sumo wrestler that needs to eat to win and the guy looking out over the water thinking a picnic sounds great right now and it's just... tedious.Everything about this fantastic bombastic samurai drama is ground down into .And that's painful.The ending was... such an ending I just uninstalled from there. Should've done it 15 hours in when I wanted to quit then. But now I can say I've played it, and I don't think you have to. (I'm not saying this lightly, either. I liked Dead Souls.)

_childDocuments_.review: - Like A Dragon: Ishin! is a solid entry in the LAD/Yakuza series, but it's far too grindy and its real charm is in its unique historical setting and its real brilliance is actually as a piece of historical fiction most westerners won't get the references to. - In terms of core gameplay: Ishin! is the middle point between Yakuza 5 and Zero, with a fun style switching combat system that's a bit underutilized due to lacking enemy design to hard counter style choices. There's a ton of side content that's fun, including strip Rock, Paper, Scissors that has a catchy-as-heck chant and surprisingly strict timing on the Buyo Dancing mini-game, but also a solid chunk of side content that's WAY too grindy. The "grind out money on the farm to grind out swords to grind out the dungeon to grind out money on the farm" loop starts feeling sisyphean well before the half-way point on any of these progression circles, and you could cut all of these elements in half and the overall game would've been better for it. The other big negative is that RGG Studios was obviously inexperienced with Unreal 4 when they made this, and there are myriad small problems and lacking optimization in this release compared to games they've made with in-house engines and tools. These issues can be tweaked away on PC though, thankfully.What actually makes Ishin! one of the better and unique entries in the LAD franchise is its setting and premise. While there are other games set in historical Japan, few do the Bakumatsu period and even fewer are centered around retelling the story of Sakamoto Ryoma specifically.I didn't know much about the actual history myself until playing the game and when I started looking into the Shinsengumi, the Satcho Alliance, the Ikedaya Assault and other historical events and characters featured over the game's narrative. But once I did, the actual brilliance of how the RGG writers play with the real history to tell a story becomes VASTLY more apparent and interesting. I'm not going to say that Ishin! is on the level of "Pillars of the Earth" or some of the absolute *best* historical fiction out there - it's still a Like A Dragon series game, which comes with series-wide extravagances and touches of complete OVER-THE-TOP-TO-THE-KIWAMI nonsense that's more fun than smart - but many of the twists the game takes with its historical characters are genuinely clever and more interesting the more you know what they're referencing or how they're twisting the real events to fit into the game's fiction. It doesn't go full on Harry Turtledove either, but manages to turns Sakamoto Ryoma into a Forrest Gump of Bakumatsu Japan - in the best sense of what that means. At the end of the day, if you're a Like A Dragon/Yakuza enjoyer, you owe it to yourself to play this one. If you haven't played one before, this makes a decent first entry as it's not (directly) tied into any of the series long lore or character development and is a stand-alone "historical drama" version of those games. And other than Bakeru or until Konami finally releases a full Ganbare Goemon/Mystical Ninja Collection, if you want a fun action game set in the late Edo period of Japan, this is one of, if not the best option here on Steam. Which is to say, this is really the one and only . . . Ryo Ga Gotoku game out there!(I apologize for the 2.7 people who actually understood just how bad that joke is in advance)

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a spin-off of the Yakuza series that takes place in the Bakumatsu era of Japan, and while it's not the most polished yakuza game, it still manages to be a fun experience. Here's my review of the game: After playing Lost Judgment, this game’s combat doesn’t feel as smooth. Parrying doesn't work half the time for some reason. Dodging doesn't always work because some enemies have the wide slash move and they will always hit you no matter how well you time your dodge. Despite the issues described above, the combat styles in the game still manage to be fun in their own way, with "Wild Dancer" being my favorite because of its style and agility. The graphics in this game are beautiful and the attention to detail in the environments is amazing. The world feels alive, and since this is still a „yakuza game", there are plenty of charming substories in which you can partake. The game features a lot of minigames to enjoy, and the voice acting is really good.The soundtrack is amazing, with my favorite song being from where you train at the Ginryu Dojo. Heat actions are dope as always, and the weapons have cool effects that impact combat. However, some people might be turned off by the amount of grinding required for said weapons and equipment. Another thing is the introduction of trooper cards. Some people might hate them because of their unrealistic nature in gameplay, but I think they are a cool way to incorporate cameos from other Yakuza games. If you don't like them you don't need to use them to enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Yakuza that is not technically Yakuza.Has all the jokes, emotional stories and cool moments just like in 0.Story actually makes sense as opposed to Yakuza games..Ryoma is amazing and is very quirky, even more so than Kiryu.I love Kiryu but he's way more sad and tragic, which can sometime be unfitting of the jovial vibes the mini games have.Imagine just seeing random people doing a dance on the street and joining them. That's Ryoma for you.Or better yet play house with some local children. Ryoma gets to live the life Kiryu's always dreamed of, and I'm here for it.Every interaction matters and is either a substory or leads to a short storyExample: You feed a cat 5 times wondering "why am I even doing it, it's tedious"You then get to see the cat's story and you adopt said cat.Or you buy from a certain merchant a few times, he gradually tells you his supplier is late, you then get to sell him produce from your garden that you grew yourself.This makes this game very unique and cool.It makes you feel like you're always in an arcade.The graphics are amazing. Every location is gorgeous.UE4 really made this game shine.Usually Yakuza games have heavy problems with aliasing (the edges always dance and shimmer)The newer Dragon Engine is particularly bad in that regard. (also the physics are wonky)The facial (and idle) animations of dragon engine are stiff and lifeless.Such problems are absent here. Really wish they'd use UE4 for all Yakuza games.Best LAD game in my opinion. I mean look at my hours (and I'm not even done yet)I usually binge game but not to the extent this game makes me.It's just too fun to stop.Every few steps you make there's an interaction.You never feel lonely in the world of Ishin.You plan to go somewhere, and then get derailed a 100 times (of your own volition) and end up doing something completely different.I mean, can you really walk by the cat without giving it a fish?nahhhhhDon't listen to people saying it's grind-y.You can choose whether to grind or finish the game in 15 hours insteadThe grinding isn't mandatory and doesn't really affect progression (i.e. you're not forced to grind to better your gear, because gear good enough to finish the game randomly drops and very often so)But in case you want to grind, you will be rewarded with story bits and world building.You only grind because you want to see that extra scene/interaction or complete an achievement.Anyway amazing game easily on par with Yakuza 0.This game is what westerners so desperately seek in order to refresh the open world formula.This is how you make an open world feel alive as opposed to the barren lands of western games.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a spin-off of the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series set in 1860s Japan. The game's story is based on that of the historic figure Sakamoto Ryoma's, but with many additions and changes that make it much more entertaining and bring it more in line with the rest of the series.Ishin! has a huge cast of characters, the majority of which are loosely based on historical figures, all primarily being portrait by various characters from games within the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. The bulk of the characters in Ishin! are portrayed by characters who have similar personalities to those that they are portraying, however, the characters in Ishin! still manage to stand apart and feel distinct from the ones they are portrayed by.The world of Ishin! is one that feels familiar to other worlds within the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, the crowded streets and substories encounters scattered all throughout the world are exactly as you would expect from any game in the series. But the overall setting of 1800s Japan makes the world feel very distinct and unique from the rest of the series, leaving Ishin! feeling somewhat refreshing despite it's overall similarities with the rest of the series.The combat in Ishin! plays the same as other games Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, the main difference to the combat here is the unique combat styles present in the game, Swordsman, Gunman and Wild Dancer. These three combat styles are each very distinct from one another and each have their own uses. Swordsman sees you utilising a katana for close one-on-one combat, Gunman lets you use a firearm for a variety of ranged attacks, and Wild Dancer combines both sword and gun into a more all-round combat style. The game also features brawler combat style which plays similar to the hand-to-hand combat typically seen in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games. Overall the combat feels well balanced, although the Gunman style can easily trivialise much of the game's combat by staying at range.Ishin! also introduces the trooper card system. While originally constrained to a side mode, the remake of Ishin! now allows you to utilise trooper cards throughout the whole game. This system allows you to assign various cards that grant various abilities when used, these can range from small temporary buffs to damage to unique powerful attacks. The cards have a cooldown between uses to prevent you from spamming their abilities. The rarer cards can be massively overpowered, allowing you to trivialise any encounter. The cards don't seem too bad in the context of the side mode, but utilising them during the main story will destroy any sense of challenge the game could have provided.Ishin! also has a wide assortment of side content available. Much of the typical side content found in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games is present, such as gambling minigames, karaoke, and the arena. However Ishin! also comes with an assortment of new side content, buyo dancing, chicken racing, cooking and tending to your farm. The side content in Ishin! is all good and offers a lot of variety, providing you with a huge assortment of interesting things to do outside of the main story.Overall, Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a unique spin on the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series that feels familiar yet provides an experience that is both unique and engaging. The world, story and gameplay are all excellent and all come together to make Ishin! a game worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It has a decent story, well-acted scenes, amazing graphics, okay-ish gameplay, but suffers terribly due to its unneeded KIWAMI upgrade and the port to Unreal Engine.Back when this game was first announced, I was ecstatic to finally try this game out for myself, having only watched subbed playthroughs of it from various YouTubers. The graphics looked great, the trailers they've shown was sufficient enough to make me think "maybe this remake won't be so bad?" and got me to buy the Digital Deluxe edition to play this at the earliest. I played it, I did some side content, I grinded for some weapons, I played minigames, then I finished the main game. While I do appreciate the graphics overhaul it received from being ported over to Unreal Engine, the gameplay was rough. It was nothing like I had seen before from the original, bosses had superarmor, which kind of made fighting them unsatisfying, and the whole trooper card system and KIWAMI style skills that they had trivialized some fights hard, 99% of the time causing me to just go "wow, that was it?" whenever a boss fight would end. The combat did have the feel of a regular ol' RGG game, but it was  The impact it left behind on me was that of an indie game trying to emulate the feeling of Yakuza's combat.Some styles (ie.  and Swordsman) just utterly overshadowed the others, making them kind of useless if it wasn't for their universal skills and situational advantages, which I've noticed, seems like an issue that is only present in this "remake." Add fights were questionable, most of them ending quick due to the new trooper card system, or just the balancing of the styles in general, boss fights, as I've stated, were unsatisfying, most of them having superarmor to the TWO-HANDED sword style, but staggering to the dual wielding gun and sword style.  The story was decent, I liked the recasting, and the fights had awesome choreography as always. The soundtrack was amazing, the setting, the dialogue, and the storytelling is still one of RGG's advantages when it comes to games. It's just the fact that several of the new features they've given us and the balancing they've done, and the port of the battle system to the Unreal Engine ruined this game's charm, the thing that makes all RGG games feel special, that being the combat. 99% of the time, you'll be spending your time in battles, and the fact that they are generally unenjoyable (again, in my opinion) disappoints me greatly.And while I'm here, I don't appreciate these DLC practices. I do like the idea of more content, like they did with Kaito Files in Lost Judgment, but the price tags are unexcusable, and the fact that they've put basically micro-transactions into their game makes me want to just support them less.Please let this be a lesson to the team, it's great to try new things, but when it ruins the enjoyment and the drive to play the game for your consumer, it's typically not a good idea.Overall, it's bearable, I'd still say this is a game worth getting on sale if you're a big RGG fan, but I'm personally just very disappointed in this remake. The game itself was fairly recent, it genuinely just needed a remaster using the same old engine. I'd rather have the old engine without the fancy new graphics with fun gameplay than whatever we got with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! has been quite a surprise because, a priori, looking at the setting, it looked like a completely different mood compared to other games from RGG Studio, in this series but, right at the start of the game, we can already see that this will, in fact, be a great game within this franchise.I’ll start talking about PC performance, on my  system, this game performs amazingly, it’s pretty easy to run it way above 60 FPS at 1620p DLDSR downsampling (from 1080p native, my main resolution), Max Settings, and no need to use Upscaling at all.I choose 1620p DLDSR over 4K DSR because I find it looks better in this game, but 4K is also doable at 60 FPS, might need some Upscaling though (in which case I suggest XeSS over FSR 2.1, the former looks a bit cleaner overall, particularly at Ultra-Quality, but both can experience some temporal shimmering artifacts though, be aware, minor ones…but they exist).In the PC port we can find the expected settings from previous RGG games, so it’s all in there, including an FOV setting and pretty Customizable Controls.With the 1.03 Update, the game is free from any Shader Compilation Stutters, it runs pretty smoothly now, except very small hiccups right when a loading screen happens, nothing major there.When it comes to , this half remaster, half remake of Ishin brings back some good old favorites from previous games in the series, which is really nice to see because I really like their actors’ performances, both here and in those other games, of course.The  is the usual high quality from RGG games, with some character specific tracks from previous games coming back but with new arrangements fitting the era this game takes place in, a nice touch indeed. wise, I mostly found the combat to be pretty decent, this is after all a PS3 game with some improvements and the combat feels it’s from that era, but it’s not too bad once you get used to it, definitely it’s not the worst in the series.I played on Hard Difficulty and the game felt relatively balanced, except in a couple encounters here and there.The more skill points we get, the better the combat becomes, that’s for sure, and that’s a good thing. Again, not the best in the series, but I enjoyed it for what it is.Speaking of balancing, I found the Crafting system to be the weakest link here in this game, it’s nice that we have it, but it creates an unnecessary grind, if we want to level up the Blacksmith to a decent level to take advantage of discounts, or to unlock all the crafting variants.Surely, it’s meant to be combined with the rest of the “Another Life” activities such as Farming, but it’s a grind, nonetheless, and some people may not like that.Optional, for sure, because you don’t really need to craft anything in order to complete the game, you still get decent weapon drops and other items when defeating some bosses, but if you want more cool items and such…yeah, you either use certain money making exploits, or grind.All in all, I’ve enjoyed this game quite a lot, the story is pretty moving, with many epic moments and boss fights, it’s full of characters with so much charisma and the ones that got changed, from the OG release, to this remaster/remake, fit in so well in the story, because their actors are top tier.After playing this game I am now more eager to know about the next game in the series, Like a dragon: Gaiden, and of course looking forward to the day where Like a Dragon 8 arrives, likely next year.

_childDocuments_.review: At launch, the PC port has a stuttering issue where any time a new effect is used, the game stutters, including in heat moves and cutscenes, so when major characters die during dramatic moments, chances are Ishin will stutter. Additionally, all cutscenes and some minigames are locked to 30 fps. The keyboard and mouse support remains laughable (pause is mapped to M), so a controller is required...Beyond just the PC port's (hopefully) launch issues, Ishin is an interminably boring boring game. The combat is the biggest offender with even regular enemies being damage sponges and, of the four different combat styles, only two are truly useful. Gun-style is borderline useless because of how little damage the gun does (I racked up a 99 hit combo on a random encounter), not to mention no fun since the gun does not have any combos. Brawler is straight up useless because it does so little damage. Sword and Wild Dancer styles are both fine, but extremely boring since you'll mostly spam the same combos over and over again... Other, better Yakuza games let the combat open up more as the game progresses, but the upgrades you get in Ishin just do not change the combat substantially. A lot of the heat moves you can get are hidden deep in the skill trees and locked behind finding a collectible or training missions, not that you'll be able to use heat moves since it takes an obscene amount of attacks to build up one bar of heat. On top of that, heat moves don't reliably do a lot of damage, for instance some random encounter thugs can just shrug off heat moves like they are nothing...Adding to the boredom, Ishin also has a lot of chapters that primarily involve running from the inn you stay at to the barracks you work at. Just back and forth repeatedly. I have never used fast travel more in any other Yakuza game, but in Ishin I used it at least over 30 times mainly because of how much you get sent back and forth between those two locations. Other Yakuza games were not perfect, but neither were they this bad either...Something that kills me with Ishin is the step back in presentation compared to the dragon engine games. Ishin is a full priced remake of the game of the same name from 2011, and despite being a remake, it still seems to share a lot of the same animations and technical limitations of the game. For instance, in Yakuza 6, from 2016, you can seamlessly walk into almost every playable area in Kamurocho, including buildings. That has been the standard for the last seven years. Now, in Ishin, we're back to loading into buildings. I really loved how perfectly the Dragon Engine games captured the atmosphere of a busy city, and seamless transitions between playable areas added a lot for me...The graphics also just do not look as good to me as the Dragon Engine games. Ryoma's walking and running animations all feel like the pre-6 Yakuza games too, which is maybe a plus for some, but I appreciated the grounded feeling of the movement in the later Yakuza games. Lost Judgment in particular feels perfect in both regular and combat movement. I wish Ishin felt more like that, rather than a really basic version of Yakuza 0...The story is fine, the usual mix of Yakuza's trademark compelling melodrama. I wish the game did a better job offering context for its setting, but then again, it ends with a nationalist screed before cutting to black, so maybe it's better that it doesn't. ..PC port issues aside, the Ishin remake is still one of my least favorite Yakuza games with an excruciatingly boring combat system, step back in presentation, and mediocre story with a bizarre ending. Still, I'd love to see a remaster/port/or remake of Kenzan, just hopefully priced appropriately and with a better PC version.

The single biggest problem in this game is the combat and systems relating to it.TL;DR: if you just play the main story, you can have a good time with it. If you go for all substory completion (e.g. ) or -- god forbid -- 100% completion, you will probably hate this game.Every enemy feels like they have 2 or 3 times more health than they should have, you feel like you have 2 or 3 times  than you should have, and half the styles do garbage damage. I think they expect you to use the trooper abilities that erase squads, otherwise you're sitting there for an eternity mashing buttons.Getting good equipment to make your damage output  more favorable is locked behind a ridiculously tedious equipment grind. I sidestepped this entirely by buying a "light of heaven" sword from that one shady dude in town, then just using the swords given to you in the main story. Very little else ever felt even remotely worth it.In other game in this series, many of your moves have secondary effects, like stuns, guard-breaks, or knockdowns. There are very few moves in this game with those effects. Additionally, many enemies are immune to these effects (this is the hyper armor problem others have mentioned), so they'll face-tank your attacks and chunk your health bar.Every style feels like it has half the utility of a style in another Yakuza game. The reason for this is that they expect you to get that ability that lets you switch styles mid-combo, then use that for the whole game. Unfortunately, this system is nowhere near as fleshed out as it should be. Kiwami 1 did this  better. Brawler and Gunman feel very under-baked. Swordsman has a lot of counters, but they feel stiff and awkward to use, and sometimes seem like they just don't work. Wild Dancer has the most fleshed out moveset, but it's kinda just mash light attack then occasionally dodge.Then the dungeons. Oh my god, the dungeons. Don't even bother. They're only good for grinding materials, and they are so mind-numbingly boring. There's like 40 of them, and they get longer and more tedious the further you get.Finally, the "reward" () for doing all the substories . It's one of the worst in the series, and is just more of the same crap but with worse numbers. If you really,  want to do it, just download a save.I'm kind of amazed that testers played this game and said "yeah, this feels good". This game desperately needs a modder to come in and overhaul all these numbers. Unfortunately, because this is a new engine, the modding tools just aren't quite there yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend “Like A Dragon: Ishin!” to existing fans and newcomers, but with some caveats. I’ll start with the good and then mention the bad!Positives:-An engaging melodrama based on an exciting time in the history of Japan-A helpful “Glossary” function to help clarify things that those of us not familiar with Japanese history (myself included) can benefit from-Exciting combat with four unique styles-Lots of minigames, including Karaoke!-Great (Japanese) voice acting-No performance issues on an older rigNegatives:-It’s a remaster of a ten-year-old game, and the game mechanics are a bit outdated-Still has some of that Yakuza-cringe with how women are represented in minigames-Similar to other Yakuza games, it’s not especially polished in the graphics departmentAll in all, it’s a fun Yakuza game and easy to recommend. If you’ve not played a Yakuza-style game before, this is a great point to jump into the series! In my view, the Yakuza games have always had a B-movie charm, with serious melodrama juxtaposed with silly side activities, and this game doesn’t disappoint. Even though I’m only a chapter and a half in, it’s already making me laugh.
