_childDocuments_.review: LIKE A SAMURAIThis game takes place during the end of the Tokugawa period or the Edo period, a piece of history that is not really abundant in current modern entertainment and media, or atleast not from my experiences. From what I know, a samurai is a katana-wielding warrior usually highly regard by the people for their bravery, skill, and more. This game delves in deeper about being a samurai that is actually very interesting especially the time period being kinda the end of the samurai. Unlike in most other entertainment, samurai here is depicted as wielding guns too since the British made contact with Japan exchanging weapons such as firearms and such. I don't know realistic it is when compare to the real life period but this tiny bit of piece adds to how unique LAD: Ishin! is when compare to other samurai-focused entertainments.Like A Dragon: Ishin! is a brand new Yakuza game by the chads in RGG Studio and also a remake of the Japan-only 2014 game Ryu Ga Gotoku: Ishin. This game is rebuilt from the ground-up with Unreal Engine 4 and new additions compare to the original. I haven't played the original RGG Ishin unlike other Yakuza games since its not available in my country and also I need PS3 hardware or an emulator to play this game. Therefore I will not be making any comparisons to the original but from what I've seen, the games is pretty much faithful with the addition with a new mechanic which is the Trooper System.In this game, you play as a samurai, Sakomoto Ryoma, on his journey to find out the truth of a certain event that happened earlier in the story. Eventually, you playing as Sakamoto Ryoma, in typical Yakuza fashion, will find out about the pieces at play being controlled by the powers of Japan, samurai organisations, other warriors, and more that is very enjoyable to experience. More importantly, the events you'll experience as Sakamoto Ryoma also happen in real life during that period of time so some context about history adds more to the experience. Not 100% accurate though but the additions for me are very creative and well-thought by the writers team.In typical Yakuza way, the action here is phenominal. I'm referring to both the combat and action scenes. For combat, the game have the style-switch system that is present on other Yakuza games like Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami, Judgment, and DMC 5 where you have the Brawler style which is the classic Yakuza style, Swordman that is good in 1v1 situations, Gunman which is a more range and fast style, and Wild Dancer which is a full-offensive style combining both sword and gun. Combat is awesome with combos you can string together in-between styles. Addition to the combat system is the Trooper system where you can assign 3 or 4 cards in one style to execute special moves that rivals Yakuza 7's specials. Most of the cards are just stat buffs but the special ones can make Sakamoto Ryoma shoot a beam of light between his palms or open a black hole to the shadow realm. Personally, I didn't use much of the Trooper system except in the Battle Dungeon minigame. Battle Dungeon is a mission-based minigame where you can do to get materials for equipment and crafting. Equipment here felt much better to use here than other Yakuza games since it is realistic to wield swords and polearms in this game. The crafting system is also similar to Monster Hunter which is an A plus in my book.Returning back to the story, the story is good. I'll admit I didn't fully understand since there were many factions and terms at present like the Choshu Domain, the Bakufu, and more that kinda made me confused on how the world works in Tokugawa Japan. To alleviate this, the game has a glossary that highlights certain terms that are important to know like Sonno Jouie, Shishi, Joshi, Goshi, and more during dialogue scenes. Being Japan af, the names of every character are also arranged accurately to how it is called in Japan with the family name being the first. Sakamoto Ryoma with the old arrangement is Ryoma Sakamoto with Ryoma being his first name. Like Naruto Uzumaki changed to Uzumaki Naruto, or Kazuma Kiryu to Kiryu Kazuma. Since the game is Japan af, might as well go all in. This is also applied to the actors name and the devs in the credits. Although I was dazed and confused during the credits, a quick Google search about the history of the characters and the time period really brings out all the references the game made along the way. I do understand why it wasn't released in Internationally since it has too much content and references about Japan. I commend the translation team for the effort in bringing this internationally and making it more accessible.The soundtrack is straight up fire. Other than that, the main story is only a percentage of the full game. The side-content is usually one of the important things to do and have fun ingame. You can do Karaoke, or Singing Bar, a typical Yakuza staple, Buyo Dancing, a traditional Japanese dance, selling Udon, farming, selling crops, cooking, and more. Yakuza games can be defined as a hybrid of action and slice of life game where you not only do what the character does, but also become one. Other than the activities you can do, there are also substories which are little events that are very entertaining. These substories other than giving you rewards, also give you features in other minigames, tidbit lore of the world, and more and never are there a chore or bore to experience.Alas, not every game is perfect. This game have a friendship system where you have to interact multiple times in order to maximise them. Not all of the NPCs you interact gave any meaningful reward, atleast from how much I have played. There are tons of NPCs, like TONS of them in every nook and cranny, shops, that you have to kinda interact with either giving items they want multiple times. Some are funny but most are just kinda tedious to do and felt like giving out items that I could have used better in other situations like in the Battle Dungeon. I have not done all of them so my opinion may change, but for now, the relationships are tedious to fulfill and have no reward in fulfilling them.Other flaw is that there many spelling errors, like too much for a Yakuza game. Kinda sloppy. The translations confused me especially the differences being Joshi and Goshi, which I can understand it being mistakenably written. More quality assurance for better spelling please. And also some button prompts can bug out, menus being slow, but these tech issues I can give forgive since I have a high tolerance for it. Its just the spelling errors that are quite many that its noticable.Overall, a classic Yakuza, or Samurai game.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: I understand why this game has mixed opinions, especially when played on mouse and keyboard.The fact you cannot assign menu/pause key to escape button, feels like a huge mistake on the programming, fighting itself feels nice BUT there are situations, where using a dodge feels like it doesn't matter, with some homing missile attacks from Ninjas and few final encounters. There's also very weird way they approached the 3rd division, with collecting cards, and allowing you to fuse them to empower them- only for the game to immediately delete records of owning that card. The fact those cards were essentially stronger than any attacks made by player character, and yet still feeling like a grind fest in dungeons. I still feel it's a game worth playing, if only for a chance to actually have Yakuza game where you can use weaponry, with very good writing for most of the game... but don't treat it too seriously. It's best to approach this game for the fun of combat, than to go crazy with it.

_childDocuments_.review: You'll see that 90% of the negative reviews of this game all only talk about the DLC being one time consumables, while I agree it's stupid, the simple fix is to just not buy them.To beat the game on Legend difficulty not too much grind is required, just cheese the chicken race for money and fight well. From what I can tell, on higher difficulties, the game doesn't make the enemies super tanky, it makes you very easy to kill which I think causes a lot of great adrenaline inducing moments as you hang on to a tiny amount of health waiting for one of your healing cards to recharge as the enemies try and hit you. The story is excellent and the members of the Shinsengumi are mostly very interesting. Not my favourite RGG game (that one still goes to Judgment) but still up there as one of my favourites and the idea to make Legend difficulty available from the start is a brilliant change.

_childDocuments_.review: It's enjoyable. Just be aware that this is a spin-off that will let you see a lot of familiar faces (you most likely noticed already while looking at the promo material). To avoid cringe, total loss of immersion or your suspense of disbelief being stretched to its limits, just stay on the meta-level. Imagine that this is a stage play inside some weird time anomaly in which all the prominent people within (and without) the Yakuza reenact a samurai story for the entertainment of some unknown entity. You can even give Kiryu his normal outfit and pretend that he is time travelling - or really isn't into cosplaying. For more realism, you can use the brawler style exclusively to explain that fights with swords and guns ever only result in bruises as long as there is no cutscene coming up. This Kiryu does occasionally kill, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game that uses your preconceived notions on yakuza world characters to create a narrative that is a beautiful faux-history that feels truly by RGG studios. Games a little light on substantial side-content, the majority of it I found to be a tad tedious for very little reward, or even dialogue. Main plot and the 10 or so hours I did of the side stuff was while worth it though in both drama and laughs, but I imagine completionists will have a more frustrating time than a typical RGG game. Guys please buy this game so they translate more of the lost RGG games, I don't normally make reviews but I want this to be a call to action.Lastly, while I'm the LAST gamer to talk about this, as I have no problems with what people would consider "poor switch performance", but this is probably the least optimized PC port of RGGs games. Frequent lag while hitting a lot of enemies with trooper cards, some weird glitchy parts of the chapter 11(?) gauntlet in Edo, and one of the most important cutscenes, the one at the end of the second to last chapter, was flashing a black screen sometimes. Nothing awful, game looked beautiful and run well 99% of the time, just hope these are ironed out.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've unreviewed and re-reviewed this game a bunch of times.I love this game, but I have minor nitpicks with this remake itself.History time, this game is actually a remake of a Japanese-only PS4 game of the same name, with some changes. The original game was released around the same time as Yakuza 0, so if you're wondering why some things look similar, that's why, a lot of the face actors are the same people. Pretty much every familiar face is all based off a specific person, like Bacchus for example is based off a real person.Trooper Cards used to only apply in battle dungeons, now they apply everywhere, but the game isn't balanced around it so they break the game outside of battle dungeons. In the original game there were food bonuses instead, that provided passive stat buffs, but they weren't as high.Randomized affixes were turned into seals, at original launch of the remake people complained about them being less varied, turns out the drop rates were ♥♥♥♥♥♥, this got fixed. Almost all of the affixes now exist as seals, which can be collected and used as you please, rather than being even more at the mercy of RNG.The crafting system in general was reworked, with weapon paths being more cleanly displayed, and the single timed button press "minigame" being removed. That being said, it's still cryptic as ♥♥♥♥ where to find the dude who lets you make magical weapons. He's in Mukurogai, if you didn't check.The battle styles were reworked slightly, as in Gunner was changed, but not nerfed. In the original, gunner's attack speed was relatively constant, allowing for run and gun, and it was actually pretty powerful, because knockdowns are a mechanic. In the remake, shot speed is tied to movement, if you stand still, you fire faster. The actual DPS is about the same, but now you play as a turret. Wild Dancer still works if you like run and gun.Brawler always did the damage of a wet noodle because you were expected to use affixes or seals to improve Brawler, use the Fundoshi you get after the Ryuji fight, it multiplies your brawler damage pretty high. However, if you don't like this, I recommend using a mod that changes brawler damage, they exist already. The Yakuza/LaD/Judgment modding community is very active, and Ishin got a lot of good mods close to release. The modding discord is a friendly place filled with a lot of people who put effort into their projects.The story is very loosely based off Japanese history, so if you want to complain about the story, it's basically the TV Soap Opera version of the very real legacy of Sakamoto Ryoma. All of the characters are based off people in that era, but played by face actors who played people in the main Like A Dragon series.The top review complains about how sidequests work, Only an admittedly sizable fraction of the quests use it, and the friendship system isn't new, it's actually used in a ton of the later numbered Yakuza games, as well as Yakuza 0, but is also used in Judgment, and in my opinion, Judgment handles that system the best.I actually like the battle dungeons, they have problems but I just like actually having long encounters in these games that aren't apart of the story, where you move through a big area. The Kiwami 2 bouncer missions are similar, and I like those too.All this being said, I do think the price is too high for a remake that isn't terribly expanded over the original. This game has about the same amount of non-dungeon content as Judgment, which is reasonably priced on PC, and is also based off the PS5 remaster, similar to how this game is based off the PS5 remake.The game had some shader stutter on release, but it's not as bad now. There's a hidden DX11 mode that might help you avoid shader stutter if you get it.8/10, not the best Like A Dragon game overall, but I like it and it's worthy of being put up next to the others.

_childDocuments_.review: Saying that I "recommend" this game is a bit of a stretch. It's very complicated. I only recommend this game to a select few people, being those that are already huge fans of the series like myself that wanted to play all the games. Ishin is a love letter to the fans and the series as a whole in almost every single regard, and you owe it to yourself to play it for that reason alone. The story is also probably the best the series has to offer, if not second to Yakuza 0. That said, if you are just a casual fan of this series or if you are looking for an entry point, I advise you look elsewhere, unfortunately. The enemy health pools and overall difficulty curve are impossible to keep up with unless you want to resign yourself to tens of hours of tedious grinding. If you want to get into Like a Dragon, check out Yakuza 0, Yakuza: Like a Dragon, or the Judgment duology instead.

Overall this is still a game I'd recommend to anyone who likes RGG games or wants to get into them!

_childDocuments_.review: I would only recommend this game to people who are previous fans of Yakuza, mainly because you get to see a lot of your favorite characters from throughout the franchise in it, however one thing that I found extremely hard was to keep up with the story.Every character that you know now has a new name which makes keeping up with the story extremely hard, at least for me.You get introduced to a lot of new characters all the time and they pretty much expect you to remember them all. They do have a glossary, where you can press a button in conversations and it will tell you more about it, but that is mostly for city and clan names. Sometimes I honestly had no idea what they were talking about, only later when they actually went and physically did what they were talking about I understood.The combat is not as exciting as some of the older Yakuza games. If I for example compare it to Lost Judgement it's way less enjoyable, you basically get 4 different styles which two of them were basically unusable for me. When games give you choices but only a few of them are actually good it starts to feel a bit meaningless.The combo game didn't feel as good as the older games either.However, it has all of it's usual Yakuza story plots and action, so I will recommend it, however I believe that you will enjoy it way more if you're already a Yakuza fan.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ten hours into early access, and it's really cool so far. Runs very well. What I thought might end up being a gimmick game is actually a fun edo-period revenge story in a Yakuza skin.The neat thing is that the characters are all ones from past (er future) games, but narratively they don't actually need to live for continuity. The gunplay is actually really fun too. The key to this one is not to go in taking the story super seriously, or expecting it to be really challenging. If you can just strap in and enjoy the ride, I think it's worth it. One big con for most people is going to be that it doesn't have the graphics of Y6/YK2/Y7/Judgement/Lost Judgment, but it's a rework of a game from 2014, so I get not remaking it from the ground up. I do think it's a shame this didn't come to the west back then, because it would have been the perfect prequel to yakuza 0. One thing is for sure, this is a full game, worth the price, and it's doing it's own thing. Pretty fun, another great game going into 2023. It's nice to have a franchise like this that you can count on.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun, like watching a really well thought out and well executed samurai movie/tv show. Gameplay wise there is little to really comment on, the combat is mad simple and while that would usually be a drawback to getting into the game I don't think you play these kind of games for engaging and exciting combat (if you want something like that go play DOOM Eternal or Dark Souls or Zeno Clash). The story really shines, all the voice acting is phenomenal, perhaps the only complaint in that regard is that there isn't enough! As much of a pipe dream as it may be, I really wish that everything was voiced--certainly these games make enough to have some sort of significant budget--and not just significant character interactions. Really that's a nit-pick though. The game is great, I love these kinds of stories, I'd for sure recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of heart and sincerity, much like what people have come to expect from these games, but it also does a lot to set itself apart from your traditional Yakuza experience. About a day before I picked up Ishin I finished Yakuza 0 for the first time, and oh man am I in love. I enjoyed Yakuza 0 but I had a lot of problems with it that this game fixes entirely for me.If Yakuza 0 is more of a beat-em-up River City-esque game in a 3D space I would say Ishin! is an Action-RPG with brawler roots. Potentially this might turn off some fans of the series but I'd like to run down a list of things that really set this game apart for me: -New abilities are no longer paid for with money. Using your different styles levels them up and allows you to spend orbs on them to learn new abilities. This means that using your favorite styles rewards you by making them stronger, rather than grinding out a separate resource for them.-You can block or Parry out of almost any rush attack immediately which means that combat feels extremely responsive. Even if you are in the middle of an attack if you time your guards right you will cancel out of it and parry the enemy. Overall this makes the combat feel far more aggressive if you're able to pull it off consistently. -The heat gauge is no longer tied to unique moves on the different styles. This means that if you go for a tiger drop, or one of the other parry options you don't have to worry about where your heat gauge is relative to what you're able to do. I remember in Y0 there were some moves that were only usable at heat level 1/2/3 and this would lead to unnecessary clunkiness. The heat gauge is now almost strictly used for Heat Actions and each style's 'Ultimate' attack. It no longer drains in combat either, but it goes up a little slower, which makes heat items a little more valuable. -The enemy variety is good, and the styles have more niche uses. There are by far more enemy types in this game that demand you to pay attention to their movesets a little more than normal. The minibosses also all feel by far more unique than anything I encountered in Y0. Even between enemies using katanas you'll notice there are 4+ different stances they'll take that change up their movesets.-There is a monster hunter-esque weapon tree for the 5 different weapon types and armors in the game that require you to farm materials from different places along with a weapon quality and enhancement system using different gem sockets to further customize your play style. There are some +5% skills here and there, but there is also a mix of unique modifers that change how some things in combat function, like a special glove passive that allows you to block with brawler and gunslinger syles for example.-The trooper cards aren't too obtrusive and you're not required to use them, but I think they're fun an add another layer of customization to the game. I don't mind pouring over their active and passive effects, and so far there seems to be a decent amount of configurations therein. I can see why they would turn someone off, but they just add another layer of depth to the game for me. As for actual combat challenges there are now dungeons to explore that drop loot, different weapons, and allow you to further level up your styles and character. If you enjoy the combat you can now more freely just engage with these combat encounters alongside the arena with special boss fights as well. If you ever felt there wasn't enough ways to just jump into Yakuza's combat and try out your new moves on mooks and bosses alike this game really rectifies that in multiple ways.There is a lot going on with this game that makes it hard to cover everything. The locales are all bright and colorful. They feel lively and well put together. The CP system is gone in favor of a more easily accessible Virtue system that gives you points for pretty much everything you do, meaning you no longer have to seek out to do specific tasks in order to access the meta-progression systems. The mini-games are all rather fun. Some returning, and some new. I particularly like the farming and cooking mini-games that function as this game's primary money-making activity. The substories are still a mix of silly and touching. Some are better than others, but none of them feel outright bad. The story and setting are a huge draw for anyone who misses old games like Way of the Samurai, and similar life sim-esque games. The cast is extremely strong, obviously there are a lot of character 'cameos' in a sense that historical figures are replaced by Yakuza character models and voice actors. Also you can finally quit the game from the pause menu rather than having to go back to the title screen or hitting alt+F4. You can save anywhere, so you're no longer stuck having to run to phone booths or being stuck in longer stretches of gameplay without a way to save. If some of these QoL features are in later titles I wouldn't know, but they stuck out to me in particular jumping right in from Y0.There is a problem with this game's shader optimization. You WILL get a lot of microstutters in the beginning of the game until it finishes building a shader cache, but once it's done it runs extremely well. This game might be a strong contender for my personal game of the year, but we'll see what the rest of the year holds. Well worth the asking price for me. Even if you're not a fan of Yakuza, or you bounced off of the other ones, give it a shot on sale maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm starting to get really tired of how RGG Studio treats their older titles.This remake is nothing but an insult to all the fans of the series, whether you even realize it or not.It took nine years of fans outside of Japan asking for Ishin to be released worldwide, just for Sega and RGG to de-list the game from the Playstation Store and replace it with an inferior remake that no one asked for. The fact that they somehow managed to take a Japan-only Playstation exclusive and make it even less accessible than it already was is absolutely mind boggling. It  saddens me that now, the original game will most likely  be released worldwide and freed from Playstation exclusivity since the average player (understandably) has not played the original game, and does not know just how bad this remake actually is.Good :Two new karaoke songs (though only one of them is actually new, the other is just bakamitai for the fifth time)New substories (though they're pretty mediocre)Can change the haori of Ryoma and even all of the Shinsengumi captains whenever you want, no need to be in the post game.Mixed :Character recasts. They're just  for the most part, but I miss Baba as Todo, and I really don't like Shibusawa as Takechi. Han Joon-Gi is also a very unfitting recast for Yamazaki and it's very obvious that they lazily re-used the animations. Oryo is the only recast I think I actually liked more than the original.Bad :One substory was cutOpening movie was cutRhapsody of Chivalry was replaced with Town Bully from Yakuza 6 for some reason.The final cutscene involving a father and son in the present day looking at a statue of Ryoma and talking about him was cut from the game. It makes absolutely no sense why they would remove such an interesting and unique cutscene. Even Kenzan didn't have anything like that.Menus are strangely slow, takes like a full second after clicking something for it to appear. The menus were more responsive in the original Ishin.The combat is just worse than the original. Enemies have way more health since they rebalanced the game around the troop system rework and you can say goodbye to the wall bounding and back attacks signature of the original game (and many other older RGG games) because for some reason they thought giving every enemy hyperarmor was a good idea. Brawler style was also nerfed into the ground, practically making it a useless style. The damage is absurdly low and the parry buff does not last nearly as long as it did in the original. Bosses also love to immediately break out of grabs (or literally just can't be grabbed at all) unlike the original game.Who asked for the troop system rework? It feels like RGG was just desperate to find some new mechanic they could force into the core gameplay to have a reason to re-sell it to their Japanese fanbase. I find the argument that some people make that the troop cards are "optional" to be total BS and shows that they have no idea what playing the original game is like. Simply unequipping the cards yourself does nothing to make the game play like the original. The balance changes made to accommodate the troop system rework changed the combat for the worse as mentioned above. These magical abilities that bosses use now are not only unfitting thematically, they don't even add anything to the boss fights gameplay-wise. They were so lazily implemented that they just break the boss AI and don't act the way they would in the original game. Where they should often be performing long combos and follow-up attacks, they instead just favor using these lame magical attacks with long wind-ups and i-frames that really serve no purpose but to delay the fight. Tokugawa Yoshinobu will almost never actually do his follow-up attack after hitting Ryoma with a throwing knife, instead he'll just fire a giant laser beam at him like this is Dragon Ball and not a historical drama.The troop system rework also made grinding in general, but especially materials for Amon's sword (which isn't even as good as it was in the original; it no longer has the unique ability to create projectiles with every swing, now it just gives miniscule life leech that other weapons can have), even more tedious and take much longer. The best way to clear the last battle dungeon in the original Ishin with the troop cards takes about ten seconds to clear the whole room with four attack cards since they actually stack damage properly unlike the cards in the remake. Best way I could find to do it with the troop rework in Ishin Kiwami forced me to take them out one-by-one since the damage buffs didn't stack, making it a  slower process. Grinding was already a big issue in the original Ishin, and they somehow just made it even worse here.What the hell were they thinking with this atrocious blacksmith rework? Forging costs were increased so much it's actually insane. For example, the Bonbori Lantern used to cost 3 Ryo and 6000 Mon to forge, and now costs 116 Ryo 4600 Mon. That's an increase of over 30x the original price. WHY??? The reworked seal system is also some of the most asinine, RNG dependent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a game mechanic I have ever seen in my life. When enhancing weapons in the original Ishin, you would just sacrifice the weapon with the seal you want to use on another weapon and it would always work. There was even a small mini-game that determined how good the enhancement would be (which was not left to RNG at all). In Ishin Kiwami, the seals that come with gear you make are locked to that piece of gear, so you can't just dismantle it and use it on a different piece of equipment, you have to exploit a mechanic the game never informs you of, which is randomly getting an extra seal when making a piece of equipment. The best way to get the seals you want is to save your game, forge cheap weapons with an empty seal slot such as a bronze cannon over and over again until you get it with a random seal, reload your save and make that many cheap weapons minus one, then make the gear with the seal you want (which I had to refer to a spreadsheet some poor soul had to fill out to figure out what gear gave seals I needed for completion) and hope you get it. Then dismantle it to be able to use that seal on another weapon, then there's only a CHANCE that it will be added to the weapon when enhancing it with the seal. If it fails (which it has failed at a 2% chance of failing SEVERAL TIMES for me), reload your save, and then enhance with a completely different seal because the chance is pre-determined for some god forsaken reason, then try the seal you need again and MAYBE then it'll work. IN WHAT UNIVERSE IS THIS GOOD GAME DESIGN? I have 100% completion on both versions of Ishin, and the remake was FAR worse because of this.DLC is egregious. Nothing before launch said that the material pack DLCs were a ONE TIME USE. Not even once per save file. You can't even claim it again on a new save, you'd have to buy it again. Haori that were free in the original game are now locked behind DLC and the new difficulty is DLC.Why are there giant enemies like three times the height of Ryoma now? They're so strange and out of place.Amon is PATHETIC. In the original Ishin, Amon was one of the hardest fights in the series. Now he is the easiest. I did not even have to  to beat him. ON LEGEND DIFFICULTY.Censored QTE in the bath house fight with Saigo in chapter 2.Cutscenes are STILL locked at 30FPS.I absolutely dread to think about what they might do to Kenzan at this rate. It is one of their most important games because of the improvements and new mechanics that it brought to the franchise among other unique elements and they will likely throw that game away in favor of another terrible remake.TLDR: This is a vastly inferior, insulting version of the original Ishin that has nothing going for it apart from it actually being released outside of Japan.

_childDocuments_.review: I found  to be a bit of a mixed bag, but would recommend . is a remake of 2014's Playstation and Japan exclusive , which is a samurai-themed spin-off of the main / series.The action moves from modern day Kamurocho to Kyoto during the  period of the 1860s. This was a pivotal point in Japanese history, as it led to the overthrow of the Bakufu military government, the Meiji Restoration and ultimately, the modernisation of the country. We play as Sakamoto Ryoma, a ronin searching for his foster father's murderer. Ryoma travels to Kyoto and discovers that the killer is among the leaders of a notorious Bakufu-organised police force, known as the Shinsengumi. Ryoma is forced to infiltrate the organisation in order to find the culprit.Ryoma has the likeness and voice actor of Kiryu and several other series mainstays appear in alter-ego form, such as Majima, Akiyama, Saejima, etc. Many of the characters are loosely based on real-life historical figures and the game has some fun with this set-up.As in any  game, you can engage in a variety of mini-games, such as Karaoke, Gambling, Fishing, Mahjong, etc.  also has a few unique side activities in the form of "Another Life", where you manage a farm and "Battle Dungeons" where you fight through a series of labyrinths to gain rewards in the form of XP, money and crafting items.Fighting styles return and Ryoma has 4 options to choose from: Brawler, Swordsman, Gunman and Wild Dancer (a combination of Sword/Gun styles).-I found the historical setting to be very engaging to the point that I was inspired to read-up more on the real-life events.-It feels like a tribute to the  series as a whole. There's fan service aplenty and long-time fans will get a kick out of seeing some of the returning faces from past games, like Nishiki, Ryuji Goda, Mine, Kuze and Awano, along with some more obscure ones.-As in all games in the series, the music and voice acting are top notch. Some iconic series themes make a reappearance in remixed form.-"Another Life" is a fairly chilled out diversion from the main game, where you can grow and sell vegetables on your farm and cook meals with Haruka, as part of a side story where you need to raise money to pay off her debts.-Karaoke as always is thoroughly enjoyable - there's a few other interesting mini-games like the buyo dancing, running the noodle shop and cannonball training.-Some of the substories are up with the usual  fare of zany and surreal - the "Ee ja nai ka" series comes to mind. There's some neat references to real-life figures like Natsume Soseki as well, helping to reinforce the historical setting.-"Majima" aka Okita Souji, plays a prominent role in the game.-The story definitely loses its way in the 2nd half - without spoiling too much, there's one particular plot twist mechanic that gets overused.-The Battle Dungeons are a real drag to play through. They tend to be filled with lots of spongy enemies and can be quite difficult to navigate. They're also required if you want to fully engage with the game's crafting systems. I think there's 40 of them in total to play through, but honestly I lost interest after the first batch.-Speaking of which, crafting the best weapons and gear is going to take a hell of a lot of grinding. The top end items will cost obscene amounts of money, not to mention all the materials you'll need.-Combat in general feels quite stiff (especially coming off of ) and I found I only used 2 of the fighting styles regularly. Gunman is very situational and Brawler simply doesn't do enough damage.-One of the most controversial changes implemented in this remake is the implementation of the Trooper cards system outside of the Battle Dungeons.  Damage and health values have been adjusted for both Ryoma and enemies to account for this and use of the cards feels essential to avoid every fight turning into a long, drawn-out slog. Many bosses will now have "super moves" that can quickly drain your health as well.-Many of the substories are really lacklustre - so many of them revolve around bringing a character X number of items (usually vegetables) to complete a friendship and they're so tedious to play through.-There's not a huge variety of mini-games, unless you happen to enjoy gambling!While I'm glad I played  and generally enjoyed my time with it, I found it to be one of the weaker entries in the series and it's definitely not worth it at a full price of €60 (or your regional equivalent).Any fans of the series should enjoy the callbacks and nods to previous games and it's worth a run through the main story. I'd advise anyone interested to temper their expectations though -  does suffer from some frustrating mechanics and unless you're a masochist, a Completionist playthrough should be avoided.

_childDocuments_.review: The 2023 remake of Like a Dragon: Ishin! brings a fan favorite entry in the series I will continue to call Yakuza to international players for the first time, albeit with a Kiwami-style treatment. Ishin eschews the normal crime drama of contemporary urban Japan in favor of an Edo period samurai drama with the roles played by major characters from the rest of the series. This change in setting makes for a nice change of pace, even if Kyo is awkwardly structured. This game also lets you switch between different combat styles on the fly a la Yakuza 0, and these new styles are for the most part quite fun to play. The new Another Life side activity also adds a nice, slower-paced farming sim-esque component to the game. Otherwise, this is Yakuza, with all that that entails.Ultimately, I find myself preferring the series' more typical tropes, but this is a very worthwhile detour if it at all intrigues you.

Maybe it's just me but these little details make a game feel more realistic and even though this is supposed to be happening during the 1860s in Japan I could relate.Absolutely loved how the love-hate relationship between Kiryu (Ryoma) and Majima (Okita) was kept alive.What I didn't like: Special effects being used by enemies (and having these myself with the help of troopers) and the giant enemies. _childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon: Ishin is a action-adventure video game developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and published by Sega. The game is set in Japan’s late Edo period and features a unique blend of action-packed combat, an engaging storyline, and a wide range of side activities. The combat system in Like A Dragon: Ishin is a major highlight of the game. The game features an action-oriented combat system that allows players to switch between four different fighting styles, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. The four styles are swordsmanship, hand-to-hand combat, firearms, and dancing style (a combination of swordsmanship and firearms).The combat system is challenging on harder difficulties, but also incredibly satisfying, and the variety of fighting styles ensures that combat never feels repetitive. There are easier difficulties as well if you’re not familiar with action-based combat. Heat is gained from defeating enemies or from eating or drinking certain foods (usually alcohol). The Heat moves are flashy and over-the-top.The game’s storyline is also a strong point, as it features an engaging plot that keeps players hooked from beginning to end. The game’s protagonist, Sakamoto Ryoma, is a historical figure who is caught in a plot where rebels want to overthrow their government. The story is filled with political intrigue, personal drama, and plenty of action, making for a thrilling experience and a fun history lesson, though of course the historical events are exaggerated.One of the strengths of the game’s story is how it shows historical events but with Like A Dragon characters instead. The game’s developers have done research, and many of the characters and events in the game are based on real-life Japanese history but it’s really interesting that the characters are represented with Yakuza and Like A Dragon characters (and it works surprisingly well).In addition to the main storyline, Like A Dragon: Ishin also features a wide range of side activities to keep players entertained. These include gambling games, fishing, dancing, and farming.Substories or sidequests are an integral part of the Like A Dragon series, and they offer players a wide range of optional activities to engage with while exploring the game’s world. These sidequests typically involve helping out various NPCs around the game’s world. They’re fully-fledged side stories that often involve a series of quests that are linked by a common narrative thread.Dojos are specialized training centers where players can improve their character’s abilities and learn new moves. Dojos are scattered throughout the game’s world, and each one is dedicated to a specific type of combat style or weapon. The sensei will offer a series of training exercises or challenges that the player must complete in order to improve their character’s skills. You can then purchase new abilities after completing the training. The types of training available at each dojo will depend on the combat style or weapon that the dojo specializes in. For example, a dojo that specializes in hand-to-hand combat may offer training in martial arts moves or techniques such as counters, while a dojo that focuses on swords may offer training in different sword styles and techniques such as parrying with the sword.The friendship or bond system is a key feature that allows players to build relationships with various NPCs throughout the game’s world. As players interact with these NPCs and perform various tasks for them, their friendship level with them will increase, unlocking new rewards and benefits. One of the benefits of the friendship system is that it provides additional incentive to explore the game’s world and engage with NPCs outside of the main storyline. By building relationships with various characters, players can unlock unique insights into the game’s world and lore, as well as unique rewards that can’t be obtained through other means.The farm is a key feature that allows players to grow and harvest various crops which can be given as gifts or sold for money, as well as raise and care for animals which you can befriend. By managing their farm effectively, players can produce a variety of resources and items that can be used in the game’s crafting and cooking systems allowing for the creation of more powerful weapons, accessories, and food (healing items).By managing their farm effectively and growing a variety of crops and raising animals, players can become more self-sufficient and profitable, providing an additional layer of depth to the game’s economy and resource management systems. Like how Yakuza games in the past often had businesses for you to manage, in this feudal Japan era game you instead have a farm to manage! The Battle Dungeon Missions are a set of challenging combat scenarios that can be accessed by speaking to a specific NPC located in the game’s world. These missions offer players a unique way to test their combat skills and earn valuable rewards and experience points. The Battle Dungeon offers players a set of increasingly difficult missions, each of which consists of a series of battles against powerful enemies leading to the superboss of these games. The Diligence Records is a system that tracks a player’s progress and achievements across various activities in the game. These records are essentially a form of achievement system that can be viewed in the game’s menu, offering players a way to track their accomplishments and earn rewards. Diligence Records are divided into various categories, each of which tracks a different aspect of a player’s progress.In addition to substories and bonds with friends, there is a wanted system that allows players to hunt down and defeat powerful criminals who are causing trouble in the game’s world. These criminals are known as “Wanted” targets, and they can be found throughout the game’s various districts. These battles are typically more difficult than regular battles in the game, as the targets have higher stats and unique abilities that make them formidable opponents.However, the game does a good job of gradually introducing players to its various systems and mechanics, so even inexperienced players should be able to enjoy the game with some patience and practice. One nice aspect of this title is that there’s no missable content unlike the older games, so if you want to do the main story first and then tackle the substories that’s perfectly fine. In terms of graphics and sound, Like A Dragon: Ishin is top-notch. The game’s visuals are stunning, with detailed character models, gorgeous environments, and impressive special effects. The game’s soundtrack is also excellent, with traditional Japanese music that perfectly capture the game’s blend of historical authenticity and over-the-top action (like in the bathhouse fight scene).Another criticism I have is that there is unfortunately no English dub, you’ll have to play it with Japanese voice acting and English subtitles, which is too bad because we’ve been spoiled with English dubs for several games now.As far as I know, there really is no other game that fills the niche that Yakuza, Judgement, and Like A Dragon does. When I was much younger, I had a lot of fun in Shenmue not just playing the main story but also have fun with optional content such as playing in arcades, and over 20 years later I find myself feeling the same when I play Like A Dragon: Ishin. I really enjoy the dramatic cutscenes and the art style, specifically how the characters look realistic.Like A Dragon: Ishin is a very fun game that offers a unique and engaging experience for fans of action-adventure games and Japanese history. With its challenging combat, many different combat styles available, an addicting crafting and upgrade system, engaging story, many mini-games and substories, and attention to detail, it is a must-play for anyone looking for a satisfying gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the series who has played every game available, even down to emulation, LAD: Ishin is something I'd say you need to buy only when its on sale.First, the positives. The setting is very unique for these games, and the combat can be just as satisfying and punchy as the mainline entries. The story is enjoyable, with its fair share of twists and turns, and the side content is as stacked as usual.This game, however, has obvious negatives that originate from both its status as a SEGA branded rerelease, and as an experimental series entry. The combat having 4 styles is nice, but only two are properly balanced, Swordsman and Wild Dancer. Swordsman suffers from godawful combo speed in the early game, and Wild Dance not having a proper guard sucks. The other two options, Gunman and Brawler, are on different ends of the usefulness scale. Gunman is far too easy to abuse, even in the early game, and tears through most non-hyper armor encounters. Brawler, by contrast, despite having all of the previous Komaki tech, does no damage unless you equip items that heavily buff the style. Boss fights also suck, as they utilize way more hyper armor than the original game, which makes them wars of attrition, and even ruins the drama of certain boss fights (looking at you final boss).The graphics make it really obvious that this is the RGG team's first delving into the Unreal engine. While I do agree it was necessary in order to better portray the more naturalistic tone of this entry, it comes with all the traditional issues of shader compilation stuttering and fps slowdown, along with low res textures. Side Content is probably where the experimental aspects of Ishin shine through, for better and for worse. On the one hand, currency for side content completion and Friendships are cool. On the other hand, most Friendships are either lengthier repeat fetch quests, or merely reskinned completion parameters, such as money spent on stores. The content centering around the home is cool, but either incredibly repetitive (farming and cooking) or fetch quests. AGAIN. The crafting system is probably the worst part though. The original game had sane costs for upgrading weapons, but the material grind did suck. Here, money required has increased one hundred fold (I am NOT kidding), and still keeps the old materials grind. The method by which you get these materials? Battle Dungeon. Which has higher enemy health pools than the original, necessitating use of the cards system, which clashes heavily with the more grounded themes of this game, and also alters the base game's content (reducing skill wheel health upgrades to incentivize card use, which inadvertently makes content that locks off cards way harder) The battle dungeon was a big grind in the original, but here it might as well be a part time job for the player in the worst sense of the phrase. And the only way to grind out the cash requirements for this game is through the chicken race, which is a lengthy and hellish process. Just use mods if you're trying to 100%, unlike in other games, its just not worth it. All in all, Ishin is a clearly experimental franchise point both at the time of its initial PS4 debut, and now in its rerelease. The gameplay hasn't either aged well, or has been marred by the quality of this rerelease. Some concepts that come with this are cool in theory, but they just cannibalize the original game to be properly integrated. This isn't a bad game by any means, but it sure is one of the worst Yakuza games I've played, which should tell you all you need to know.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you beat the last boss in Sekiro and go “I wish I was that guy”? Have you ever wanted to be in a Kurosawa film? Look no further.In Ishin, you too can be a Glock Saint in a samurai tale full to the brim of: love, revenge, secret techniques, secret identities, political plots, manly men yelling at each other, manly men crying at each other, manly men beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other, and epic one-on-one duels. And in between? Karaoke with the boys.Ishin is a Yakuza game through and through. And that is the best recommendation any game could ever receive.Unfortunately, there are some technical issues that hinder the experience. Partly due to the fact that the game is the first one made by them with the Unreal Engine. It’s a very good first effort but issues to show. Micro stuttering is definitely an issue throughout the game. Much more during the beginning but some will happen sporadically in cutscenes later in the game. The lighting in the game also has a couple miss steps. There are occasions where a character seems way too bright for an interior scene.Gameplay wise, the actual fighting can seem a little rough. Especially when you're using the gun where it seems like the game needs two to three shots to miss before it actually targets an enemy in a group. Smithing in this game is basically non-existent due to how grindy it is just to make stronger gear. However, on Normal difficulty, that's not an issue. The game will drop stronger gear sporadically after specific boss fights.The game is friendly to new players of the series since it's basically a side story. However, because they use faces from characters throughout the whole series as well as their theme songs, the game is much more appreciable for people who have played the other games.Still, if you can ignore the negatives (which is a pretty easy thing to do, in my opinion), you’ll have an awesome time with the game. Best OST of the series. One of the best stories in the series. Probably the best final fight in the series. Because of the issues, the highest I can give it objectively is an 8/10. If they can fix their stuttering and lighting (or if you can ignore it), 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon: Ishin is either the first Like a Dragon game in the West or the latest in a long line of a major franchises, depending on your view of the naming convention.  This was created by RGG Studio and they are well known for their “Yakuza” series, though that series is now named “Like a Dragon” which is a direct translation of the original series title, Ryu Ga Gotoku.However, Like A Dragon: Ishin, or Ishin as I’ll call it for brevity’s sake, is a stand-alone title, for the most part.  However, the connection to the entire Like A Dragon Franchise is important.  While this is a fresh new story in a new time period with new characters, every major character in Like A Dragon: Ishin uses a similar face to the rest of the Like A Dragon Series.  This might be the most important part of the game because for some it’s a little too on the nose, and for others, this is pure fan service, which is what fans of the series might enjoy.  Many characters who no longer are part of the larger franchise, appear once more in Ishin, and in many ways, this works. Seeing some of the great heroes' and villains' faces tell a new story is entertaining, however, there’s a bit of an uncanny valley for many of the characters.  It was often that I could tell that certain characters were people I knew, but sadly with a change in hairstyle and clothes it was hard to place them, again this is something some players may love, and some players may hate, and this time around it bothered me just enough that I feel like I should mention it. The one big negative though with this is that every character plays to type, meaning if the character is a villain in Like a Dragon as a whole, they’ll typically be a villain here, the same with the heroes.  While every character is different, it’s a shame that there wasn’t more of a mix between the heroes and villains of this story.That being said, the story told here is rather solid.  The game focuses on “Kiryu Kazuma”’s character Sakamoto Ryoma who is based on a rather famous historical character.  After a tumultuous first chapter (This is a Like a Dragon game after all), Sakamoto Ryoma adopts the name Saito Hajime.  Rurouni Kenshin fans will instantly perk up because that’s also a name of a major villain there, and sure enough both Ishin and Kenshin have characters based on the same historical character.The basis of most of Ishin’s story is rooted in historical facts.  Saito Hajime eventually joins the Shinsengumi, which is run by Kondo Isami, he’s befriended by Okita Soji (played by the same face as Majima Goro), and they are defending the Bakufu (shogunate).   This and much more of this story is based on historical fact.However Saito Hajime and Sakamoto Ryoma are not the same people, and a majority of the story is fictionalized, this is historical fiction, but similar to Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Like A Dragon: Ishin will make players more interested in the time period and the real characters behind this story.  Though Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a little more historically accurate, both of these are entertaining for the fictionalized accounts.The story in Ishin is mostly well-paced.  There is at least one chapter that just seems to have a minor reason for existing and the final chapter seems to load multiple unnecessary diversions for time, but overall, if players enjoy the typical Like a Dragon style, born from Yakuza movies, Ishin will feel right at home even if it’s based on the Samurai and the Bakumatsu time period (essentially the time period after the Black ships have arrived in Japan to “open up the country”).Sadly what is supposed to be the biggest twist in the story is given away almost immediately especially if players are familiar with Like A Dragon’s flow, but overall the story is well told and still will hold many surprises for fans of the series.  Though the story is only one of the major features of this franchise.  The combat will be where players are spending most of the time and in that Ishin is a little unstable.  The main draw of Ishin is to return to the Samurai time period, and that may make people think of a lot of sword fighting, but within the Bakumatsu time period, guns have entered into the mix.  The good news is Sakamoto Ryoma can use both, as well as combine them and use a bare-handed style as well.  That means there are four different fighting styles in the game, and each one feels different enough to be worth including.  Even the combination of sword and gun feels unique to both.  Bare-handed brawling against sword-wielding goons sounds dangerous, but there is an enhanced amount of defensive parry ability that helps offer a higher risk-reward structure in theory.In practice, however, Ishin boils down to two styles.  The sword is so powerful almost no other style is necessary, and there are only a few moments when the range is required.  The guns on the other hand can stun-lock large groups of enemies to the point where if players want to they can just rain fire down on enemies.  Ishin tries to balance this with enemies who have armor, which does weaken the gun’s power but just requires players to switch to the basic sword mode.  Bare-handed and the combined sword and gun style have neither the power nor the utility to be necessary and even though I tried my hardest to use the Barehanded mode, it’s a foolish move that will only make the game harder. Add in the fact that equipment exists in this universe and players will be able to get better guns and swords, and the focused styles also will provide more of the bonuses of either, there are only two of the four styles worth spending time with. This isn’t a negative per se, as long as you’re a player who is willing to accept that there are styles of fighting that have no purpose, but it’s a shame that the developer couldn’t balance the four styles to be more useful.As for the rest of Ishin, it has all the typical drapings of a Like a Dragon title.  Outlandish side stories, interesting characters, unique moments, a wonderful self-contained map, and a memorable location.  Mini-games return and with new additions added players will have everything from the classic Karaoke, mahjong, shogi, and casino games, to chicken racing and a Geisha set of mini-games that feels just explicit enough to make someone blush. But this is ultimately what a LIke a Dragon title is, which is also how Like a Dragon: Ishin has been sold.  Ishin was intended to tell a different story, and provide an odd form of fan service in that many characters already in the universe could return for one more game.  At times it feels almost like a play, with characters playing similar characters to their originals but telling a different story, but that’s also what makes this charming, it’s a chance to see new pairings, but also one more chance to fight Ryuji Goda, a chance to see an alternate history for Majima Goro, a chance for Kiryu Kazuma to hang out with friends once more and fight against a secret cabal once more. And in that, Like a Dragon Ishin succeeds.  It also succeeds in one other way.  As amazing as the Like a Dragon franchise is, many characters feel so well developed it’s hard for them to surprise characters once again, and Ishin allows a way to tell a new fresh story using characters fans are already quite familiar with.  Ishin is a breath of fresh air in that it can show there’s still a lot of life left in the Like a Dragon formula, even if it isn’t in a typical Like a Dragon game.   That’s perhaps Like a Dragon: Ishin’s strongest point, it’s the perfect game for someone who has played the entire franchise and wants to play a similar game, but not another of the main series entries.  And you know, I’m really happy to have played through this entire game and go another wonderful story out of it. 8/10 If you enjoyed this review, consider checking out my Youtube channel where I review games .

_childDocuments_.review: The story is fun and interesting, in classic RGG fashion a bunch of plot twists. The combat is weird, it works and doesn't work. I do enjoy the Katana style, but I also find parrying to be very slow and off. Graphically it looks good, it runs pretty good too. I was seeing some negative reviews mentioning stuttering and low fps but I didn't get any stuttering and I am on a lower end laptop playing this. My BIGGEST complain though is the minigames/side missions, specifically the arena and shenegumi battle missions. I found both of those I can't progress in as it just softlocks me without spawning more enemies or allowing me to pickup the requested item to complete the quest. So those 2 minigames are completely barred off from me playing, leaving really only the lackluster sub stories and the main quest line. If you want the expected story you'll get from RGG games then go ahead and get this, but if you're also looking for all the fun substories, combat, and minigames the mainline series has, this is not worth the $60-$70 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, it's important to clarify that this is a remaster, not a remake. The original game used a different engine, and this version has been rebuilt using Unreal Engine 4, with additional visual adjustments. This is significant because it requires much less effort than a full development cycle, resulting in a faster and more cost-effective product.The base game is currently priced at 59.99 EUR, with the Digital Deluxe edition priced at 69.99 EUR. Comparatively, Hogwarts Legacy, which was released in the same month, is priced at 59.99 EUR for the base game, and took approximately five years to develop with an estimated budget of 150 million USD. Despite using the same Unreal Engine 4, Hogwarts Legacy features the latest technology, such as ray tracing, and boasts impressive visuals and performance, including shader pre-compilation on PC.Although the remaster might have been worth the price if it were flawless, it unfortunately falls short in some areas. For example, cutscenes run at only 30 FPS, which is a jarring contrast to the game's 120 FPS, which can be immersion-breaking. It appears that the cutscenes are rendered in real-time, not as video files, so there is no reason for them to run at a different frame rate.Additionally, the intro and other cutscenes are not skippable (*), and there is no shader pre-compilation. Despite being a brand new remaster, the visuals are completely dated and do not compare favorably to other games in the same price range. For instance, Judgment, a game from the same developer that is older than this remaster, can run most of the game at 120 FPS, including cutscenes (with only a few pre-rendered scenes), has skippable cutscenes, zero stutter, and looks even better than this game.In conclusion, while the base game is great, the current state of the remaster does not justify the price tag, especially when there are other games available at the same price point with better visuals and performance.* I've started the game with mouse+keyboard and tried pressing several buttons to skip the intro, including the ESC key - none worked. Apparently, you can skip intros by first pressing "M", then some other button on the keyboard. With a controller it's more natural: pressing the start button (which is usually mapped to ESC on keyboard, but not in this game), then pressing "A" / "X".

_childDocuments_.review: i love the LAD games, but definitely skip this one. major problems abound, including:1. so, much. grind. the game's reliance on skill tree upgrades to increase combat damage is good, but all but one of the styles rely on weapon damage to bring damage up to snuff as well. how do you get good weapons? grind hundreds of thousands of units of currency, collect materials on stacked rng systems, and you'll still feel like you hit like a wet noodle. why? well, that brings up complaint 2 and 3.2. brawler. just as a fighting style. has some of the most useful counters and heat actions in the game but does utter garbage for damage. even the tiger drop is generally useless in this game, but fully leveling the style is necessary for major sections of side content (as well as essential upgrades like faster heat build, quickly changing styles, and health upgrades)3. the engine and combat. like a dragon: ishin! was remade by a studio that is not RGGStudios, and consequently, they didn't use any of RGG's in-house engines like the dragon engine or yakuza 5's engine (the engine that the original ishin!, yakuza 0, kiwami, and of course yakuza 5's gameplay are based on). for gameplay this means two things: firstly, juggles are gone. completely gone. enemies do not bounce off of walls or the floor, enemies can't be cornered for long combos, etc. secondly, the rules of engagement are completely screwed up; frequently bosses and enemies will turn around during a backturned rush combo, resulting in frustratingly inconsistent damage opportunities. all of this compounds with the following...4. you feel weak. damage always feels too low, and enemy damage always feels punishingly high. the only way to remedy this seems to be dropping the difficulty down, but as someone who has played many many past LAD games on hard or even legend difficulties, it is a stark and frustrating difference. only a few mistakes can result in complete failure, but your damage is so low and your combos so slow, damage windows so inconsistent, that playing the game itself feels like spinning a slot machine. in conclusion: this game sucks, play literally any other LAD/RGG/Yakuza game to have an infinitely better time. if you're a newcomer, play yakuza 0. peace

_childDocuments_.review: unfortunately, like a dragon: ishin might just be my least favorite RGG game. as a big fan of the yakuza games and having played through all of them including the judgment spin-offs, i can't help but feel disappointed by ishin and here's why:the plot:simultaneously rushed and very slow, which is quite a feat but nothing new in a yakuza game. even though i did enjoy most of it, the ending left a sour taste in my mouth - particularly the instance when the "puppet master" shows himself. not only was this moment rushed, it was incredibly jarring. he jumps in the middle of an emotional moment between two characters as the story is about to wrap up and acts like an absolute cartoon villain. i was actually flabbergasted by how terrible it was. you've got the whole nine yards: shows up out of thin air? check. machiavelic laugh? check. starts spewing his entire plan with a smug expression? check. pisses and ♥♥♥♥♥ himself when his plan takes a turn for the worst (surprise) in the matter of a few seconds? check. the yakuza games are notorious for having moments like these, but MAN this one was horribly executed especially because it's his first appearance in the story as well. combat:you've got four styles this time around: the swordsman, the wild dancer, gunsman and brawler. out of all of these, only the swordsman and wild dancer are actually useful in a fight. - the swordsman is the most frustrating style in probably the whole series. it's slow, clunky and you will fail to connect most of your attacks, but it deals the most damage. recommended for 1v1's against stronger enemies. - the wild dancer is very fun and also the only style you should really use throughout most of the game. even though it's very fast and flashy, it lacks any substance. after you've unlocked a specific rush combo ability, you will be able to mash the dodge and the basic attack button through literally ANY enemy in the game which becomes boring very fast. - gunman: you shoot guns. that's it. you don't even have to reload! just run away and shoot them at a distance (if they don't deflect the bullets).  - brawler: even though it can get very fun, it hardly does any damage. i could kill my enemies faster with words of affirmation than with my fists in this game. shucks.overall a very frustrating experience. enemies will hit you anyway after failing to connect their attacks, your swords will go through them and not do damage at all, the list goes on. crafting:the blacksmith is a very interesting mechanic that sadly falls short. you've got these massive trees to craft different kinds of swords but all of that becomes trivial when you realize the game hands you over much stronger swords by simply completing the main quests. what's the point of grinding in the dungeons, collecting materials and saving money only to get a better sword anyway by just progressing through the story? i spent around 5-6 hours gathering everything i needed to craft a good sword only to get a much stronger one for free an hour later. the music:both the new songs and the remixed ones from past games sound great and they're one of the strongest points in this game. unfortunately, RGG had the bright idea of reusing awano and kuze's theme for their respective boss fights here. why not just remix them and turn them into their own thing? what's the point of reusing them? i'm not sure if it was laziness or fan-service but either way i didn't like much of that.conclusion:if you're a die-hard fan of these games, try this one out. the cinematics are still very entertaining and every character has the charm and presence you'd expect, so everything will still feel very familiar - but do be prepared for the worst features of every yakuza game to be present here and dialed to 11.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! Is a perfect standalone experience to get yourself into the Like a Dragon franchise. You do not need to know any of the other extensive personalities that surround the franchise and can perfectly stand on its own without its older brothers. There is little to complain about when it comes to this game outside of a few gripes when it comes to balancing and one hundred percent completion. There are four unique fighting styles you can experience, however to be frank you'll most likely use two out of the four extensively and towards the end of the game just one due to how broken it is. The mini-games in this collection are great and can keep you busy for hours if the dramatic story becomes too much for you to handle and you need a break. You can do anything between fishing, working at a noodle shop, hunting down bounties, the infamous mahjong that Like a Dragon is known for within the community and plenty more. The story is a fantastic setting set within 1860s Japan during the Bakumatsu era at the end of the Edo period. You play as Sakamoto Ryoma a real-life historical figure who gets tangled in his own revenge scheme, finds himself embroiled in the tumultuous socio-political climate of the era. I have left out countless activities and didn't even mention the RPG like leveling up system, down to the blacksmith where you can upgrade your weapons and armor.If you like feudal japan settings, drama, RPG like qualities, goofiness within minigames, and can look beyond a few questionable balance choices! You will undoubtedly find a fantastic time within Like A Dragon: Ishin! PS: Okita Soji is husband.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a mediocre 2014 game with new, good and bad adjustments for 60 dollary doos. Yikes. (Wait for a sale.)Want a good Yakuza spin-off? Buy Lost Judgment.I love the Yakuza series, but LAD: Ishin is so painfully average. There was not a point where I cared about whatever was happening. So much talking and so many cutscenes, yet nothing of value is told.It's either: historical exposition, stating the obvious 3 times in a row or rarely actual interesting stuff (character conflict, motivations or banter).The protagonist is barely directly involved in the plot for most of the game. He either gets told what to do or tries to intervene too late.You have this "Avengers assemble" type of deal, with all these actors / characters from previous games together here and they barely interact or do anything.The plot twist is crystal clear from 2 hours in, so have fun chasing the obvious for 20 more hours. I must also note the main character, Sakamoto Ryoma, is so bland. He's this goody two shoes, always morally right. This might sound weird, since he's almost a copy of Kiryu Kazuma from Yakuza, but hear me out. Kiryu is a criminal, this is the card life dealt him. Constantly using violence and breaking the law, because he knows no better. He was raised this way and himself notes many times, isn't smart enough to find another path. You could say, he's a flawed character.Compared to Sakamoto, who's 100% right 100% of the time.About the main villan:I do love my boy Mine (Hijikata) here, character from Yakuza 3. He is given a lot of screen time and done justice. They did my boy right. Mostly because he's the only interesting character in the WHOLE game. He's got some ambiguity to him, you can never be sure what he's up to.Everyone else is so one note, you could read their minds.Select Wild Dancer style and mash X button. Not a SINGLE encounter in the main story and my encountered side stories requires any strategy. To boot, the other styles are complete garbage and not worth using.Now, I know none of Yakuza games had particularly advanced combat, but you could mix up your approach a bit. Ishin and Yakuza 0 are extremely similar to each other, so lemme compare them, as they basically released at the same time (2014 and 2015). In Yakuza 0, let's say you use the Beast style. It is most useful against groups of enemies, since your slow, wide attacks can't be interrupted. However, it's unhandy in fast 1v1 boss fights, but you COULD make it work in your own way just by attacking at the same time as the boss and trading damage. In most cases, it felt good to be this unstoppable tank. In Ishin, Brawler style is similar, but you cannot block or tank attacks from the bosses, because all of them (and most basic enemies) use a blade, thus knock you down before you hit them. This means you must constantly parry with strict timings and chip away with low damage, if you prefer the unarmed Brawler style.Or you switch to Wild Dancer style and ignore almost all mechanics. It's just boring. It feels unnecessary to use other 3 styles. Stunningly beautiful and as good as any Yakuza games. Overflowing with activities like dancing, singing and mahjong. Plenty of side stories, which are well written and funny, like having to translate a letter between lovers. Or some sort dance mob that would only happen in modern times, yet there it is. It's all so bizarre in the most fun way. Unlike Yakuza 0, you can enter most shops without a loading screen (wow, next gen, I know).Yet, there is an annoying delay to skipping lines of dialogue, that was fixed in Yakuza Kiwami 1 onward, but is present here for some reason. The line must play for like a half a second before you can skip (even if you hold auto-skip with R1+A buttons). I believe it all comes down to greed. This is not worth a full 60 bucks price tag.I did not like most of my time with it. I only finished it because I really love this series, but was kinda bummed in the end.There is definitely a bit of enjoyment to be had here, which would be fine if bought on sale.Story and combat are such a snooze-fest, I cannot be bothered with completing the good side stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Yak- I mean Like a Dragon  If you like these games, get it  If you've never played these, though, perhaps start elsewhere  This has its own self contained story as a past era spinoff, but the historical characters are essentially played by Yakuza/Like a Dragon characters, and knowing their normal incarnations is part of the entertainment of this game   But keep in mind that Sega has introduced microtransactions into the "trooper card" system  Please do not pay for these   Editing after putting in quite a few more hours and also finishing the main story:   I stand by the early review I did, as I enjoyed the game quite a bit  The game is pretty much exactly what I expected from a Bakumatsu Yakuza spinoff, and the game had me glued to my seat for many hours   But I am also a little disappointed by the overall situation of this release   Cutscenes and minigames capped to 30 FPS  Additional difficulty locked behind paywall (This personally doesn't matter to me as I play Normal, but shady business practice is shady)  Consumable items sold as "DLC" that work only for one savefile, and you have to rebuy them if you want them again in a different playthrough  Game sold at a $60 pricepoint as a "remake" but outside improved graphics and character replacements, nothing is really remade, and the gameplay has seen no improvements since the Ishin/Zero/Kiwami1 era  (Ironically, it's not faithful to the original either due to the character replacements. But at least this shouldn't be an issue for most English speaking players who haven't played the original Ishin)  Switching to UE4 is being marketed as some big deal, but in the end the only thing it gave us is DX12 shader compilation stutters (use the command line switch -dx11 to reduce this problem). I do hope this is the first and last time they use this   Feels a bit like Sega executives are letting the recent success of RGG games get to their heads
