_childDocuments_.review: I've been keeping an eye on this since it dropped the little demo almost two years previous.  I'll start this by saying This game is  gorgeous.  Its hand drawn environments and fully animated cut-scenes ooze style and originality in their Taoist come cyberpunk setting.  There are even some sections that are done like little comic strip cutouts along with a wealth of  distinctive flairs that set this apart from other hand drawn games that have been copied to death recently; *cough* Hollow Knight clones.  The combat is  inspired by Sekiro to the point where this feels like I am actually playing a 2d version of Sekiro; right down to bopping people on the heads when they charge a red unblockable; the only thing missing is a kanji symbol.  The controls are hyper tight, the parry is well timed and very responsive and the enemies are vicious and formidable after the tutorial.  Gameplay and exploration is along the same line as Blasphemous or aforementioned Hollow Knight, but there is a genuinely intriguing and grim/beautiful narrative unfolding that's a little less vague than a lot of soulslikes and metroids in the way that it is delivered. Be prepared to stop and take a little beat every now and again instead of all out action continually, especially at the start where there is a decent bit of exposition; don't worry though this doesn't disrupt gameplay flow after the first hour/tutorial zone. >You start with a very minimal toolkit but you WILL unlock all the things you might imagine would make both the combat and traversal more fun, just give it a while to let the game unfold. >Enemies and bosses start super manageable but quickly amp up in difficulty. They never feel unfair, but rest assured to those looking for a challenge, don't be put off by the gradual ease into difficulty.>This game is dark as ♥♥♥♥, with a lot of violence, brutal narrative decisions and world lore. It's also really beautiful and heartwarming in equal measure, but don't be fooled by the cute character design and art style, this setting has a lot of grit to it. I have loved pretty much everything about the game so far and I urge everyone with a spare 25 euro to check out this absolute gem of a release if anything I've said in this review sounds interesting or appealing. It's beautiful in content and presentation, its combat mechanics are amazing and there is a metric tonne of heart and soul pouring from every pore and pixel.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my few 10/10 games (one of the other being Hollow Knight) - and guess what, I hate platformer.When I first know about Nine Sols, I thought "oh, HK, but with cat instead of bug". However, this game was not "just more HK" as I first thought: it reminds me of the first time I played HK. I feel like I never actually wanted "more HK" (that is what Silksong is for), I just want to experience the joy of playing a wonderful game like I did with HK.While the game takes a fair amount of inspiration from HK, the vibe and feel are different. First of all, this is a story focused game, and it has a very good story imo. While I love HK, that game story is pretty much Dark Soul 1 (and I do like both games, I cannot really say their stories are engaging). If you are interested and familiar with east asian culture and mythology, you will have a great time spotting the influence and messages. I also like that its story is rather straight forward, but complex due to the theme and characters, rather than just twists and drams like modern writings. I guess I should not be surprised given that the developer's previous 2 games are highly rated story games.The second thing worth mentioning is the difficulty. I do think the game is on the challenging side, but somehow I always feel the game is "easy". Perhaps it feels so because the gameplay is "fair" most of the time: you can dodge and parry pretty much anything with very forgiving windows. However, the game is very punishing when it comes to misplay - you have fairly low health and can be two-three shot by the bosses if you button smash. The playstyle is also surprisingly flexible, having multiple styles to choose from and mostly balanced.I want to note that I consider myself an awful platfomer player, hate it even, and I also play only on keyboard and mouse. Yet this game feels much easier and better than Hollow Knight (I believe keyboard and mouse is just awful to play for platforming games like HK, since you need very precise movement). Some people complain about the hitbox, which I guess is kinda fair, but then again most enemies and bosses have easy to recognise attack pattern. Again, unlike games like HK, this game is less about precise movement (so it's not like you try to dodge enemy hitbox), but about timing. The game has more Sekiro DNA than HK as it does suggest in the game description. I actually like Nine Sols combat slightly more than Sekiro because Sekiro combat later on relies too much on counter.Do note, if you do have trouble with parry-style combat, the game has a very flexible difficulty adjustment in the Story Mode! I consider the story a huge part of the game, so it's total ok to enjoy the game with less punishing combat.There are quite a lot of other praise or nitpick I can say, such as the music and sound, characters and tropes, etc. but that would be too long for a Steam review. I had one small bug while playing but it is fixed pretty much the next day; performance is much better than HK at launch as well. The ending makes me quite moody for a while, both sad and happy. Really though, it was quite an emotional experience and I hope people will also enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super sick.  Story is really great with a super strong and interesting theme.  It looks and feels like playing a manga, and I'm not a super big manga or anime guy, but it has a really cool presentation, I loved it.  Combat is fantastic, the boss fights really shine, the game isn't easy, but it is absolutely cool/fun enough to merit it's difficulty.  I bought it at full price (a rarity for me these days) and I would buy it again, and I will definitely play it again at some point.  My only minor suggestions to the devs would be to visually outline some of the projectiles a little in some of the Boss Fights near the end, and maybe explain (maybe they did and I missed it, but I don't think they did) that grounded parry must face the opponent's attack, I didn't find this out until late, late game, and I could see others not figuring this out on their own.  Really great game, I will buy whatever this dev makes next.  Lot of passion in this one.Two things of note1.  This is more combat focused with a metroidvania style sprawling map, but there is not a lot of backtracking for exploration and super hidden secrets, though the exploration is not mind numbing either, it is still there, just minimized and takes a back seat to the very fun combat and excellent story.  Chances are you'll have missed a couple things by the time you have all the traversal abilities, but its fun to go find the few things that slipped through the cracks.2.  I've seen a lot of reviews reducing this game to 2D Sekiro, but while I do think it obviously takes some ideas from Sekiro, it also has a couple of it's own and the nature of the extra/added mechanics makes this it's own game.  I know most people are comparing it out of love, but I almost missed this extreme gem of a game due to it being explained that way to me across multiple reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty freaking sick, not gonna lie. It's like Chinese Hollow Knight but furrier, edgier, gorier, and in space. The protagonist is lovingly talking to a child one second and then brutally executing someone the next. The protagonist is also a chain smoker and an alcoholic which is great for representation; he's constantly talking about how he can't wait to drink alcohol, just like me. Game is actually pretty linear because your AI assistant tells you where to go and what to do, but there are some secrets. Combat is pretty good when you get used to it. In this game you walk into a room with the boss and they start wailing on you and you better learn to parry them. You can die instantly because there's almost no I-frames between damage. It's very easy to get combo'd and die instantly especially when multiple enemies or floor spikes are involved. There's also a few moments that will make you go "holy cow the boss has another phase?" which is a huge plus. I like the setting and the lore and the story here. I also like the NPCs, I wish there were more you could talk to. Dialogue and text is pretty good despite being made in Taiwan. True final boss is very difficult and the hardest part of the game, as it should be.Overall, I give this game a 9/10. It's freaking sweet. This game is only not as popular as hollow knight because Dunkey hasn't told people about it (as of this review). WARNING: This game contains a creepypasta jumpscare which may make you poop your pants and give you nightmares.

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment I stepped into New Kunlun, I was hooked on Nine Sol's dark, cryptic lore and fantastic "Tao-punk" art direction. The parry system and combat mechanics are genre defining and this title really came out of left field from RCG. The map designs are immense and very well sequenced, and I found myself wanting to explore every area several times as I acquired new movement abilities. The combat Nine Sols delivers will force the player to adapt their play style/gear and make strategic decisions before and during combat. This makes winning fights extremely rewarding. There really is nothing like the feeling of chaining several successful perfect parries and then hitting a max Qi charge talisman for some massive damage 😊.This game took me by surprise and I wish I would've picked it up sooner. If you like Sekiro, Hollow Knight, Souls games, or really any other titles that punish you for mistakes and force you to adapt, this is for you. That being said, don't let the difficulty stop you from making this purchase. There is a "story" mode and for a mere $30, Nine Sols is 100% worth that for what it offers lore wise.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is an absolute home run for me in all aspects. The gameplay is fast, exhilarating, and challenging - but it wasn't soul crushingly difficult. I love the parry and talisman mechanics. There are difficulty spikes and certain bosses are relentless (and kind of annoying), but nothing felt impossible or unfair. Even at the toughest bosses I could feel myself improving on every subsequent try. The hand drawn artwork is gorgeous and stylish, despite the UI being a little bit awkward. The audio and music are 10/10. Nine Sols also has one of the best stories in recent memory.Overall a total masterpiece game worth your attention. It doesn't have the same turnoffs as other soulslike metroidvanias; the exploration isn't super tedious and the difficulty isn't insurmountable. Even if you aren't into the genre, give it a try. But make sure to use a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard, but if you like Sekiro, which focuses on reacting to enemy attacks, once you're familiar with the parry timing, this will be the most satisfying Metroidvania combat for you. The core of Nine Sols lies in its parry combat system. The mechanics are intuitive yet challenging, requiring precise timing and strategic thinking, making each enemy encounter a test of skill rather than mere button-mashing. Boss battles are intense, multi-phase encounters that require a deep understanding of the boss's mechanics (I tried the final boss for 3-4 hours until I beat it... other bosses may take 20-30 minutes to get familiar with their mechanisms). Additionally, character customization allows players to tailor their abilities and playstyles; I did change my setup a few times to make some boss fights easier.Art style plays a very important part in a Metroidvania game, in my opinion. Since we run around the map a lot, the background must be interesting enough to keep players enjoying the journey. And one of Nine Sols' most striking features is its art style. I think it might be the most unique style in the Metroidvania genre right now. The game world is beautifully crafted with detailed, hand-drawn environments with Taoist mythology aesthetics.Must also mention that Red Candle is known for making horror games, and the nightmare part of this game is very unnerving, even if the boss there is a furry lynx mommy.Both are incredibly good. The perfect parrying sound effect is really satisfying, and every time you attack, you can hear the long sleeves swinging. The soundtrack of Nine Sols is another highlight, perfectly capturing the mood of the game. Every main boss has their own unique theme; some of them even change with their phases, really hyping up the fights. I love the Chinese religious vibe of the music mixed with the electro genre; the soundtrack is well-composed and complements the game's tone effectively.The narrative provides enough context to keep players engaged. Plot might be the weakest part of this game, but I still enjoyed the interactions with NPCs and bosses.A must-play for fans who appreciate reaction combat systems and the Metroidvania genre. Its Tai Chi-style parry combat is a breath of fresh air, offering a level of engagement and challenge that is both satisfying and addictive. The overall experience of playing Nine Sols is one that will definitely stay with you long after the credits roll.    A very polished game, as seen from the boss and map designs.    Fluid and engaging parry combat    Unique art style    Well-composed music and satisfying sound effects    Some respawn points are a bit too far    Early stages may feel annoying hard if the player hasn't found abilities like air dodge or double jump.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best indie soulslike games of the year—and potentially of all time if you're into this kind of game. Given how popular Hollow Knight is, I'm surprised this game hasn't gained the same level of recognition. As many have noted, it plays like Hollow Knight with a unique twist on Sekiro's parry system. The combat is simple yet incredibly fluid, offering a challenge without being overly punishing (you can change to lower difficulty if you prefer). Once you become familiar with the wide range of available skills, you'll find yourself pulling off impressive and satisfying moves.The art style is stunning, and the story is engaging. However, if you can read Chinese, you'll find the experience significantly richer. Many of the characters and locations are rooted in ancient Chinese mythology, which adds a fascinating layer of depth. While this cultural exploration is a major plus for me, I can see how the names and references might feel obscure if you don't speak the language.Although the overall world-building is decent, the weakest aspects of the game are probably the dialogue and character development. The dialogue can feel a bit flat, and most characters come across as one-dimensional.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get the negatives out of the way first. The thing that bothered me the most about this game is the fact that there's a ton of cutscenes and dialogue, and you have no option to skip them aside from fast forwarding the text. Why this is still a thing games do in 2024 I will never understand. It especially sticks out as a flaw in a soulslike / metroidvania like this because a lot of players will naturally want to replay and speedrun it, and they'll end up spending a lot of time just sitting there waiting for the cinematics to end. Even playing casually I found it just slowed down the pacing too often for my liking. There's also a little bit of jank with the hitboxes. They're consistent once you get used to them, but some attacks just aren't very intuitive visually and lead to that feeling of "wait, how the hell did that hit me?"All that put aside, I still think this is a fantastic game overall, and definitely the best game in its genre I've played in a long time. While it's easy to tell it takes inspiration from Hollow Knight, I think it sets itself apart through the style and setting more than enough. There's a really cool blend here of eastern mythology and cyberpunk aesthetics that makes exploring and getting lost in this game's world a joy, and each area feels completely distinct through both atmosphere and gameplay. I'm also just a big fan of the artstyle overall, I always love 2D hand drawn art in games and this is a beautiful example.The combat system also strays pretty far from what you'd expect in a typical metroidvania, being highly focused on blocking / parrying attacks and waiting for openings rather than playing aggressively. There's definitely a learning curve, but improving at it and taking down some of the tougher bosses feels extremely satisfying. I honestly think it feels pitch perfect, and the fact you're still getting new attacks and modifiers to add to your kit late into the game make it stay fresh to the end.Lastly, the map design. In the grand scheme of this genre, this game isn't all that open ended compared to something like Super Metroid or Hollow Knight. With a few exceptions you'll be going through each area in the order the game wants you to. It's something I'm personally fine with, since it allows for a better difficulty curve, but I could see others being a little disappointed with the linearity. Each individual area does atleast feel pretty open and expansive, with tons of secrets to find. I also appreciated how you never feel like you do too much backtracking in this game, especially since you unlock fast travel not too far into the game.Overall, this game will definitely be a highlight of 2024 for me, and I'm really glad I decided to give it a shot. I'm usually pretty intimidated by soulslikes just because I've definitely dropped off of a few of them pretty early on, but this game felt a little more reasonable with its difficulty than most. (Plus, not having obnoxious runbacks every time you fail a boss is a nice bonus.) I had so many moments where I felt overwhelmed when first attempting a new boss or learning certain attacks, but eventually being able to overcome those parts was just so rewarding in a way games haven't made me felt in a while, and I think that feeling is what I took from this game the most.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely amazing metroidvania game, the music, combat, and story all really come together to make a memorable unique experience. The combat is fair with the balance for parrying being really solid even if its not perfectly timed the game encourages you to keep trying with the internal damage mechanic which definitely sets apart from other games parry systems where if you miss it or time it improperly you are punished severely. Basically non perfect parry will still counter the attack but you take regainable damage. _childDocuments_.review: I was initially recommend Nine Sols by a friend who pitched it as 2D Sekiro. I've never been that big on metroidvanias (bought Hollow Knight but never made it past the first few hours), but I absolutely adore Sekiro so I decided to give Nine Sols the good ol' college try. RedCandleGames has really created quite the gem here. While Nine Sols is by no means perfect, it absolutely nails the rhythm-game-esque feeling of Sekiro's parry system, and there is a decent amount of customizability through the jade system. The boss fights are a joy, and the two 3-phase bosses for sure rank up there with the likes of Sword Saint Isshin, Lady Maria, and Malenia (not to mention the OSTs!)What honestly surprised me the most was the storytelling. While nothing absolutely groundbreaking/mindblowing, the story is well-written and well-executed, and definitely has moments where it hits you in feels. For a game that I expected to just rush through smacking things, I found myself actually slowing down to read bits of lore and dialogue. TLDR: Play Nine Sols now

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the entire game, and it was a hell of a ride.The game is extremely unforgiving but very fair, you can't compare it to Hollow Knight because they are fundamentally so different, you jump in and attack then dodge in Hollow Knight, in Nine Sols you can't just jump away from the attacks, parry is a must, and when you get into the flow of the fight, it feels so rewarding to perfectly parry everything the boss throws at you.The game forces you to be patient, if you try to end a fight quickly most likely the only thing that will end quickly is your life. Stay calm, feel the rhythm, and try to parry everything, since literally everything hits like a truck (even the common enemies, never try to rush).As I said, Nine Sols is super hard so it might not be for everyone, but the game is NOT unfair, there is not a single time where I felt the fight was out of my control and that the game is just throwing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at me, I always feel like I can win it if I just calm down and be more precise, I never felt like it's unfair even when I literally took 5.5 hours to beat the final boss.The game also has a very good story that keeps me invested until the very end, there is a lot of dialogues to read, but they're all very good for people that can appreciate a good story.I decided to try this game after hearing people said it's a good game to play while waiting for Silksong, but I was wrong, it's a game that deserves to be picked up by anyone, not just for people that are interested in Hollow Knight. Also Nine Sols' price ($30) is not expensive in my opinion, the game is worth $30, it's just that Hollow Knight is ridiculously cheap at $15.

_childDocuments_.review: Outstanding game! Not only is Nine Sols a delight to look at with its gorgeous art-style, it's also filled to the brim with memorable boss fights and a world that feels expansive and interesting to explore. The story is on the darker side and it isn't afraid to takes its time. That part may not be for everyone, but in my opinion, the time spent on character development made the (true) ending hit that much harder. That being said, this was easily one of the most rewarding experiences I've had finishing a game, due in no small part to the strength of the writing and the tough but tremendously fun combat. Once you get the hang of the timing for parrying and how to use your talisman, the fights start to feel really, really good. So if you're looking for a story-driven metroidvania with a deep focus on combat, this is one to try. Also, best boy Shuanshuan <3

_childDocuments_.review: Man I wanted to like this game. Beautiful artstyle, interesting setting, cool gameplay setup etc.But the combat system. Holy crap the combat system. It is NOT fun, it is purely frustrating and only serves to kill the immersion constantly. This is the worst way to implement a combat system revolving around parry that I've ever seen. I've 100%'ed Sekiro, MGR and God of War, and I hate trying to parry in this game. It gets even worse when you're forced to fight very nimble enemies in a tiny arena with foreground objects obscuring them, and when I got to the area that is full of enemies that explode when they die (and also jump onto you at extreme speeds when you're trying to hit something else so that you end up detonating them in your face) is the point where frustration > enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option for reviews here on Steam.The mechanics? Gorgeous. Parrying is fantastic to do, and in general very worth it.There is very little endlag to moves, everything is snappy.I've played Hollow Knight,  I'll try my best to refrain from comparing Nine Sols to it, that seems unfair.Healing is something I would like to compare though. You have limited charges in your healing pipe, and you can't get them back without properly going to a "bench". That, on paper, is perfectly fine. Several games have done similar for healing, such as Tunic's Healing Potions. You have an innate autoheal, but I dunno about you, I don't wanna wait in the case of me getting on low hp.But the issue isn't in the healing. It's in the damage you need to heal.I'll admit- it's probably a skill issue and I might be salty. But it feels like enemies do just too much damage. It feels like enemies kill you in ~4 & 1/2 hits. Weird metric, but hopefully that gets the point across. At least where I'm at at the time of this review, an annoyingly consistent number of enemies typically use multi-hit (2 hits 90% of the time) attacks. So that ~4 & 1/2 hits goes down to ~2 combos.It doesn't help that this game has a mechanic equal to HK's Shades or Tunic's Spirits, you lose your stuff until you get back to where you died.Here's the kicker for me though- if an enemy kills you, it inherits your stuff. You need to  it to get your stuff back.But if you died to a tough enemy, and now that still tough enemy has your stuff, how do you beat it?My overall opinion of this game is just meh. The best way I can put it into words is that a gem of a game tries its best to make you dislike it. I am constantly switching between great joy and insane frustration.Not for the faint of heart!Edit: Final boss has some total bs in there, took me >1hr, a lot compared to the other bosses

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, truly. Probably my personal GOTY, at least as of the time of this writing.Both the story and the combat start out a little slow (especially in the first hour or so of gameplay), but after playing through the game twice now I actually kinda like this - the primary combat tools that you start out with (parry, dodge, slash, talisman) are going to be your bread and butter for the majority of the game and so spending a while getting acquainted with them makes a lot of sense, and from a narrative perspective I appreciated getting a feel for the characters a bit before they started dropping a ton of Proper Noun Exposition into the mix. Once the game gets going though, it really gets going - both the plot and the combat evolve in fun and interesting ways, and while the combat remains focused on parries throughout I was pleasantly surprised at the variety of different "builds" you could do, though once I found my favored setup I mostly only switched it up a few times for very specific enemy types towards the end of the game.Story wise, this game pretty easily has one of the best stories and narratives of any metroidvania I've played in the past few years. At first it felt like they were going with a "we're not really going to give you a clear plot" idea that so many metroidvanias have utilized recently, but that was just a setup to get you familiar with the setting and the characters - the story and world are fleshed out both in some story scenes and flashbacks, but also just in the world around you through lore pickups. By the end I was very invested in the characters and the story, which is impressive to me in a game where probably a full half of my first file's playthrough was spent bashing my head against bosses.All that to say - if metroidvanias appeal to you, you should probably give this game a try. I thought for sure that the combat would be too hard for me, but once you get the hang of how the game works it is actually fairly forgiving - and the story is well worth the time it takes to get used to the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. The artistic style is fantastic, the characters are amazing, and the environments stand out, each new zone having an unique theme and score to it. However, I am still unable to recommend this game as the combat, which is its primary feature and mechanic, is the most frustrating thing about it. This is exemplified extremely well with the boss Yanlao: the game has a stun feature where Yi can get knocked to the ground by certain attacks; however, like games in the Soulsborne series, Yi is NOT given some i-frames to recover here but is entirely susceptible to damage. This becomes a clear problem when fighting Yanlao since missing a SINGLE parry in the second phase can knock you down, get you hit, thrown into a laser and hit again and you will die in one single combo that you cannot do anything about. Outside of this particular boss, this mechanic has killed me so many times where it is straight up unfair and can only be boiled down to poor game design. In addition to this, the game's respawn system is the most atrocious thing I have ever seen. Once more, if you get hit by spikes or something of the likes, you respawn, ONCE AGAIN without a single i-frame meaning that the enemies around you immediately attack you without you being able to do anything about it, often leading to undeserved and stupid deaths. This is honestly game-breaking and I am stunned that it made it through testing.

The only souls-like I had completed up until now was Steelrising, partly because it is relatively forgiving but also because I liked its style and the setting. It took 35 hours, but I finally finished Nine Sols (standard mode, normal ending) as well. A more skilled player would need much less time. The later bosses took me a long time to learn, and the final boss took me three sessions of one hour each. _childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols really surprised me. The level of detail and thoughtful craft put into this game is seriously impressive. It’s one of the most satisfying experiences I’ve had with a game in years. If you’re a fan of Metroidvanias and Souls games, this game is worth your time.You’ll no doubt read about how the game is hard. It is, sure, but it’s equally rewarding, and you  have to be a Sekiro player to enjoy it. I wasn’t. I’d never played game that placed such a strong emphasis on parry mechanics. From my perspective, the game does a great job onboarding players with that style of play in the early game by being thoughtful about enemy density and attack patterns. As the game progresses, there’s appreciable variation in enemy behavior and quantity, such that there’s a benefit to approaching encounters in different ways fairly often. Some enemies benefit from being engaged aggressively, some defensively. Developing a sense for that and learning how to execute the games mechanics skillfully was  satisfying. The implementation of the internal damage system, in particular, was something that stood out as novel design which yielded satisfying gameplay. The game also provides the player with a fair amount of progression and customization options in its static skill tree and separate configurable skill slot systems. Nine Sols rewards thoughtful selection of Jades, talisman style and arrow type, and in the cases of its most difficult challenges, demands it.The bosses, in particular, are what elevate this game from an experience that I liked to an experience I loved. Yes, I died . However, for me, learning the attack patterns of bosses—when to parry, when to punish—was the ideal mix of frustrating and rewarding. The game has that exquisite alchemy of making some encounters feel nearly impossible at first, but each attack, each movement of the boss communicates how to approach it, so that when you’ve learned to read a boss and defeat it, it is immensely gratifying. I’ve played Hollow Knight, Dark Souls, Elden Ring, etc. For me, Nine Sols has among the strongest, most consistent quality of boss design I have ever seen in a game. The final boss, in particular, was an incredible challenge, and the experience of overcoming it cemented Nine Sols as an all-time game for me.As a frequent Metroidvania player, I found a lot to love in the level design. The game does a great job of tucking away secrets and rewards, difficult to access areas, and hidden bosses. The game really rewards exploration and I had a great time scratching the corners of each map trying to find everything. The game doles out movement abilities over time, such that playing the game a dozen hours in feels significantly different than playing the game just a few hours in. The game is also good about ensuring that these new movement abilities have utility in combat as well, giving you different ways to approach or deal with enemies apart from using the standard parry. The game gives you some prompts about where you might go, but it absolutely does not hold your hand. In my playthrough, I wound up in a few frightening areas on a couple occasions just from exploring thoroughly, which I always enjoy, because it serves as foreshadowing and makes the world of the game feel expansive and non-linear.The narrative of the game took a while to get its hooks into me, but when it did, I found myself invested in the world, characters, and mysteries of New Kunlun. The lore, delivered both in dialogue and found objects, really drew me in over time, and I was engaged by how the long history of the Solarians informed the aesthetic of the game and its narrative direction. I do wish there was  more to directly reference in the game’s database (“what was the difference between  and  again?”), but I suspect the lack of an explicit glossary was intentional. The net affect is that it takes some time for the full picture of the world, and context in which Yi is operating, to unfold. The different elements gel really well by the end of the game. The full scope of the events which preceded the game and the core thrust of the narrative arc unfolding in the present reveal themselves around the same time, in way I really enjoyed.I was not  drawn in by the characters at first, but the game does a fantastic job of giving them depth and complexity over time. Shaunshaun is an excellent example of a character who I did not like at first and who seemed to be operating in a fairly flat way, but over time really grew on me. I think the game still may be guilty of saving its most interesting characters for the end of the game and not giving as much screen time to some of the Solarians who engaged me the most, but on the whole I think the game punches above its weight in its character development and dialogue. That’s not necessarily what I come to this kind of game looking for, so the game far exceeded my expectations on this level.Similarly, I was not  captivated by the taopunk aesthetic. However, after combing through the different areas, admiring the architecture and level design, taking in every frame of the lovingly detailed animation, and listening to its gorgeous score, I walked away enamored with it. Nine Sol’s aesthetic feels distinct and unified in a way that is rare and notable. The game has a visual identity that, over time, is layered and coheres, leaving a strong impression. One particular element I loved was the way that scenes were occasionally conveyed in manga-like panels. This is not just an interesting stylistic choice, it gives more opportunity for shifts in scene perspective and character expression. The game packs a lot of drama, tone, and characterization into these scenes. I’d guess that the effectiveness of this visual style plays a large part in why I grew more engrossed in the narrative and characters over time.On the whole, Nine Sols is among the best experiences I’ve had in years. There’s so much to love here. If you’ve taken the time time to read this, I hope you will consider giving this game a chance. With Nine Sols, Red Candle Games has crafted something stellar and singular.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is a recently released Indie Metroidvania set in a hand-drawn Taopunk world, with challenging combat that puts a main focus on parrying mechanics. TLDR at the end for those who don't want to readPros:I don't think I've had as much fun with challenging combat since my first playthrough of hollow knight; The main character is snappy and responsive to control, with a satisfying parry mechanic which can be pretty hard to get perfectly right. The combat itself is intuitive and pretty easy to grasp, but takes a while to get good at, and the enemies are varied and relatively interesting (I'll get onto that later).The story is also of a very good quality, with a seemingly well detailed setting & some good old mystery to keep you engaged. The story also seems to be (so far) trying to tell a more morally grey tale than the average game, the protagonist especially has very pronounced flaws and the beginnings of a really compelling character arc.Another thing to mention, though rather obvious, is the art. The art looks really good and the aesthetic is interesting. Not much more that I can add there really.Cons:The game is not without drawbacks though. The currency system is quite punishing; you die once and your money is dropped or absorbed by the enemy that defeated you, if you die again without picking it up, the money is lost. Considering how easy it is to die in this game, it is quite easy to lose all of your hard-earned currency due to a few small mistakes or bad RNG, which can be very frustrating. Another issue is the dialogue, which is just text (and there can be a lot of it), which some players may find difficult to read, and the font does look a bit goofy at times.To elaborate on the enemies in the game, the AI is... not good. Enemies have a habit of standing still for a while in front of you without attacking, which I assume is to make it more manageable to parry when fighting large groups, but when fighting single enemies, waiting 2-3 seconds for them to make an attack while standing directly in front of them can be a little immersion breaking.To concludeI think that 9 sols is something special, from what I've played of it, it has been imaginative and engaging with gameplay mechanics and (to a lesser extent) story. I would definitely recommend it to anybody who enjoys metroidvanias or even anybody who is just interested by the combat shown in the trailers.TLDRpros:-Really fun combat-Interesting story-Pretty artCons:-Punishing currency system-Lots of text to read-Lobotomised AIAddendum: I am probably biased in this game's favour, as I am a MASSIVE fan of Metroidvanias, and will generally enjoy a game if it's a Metroidvania. This is also the first time I am writing such a long review for a game, so my apologies if the format or language is hard to read / interpret. There are also a few things that I found a bit too subjective to insert into the review, a lot of which is covered in  (which I also ripped a few points from), so read that if interested.

_childDocuments_.review: "Enjoy a sublime eternity amongst the evergreen foothills! New Kunlun: the second home of your dreams."I find it funny how incredibly sinister, obvious, and stereotypical that message is. Where we are is doomed, alright, we must trust the Council and migrate to this other plant in which life will return to normal. The game even plays on this by allowing the player to find an item, its description is about a guy who has been super unlucky his entire life, all the annoying things happen to him all the time but when he gets accepted as an immigrant to new Kunlun he thinks he finally caught a break: "Could all those unlucky things that happened to me were the price to pay to get this ticket?" little did he know that this ticket will be the completion of his bad luck, and the one that will end his life in one of many heinous ways.Furthermore, even those who didn't get accepted to migrate were also doomed... The scale of the tragedy engulfs all and everything, in the face of such a predicament, difficult choices must be made. Or so did the Council believe.Why? How did it come to this? Yi said once: "Greed is in our very nature". Maybe none of this would have happened if we, or them, the Council members, were content with what we have. We always want more and they wanted more, they wanted immortality. Maybe none of this would have happened if people didn't lie if they admitted that their technology cannot do what it's being asked to do. There's always a price to pay for the lies that we say. The debt is accumulated and eventually demands to be paid. The bigger the lie, the bigger the debt.How Nine Sols merges religion and science is nothing short of amazing. We are in space, we are in a virtually created world yet we see the temples of those before us who worshipped and prayed tirelessly. We come from religious tribes and people yet Yi refuses to embrace it or even accept it, "Superstition this, superstition that". Yi's life was once saved by the same superstitions that he refused to accept: "No! It was my mentor who saved me."Yi the kind of person who thinks everything can be understood by science.Throughout your journey, you see how one person's views can change thanks to their newfound experiences and... friends.The NPCs in this game are verified souls-like NPCs. Their humor, functionality, and importance are just perfect, itched in my memory, and will never forget them. It's always great how those darkest games have the brightest humorous moments as if it is to say: "No matter how bad it is outside, between friends, all is well."We, humans, like to boast about our human rights, the right to live and exist, the right to freedom, happiness for all, dignity, liberty, equality, brotherhood, and so on. But let's assume hypothetically that on a distant planet lived a different species, to whom our existence is tied. We must kill them to live and survive. Would our human rights theories stand in our way of surviving and doing what we must? No, it won't. But why? Because this species isn't humans? is our human rights theory a lie? Is it because survival is more important than anything else? Is it because they are not as smart as us and they would go extinct on their own anyway?Well, and so did the Council of 10 went on to justify, each according to their character, the invasion and enslavement of a different species. And so did the the lies begin and so did the debt started to accumulate for centuries. I don't think any of the 10 envisioned or imagined how grave their mistakes were or the cost of it all. Not to excuse them, that is.The thing that I probably found most interesting about this game and at the same time, most annoying is how blurry the lines are. It's never black and white: "What is justice? black and white? Good and evil? It all depends on the eye of the beholder." said Ji, leaving me very conflicted about how to feel. Even in my moments of victory, the game would never let me have it. Would never let me believe I did a 'good' thing and instead the opposite, making me feel like I'm the bad guy... and maybe I was.Ultimately, no matter your circumstances, your actions have consequences. We could sit here and try to justify them till tomorrow, but it won't change the fact that Pengali is a deserted deathbed and the Pale Blue Planet is nothing but an apocalyptic farm where delaying the inevitable ever sinks us deeper into a delusional coma.The combat is fantastic. It's very Sekiro-like, your parry is your everything. Exploring the world was fun, side quests were meaningful throughout which you saw the world and your friend change as you went on your self-righteous journey. The music. Now this is what I like. _childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is an excellent game and absolutely worth it for the current asking price. Nine Sols is a solid take on the metroidvania genre - If you've enjoyed games like Hollow Knight, Metroid Prime, or Ori and the Blind Forest, then Nine Sols is a must try. The game also combines elements of Soul's likes well, particularly Sekiro. It's a very parry heavy game. The combat is tight and engaging. Puzzle platforming is fun and of expected difficulty, although it doesn't quite reach the White Palace challenge of Hollow Knight. A unique element of Nine Sols is your AI Whisp companion that allows for limited platforming to unlock mechanisms further away from your character, it's fun, but under utilized.The story of the game is good, not new, but good. It's not often we get to see Cyberpunk Taoism and the atmosphere and lore kept me consistently engaged. The game doesn't really have any twists or turns, but the characters are well-written and interesting throughout. It's very trope heavy, but the tropes are done interestingly and compellingly. The scope of the story starts small and rapidly pulls back creating a compelling narrative, even if we've seen stories like it before.All-in-all great game, worth the asking price, and it did what any good game should - I was sad when it ended because I wanted to engage with the world more.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure this game has already drawn a lot of comparisons to Hollow Knight, and even though it's an apt comparison, I think it's worth examining more closely. It's not similar in worldbuilding, gameplay, or art style; the level of difficulty is arguably harder (it involves a lot of precise timing of attacks with little wiggle room, precision being one of the worst things for me personally), and you start out with most of the tools needed to navigate the map, making exploration a lot more accessible. These are all traits that make Nine Sols stand out among competitors, and worth playing.But the ways Nine Sols is similar to Hollow Knight also makes it unique, in a way. I keep bringing it up because I (along with many people) think Hollow Knight is the industry standard of the Metrovania/Souls-like genre, the one to imitate or surpass. And although Nine Sols will probably never reach the same level of popularity or notoriety, I think it gets the closest to capturing the essence of what makes the game truly great. Whereas a lot of games would've tried to match the art style, mechanics, or tone of Hollow Knight, Nine Sols rebuilds it from the ground up, creating something both like and very different from other Metroidvanias.The way the story unfolds is far more akin to an RPG than anything else, populated with a lot of colorful characters to interact with, a set goal known from the beginning, and a heavier emphasis on exploration outside of the typical "point A to point B" formula. I've only played about 12 hours at this point, and I suck at boss battles (especially in games this difficult), but I've still traversed all over the map. Instead of new equipment or skills needed to proceed, more often than not, the main roadblocks for progression are extremely powerful enemies that will wipe the floor with you if you aren't strong enough; so, technically possible to beat, but far smarter to go a different way first. This is emphasized by the fact that you have a home base that you can fast travel to, but you can't fast travel from one location to another, making the map more of a web than a dungeon: if things get too hard, go back to the beginning and go a different way instead.The art is beautiful as well; filled with saturated colors blended in a way that evokes Chinese watercolors. A lot of Metroidvanias focus on darker, dreary tones or expressed through the kind of lens filter a DC movie would use. A downside to the graphics, however, is that it really slows the computer down. As long as I have my laptop plugged in, I can run most 2D games without any trouble, but I had to greatly lower the quality to run certain parts of Nines Sols smoothly. A little lag isn't always a big deal, but when a game focuses so much on timing and precision, lag can be fatal.The other positive for players like me, who are terrible at Souls-like games due to difficulty but find less challenging games too easy, is that Nine Sols has a custom scale option at the beginning, instead of the typical "easy, normal, or hard" modes. Here, we have "normal" or "story mode," which allows customization. I chose to play it at normal difficulty, of which I'm honestly regretting, but if I decide to go back and start a new save file using story mode, I know the game will be fun enough to retread old ground.TL;DR I cannot recommend Nine Sols highly enough. $30 seems like a steep price, but I don't think it's asking too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is quite comfortably my GoTY for 2024 as of mid-June, and I fully believe that it is the new champion of the Metroidvania/Soulslike genre, and by a comfortable margin as well. While it might not be top of its class in every single field, I think that there's a real argument to be made for it being a runner up across them all, which is extremely impressive. I don't think I've ever played a game with such a strong fantasy style. Taopunk is such a fresh take on a very traditionally medieval genre, and the bar Nine Sols sets is not one that will be topped any time soon. The game's philosophical and touching story are a real breath of fresh air when contrasted with its muddy and more speculative Souls siblings. The world is rich and a lot of quality effort has clearly been put into expanding on the cultures and histories of the various Solarian factions. While I don't think that the game's music is best in its class, I feel that simply calling it serviceable is disrespectful. I didn't have any big Greenpath Theme or Slave Knight Gael moments with it, but it was reliably pleasing nonetheless. The world and movement are all quite good; exploration is smooth and the enemy populations are well balanced. Nine Sols understand that its combat system is oriented towards one-on-one fights and for the most part it allows you to isolate each enemy, while also leaving room for enemies to bunch up if you get careless.All of that said, where Nine Sols really shines is its combat. I'm of the opinion that Sekiro has the best melee combat system of any game I've ever played, and the inspiration shines through extremely brightly through Nine Sols, a game that, if I may be so bold, rises to Sekiro's challenge, and perhaps even surpasses it in areas. While Sekiro places a greater emphasis on rhythm, which does make it a more consistently satisfying system to learn and pull off, Nine Sols incorporates Sekiro's parry system with a more weaving-oriented approach. Given that there is no posture system, your goal is instead to sneak the heaviest attack you can in between each of the enemy's, parry, and repeat. It works fabulously. The internal damage system is a bit superfluous when it comes to enemies; most of the time only serving to encourage aggression. However, talisman blasts have the delightfully satisfying side effect of converting all internal damage to direct damage. Often you will build up a large amount of internal damage on a boss and then consume it all to decimate its healthbar. It's a deeply enjoyable experience, and in my opinion rivals the satisfaction of breaking a boss's stance in Sekiro. A place where I believe Nine Sols has a leg up on Sekiro is visual readability; the 2D medium makes boss attacks much easier to perceive and react to quickly, which is essential for the fast-paced combat. The readability alongside near-impeccable difficulty balance and hitboxes make for one of the fairest combat systems I've ever encountered in a game. Despite the game's pretty challenging boss fights, there was only one where I ever got frustrated. When the game slips in this regard (which it does on said boss, in my opinion) it is very noticeable, though that does come with the side effect of it being all the sweeter once you get back to the status quo of the game absolutely nailing it. Nine Sols's combat is its most impressive achievement among a series of genre-defining accomplishments. It means a lot when the only complaints I can think of for a game feel more like nitpicks than real, significant problems with it, especially when they are so few. I cannot praise this game more highly. It is rare that a developer's vision for a game is so clear and so purely, perfectly realized. The already high bars for the Metriodvania and Soulslike genres have been substantially raised. I strongly recommend Nine Sols to anyone who is willing to overcome the ample challenge it offers, you will be rewarded with one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't leave reviews for most games I've played, but Nine Sols is probably one of the best games I have ever played.     It is a cross between Sekiro styled deflection (parry) centered combat, and a beautifully stylized 2-D Metroidvania similar to Hollow Knight. Though the size and scope of the world is not quite as big as Hollow Knight, there is still plenty of secrets and other hidden items to find. It also has a very unique style of what could be described as a mix of Taoism and Asian culture, and a Cyberpunk sci-fi setting, or "Taopunk" as the steam trailer describes it.   Nine Sols is also much more story and character focused than Hollow Knight or similar Souls-like games, and has some of the most interesting and compelling writing I've seen in a game in a very long time. The protagonist Yi also becoming a new favorite main character of mine. I know that not everyone has the patience for games with a larger narrative focus as they just want to get to the game-play or "meat" of the game, but if you are looking for a game like Hollow Knight or Sekiro, or just a fantastic Metroidvania with a somewhat larger focus on the characters and story without any sacrifice to the quality of the game-play then Nine Sols is definitely worth playing. Also, for those who don't care about the story or characters, it is not too difficult to just skip or speed through much of the dialogue and cut scenes if you want to, though I strongly recommend to give them a chance.   The boss fights and battles against common foes can be described as a dance of sorts, just like with Sekiro, with a satisfyingly strong blend of offense and defense. The bosses in particular (the Nine Sols) are definitely a highlight of the game, and are some of best, most memorable, and fun Bosses I've fought in a long time. I would rank some of these fights as being worthy of some of the best bosses from Sekiro and Hollow Knight, as well as Furi for anyone who has played that. They also recently added in a battle memory mode into game that lets you re-fight any of the Sols if you have achieved an ending in the game. It is not a true boss rush, but it is a welcome addition regardless to be able to enjoy these fights again, and to be able to practice them without having to replay the entire game to do so.   Also for anyone who may be hesitant to give the game a try due to the inherently higher difficulty of souls-like games, fear not for there is a story mode that can be enabled that allows control for damage taken and given, though I would encourage to give the standard difficulty a chance as this kind of combat is not as satisfying if you adjust it to just let you tank through everything and kill enemies in a few hits. The difficulty I would argue also helps to enhance the atmosphere and the at times bleak and brutal feeling of this world.   It is also worth touching on that not only does Nine Sols has a beautiful art style, but much of the sound design and music in the game also matches the visual quality. I would describe some of the sound track as being hauntingly beautiful and somber.   I also did not experience any notable performance issues with the game, as it ran quite smoothly for me with a stable FPS and no notable glitches. But I also have a good quality PC, so your mileage may vary depending on your setup.   Overall I have very few issues with this game as I feel it is as close to perfect as game like this can get, but while I may not have any major complaints about the game I do have some minor nitpicks. There are a couple of attack animations that do feel that they could have been tweaked to telegraph the attacks a bit better on a handful of enemies as they feel a little weird, but these are very few and far between so its a rather minor issue that many people probably will not notice. The hit boxes for a couple of attacks also seem to be a bit larger than they appear to be which can make it look like you got hit by an attack that shouldn't have been that close to you, this is also a rather small issue but it is worth noting.   I should also mention that while it did not bother me, this game can get rather gory and violent and does have some moments of cruelty, so if you are easily bothered by such things you may not enjoy this game. I will also note that while I did not have a issue with this, some people have complained about the final boss of the game having a rather sudden difficulty spike, especially if going for a specific ending. While I personally think the final boss is perfect as is, I can understand that it may be a bit much for some people. So if you struggle with this fight I would recommend to try changing up your strategy with equipment and abilities to see what works and what doesn't as I also had to do this. Some optional abilities you may have glossed over during the rest of the game may be very helpful here, I would recommend the water flow talismans when learning the fight and attack patterns, and the full control talismans for more damage to get through the fight more quickly once you get comfortable with it. As a tangent the full control talismans became my favorite style to use after beating the final boss and will definitely be used more on future playthroughs.   I could go further into describing the different aspects of the game and the combat and story, but this review is already rather lengthy and I don't want to spoil the game too much with regards to mechanics or said story. Though I will say that I would consider Nine Sols to be my personal Game of the Year for 2024.   TLDR: Nine Sols is an amazing parry focused Metroidvania with strong characters and story that I would strongly recommend to anyone that enjoys games like Sekiro or Hollow Knight. And even if these kinds of games are not something you would normally enjoy, I would at the very least try playing through with story mode to experience the story and characters if you more interested in the narrative of the game than the game play. Also you play as a lonely, depressed, and sometimes very vengeful cat boi so I'm sure that's a plus for some people.  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: really hard, really good. some of the most creative and visually inspired boss fights and world, and now i'm kicking myself because i was one quest away from reaching true ending before fighting the final boss. like a lot of other reviews say the final boss is definitely the most difficult but it felt so satisfying to finally beat them. highly recommend.i read some other reviews about the combat system being unpolished, specifically the need to face the same direction to parry and getting comboed by enemies; but i would say after getting used to the gameplay facing the same direction is second nature and getting comboed is not a real complaint to me, because you should be appropriately punished for messing up. there are a lot of options to avoid getting trapped in a string and parrying is pretty lenient, all things considered. so if you don't want to struggle too much then just play the story mode, but you're really missing out on some of the best adrenaline rushes out there if you do.The story is also pretty good, there's a lot of environmental storytelling and bits of lore to find, and you get a lot of the story shown to you through flashbacks so piecing everything together isn't too crazy. However, I do have to agree with a review i saw where they thought some of the npcs are a little too dialogue heavy and just repeat what is already being shown to you, so it can feel redundant and kinda ruin some of the show don't tell aspects of the story.overall, 9/10, game isn't too long and the fights are the best.

I'm intrigued by the game, the game disappoints me, I uninstall it, I give it a second chance.Some specific thoughts:- Map shows icons for NPCs but doesn't specific WHICH NPC it is. That feels needlessly obtuse, and speaks to a larger pattern of lacking quality-of-life game design that it could've borrowed from all the other Souls-like games it's copying.- Hitting environment areas that hurt don't simply take damage and give you a moment of i-frames to step away; it's an instant black-out, teleport back to a previous area, which sometimes means you're dropped right in front of the enemy you were fighting while they're winding up for another attack, so you get pinball bullied to death.- Enemies give out paltry scraps of XP that don't seem to scale, so when typical Souls-like permadeath loses you the XP you'd been grinding for an entire boss zone, it's gutting like no other Souls-like.- As you'll see others mention on Reddit, parrying works better when in mid-air, which is limiting.- I appreciate the art style and characters' different personalities. the story drip-feeds enough.Overall, I'm still disappointed. I remember liking the demo; but I still regret paying for the full game. :'-(

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I ever written a review for a videogame, but I think this one deserves it. Nine Sols is a game that excels in every department: art/presentation, gameplay, storytelling (I loved the manga-styled cutscenes and almost cried at the end), and especially the soundtrack (jesus christ the OST... you get this banger during one of the first bosses:) I could spent hours admiring this game, but instead of stirring up expectations, I prefer to warn you that...- Though the 2D models are gorgeous and have their charm, it's pretty grim, dark, bloody and even have some small body-horror elements. .- . Sometimes you feel you are getting the hang of it, then suddenly you are retrying a boss fight more than 10 times. I didn't test the "Story Mode" difficulty, but I can tell you that "Standard Mode" will test your perseverance over and over again. If you are not into repeating (pretty amazing) boss fights until you can master them, then the "Standard Mode" isn't for you, especially with the final boss. I don't meant to flex, but Sekiro's final boss felt like a pushover compared to this one. This is surely subjective, but in my decades of playing challenging games, I never thought I would have to repeat that kind of (lovely) experience again where I had to spent at least 1 hour trying and trying until I beat it, but I can see why that may frustrate some players.- . You can tell the developers had pretty competent writers and it's truly a labor of love. But if you are not into reading lots of dialogues, interacting with every single character and logbook, you will be missing on a 50% of what makes this game so great.- . Sure, it borrows one or two mechanics from that game, but just like the game description says, it's heavily inspired by Sekiro, which means you need to have a sense of rhythm and reflexes in order to parry instead of attacking. I have to make this warning because I suspect people will buy this game thinking "oh, I loved Hollow Knight, I'm surely going to love this one". Nah, they are completely different experiences. I'll quote what another user said "Hollow Knight is the 2D version of Dark Souls, while Nine Sols is the 2D version of Sekiro". The only thing I can gladly admire that it shares with Hollow Knight is that every area plays a role in the storytelling, instead of what most Metroidvanias do where they insert random traps and monsters here and there "because it's cool".- Also, , though it has the basic elements of exploration and platforming, which are very satisfying, and you always have the liberty to go wherever you want as long as you have the necessary powerup, this game is mostly linear and there aren't that many optional areas to explore.- If I had to list the things that I personally think they could improve:Nonetheless, it's a pretty complete 20-hour package, with an amazing story told with philosophical elements, a good pacing that keeps you wondering about the main character's true intentions, and thankfully it doesn't rely on overly-expositional dialogue: it's not until the very end that you get the whole picture of what's happening.Since the very beginning you can tell that every piece of this game is high quality and made with ton of effort. I highly recommend supporting the developers even if you buy it with a small discount.

_childDocuments_.review: A platformer that looks and sounds absolutely gorgeous.Unfortunately, it's more about combat than anything else. While classified as a metroidvania, it's pretty linear with little reward for exploration, and no real sense of getting lost in the world. Not only that, exploration is actively punished by its money dropping mechanic. Also, if you die on the way to your money-holding gravestone, you'll lose everything you had. No joke.Gameplay here is ALL about fighting, and to be more specific, about parrying. This isn't a metroidvania!It's a parrying simulator with all the rote memorization that comes with the territory. It's more like a punishing rhythm game, where you absolutely need to know every enemy/boss telegraph by heart, and even that's often not enough. Some prompts are virtually indistinguishable from each other, and if you fail to react correctly a couple of times, it's game over. (Then again, I assume that's what they mean by the "Sekiro-inspired" marketing phrase.)This is a huge issue, as bosses kill you in a few hits, while you have to get in dozens. On its "normal" difficulty, even mini-bosses are ridiculous sponges.As for the inevitable "git gud" choir of unemployed gaming gods: practicing fights in Nine Sols sucks, for the aforementioned reasons. You die fast, and to get another try, you need to make your way through the mostly boring environment to where you died - and most likely be forced to wait for elevators and whatnot while you're at it.Not good, unless you have unlimited time. You either check the correct strategy on Youtube or play the trial-and-error game for extended amounts of time.Note: The game does have a story mode which can be adjusted make everything more tolerable. Personally, I wasn't that interested in the story, so I opted for just uninstalling.I bought in to the "stop waiting for Silksong and buy this" hype and it really didn't pay out.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played the demo for this game about a year and a half before release, and ever since I was incredibly excited to get the full experience. I didn't get it recommended to me by anyone, I just stumbled across it on my own on Steam (probably the first time ever discovery queue has done its job). Regardless, when I got my hands on the finished product, I was far from disappointed.The combat in this game is hard. It is very hard. But it's the type of hard where you immediately recognize what you did wrong. No part of combat is unfair. It just requires a lot of focus and patience. Being too greedy with combos is a surefire way to get domed by an enemy attack before you have the chance to parry it. The best strategy against almost all opponents is to parry/dodge until you have an opening. This is in no way bad by the way, this flow of combat is incredibly satisfying. The calmness with which you need to approach combat, if you pardon the journalist-y language, really makes you feel like Yi. Past parrying, you have a decent amount of freedom with which you can approach combat, but explaining more would get spoiler-y.This game is not exactly a metroidvania. Given its focus on story, progression goes fairly linearly. You get new abilities in a set order and fight the bosses in a set order, but there is plenty of room for exploration in between. It's more like Sekiro than Hollow Knight in that way. Straying off the beaten path often gets you heaps of money, upgrades, and optional minibosses to challenge, which often give you some good rewards.Nine sols is, through and through, an absolute treat to the eyes. Every sprite, background, and chunk of flesh is beautifully rendered in a style that is (for all I am aware of) wholly unique to this game. The strong linework and bold colors of Yi, his enemies, and their attacks make sure you know exactly what is going on at all times. Glow and screen flash effects are used sparingly and tastefully, minimally obscuring gameplay while still providing punch to important actions. 3D elements are also often used to represent complex structures or objects, but they are not at all jarring to look at. They blend in with the 2D art extremely well. Past just the art, the animation is also excellent. Enemy attacks are easily readable (except for the times when paying close attention to tells is part of the challenge (it's done in a really good way trust me)), so you can always figure out how you need to get around an enemy attack. The animations for bosses especially are excellent. Character animation is also wonderfully done, with a wonderful array of cute, cool, disturbing, and heartwarming. Cutscenes are done in a variety of ways, either with the characters on screen, in a comic book format, or fully animated, all of which are done excellently.All of the sound design is excellent. Parries and hits are snappy and satisfying, and in general the world sounds great. The music sets the vibe extremely well, both the battle and atmospheric tracks are excellent. I don't really have much more to say other than it's really good.tl;dr the game is really good

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a review guy, so a tl;dr for a reasonably short review: ╚{The mechanics and 'easy to learn difficult to master' difficulty skill make this worth picking up alone.                   ╚{The story is memorable and worth experiencing these characters painfully learned truths through a window of your own perspective.The gameplay is silk smooth, and plays off the metroidvania "use little to no keys" mentality. Plenty of ques/hints, historic genre techniques, and solid story/character development elements keep you invested in going forward.   I could recommend this game off of the polish they put into the game mechanics... The .I'm a sucker for science fiction and fantasy. That being said this is an incredible fusion of the two and really had me locked in on the wonderful environments. With that bias out of the way I really want to focus on the glimpses of perspective you get in this. The exhaustion (sometimes literal hand cramps) mixed with the quiet and surreal 'windows' leave you with a gratifying and hollow sense of victory over some foes... and others leave you wanting to hunt them down yourself again and again. Looking at you Eigong.Additionally (spoiler)I walked into this blind and it was a pleasant find so I'm sure there'll be more to dig up later as I haven't hit the 100% just yet. I was confused why a mature game would use anthropomorphic characters to skirt certain issues. That is, until the better half of the game when I realised just how much fun the devs were using it to approach several different philosophies and views from a left field sort of stance. There are a few times it's used to help explain aspects of the world, cultural tastes, and other awesome soft-handed world building techniques. (Plus one ha ha joke to help break just a bit of end-game mental tension; cause the hooks in this story were meant to dig deeeeeep)

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AFTER COMPLETING: It remained very strong all the way through! There was a bit of a difficulty spike with the last few bosses but it was sick. Like... 8.7/10. Fantastic execution of the hollow knight formula.They updated the map system to make it friendlier. I was fine with it being more obscured previously but I can see how that would have alleviated some of my personal pressure points earlier in the game.THE REST I WROTE ABOUT HALFWAY THROUGH THE GAME BUT STILL AGREE WITH: An excellent entry in the metroidvania + soulslike fusion genre. It takes many mechanics from similar games and executes most of them very well, all while featuring a great art style and soundscape.Map exploration has been great so far. I like how large each room is and how it shows up as a defined area on the map, and then you can find a data chip that unlocks a detailed view of the area later on. There's a few bugs with using a controller on the map screen so I've ended up having to use my mouse a few times to be able to navigate to areas.Root nodes (the game's benches/bonfires) provide the ability to teleport back to your hideout, and then later on you can teleport to any root node that you've found. This is pretty standard amidst these games, though I personally prefer Hollow Knight's travel systems with the stagways, trams and dreamgates over simply being able to teleport anywhere.In usual fashion, dying gives you the opportunity to lose accumulated money/exp. There's plenty to buy with money and I mostly run with the charms that give me more money, so I haven't felt like I've lost much progress even when I did make some silly mistakes and die. It definitely felt a lot more punishing in the first few hours of the game though. At the point of the game where I'm at, I have a few shopkeeps in my hideout so I'm never more than one node away from spending money.Exp and the skill tree feel like extraneous systems to me. In terms of losing exp, you can only lose accumulated exp to your next skill point which really isn't that punishing imo. In general I'm a little tired of skill trees but it doesn't necessarily detract from the game.Combat and movement feel very smooth. Directional parry took a bit to get used to but feels great. Enemies from above can occasionally cross you up but it's not a big deal. Some enemies also turn on a dime so dodging through them during a flurry of blows is dangerous if you're not careful. A horde of enemies surrounding you is genuinely dangerous. I'm still feeling out the 'unbounded' counter move which lets you absorb/reflect completely unblockable moves though at the moment it feels very strange.There is a good bit of unskippable cutscene/dialogue that (if it remains unskippable on repeat playthroughs) would hurt the replayability of the game. I enjoy the characters quite a bit otherwise, though a few cutscenes are a touch too long in my opinion.All in all, a great package so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Deep, emotionally rich, and meaningful game that, like a lot of Red Candle games, speaks eloquently to the Taiwanese identity, in a way that very very few pieces of literature can do. I get the same "me vs. game" vibes going through this as I got with Elden Ring, which is not necessarily a bad thing if you're into that. That being said, the developers do have an "easier" story mode that you can switch to if it gets too frustrating at any point. So if you feel yourself frustrated at any point, or just want to experience this rich and deep world and story with minimal frustration, there's no shame in switching to easy mode (honestly I might switch soon myself because I'm just so engrossed in this story)Also this targets a more mature audience. This isn't a game for kids. Be warned.
