_childDocuments_.review: Really well made metroidvania, with a good amount of polish and not too long. Definitely worth playing if you are a fan of the genre. I played through the game on standard mode and these are my thoughts on the game. Pros:- Engaging and unique combat that you won't find in any other 2d game- Each boss is very unique, the presentation of them makes each one feel super fresh.- Different parry types keeps combat engaging, its not just "press the parry key", sometimes you have to tap parry, sometimes you have to hold parry, sometimes you have to air parry attacks. This makes playing well extremely satisfying.- There are more character interactions through out the story compared to the average metroidvania, making it easier to get invested in the world.- The story is well written, with plenty of foreshadowing if you explore well and find the logs. I personally played through the game 2 times and found a lot of the side characters charming, even on 2nd play through.- Spawn points are usually placed close to bosses, making the trek back very quick.Cons:- Map design in certain areas can get pretty frustrating at times. The maps are small so its not a huge problem, but traversal can get annoying at times.- Damage is very high, so it only takes a few missed counters to die sometimes.- Dieing before picking up your "soul" can be extremely frustrating, losing large amounts of currency. Luckily the is somewhat mitigated by the excessive amount of jin players can get by exploring.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't downvote a game that kept me hooked this long. There's definitely a lot to like here.There's obvious influences from Hollow Knight and Sekiro, and the gameplay feels great. The movement is clean and crisp, and the parries have plenty of wiggle room (in my opinion).At the same time, there were a number of things I really disliked.First, this game desperately needs a way for players to skip cutscenes, including the cutscenes where Yi jumps into a box to be transported from one region to another. I'd replay the game but I don't want to rewatch the cutscenes. Even the first playthrough felt agonizing at times because of having to rewatch the slow boss transitions. It at least begs for a speedrun mode that has no cutscenes at all.Especially the boss of the brain room. Fighting that boss felt awful. The fake difficulty of not having a hud (and therefore unable to see my HP), and the fact that the battle lasts 3 phases, and the way the action dropped between phases - which took me out of the flow experience - and the fact that it all felt unjustified for that character to be that strong, all just sucked. I don't want to fight a 2 phase boss. I definitely don't want to fight a 3 phase boss. I hated that fight.The power scaling felt bad too. At the start of the game, it takes a full 3-hit combo to kill anything. That felt like too much. But every enemy after that takes more, so that instead of getting stronger as the game went on, I felt like I got weaker. The final boss really takes that to an extreme, where a Full Control explosion does less than a quarter of their health. To me, it felt like I had to spend excessive time killing mooks, and like I did paltry damage to bosses even with my most damaging skills. It especially stood out because every tao fruit said in its description that it increased my damage. And yet a normal attack against a boss only did a chip off its health. That really sucked.One last thing: stop sending me back to an earlier point in the game after the ending! I don't want to do the last part of the game again in order to fight the boss with a different jade setup.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exceptional.  It may be the second best metroidvania I've played, and if people felt this was better than Hollow Knight I wouldn't fight them too hard.This is a story rich, beautiful, and *damn* hard game, mixing fun and fluid movement mechanics with Sekiro-like parry based combat.  The standard difficulty is *really* tough, even for a well played souls player like myself, but it also has the same trait as Sekiro - when you do finally beat a tough battle, it feels exceptionally well earned.I particularly like the story in the game, and the slow reveal of the world and the character motivations.  This is a darker game than I initially expected, and it's worth calling out that there are some pretty heavy themes at times.  That said, I really started to fall in love with Yi and the characters immediately around him.  If you have any interest in games like this at all, you can't go wrong here.  Just... maybe consider that "standard" difficulty is basically "Sekiro" difficulty, and if you find it too hard there's no shame in dropping down a level to see the game through.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as a recommendation from a friend and once I picked it up I couldn't put it down.The story is easy to follow and really does a good job on introducing characters, establishing who these characters are, and it really makes you feel for them.Art style and design are amazing and always nice to look at throughout the game! Never felt like enemies or areas looked too similar and the maps pretty easy to follow along!The map is a good size, doesn't feel too big or too small, feels nice and easy to navigate. checkpoint placements also feel fair, never found myself frustrated because of the route I had to take to return to the boss.Combat is fun and feels good, the song and dance you do with all the bosses feels amazing! The dashing, dodging, blocking, etc. all felt very nice to execute during fights and you can make some very nice 'jade' combinations to help.Soundtrack I would give a 8/10, while I enjoyed the soundtrack (there are some BEAUTIFUL tracks) I really didn't find myself having the urge to stop and take in the music. Sometimes I did but other times I just thought 'this is nice' while dashing through an area or it was just music that was 'there'.I loved loved LOVED how this game handled exploring and getting chests/items. All items felt fair and intuitive to find/get, even ones that you couldn't get till' you unlock certain skills felt easy to understand we'll come back later. I never felt like I HAD to go out of my way to get items/treasure and some had fun 'puzzles' to solve! There is one 'locked' door for a side quests that's only unlocked during a crucial endgame moment and feels like the timing to unlock it is odd and easy to miss.Some things I would've like to see are markers for past treasures you obtained or if you already have a visual of one an unopened chests Icon or something that helps up better keep track of treasures. There were small moments where I went back to an area for one last thing and despite having the whole area unlocked I found myself playing hide and seek and having to comb the area again to remember where it was.Reading other reviews I'm seeing some talk about the final fight, so heres my 2 cents.The fight is BRUTAL!!TLDR; Overall 9.5/10Get it if you like platformers, metroidvanias, and a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly the combat feels so polished and unique, it takes a while to get used to this type of hit-hit-parry combat sequences, but once you do you'll freaking love it, its hard (if you want it to), its refreshing, it keeps you on your toes and IMO I think this type of innovations and appropriations from other genres are what makes this metroidvania games so popular and captivating these days.If you like games like Hollow Knight, Ori, or any other metroidvanias, this game is for you, a game with their own unique twists and features that will leave you baffled and thankful that there's still developers that are  not afraid to innovate and go outside of the already established in order to create their own unique experience, and on that note I can't recommend Nine Sols enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember when I beat NKG in Hollow Knight (don't worry it'll make sense).  5+ hours trying to avoid a pretty gnarly move set and finally achieve victory.  In that victory I had 2 realizations.  First is that's about as hard as any fight can be... for me... and still be worth doing.  Second was that a fight that hard was only worth doing because the game was Hollow Knight.  So I got to this game's first 3 phase boss fight (yeah i know P1 isn't that hard), was about 2 hours deep and wondering how close to the 5 hour mark this boss was going to run.  I asked myself "Are you having fun?"  I don't think I'm gonna finish this one.Yeah, it'll get the thumbs up.  Its got a unique and well realized art style, does a solid job with its story telling and characters, and of most importantly does a really good job with it's combat for what it is.  It's not Nine Sols' problem that I've had Souls-like fatigue since the moment that term was coined.  I guess I could also just crank down the difficulty but at this point I'm also kinda burned on it so  just moved on to something else.I get the impression souls vets take about 1/3 to 1/2 the time I do to beat these fights, and if I were executing on that level then I'd probably have as much fun with it as they do.  So if that's you, consider this a strong recommendation. 8.5/Hollow Knight

_childDocuments_.review: This is a long one.In short, this game is incredible. Extremely well rounded combat with just enough variation to keep it interesting along with a Jade system that allows you to create whatever kind of build you like. The boss design is excellent in this game, but I will say that it takes a minute to get to the truly excellent bosses. There exists a stealth section in the game, and I'd say the boss at the end of that section isn't bad, but it's the worst one in the game. After that boss, the overall lineup sees a major boost in quality. My biggest gripe about bosses is the healthbars. Every major boss has multiple, and I don't think that's a great design choice. I love that the major bosses all have more than one phase, but do we really need to dedicate individual phases to their own unique healthbar? What's wrong with having one big healthbar and starting new phases after a certain HP threshold? A big healthbar is meant to be indicative of how much health the boss has left, not how close you are to the next phase. There's even a boss that has three healthbars, which was completely unnecessary and made an otherwise excellent fight drag on for way too long. Overall, the bosses are well designed and are all fair, despite some being quite difficult. The learning process never feels overwhelming, and once you do learn it, the bosses are a joy to fight against. The combat in general feels very satisfying. The game is centered around deflection and parry timings with an internal damage system to keep imprecise parries from being too punishing. The flow state that can be reached during some combat encounters is genuinely euphoric. "Hollow Knight meets Sekiro" is likely a phrase you've heard regarding this game, and it's very true. The player moves like Hollow Knight and fights like Sekiro. It's a perfect balance between my two favorite games.Platforming is not the main focus of the game, but that doesn't mean the platforming isn't also great. Dashing through the masterfully designed levels in this game were some of my favorite moments of my first playthrough. There aren't very many particularly challenging platforming sections, but a large majority of the platforming is very fun and well executed. The level design is top tier for multiple reasons. Every area has branching paths with different combat and platforming challenges that all lead back to the central save point of the area. Unlocking doors and discovering shortcuts has never been so satisfying. Next thing I want to touch on is the story. This game is dark. It has themes of life, death, disease, corruption, sacrifice, and more. The lore goes deep in this one. I found myself falling in love with the characters and really caring about their stories and motivations. The protagonist, Yi, is particularly well written and has quite the journey. Some people may be turned off by the amount of dialogue in this game, but there is an option to speed up dialogue in the settings, though I didn't find a way to skip cutscenes (Red Candle you should fix that). The story isn't as cryptic as something like Hollow Knight or the Souls games. It gives just enough exposition and lore to keep the player in the loop while still keeping some secrets hidden to create mystery. It's an excellent narrative that has its twists, turns, ups, downs, wholesome moments and heart wrenching moments all the way through.Last thing I'd like to focus on before I get into spoiler territory is the soundtrack. This game's music is hauntingly beautiful. There are somber tracks, epic tracks, blissful tracks, sorrowful tracks, creepy tracks, and everything in between. Some of my personal favorites include Ji, Yingzhao, and the final boss. The music always excels at creating an atmosphere that perfectly fits the situation. That doesn't mean it isn't disturbing sometimes, but the situation usually calls for it. Overall, the music heightens the experience and executes its job perfectly.I will now be moving into minor spoiler territory. I won't say any names, but I'm going to talk a little bit about the final chapter and it's implications. No critical information will be revealed and if you're doing a blind playthrough you can still read this part and not have too much spoiled. If you don't want read any further, that's okay. As a final statement, I rate Nine Sols a 9.7 out of 10. I adore this game and would recommend it to anyone seeking a fun combat-heavy metroidvania experience.--MINOR SPOILER TERRITORY--This game has one sequence that I think genuinely sucks. The one and only bad part of the game is the Point of No Return. The autoscroller section where your HUD is completely removed is aids. I'm really not sure what the rationale was here, but my experience kinda tanked during this part. This game went from being a 9.3/10 to being a 8.4/10 during this 30-ish minute section. Even after the autoscroller is over and your HUD comes back, the enemies here are quite annoying. Being forced to use a talisman to kill them makes for a pretty irritating and overly lengthy section especially due to the story implications at this point during the journey. The emotional impact that this part is supposed to have is negated by the tedious combat section. I wish the enemies were easier to dispatch, or that they weren't mandatory to kill so we could skip past this part. The good news is that after this part, the game reaches new heights. I will now be talking about the final boss. I will not say names or descriptions, but I will talk about my experience.---Nine Sols's final boss is the best boss in the game. I think it's the greatest final boss since Sekiro. The flow state is absolutely unmatched in this fight and nothing ever feels unfair. The music here is epic, but it cranks it up to 11 in the hidden section. I won't reveal specifics here, but there is a way to unlock an alternate version of this fight, and the music here is the best in the game. It's the insanely epic climax to a crazy journey full of surprises, and the last surprise reveals itself as you fight your way to victory. This is, in my opinion, a perfect boss. It's also one of the hardest bosses I've ever beaten. The original version stands on even ground with a decent chunk of Sekiro's medium-difficulty bosses, but the alternate version stands toe to toe with Sekiro's final boss and I think it might be harder. This is a MASSIVE uptick in difficulty from the previous bosses, and I regret to admit that a lot of people may quit due to how difficult this boss is, but if we're being honest, story mode exists. If this boss gives you trouble, switch to story mode and fix your damage multipliers to your liking. You might regret it though, because the triumph over this boss on standard difficulty is the greatest feeling in this game and you will have robbed yourself of the feeling by tapping out at the very end of the game. The entire experience with the alternate final boss boosted my final rating up to a 9.7 out of 10. This game is beautiful and is so well worth the money. That's all from me, and if you actually read this far that's amazing. Definitely give Nine Sols a shot.

Yi, the protagonist is one of my favorite mc’s in a game that i’ve seen in a while. Hes complicated, and a perfect figure for the central question of this game which is: “is there ever really a right answer?” He’s helped by a brilliant supporting cast who I deeply cared for by the end of the journey. And while i wasn’t entirely satisfied with the finale “ (im sure i didnt even get the true ending) i thought this was a pretty damn good narrative overall.I didnt even talk about the combat, sekiro fans eat your heart out. I had been craving some more deflect fun time and this game surely delivers on that. Oh yea and it has an absolutely stunning art direction. And soundtrack. Just about everything you’d expect from a sols like, with all of the quality and care to back it up. My gripes would probably lie in the map. Most of the areas in the first half look pretty samey, which makes backtracking of any kind absolute hell. It doesn't help that the map is awful, and couldn't be less descriptive. However there is some variety in the second half of the games areas.This is one of the best sols likes around. And after this, the eternal wait for silksong feels a little easier… kinda. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game through and through, and highly recommended if you like Metroidvania-type games or the combat of Sekiro. Great, inspired setting, wonderful art and character designs, fantastic music with some truly stand-out tracks, and spectacular action. The combat is challenging but rewarding, with bosses reminiscent of Sekiro that feel just unstoppably powerful until you find yourself deflecting their every move, which is very rewarding.Nine Sols also contains my favorite new game mechanic of the year in the Unbounded Counter, sort of an advanced late-game parrying technique that meshes perfectly with the theme and is super satisfying to pull off.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts really slowly, showing you many dialogues and exposition. But after the first hour the pace is perfect in my opinion. The game is hard and often compared to Sekiro but Sekiro is much harder if you ask me. The parry mechanic is pretty forgiving and once you get the hang of it, it's like a choregraphy espacially for the boss fights.All bosses are pretty unique with some sticking out creativately. The final boss could even have another phase in my opinion.The story is well thought out and gets more interesting the longer you play so it's worth to keep on playing. Some not so unique but also unique takes on the cyberpunk genre but everything in this Tao inspired setting which I haven't seen elsewhere.After all there is not much to say negative but that it ended too soon. Only the hitboxes for dashes could be a bit more clearer, but since this is a parry game you are emphasized to use it instead of the dash. Great game. _childDocuments_.review: Summary: A fantastic game with more mature themes that surprised me with its quality and content at every turn. I enjoyed every moment and will continue to think about the plot and characters into the future. I recommend this game strongly to most individuals. WARNING: slight horror themes.Until a few weeks ago, I did not know Nine Sols existed. I only stumbled upon it after a recommended YouTube video. Curiosity struck and I decided to give it a try. I am pleasantly surprised with the game, and I believe it deserves every positive review it has received.THE GOOD (Spoiler Free):First and foremost, the setting and world building is fantastic. While the plot can be a bit slower at times, it still felt well paced, keeping me on the edge of my seat as I learned more and more about who the characters were, what was going on, and why. This was further supported by the amazing soundtrack.Following up that was the combat system. Nine Sols is built on a counter-based combat system similar to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Without going into too much detail, you are introduced to a way to block attacks, with you getting rewarded for perfect parries and partially rewarded for imperfect ones. The whole game and all combat is built around this system. While it adds a good deal of difficulty to the game, it also makes the game significantly more rewarding and satisfying when you execute your parries well. I also want to touch a bit on the story and themes of the game. While I definitely enjoyed them, they are more mature. Without spoilers, they deal a lot with death, loss, hope, horror, and more. There are some areas that are spooky or unnerving, but as I tend to like themes like that I enjoyed those parts. If you don't handle horror well, I recommend looking into spoilers first, then playing the game.Lastly, the progression felt smooth. No progression item or ability felt absolutely mandatory to success, but they all provided meaningful aid. There were plenty of ways to play the game without sacrificing the core game play of the counter system. It felt very well thought out. The story and area progression and pacing also felt good. While some areas and bosses did have difficulty spikes, nothing felt abnormal or out of pace. Things flowed well with the story beats, keeping me invested in every area.BAD:I only have two complaints about the game. The first is that there are very few i-frames as a design choice for the combat system. This means that enemies can combo you if you make mistakes. While frustrating, it does not subtract from the well built combat in my eyes. Additionally, it makes success feel all the more rewarding.The second (VERY MINOR SPOILERS) is there is no "point of no return message". The final sequence caught me a little off guard. My only recommendation is do side quests before you advance to the end of the final area.OVERVIEW:Overall, I feel this game is fantastic. While not perfect in my eyes, it still feels very close to perfection. The characters and their stories were endearing and the game-play was enthralling. 9/10, I highly recommend this game, unless you do very poorly with horror. Then I recommend the game after you look into spoilers so nothing catches you off guard.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly good game. Intriguing story with emotional payoffs, beautiful aesthetics and exceptional sound design/music, rewarding exploration and solid level design - all backed up by an incredibly satisfying combat system. I was very often incentivized to make the most out of Yi's entire toolkit, especially during the delicate dances that are this game's boss fights. I can't stress enough how much the sound design does for this game. Nailing parries feels impactful and great, and the music does so much to set the mood for Nine Sols's many beautiful areas and poignant story beats. The story itself has a good mix of straightforward cutscenes/events and dripfed lore/information via exploration and descriptions.I think the level design can be fairly linear within each area, but I personally don't mind that aspect and there are plenty of opportunities to get a bit lost here and there - thorough exploration is still rewarded. Some of the bosses are notably more difficult than others, but nothing is insurmountable and you can always switch the game's difficulty and adjust damage sliders to your liking. I didn't find the difficulty curve intense enough to feel compelled to do so but it's always a plus that the option is there. I do wish there was a cutscene skip option for future playthroughs (there's a fast text scroll but that's it), although I wouldn't recommend skipping anything on a first playthrough. I'd also love a boss rush and thankfully I think they've got one in the works.Nine Sols does SO much right and I can't wait for more people to play it. Excited for future updates as well :)

The boss fights are challenging and rewarding. If you feel that the combat is unfair maybe you're just being a baby cause the timing and flow of everything is tight. The story can get twisted but it's interspersed with humor and heart. Best game of 2024 baybee

_childDocuments_.review: I cried at the ending, so that means I was thoroughly invested and loved every bit of this game.!!WARNING!!! Rare but I actually have to specify that the gore and themes get pretty dang dark in a couple of places. I think it's still rather tastefully done, but the screenshot of gibs didn't prepare me for how hard this game would go, so be warned if you have a squeamish stomach.++PROS+++ Tight, rewarding gameplay, highly skill based with minimal screwups in design.+ Varied areas and enemies.+ Jaw droppingly gorgeous and beautifully scored.+ Incredibly intense story that I was definitely attached too. Similarly the true ending is [Barely] locked behind exploration, which I found incredibly easy to get the requirements for by just... Caring about the story, characters and each area.+ The feeling from the start to the end gives me a lot of Super Metroid vibes with how fast and efficient you can get through areas once you start getting consistent upgrades.+ The comic cutscenes are extremely visceral, and combo'd with ingenious sound design it's hard to not really feel each one.--CONS--- Final boss suffers from a common issue with parry game end bosses: The only route through them is to parry. In comparison to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice though most of these games tend to miss the addition of small throwables / gimmicks to make the fight easier. I do know you could make your way through this boss with basically zero passive upgrades- A handful of collectibles feel like they are just in incredibly silly spots and it's very possible to miss out on completing one quest due to how poorly the way forward for it is communicated. Similarly progressing quests feels a little jank.Obviously the verdict is buy it, at full price, with the soundtrack. It's VERY much worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really, really good game. if you like Hollow Knight and you're waiting for Silksong, it's a no-brainer. If you like Sekiro and also like 2D platformers/adventure games, no brainer. The story and characters are compelling; the visuals are stellar all the way through, some incredible settings to be experienced that are almost worth the price tag alone. Music serves its role handily, I won't remember any of the tracks but they were perfect ambience for the experience. It's not the kind of game that thrives on songs anyway. Taking it more in the direction of ambience was absolutely the right move for this world.The combat is outstanding - by the very challenging final boss, you'll be zipping around, using every frame you can to attach a talisman, parrying and countering, and getting a few sword strikes in. Unfortunately also has the only thing I can fault Nine Sols for, within it. Some of the hitboxes are atrocious. This isn't enough to spoil the game, but it'll kill you a few times during a playthrough. Thankfully it's pretty fast to get back into the action. When you make a game that is fast, and depends on decisions being made in a small fraction of a second to stay alive or advance on the enemy, it is just as important that the game is tightly designed in the hitboxes and hurtboxes, the timings and delays, what moves have uncancellable animations and how long they last, etc - so you don't get punished when you shouldn't have. You'll see what I mean in a couple of the boss fights. But these are something that takes a 10/10 game down to a 9/10 for me. And a 9/10 games is worth playing. Nine Sols... is very much worth playing. Stellar experience, great characters, great lore, great music, great visuals, almost entirely great combat... if you're unsure about going for this one, let this review guide you toward going for it. Very glad to have experienced this exceptionally good game. I don't keep much of an eye on specific studios, but I will definitely be keeping an eye on Red Candle games. (also, the Lady Ethereal chapter is so sick.) Salutations.

_childDocuments_.review: The Git Gud crowd is gonna hate me, but seriously, this game is ridiculously hard.The art style is good and I was enjoying the game a lot. Sure I died a few time. It's all par for the course. I run into a mini boss and it's kicking my ass, hard. I decide I leave it and come back when I have more power ups. I end up at the first real boss and... It's absurd how punishing this is. You have to learn to parry. I'm okay with that, but if you aren't perfect parrying, you will take internal damage. One hit after that and you're dead, walk back, see the intro animation and repeat.Three regular hits not parried and you're dead. And it attacks relentless. I decide to watch some tips on Youtube and I find out there's a second phase. Reading some more online about bosses and well, this is like a FromSoft game where you are supposed to die 99 times to a boss and learn the hard way.I died many times against other Metroidvania and action game bosses. I don't really mind, but there's a limit to how much punishment I can take in a sitting. And this first boss already reached it.Yes, you can turn on story mode, but I'm not a game journalist and then I might as well use a trainer. I'm not playing games for the story, I play it for the challenge as well, but this is just too much.Yeah, I didn't "git gud". It's a skill issue. IDGAF. This game is brutally hard and I'm not the crowd for that.

_childDocuments_.review: I underestimated this game, I genuinely didn't expect it to become my current GOTY, and rival my enjoyment for the likes of Hollow Knight in the genre. Granted, its design goes in nearly the opposite direction as Hollow Knight, being a mostly linear, story-heavy, combat-centric metroidvania, but stands as a phenomenal title that more people need to play & deserves to make a name for itself. It's brutal, tragic, stunning, captivating, a story of vengeance in a lore-rich world inspired by Chinese mythology, complete with engaging level design and some of the best boss fights in the entire genre. You'll get your ass kicked many times over, its Sekiro-inspired claim baring some real teeth. It's a  video game, but finally overcoming these hurdles makes it all the more satisfying. If it ever becomes too overwhelming, the game even offers a difficulty option with modifiable damage values, so anyone can experience the game. Please give this game a chance, it deserves it.Plus you play as a cute, short, angry cat that chiefs that squang in order to heal, what's not to love.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just obtained all achievements, I can now say that this game feels tailor-made for metroidvania + folklore enthusiasts like me.The combination of ancient Chinese mythology and eerie sci-fi elements (nicely dubbed "taopunk" by the devs) is something I have never seen done to this degree before and that alone makes me love this game. The visual design is absolutely top notch, from the architecture (ranging from futuristic environments decorated with traditional patterns to ancient structures inspired by yaodong and tulou) to the attire of enemies (such as the Beijing opera costume worn as armour by various mini-bosses), it is clear that a lot of thought and care went into the presentation of its mythological and historical inspirations.The soundtrack is an extremely unique combination of folk style with electronic sounds, used to great effect to establish mood and atmosphere whenever the gameplay demands. This ranges from the sinister and grotesque feel of the Processing Facility, the beautiful yet sombre tranquillity of the Yaochi ruins, to the tragic desperation of certain boss fights. Of particular note is the boss theme of a certain pair of twins, which, of all things, is an eye-opening blend of electronic music and classical Beijing opera; a collage of at least three songs performed by both male and female singers, reflecting the boss fight itself. This is something I have never seen or imagined I would see. It is no exaggeration to say that the soundtrack is an artistic achievement and innovation in and of itself.The plot brings everything together to a satisfying height. I won't go into detail here due to the risk of spoilers. To put it succinctly, this story is great for people who, while they enjoy the gloomy and solemn tone of Souls-like games as you wander through ruined sites of past calamities, would prefer there being a bit more direct narrative and dialogue.The gameplay is fairly typical for a metroidvania game of this kind, with the Sekiro-inspired parry/talisman system being the main highlight. In contrast to Hollow Knight, the emphasis is far heavier on the rhythmic parrying and countering of enemy attacks as opposed to dodging, with many enemies able to switch attack direction mid-animation and chase up to your character if you try to dash through them. The difficulty of the Standard Mode is certainly no joke, it is smart of the devs to include a Story Mode for people who just want to experience the plot. That said, the process of learning a boss' pattern and slowly overcoming that challenge, being able to look back and see how far you've improved, is indeed the kind of satisfaction embodied by this genre of game.Last but very much not least, .

_childDocuments_.review: I'll make no bones about it, Nine Sols is hard, but not unfair. The combat focused on reading the opponent and doing the right thing at the right time. Coming to grips with all the tools in your arsenal and matching that to the appropriate timing windows of enemy attack patterns in the beginning can be a bit overwhelming.     Once you start getting confident in your abilities, you will encounter bosses that will be all too happy to stomp you into the ground and force you to do a re-think. After much contemplation you will start putting the pieces of the fight together and you will be unleashing a symphony of pain against your opponents as they vainly attempt to harm you. Stringing a series of parries and counters together feels sublime and is where Nine Sols truly shines.     As much as I have drummed up the difficulty of Nine Sols. You also don't need to have perfect timing every time. An imperfect parry is better than no parry at all and will result in damage that can be recovered, so you don't need to be an absolute savant to enjoy the game.     The Jade System and Skill system will allow you to mix things up to better suit your playstyle or opponent. Bringing the same Jades that allow you to deal with multiple enemies while exploring are not going to be the most effective on 1v1 extended boss fights. As you progress through the game you will unlock abilities to regain health, alter your talisman attacks to be quick to get back in the fight, or risk it and charge them up for devastating blows.     My only real issues with the Nine Sols stems from the final side quest that only occur at the end of the game. The conclusion of these quests only triggers at a point of no return and could easily be agnostic to the main story.    In Nine Sols I had a great time taking on challenging opponents, picking up their patterns, and using the various combat mechanics and modifiers to put them down. As a person who is not big on any of the Souls games and bombed out on Bloodborne after beating the Blood Starved beast because I was simply not having any fun I was genuinely surprised that I had as good of a time as I did with Nine Sols. Nine Sols is an easy reccomendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Fascinating lore, great characters, eye-catching and original art style. One of the best metroidvanias I’ve played, and I am sort of a genre connoisseur. It is more on the linear than open side of this genre, but if a game is designed this well it is fine by me. I also enjoy many smart choices made by the developers. For example the boss introductions are done by comics. This is cheaper than making cutscenes, but they are also so dynamic and full of emotion they make a better impression than movies in many much higher budget games.One small irritating thing is the game was often forgetting some of the settings I’ve modified. Strange, but not a big deal.One important thing I have mixed feelings about is the last boss. The difficulty spike it represents is rather… insane. After having very little progress in dealing with it for 3 hours I’ve decided to switch to story mode (it is a regulated difficulty mode) and lower its damage by 50%. This way at least I’d be able to learn its attack patterns without being killed in a few seconds after it changes phases. I thought if it goes well I could always turn the damage back, but even after having it halved it still was by far the hardest boss in the game! At least with struggle I managed it with a self-imposed challenge not to lower the difficulty further…It’s great the story mode was available, but still it’d prefer a smoother difficulty curve with such spikes kept optional.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews for games very much since I'm a poor writer. However, I gotta make an exception for Nine Sols. Definitely a metroidvania type of game for people to try. Of course I did story mode because I'm baby but I really did enjoy a lot of exploratory elements in the game. It was fun trying to figure out the plot and the lore before it was confirmed while going through the game itself. As a Taiwanese-American, it's so jarring to hear Tai-nu being spoken in a game and see words you think are familiar so that was fun. Combat was difficult but rewarding once you figured out parries and such. The "social-link" aspect of the game was not as annoying as I thought it was since it contributed to character growth on a realistic scale, that I didn't mind finding such items that did so.All in all, if you're looking for a game that challenges you even in "easy" mode and for a great story, please consider Nine Sols.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AT BOTTOM OF REVIEWIf you like Hollow Knight and are interested at ALL in what it would look like with a much more interesting parry based combat system, you owe it to yourself to try out Nine Sols. I'm a huge Hollow Knight fan (played it through multiple times on 3 different platforms) and NIne Sols is the first of the modern metroidvania's that I think can compete with Hollow Knight on the same level. The platforming (at least so far, not sure how much it changes) definitely doesn't have the the same level of expression as in Hollow Knight, but the combat, IMO, is much much better (I'm also a huge Dark Souls/Sekiro fan so parrying is in my blood). Once you learn a bosses moves, you can very easily do no-hit runs in the same way as in Sekiro, but you definitely have to commit to learning the patterns. That being said, so far I have been able to beat most bosses in 5 tries or so, including some where I win first try. I would also like it if there were more secrets to find in the world, although I am still pretty early on so things like that might change. As it is right now, there are definitely some secrets to watch out for, just nothing as big as what you can reach pretty early into Hollow Knight. (I could also be missing some though)Furthermore, this game is truly beautiful. The art style is phenomenal, and the animations all look great. The music is great too, some really beautiful and atmospheric tracks that I'm sure will be stuck in my head for many hours after I finish the game. I also really like the story so far. Yi is an interesting character, and I like how much information you can find detailing the different pieces that make up this spiritual + sci fi world.Now, I will say that I backed this project a couple of years ago, and was playing the early demos and betas, and the way that the devs have improved on everything from the first demo is really great to see. I hope to see more from them in the future, and I hope we get more stories and games in this universe!Update: Having now finished the game and seen both endings, I still think it is definitely worth a play for the reasons listed above, however some of the later boss fights definitely need some tuning. The final fight in particular is INCREDIBLY difficult IMO, and this is coming from someone who has played every souls game multiple times doing various challenge runs. The main issue with this difficulty is not that the fight itself is so hard, but that you are more or less forced to change your playstyle to do only one thing in the fight (As in, change your Jades and what talisman you use in order to have a chance at winning). It is still a fight where if you learn every attack you will be able to win pretty consistently, but there are some moments/attacks with bad hitboxes that can get you taking damage when you really shouldn't have. (This is not conjecture btw, I recorded and slowed down the footage of my fights and there are clear hitbox issues) That being said, I really like the way the story ends and I think its very interesting, so it was still worth it, but if you don't like very difficult fights, then this game might not be for you.

name: South of the Circle
detailed_description: South of the Circle Deluxe Edition South of the Circle Deluxe Edition contains an additional set of digital goods including the complete game soundtrack, Eighty Two Nineteen - South of the Circle e-book written by the game’s director, and Circles EP created in collaboration with the Frostpunk OST composer. This package includes: South of the Circle South of the Circle Soundtrack South of the Circle: E-book - Eighty Two Nineteen Circles EP: South of the Circle x Frostpunk About the Game South of the Circle is an emotional narrative experience with a deep multi-layered cinematic story. The main plot asks questions about the consequences of paths taken in life and how they have influenced our career and true love through the lens of the past and the future. You play Peter, a Cambridge academic who crashlands in Cold War Antarctica. As he searches for help, his past unwinds before him, revealing how the pressures of power and his own aspirations have led him into this crisis he must somehow escape. A love story between him and fellow academic Clara develops, and Peter learns the weight of all the things he has promised. Like memories from childhood, some promises stay with us forever. MASTERFULLY EXECUTED CINEMATIC FEEL Created by BAFTA winners State of Play , the game’s beautiful aesthetic and nuanced writing underlines its sweeping cinematic scope, further enhanced by actors drawn from “Bohemian Rhapsody” (Gwilym Lee), “The Woman in White” (Olivia Vinall), “The Crown” (Richard Goulding), “Game of Thrones” (Anton Lesser), “Chernobyl” (Adrian Rawlins) and “Downton Abbey” (Michael Fox). FEATURES Compelling and immersive narrative with a unique sense of time and place. Nuanced emotional choices. Fully motion-captured performances to achieve emotional realism. Rich, authentic setting of the historical Cold War era. Environmental storytelling woven through the narrative. Distinguished and consistent art style. Crafted by State of Play Games, developers of BAFTA-winning Lumino City, BAFTA-nominated KAMI 2 and Apple Design Award Winner INKS, for audiences that seek emotional and heart-wrenching moments with a game.

MASTERFULLY EXECUTED CINEMATIC FEEL Created by BAFTA winners State of Play , the game’s beautiful aesthetic and nuanced writing underlines its sweeping cinematic scope, further enhanced by actors drawn from “Bohemian Rhapsody” (Gwilym Lee), “The Woman in White” (Olivia Vinall), “The Crown” (Richard Goulding), “Game of Thrones” (Anton Lesser), “Chernobyl” (Adrian Rawlins) and “Downton Abbey” (Michael Fox). FEATURES Compelling and immersive narrative with a unique sense of time and place. Nuanced emotional choices. Fully motion-captured performances to achieve emotional realism. Rich, authentic setting of the historical Cold War era. Environmental storytelling woven through the narrative. Distinguished and consistent art style. Crafted by State of Play Games, developers of BAFTA-winning Lumino City, BAFTA-nominated KAMI 2 and Apple Design Award Winner INKS, for audiences that seek emotional and heart-wrenching moments with a game.
short_description: South of the Circle is a deep narrative experience of the emerging relationship between Peter and Clara, Cambridge academics involved in a political conflict. The story focuses on promises made in between career and true love, where our choices burdened by our past seem to be illusory.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a movie, you have to accept it if you want to enjoy the experience. Animated movie where you just move the stick and push the button to make story go on. It tries to give you the illusion to have a role in the story, to take important decisions, to do something, but it's not the case. It's just a movie disiguised as videogame, which goes on because from time to time you move the stick and push some buttons. You never feel immersed in the virtual world or part of the story, it's more like watching a good movie that entertains, captures and amazes you, but you know you are outside the screen, seated on the sofa, it's like you're flipping through the pages of a book, moving the film inside the projectors forward.When you accept this, you can enjoy the very good, mature and smart story. Yes, it's a good movie because it's divinely written, it comes with really great characters, the plot is really original and meaningful. The graphic style is simple and effective at the same time, the right expressive style for the right story.Don't expect for a videogame and enjoy the story. Not a masterpiece, but it's an intense captivating 3,5 hours long movie that deserves your attention.

_childDocuments_.review: In the store summary page it reads: "The story focuses on the weight of life choices - between career, true love and the desire to keep our promises."But in fact all the choices you make in the game don't matter. It wouldn't change how it ends, or even how the plot plays out. It's simply presenting a story. As explained by some other reviewers here, it's just a matter of how the story is remembered.This may make a good book, or a good movie, but not a good interactive video game, at least to most players I suppose. _childDocuments_.review: I write this review a few days after finishing the game; I wanted the disappointment of the ending to fade away before I put fingers to keys (well, pen to paper, but you get it). I'll get it out of the way: the gameplay in this game is certainly limited. It's an interactive novel more than a game, but there's something very disappointing about  Taking agency away from the player was quite disappointing. Everything else about this piece of software, however, I will highly recommend. As far as visual novels go, this one is absolutely gorgeous. Whether we're in Antarctica or in the UK, the art style is striking in its minimal beauty, and it's further enhanced by solid voice acting the whole way through. Clara (Olivia Vinall) and the Professor (Anton Lesser) are standouts, but I was charmed by all of them. Sure, it's a bit heavy handed with easy political tropes (), but in such a short game, perhaps that much exposition is necessary. If you like interactive novels, minimal illustration or the 60's Cold War setting, I'd recommend this without a doubt. If you're rather looking for a "Choices Matter" game, this won't do.

_childDocuments_.review: •	Incredible atmosphere•	Unique and mostly pretty visuals •	Very good use of music•	Great, believable characters•	Very good story•	Setting captured amazingly•	Brilliant voice acting•	Achievements – easy 100%•	Slightly unsatisfactory/confusing ending•	Choices feel illusory•	Some less pretty scenes•	Price a little steepSet against the icy backdrop of Antarctica that masterfully merges with your memories of home life, South of the Circle is a deep narrative game about morals, love, determination, achievement, and friendship. The past and the present are seamlessly merged, playing out in tandem, with the contemplation of the former filling the tireless, silent struggle your character endures in the present through the snow. It is an understated journey of resilience and discovery set against that of a compelling adventure - the endless sense of loneliness in such barren landscapes making an ideal stage for the introspective, and literal struggle that unfolds - both timelines equally memorable and poignant, though sadly somewhat undone by a confusing ending. South of the Circle’s sound design was masterful. Music elevated moments, drawing out the mood expertly in a way that viscerally moved me – particularly in how it set the atmosphere of the vast, lonely landscape of Antarctica and this existential, heavy hopelessness that one feels alone while traversing it.Voice acting was fantastic – it never once felt forced, or over-acted. The actors embodied their characters fully, and delivered memorable performances that brought the game’s story to life in a way I’ve found few games truly do, especially those that aren’t AAA releases. Expression was genuine and believable.Environmental sounds complemented the music and voice acting perfectly, putting you right there in the barren wastes of no man’s land just as well as in the lecture halls of Cambridge university, contributing an understated but necessary and noticeable depth to the artistic presentation of South of the Circle. Designed in a unique blend of what I’d describe as part-animation, part-sketch, South of the Circle managed to present a very beautiful world for the most part, with unexpected levels of detail and finesse. Things such as tracks forming in the snow as you walk or drive over it, or the snowflakes blowing in the wind, both helped to create a tangible sense of atmosphere that would have come over far less immersively had they been absent. Despite the generally low-detail textures, the world actually felt very believable – alive, even. Despite being far from photorealistic, it was incredibly immersive.The only thing I didn’t love about the graphics was that when entering room interiors, the outside borders of the scene (beyond the walls of the room) were just solid black. I wish the camera view had remained completely inside the room, as this made the game feel a little like those old RPG games which do the same thing, and detracted in those scenes heavily from their immersion. Fortunately, though, this is rare, as most of the game is set outside. South of the Circle has an incredibly cinematic presentation, and the gameplay mostly contributes to how smooth this felt – though not always.Choices you can make, which affect the direction of the story somewhat, are not given as text prompts we’re all familiar with in games. Rather, there are various symbols that appear instead, each conveying a different mood or emotion which informs the tone of your responses. In some ways I prefer this because the game is quite whimsical and dreamy. The vagary of these responses are consistent with that and don’t cut through the atmosphere, but they are detailed enough that you can still make an informed decision about what response you give.While I did rather like this system, particularly as it fit the game’s theme well, there were by the late game quite a few of these moods introduced, and I’d actually forgotten what some of them were. My biggest issue with choices, though, is that they ultimately feel illusory. I deliberately aimed for consistency, yet it materialised in an ending which made no sense - the opposite of all the choices I’d made, with no reason offered in-game as to why. This left me somewhat disappointed, though because for me the value of this game is not in its ‘multiple choices’ but its atmosphere and narrative, it doesn’t detract too badly from my impression of  overall.Navigating the game world otherwise is largely assumed by the game itself in cutscenes or animations, but there are a few times, such as walking or driving over terrain, where you’ll be given control. Almost in its entirety, you’ll just be using WSAD to walk your character or drive a car. Often you can only go one way, and so as gameplay goes, South of the Circle is lacking. There are, though rarely, some objects for you to interact with in the game. Achievements relate to these, but from a gameplay perspective they were nothing that special. Some arguably even felt a bit pointless, like being able to push a plane tied to the ceiling as if to ‘fly’ it, for example. While all of these seem a little pointless, I don’t regard this as too much of an issue for the game as its atmosphere more than makes up for this. There is a dream-like quality about this game that was so quaint and peaceful, but there was also tension and a strong sense of being connected with reality, too – a haunting and powerful juxtaposition amplified in the eerie stillness of extreme Antarctica.South of the Circle is certainly a unique experience in gaming that I’m glad I’ve had. Its replayability is very low, but the story it told was memorable and the setting was captured amazingly. We are taken on a beautiful journey from the pits of plight to the heights of hope, that transcends location and time, playing out both in present and past perils and joys, as our character simultaneously endures, and remembers. While the ending was a disappointment, it did not detract from the visceral atmosphere this game portrayed, so my recommendation remains strong if this sort of game interests you.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - 3/10, tolerable story,  poorly designed game. Not worth your time or your money.South of the Circle is a walking sim that follows a linear story. The story is fine, I guess, but all the interactive elements are a detriment to it and it should not have been released as a video game.The flat colour low-poly graphics have a charm to them but are far from amusing enough to justify strolling at a snail’s pace to admire the view. Also there are a lot of visual errors and models constantly clip into each other.The story takes its sweet time taking off but eventually it does get decently captivating. I found the romance plot pretty generic but I wouldn’t necessarily call it bad. The characters are believable and well written. Except one. I could not bring myself to connect with the protagonist. Although a grown man, he would often behave like a nervous teenager which frustrated me as I was trying to keep the bloke alive. It is difficult for me to empathise with a character who keeps getting flashbacks to mild childhood struggles while in very dire circumstances during which he should be focused on surviving.I understand the game is trying to send a message (especially a feminist one), as it is not very subtle about it. This is fine when paired with an entertaining story, but in the first half when the narrative is still pretty “meh” it does feel like I’m being lectured by the devs.The biggest flaw of the game are the “choices”.  Instead of regular dialogue options you choose emotion based responses (confident, enthusiastic, shy, etc.). It is an interesting concept but executed terribly. The actual dialogue tends to barely if at all match the emotion you picked and often I struggled to get the main character to respond as I intended. Eventually I got to a plot point where I saw myself disagreeing with what my character was saying, regardless of what choices I picked. That’s when I realised that you don’t get to choose the protagonist’s responses, you can at best influence the tone in which they express them. Having the main character consistently say the opposite of what you want to say is very frustrating and makes you feel like you picked the wrong choice, which could have been entirely avoided if the devs didn’t dangle the illusion of choice in front of you for the whole game. At one point the game gives you a gun and implies you can shoot a person with it. Out of desperation to have any influence on the story I tried to kill the other person but the devs made it impossible. No matter how hard you try, the sights move away from the target.If the game was just the story then maybe, just maybe I could see myself recommending it at a discount, but all the vague and meaningless choices the game makes you believe you have make it a more frustrating than enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this is my first negative review ever. Never expected it to be in a game that I mostly enjoyed.The game is beautiful, artistically. The characters are compelling, the voice acting GREAT, and the parallel storylines work really well in the context of someone stuck alone in the freezing cold, starting to allucinate. However, I take extreme issue with how the illusion of choice is implemented.Throughout the game, you are  (I tried sometimes to not respond, but I wasn't allowed; with one notable exception ) to choose the emotion that the main character feels whenever he intervenes in conversation. I did not expect these choices to have too much of an effect in the overall narrative, but I did expect them to shape the story in some way. However, I was dissapointed. In spectacular fashion. Spoilers ahead:If you want a visual novel with some choices which actually produce (small but significant and rewarding) changes in the overall story, with a great visual style, go play Pentiment. This game, I cannot recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a bit hard to decide on but I have to recommend this game if you are interested in the type of narrative games and such. Right of the bat, South of the Circle's soundtrack, plot, voice acting is outstanding. The struggles of insecurity, guilt, and bigotry within the environment and politics of academia portrayed is one of the most relatable and realistic I've ever seen. That being said, South of the Circle commit two of the worst crimes in its designs for a choice-based game. The most frustrating part about this game is that South of the Circle design the in-game choices as ambiguous as possible. Whereas other choice-based games at the very least give you one word to describe what the character is going to do. South of the Circle's choices are offered in the design of circles with different colors representing different emotions that the character will deliver the message/choice. More often than not, the character has said and done stuffs that I didn't want him to because the choices offered are extremely ambiguous. Not only that, it has kept me strictly playing "safe" by choosing the options that are shy and reserved because I didn't want him to say anything stupid at all. Spoilers:

_childDocuments_.review: At its heart, this is an interactive movie. And not a very good one at that. I’m over 90 minutes in, and so far, the entire plot involves 1) a guy struggling with his PhD thesis and 2) a ridiculously drawn-out love story. I was bored out of my mind. There is a 3rd story about a guy searching for help in an arctic tundra, but it takes a back seat to the others.The game lets you make dialogue choices based on your preferred emotion, but it doesn’t matter at all. Just for fun I let the game run itself by not pressing any inputs, and when the timer runs out, the game makes a choice for you. The response is the same, and nothing changes. You can literally take your hand off the controller/keyboard, and just watch.Well… not quite. There are other “gameplay” elements such as driving a car down a straight road, and moving a guy through the snow. Zero fun. I’ve played through lots of interactive FMV games, and walking simulators, but I’ve never experienced one where so little stuff happens.I can only recommend this to people who enjoy narrative heavy games with no consequential choices, along with a very slow burn plot. Otherwise, avoid. I stopped at 100 minutes in.

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished South of the Circle, and I am, without a doubt, irredeemably frustrated.I'll preface this by saying that I actually put interactive storytelling above all else, and I believe that the medium is more relevant today than ever before. But the fact that this... this... this story had to be created as a game... well, that's indefensible in my eyes. I simply don't know what motivation, other than EU funding, warranted turning this story into a game.Make no mistake, I was deeply drawn in from the beginning of the story, and not just because I, like the protagonist, am called Peter and I work at a university. Not just because I am deeply concerned about the Cold War and all that it entails. Not just because it deals with serious issues, such as the office politics of the university, putting work before all private matters, or even the importance of dialogue. It is because it was supposed to be a game and it has not become one. I mean, I have played several "walking simulators" and I was perfectly fine, even moved by many of them.The graphics are captivating, with their stylized, flat, thirties-style visuals (WPA tourist posters came to mind). I loved the lifelike, sensitive and eloquent acting of the voice actors, I really felt I was in the middle of a real radio play. I loved every theme, from climate change to the feminist undertone of the work to the understated characterisation. But where does the player's role come in?Because it's a brilliant idea that the dialogues use various icons to that serve to 'direct' the protagonist, like a stage play. I'm also in favour of raising dramatic stakes by removing interactions at key poins even if the player wants to achieve something. But to have any interaction from the beginning to the end of the narrative be completely superfluous and weightless is a bridge too far. I cannot fathom what the player has done to be punished so, during this otherwise friendly three and a half hour 'gameplay'.  I can't see what prevented the makers from giving even the smallest decisions at least a bit of impact. And I really don't understand why the interactive medium was needed at all. For it is a great story that beautifully illustrates the difficult choices a compromising man makes, how we are bound by toxic masculinity even in the rareified air of Cambdrige academia, how we are at the mercy of our hearts and how we crave love and appreciation, and how the two can be at odds. But I will still not forgive myself for having to suffer through every interaction of South of the Circle. As much as I'm all for playing through the most narrative, cinematic, Davidcage-y video game possible, I wouldn't throw a stone at anyone for merely watching South of the Circle. Because while in a Telltale game I feel like every decision I make has weight, in a Quantic Dream game I'm involved in the plot, and in any indie adventure game there are exciting puzzles, dialogue trees, and tension, here in this game, that's sorely lacking. All of it.I can't help but feel that the use of the interactive medium in South of the Circle is completely unjustified, and I'm deeply annoyed that I have to press buttons to get to the end of the story, which if anything is what I've been conditioned to do since I was young. I suppose it could be said that this game is about how all your choices are inherently constrained, that physical, official and spiritual survival requires sacrifices, and that free will is the first of these sacrifices, but then again, you could have designed decision structures so that the player doesn't feel tortured all the time.So, in conclusion, I just want to say that digital gaming as a medium has every right to tell whatever story it wants to tell and I don't... okay, I moderately regret buying South of the Circle. That said, I maintain it's a textbook case for how narrative games can be diverted from their roots in play. And that is a cardinal sin.

_childDocuments_.review: So first things first, the biggest issue I had with the game was how it wasn't much of a game. And I'm not complaining about the visual novel aspect of it — I'm perfectly fine with text-based games and whatnot, but South of the Circle incorporated various interactions that made no sense and rather annoyed me as a player. For example, holding W or LMB to keep moving in a certain direction — there is no "playing" involved in that, so why not let me just click to the objective to move? And then there were minor associated issues like characters clipping through terrain and corners, being unable to turn your camera fast enough (since your character movement controls the camera) — all that is making you wonder why you give the player the tools to control the character /that/ much when they gain nothing from it. It doesn't make you feel involved in any way, it only bothers you to keep your finger aimlessly on the button for while trying to tell you that you're supposed to be enjoying the picturesque sights.And god, there are many. The game is visually stunning, I just think it could do with better interaction mechanics.Now on the subject of the story, the writing, dialogue are all great. Characters are well-presented, but — many will probably see this coming — the choice aspect is just off.So just to make sure we're on the same page here, you don't choose the specific lines but the emotions (to a varying degree) your character puts in them. Meaning if Peter is cornered to make a decision, he will have to, say, either agree to play along in a more panicky way on the one hand, resolute on the other. One major issue here is that there /does/ seem to be the intended way to progress through the story, and with Peter being the less masculine type (not putting this as a spoiler since it feels rather obvious from the first moments of the game and I love it), the less confident choices feel much more convincing. The bold ones feel misplaced, off — they're kind of along the lines of "confident complacency" at best.Which brings me to the next point, the overall plot. Which is where the spoilers definitely come in — do not click them unless you've completed the game:I realise this review's a bit weird, giving it thumbs up while mostly criticising it, and I do think that this has perhaps been rushed. Nonetheless, it's a great narrative experience, so if you dig these sort of games and aren't disillusioned to expect vital choices in this genre, it's a great pick — especially at this price.
_childDocuments_.name: South of the Circle

_childDocuments_.review: A meticulous, understated, and memorable little experience with excellent voice acting, atmospheric set design, and a solid soundtrack as the glue. This is essentially an interactive movie: a "walking sim" with very minimal exploration.There are many choices to be made but they are not in service of the plot. To be clear, this is not a "choices matter" game, at least it's not how choices are usually integrated into video games. Rather, your selections define your memories of the story. It is purely about roleplaying. But it's also about chance, because it's never clear how your choices—geometric shapes and colors—are going to manifest. Or maybe you do know how it's going to have to end? As the greatest statesman of our age has put it: "them's the breaks".People who like this kind of stuff will enjoy this game. That said, I feel the concept wasn't pushed as far as it could go. There's a purposeful restraint to the whole story that does right by its decidedly restrained characters but ends up skin-deep and rushed. Still, the designers are onto something here and I hope they get another opportunity to work on a fuller, richer game that builds on the 's potential.

_childDocuments_.review: South of the Circle is an interactive fiction game set in the period of the Cold War. It is developed by State of Play who also made Lumino City. We follow Dr Peter Hamilton, a lecturer at Cambridge, who is working on his academic paper about the clouds and climate science. He meets Clara, who is also a lecturer at Cambridge, and together they continue to research the topic of his paper. Together, they discover radiation in the clouds and the source of the radiation is emanating from Antarctica.Peter is given the opportunity to go to Antarctica to continue his research however, the plane crashes. Floyd, the pilot, hurt his leg in the crash, so it is up to Peter to go in search of help.Throughout Peter's journey, the story transitions from the present to the past. Choices he made, his relationship with Clara, his family, and co workers.It is fully voice acted throughout and the quality is excellent. The story is compelling and it hooks you in from the beginning.Since the game is mostly interactive fiction, game play is minimal and almost complimentary. It involves making decisions about how Peter reacts to situations by his emotions. The responses range from shy, concerned, enthusiastic, honest to strong. The main character is moved around with either WASD or a controller.Keyboard and mouse can be used, however, I did find that using a controller was more intuitive and relaxing to watch the story unfold.Pros:* Excellent voice acting* Compelling story* Music is excellent and cinematic * Achievements (easy to obtain if achievements are checked prior to playing)* Trading CardsCons:* No mid level savingUnfortunately no mid level saving was quite a problem and it was such a shame to see how this affected the game, which took me just over 5 hours. Saving is done automatically by an icon in the top right corner and was sometimes difficult to see because of the white background of Antarctica. Although not quite sure, but I am assuming that most of the time it saved automatically after a "scene".Rating: 8/10 (would be more but no mid level saving - luckily the story is compelling)
