_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Wrote a kinda jokey review but in reality, this game is a fantastic, silly, and inspiringly fun piece of art.  I've haven't felt so much unbridled joy and love be poured into a game since the experimental games of the early '00s and '90s.It felt like it was made in secret under a table somewhere, where the microtransactions and lootboxes couldn't find it, like it didn't care that it had to meet a quota or make a number go up on  a graph in an exec's office. It cared only that you were having fun and that it was having fun right along with you. The Cafeteria level alone is some of the most fun i've had in a game in years, and is the standard i hold my future gaming experiences too.The team at Tango GW made something that not only felt worth the price, but double that and then some, and Microsoft's decision to close the studio has completely changed my approach to how i'll be buying and enjoying my games from now on. Regardless, thank you Tango GW for the experience, HiFi is gonna be my GOTY for years to come, and I'll be listening to the OST perhaps even longer. Thanks again!

Forced tutorials, quick time events, unskippable scenes after a checkpoint, so much predictable repetitiveness, then uninspired exploration/secret finding which literally just takes a single jump in a room to discover.Sadly the biggest let down for me though was the games focus point and the main reason I played, music. It just wasn't very musical at all in terms of gameplay, Tetris Effect done a better job of that, bloody Tetris!This game is adored but I feel is tragically over hyped and I bought into that.. _childDocuments_.review: This game, is absolutely amazing. There are so many nice little touches to the characters and world in general, you can tell there was a lot of thought put into almost every aspect of this game. The fact it's only $30 is wild because it feels like it should be a $60 game. I beat the main game in about 13 hours, which seems on the short end for a game, but again for the price I'd say it's really worth it. The game continues after the main story, so I love that there's more for me to do. I really enjoyed all the different characters, and was hooked throughout the game. I also loved exploring the levels and seeing what I could try and find.One really big perk of this game is you can tell they went out of their way to make it as accessible as possible. Or, that's how it seems to me. I'm lucky to not have accessibility needs, so maybe there are things that were overlooked. But, they add plenty of visual ways you can see the beat rather than having to listen to it if you're deaf or just don't want to listen to audio. And their system of having on beat hits do more damage rather than punish the player is really nice as I have learned I can not keep time apparently.There is a little bit of a caveat here. In the videos I saw promo-ing this game, they mentioned about how you didn't really need to be able to keep the beat to enjoy the game, as it simply rewarded players. This is not *entirely* true as there are certain parts of the game/ certain enemies you need to defeat where you simply have to press buttons to the beat or you can not progress. Normally I wouldn't really point this out, and just chalk it up to making the game more difficult, but when I went in with the impression of "oh, if I can't keep time I'll be completely fine", this kinda stuck out to me. That said, there are still visual cues to help you with these things if you can't keep time very well, but yeah, just stood out to me.One other thing I really appreciated about this game is I feel like the pacing of learning new abilities/ skills is really good. I never felt overwhelmed with options for what attacks my character could do- it felt like you'd learn about a new skill or ability, have time to play around with it, and then move on to the next skill.Overall I highly recommend this game if you're even a little bit interested in it. I have some friends who just don't like rhythm games and if that's you, then yeah, maybe skip this one. But I know for me at least I was on the fence about this game and do not regret it at all after buying it.

_childDocuments_.review: - Top notch presentation with a wonderful story awaiting you.- Endearing, likeable characters with fleshed out personalities. Characters have a high level of cuteness and quirkiness.- A rhythm game that'll scratch that punk rock itch! - Great soundtrack with very creative audio effects. - Multiple difficulty levels to choose from.- Plenty of achievements and collectibles.- Hidden gems for perfectionists and explorers.- Gorgeous varied environments made in its specific style. Somewhat reminiscent of Borderlands.- Charming references to movies, tv shows, books and games.- Lots of meta humour in a game that doesn't take itself too seriously but is seriously well developed. - Characters and objects move to the sound of the beat! Seemingly simple but perfectly executed.- Accessibility options baked in from the get-go.- Very well optimized for the Steam Deck. I had a blast! - No bugs/glitches/crashes to report and near instant wake from sleep so you can resume exactly from where you left off. So cool!- All in all, the game is unique. There's nothing quite like it. Hoping it acts as inspiration for others and paves the path for a potential sequel. - The platforming aspect isn't for everyone at first, but you can get used to it. Much like the Spyro remastered trilogy.- Timing for certain moves can be tricky and lead to some frustration but with plenty of patience you can proceed. Eventually. - Inaccessible areas which require another playthrough to open. Not a fan. Understandable as to why they did it, story-wise, but still. - What Microsoft did to Tango Gameworks is beyond words. Despite that, the studio is still kicking and hopefully in more capable hands.

_childDocuments_.review: I literally couldn't love this game more than I do. That's coming from someone with decent rhythm that normally hates games like that. Hi-Fi is different though. It simultaneously helps you understand the mechanics enough with good training to let you get going without holding hands and not throwing you into something too intense. The characters and story are both typecasted things you've seen before but such a perfect distillation of those tropes that they are a breath of fresh air again. The story isn't some historical success in the artwork of story telling but yet it'll still get you invested enough to be happy or upset when the story calls for it.The only issues I had in the entire game was wishing I had slightly more movement and a better lock on system. Otherwise the entire thing was a blast. I could rant for hours but I sincerely do not care what game comes out the rest of the year. This is my GOTY hands down without question. I have heard it didn't do as well as they wanted but god I hope I see more of Hi-Fi. It's the most fun I've had with a game in so long. Too many AAA let downs. This was an amazing breath of fresh air. I wish I could play it for the first time again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a prime example of the kind of games the industry needs. Not so much the stealth release, but the interesting setting, music, art style, the presentation etc. Just something that isn't an open world realistic, "deep", over the shoulder 3rd person shooter/psuedo RPG with repetitive map markers spread all around. Something that qualifies the A and B tier state of gaming instead of needing to be supported constantly or make a bunch of money off anything other then the sales of the game. Literally the only slights I can give hi fi rush is the main character being a massive cringe lord but that's probably by design. The parry needs to be introduced earlier as that mechanic becomes the entire meta of the game and makes it more enjoyable. I've also seen people  say the rhythm fighting gameplay is also a turn off judging from some comments as well, but I at least liked it and it felt it just needed to be a little less overwhelming with options at the start. I feel like this is the kind of game No straight roads was trying to be, but with a much higher budget. My only fear is no sequel. (My greatest fear has come true)Also scottish women are hot

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game is perfect.Outstanding art and animation, incredibly satisfying character-action rhythm gameplay, all synced up to a killer soundtrack. The immense effort of designing and animating the environments to sync with the BGM makes the whole experience come to life.The writing is funny and the characters are charming. The comic-book style is seamlessly weaved from cutscenes to gameplay.The technical options are expansive and performance is stellar. The game is bursting at the seams with quality-of-life features and accessibility options.There are no cut corners, overused elements, or monetization. The game seems tailored to be as entertaining as possible at every moment. It sets the bar in every way.

_childDocuments_.review: My game play time of 10 hours is what it took me to go through the campaign on Normal while focusing on collecting, with no post-game play.Not only is the game play absolute fire, the humor is the best! Reminds me of Borderlands kind of humor, but with its own style. I found myself chuckling quite a bit, and all the characters were very thoughtfully made. Performing combos will get a crowd to cheer for you, making the combat and music even more enticing! There was a healthy balance of combat, platforming, and rhythm sections. There is also post-game work to do. My only complaint is that outfits unlock only at the end of the game for post-game use. It's nice in that you're invigorated with a fresh look, but I personally would have liked to customize a bit earlier.The only warning I have: Your head will start to bob without you knowing it while you play. You probably won't realize it until you leave the game and you sit there for a second still bobbing your head. If you have a loved one next to you, they are not immune and will also start to bob. As I type, I'm reminded of the rhythm and am back to head bobbing. You've been warned.

_childDocuments_.review: It seems like AAA companies nowadays want to follow suit with everyone else with making sequels or just adding to an already existing cash-grab genre.That being said, they announced this game 1 single day before it released, and it's already one of the greatest games ever played. Finding a single player game that breaks through the monotony this well is so rare that it almost feels like it shouldn't exist. The art style is a perfect match, all of the characters you meet are unique and likable, and to tie it all together the music and game play are terrific. The environment pulsing and gyrating along with Chai (the main character) stamping his foot and snapping along with the music gives the game this quirky one-of-a-kind experience. The combat is rhythm based and encouraged to occur on beat. Which, for the less musically inclined is no problem because the game as a toggle for a visible representation for the beat. Not to mention that this game is less than half of the new standard for game costs and its VERY polished and complete.TL;DR: 10/10 Combat rhythm game scratches my brain, if this game was $60 dollars I would still purchase it.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking over 80 hours into this game and earning all the achievements, I'm going to have to try really hard find the next game that will bring a similar experience as Hi-Fi Rush has. The unique concept combining action game combat and rhythm game elements was perfectly executed. This method design would also be applied many other interactive and non-interactive aspects of the game. The parts of the stages move with the music, all form of movement and attacking all sync to the beat of the levels. Not to mention the cutscenes and how most of them are also synced to the beat. I appreciate that aspect in almost anything because I find musical timing to what you are seeing to be very important. The music should match to what you're seeing on screen and Hi-Fi Rush nails it. My journey through the game began on Hard Mode and it was certainly an experience trying to learn this game's mechanics and trying not to die. Regardless, my first playthrough was something that I won't forget just because the overall presentation of the game. After beating the game the first time, I already wanted more to do and thankfully there were the Spectra side missions in almost every level. This also gave me the opportunity to go back to other levels and find more collectibles that I had missed. In that playthrough, I had played it on Rhythm Master (The Hardest Difficulty) and slowly began to understand the game's mechanics more and more. I knew to myself that if I was going to 100% the game and earn all the achievements, I had to get a better grasp at the game's mechanics. As I went through the game the first time, I was not using everything in my arsenal. Just learning how to control and understand what Chai is doing and the enemies around me was a learning curve for myself. I would almost say it was akin to learning an instrument (Not really though, learning actual instruments is very hard). Every playthrough on a different difficulty I saw how much better I was getting than my first two playthroughs. My timings became better as I familiarized myself with all the stage songs. I learned how to earn higher scores on every chorus. Everything I had learned was also applicable in the Rhythm Tower and I still felt as if I was learning how to play the game even from there. To summarize this section of the review, I'd say that Hi-FI Rush's gameplay, specifically in combat, is engaging enough for players to want to learn more.As I mentioned before, this game's presentation is fantastic and checks all the boxes everything that I have ever liked ever. The use of rock music culminating the game's style, the characters and how they're written, and the set pieces seen throughout the stages. Upon playing this game, I had never heard any of the bands featured in this game, but the selection all fits perfectly within the game and the combat sections. I prefer some songs more than others, but the option for streamer mode being able to change the song gave some variety on the multiple playthroughs I had done. The characters were also lots of fun to hear throughout the game. Chai definitely feels like a character inspired by the likes of Marty McFly and Scott Pilgrim. Someone who fits the criteria of coolest loser ever. Along with the supporting cast and the villains, this game felt like this fusion American cartoons and Japanese anime that isn't trying too hard and is genuinely funny/enjoyable. Also shoutouts to the cell-shaded graphics this game pulls off.If I create a list of negatives for this game, it would be same but prevalent. At times, I found myself getting bored of listening to dialog of characters over and over on multiple playthroughs of the game. There's only so much I hear Zanzo shouting in my ear about something before I start finding it annoying (Something I never did was change the voice languages for the game. That likely would've at least helped in playing through the same levels without feeling bored).As for the gameplay, my only main gripe with it was the platforming. Chai did not feel like he was designed for a lot of the stages. The worst part about his movement is his jump and the lack horizontal movement you have after it. He just sinks like a rock and you have to rely on your air dash if you're not confident in making in making a 3 ft long jump. Otherwise, there's still some fun things to on certain stages before fights, such as the zip lining segments.My final thoughts on this game would be little hard to put into a few sentences, but I feel as if Hi-Fi Rush is my game of the year and possibly decade unless I play something else that would give me a greater enjoyment and experience than Hi-Fi Rush has. I had spent almost everyday playing this game since it had launched and tried to 100% it and all of the Steam achievements. I was always busy with college or work, but I had always tried to find time to squeeze in a session of playing Hi-Fi Rush. And now since done everything  there is to that game, the only thing I can say to please play Hi-Fi Rush.

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite game to be released last year. I played this on release but I'm bad at getting round to reviewing things. I'm reviewing it now in light of... recent decisions made by Microsoft, which I'll come back to.I'm a Nine Inch Nails and Black Keys fan (and what a cracking choice of a Prodigy song) so I was drawn in from the trailers and bought this on release. The animation is fantastic, with endearing character design, it has an engaging story poking fun at corporate greed while keeping it lighthearted and comedic, and a wonderful original soundtrack fitting in perfectly with the licensed music. The audio works SO WELL with the visuals, everything syncs to the beat visually (and I mean everything, industrial machinery, lights, characters), it's incredibly satisfying when you get into the rhythm and improve as you go through the game. Excellent combat design with a nice variety of combos and upgrades. The team really worked together well on this.As a side tangent, I'm a musician but only played a couple of other rhythm games before this; in a way I kind of feel like this would be great for beginner musicians getting used to the idea of rhythmic playing, at least in 4/4 haha.It's also a refreshing to have a game without micro-transactions, isn't live service, isn't a huge time-sink (not that there's anything necessarily wrong with that, but it's hard for lots of people to find the time to commit to very long games), just 10 hours or so of main playtime for the main story, but at the same time with lots of replay-ability and extra content, some of which the devs have added since release. I haven't managed to come back for the completionist on this but I really want to when I find a good time for it, I would love to get fully immersed in this again. A real throwback to a time when games didn't have in-game predatory micro-transactions and were fully complete on release. Hi-Fi Rush is clearly made by a passionate team that really care about what they're making. A shining example of how to make a successful high quality game that people really want to engage with. This model is, in many ways, what people didn't even realise they were missing in today's climate.Absolutely incredible game, 10/10.And that's where my review should end. Unfortunately, Microsoft/ XBOX don't seem to know when they have an absolute gem. In their words, Hi-Fi Rush was a "breakout hit" for them. Go to Tango Gamework's Twitter and you see them retweeting all the various awards Hi-Fi Rush has won. Matt Booty from XBOX says "we need smaller games that give us prestige and awards", the day after... XBOX closes Tango, the studio of a smaller game that was a "breakout hit" and gave them prestige and awards.They're not just a real life parody of the malicious corporate nonsense that Hi-Fi Rush (now ironically) pokes fun at throughout the game, they're also failing at capitalism. Imagine having a successful studio, then shutting it down because you don't even want to risk the possibility of a sequel that they're pitching. Absolute joke. These clowns had a winning lottery ticket and they ripped it up. Even speaking cynically, Hi-Fi Rush 2 could've been a cash cow for them because people would want to buy it (I'd pre-order it immediately, and generally I don't pre-order games) but clearly the poor execs over at Microsoft are struggling with only a 34% increase in shares in the past year; so they just had no choice but to close a load of studios and stop those greedy devs, animators, artists, musicians and sound designers pocketing it all.♥♥♥♥ XBOX, ♥♥♥♥ Microsoft. Tango Gameworks is the GOAT. I hope you all have a great Monday 4.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun 3rd person rhythm based action game. There are platforming parts in between the fights but there is no overlap between them. All the fights are in closed off arenas. You won't be ambushed by enemies while platforming, though there are some timed jumps/doors that will ambush you instead. It takes some time to get used to the controls since  syncs to the beat, including the pulsating environment, enemy attacks,  attacks and  dashes. You always dash or attack on the beat, even if you miss time it, so you aren't actually dashing or attacking when you press the button if your timing is off, which takes some getting used to. This also makes the fights very swingy, as you tend to either wreck or get wrecked depending on well you can sync things up. It's not too unforgiving, I was able to get A and B ratings with C level timing around ~50% or so. Once you get the hang of it it's pretty fun since there are a lot of combos to unlock and you get 3 assist characters who are good against certain weaknesses and can also help you with a combo attack.The autosave is pretty forgiving too. It saves at each segment of each boss battle so if you die you start at the segment you died in instead of having to start the fight from the beginning. The boss battles are pretty tough the first time through since they are different mechanically from each other. It took me about 12 hours to finish my first playthrough on normal, so the game is short enough that it never feels repetitive. There aren't that many licensed tracks, but it does have two Nine Inch Nails songs and one Prodigy song, which are cool. The art style is very cartoony and it's definitely a game that wants you to have fun.What isn't fun are the quick time events that pop up pretty frequently. For some reason these are very random pattern-wise and don't appear to follow the beat that everything else is following at all. There are also some really weird button combos involving holds followed by immediate release+re-presses that suck. Thankfully, so many people complained that there's an option in the Accessibility menu to tone those down so you only need to hit 75% of them to pass, instead of 100%. I would have been stuck at the 4th level if not for that. So if you play this and are getting frustrated with the QTE parts, definitely go into the options and turn that on. If you play on Hard though, you'll have to complete those perfectly, which sounds painful.Also of note:+ There is a cat!+ You can pet the cat!+ You can put a hat on the cat!

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi RUSH is a one of the best video game experiences I have ever sat through and had the joy of 100% completing to its fullest extent. When I was browsing the Xbox Game Pass library one day and saw "Hi-Fi RUSH" listed under titles, I said to myself - "I'll give it a shot! Kind of looks like JSR" and that was the best choice I have ever made. This game, whether it be cutscenes, action, movements, audio - EVERYTHING is synced with the beat of the game, including environments! That wowed me quite a lot, and not to mention this was the first LEVEL. The cutscene beforehand had incredibly slick and clean transitions that you really don't see nowadays. The combat is so so so polished and silky smooth, it's almost hard to keep the beat due to how much you can get lost in just creating stylish combos and doing what you want and having fun. This game is PURE fun at its core. It's entirely user experience on whether or not you enjoy it - if you ♥♥♥♥ up, it's your own fault most of the time.I haven't even gotten to mention the absolutely PHENOMENAL soundtrack that encompasses the games' story and world. I was always a big fan of rock music, but seeing a soundtrack that nearly consists of almost that while having no duds in the OST release even on Spotify is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MARVEL. I catch myself nearly everyday so far of high school this year, in the hallways listening and jamming to the soundtrack - because that's how good it is. You don't need to play the game just to enjoy it, you can literally embrace its goodness with the 10/10 score. My favorites include The Beacon, Too Big To Fail, I Got This, Production Destruction, In A Blink, etc etc. It has so much variety - and not to mention the licensed artists are also phenomenal as well! Seeing The Black Keys alongside Nine Inch Nails in a rhythm game is a spectacle that I never thought I'd enjoy, yet here we are today. Other bands like The Joy Formidable are in there too and their music choice they gave to their respective tracks and bosses sync up with the beat very well and go alongside their personalities. I like how some songs are about how certain characters may feel and some are very on the nose with what they're referencing or referring to. My favorite song out of all of these copyrighted tracks has to be The Perfect Drug or Lonely Boy, they're both VERY good.I haven't even gotten to the characters yet, which is what I will talk about [somewhat] briefly. The main protagonist of the game, Chai, really got me connected to him - and with good reason. When I was a kid growing up, I had big dreams of becoming a world famous rockstar because - I thought it was really cool. I didn't know how to play guitar almost at all. Seeing Chai be cocky and confident due to being self conscious of how others perceive him really gives him a "hit-home" type of character feeling. Chai, just Chai, is incredibly relatable in writing and in his voice acting, done by the wonderful Robbie Daymond - who absolutely, might I add, CRUSHED it as his role. He has such a personality, and at points he really reminds me of Scott Pilgrim. He's a complete and utter boyloser who seems to ♥♥♥♥ up at every given turn, but learns to not be selfish and to help others and have empathy - and I feel like that isn't represented in media so often anymore. Chai is a jackass, and you find him corny at first - but you grow to love him and his friends, hell, maybe his personality or looks too, I don't judge. He's a character that encompasses so many people and feelings all at once, and I think him alone is a reason to give the game a shot.Hi-Fi RUSH went under my radar for over around a year. I've been disappointed that it did because after I started to play the game more, I couldn't stop smiling and/or laughing at jokes or puns made in the dialogue. This game is well worth the $30 you pay for it up front. There is no P2W methods to the combat, and everything is skilled based. While this game may not be everyone's thing, it will pull you in and make it your own. The DLC for the game is completely optional and doesn't affect gameplay at all aside from cosmetic choices. This game has given me well over 120+ hours if you combine my Xbox time (which is where I first played it) with my Steam time. I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who is looking for something spicy, something new - something DIFFERENT. There's nothing else like it.To all my friends out there? Rock on. The world will know your name.

_childDocuments_.review: Bethesda and Tango Gameworks' surprise 30 Dollar release is worth buying but I don't think its GOTY if I'm being honest. I understand why people feel this way given it feels like a statement against Modern Game Development practices (And critically executing Forspoken which is admittedly hilarious). But as a game detached from all of that, I don't feel its quite to THAT level, even if it comes close a couple times.Reason being, Pacing, The first third and The Vandelay museum can be sloggy with its overemphasis on platforming and tutorialization. I also feel like it could have used its music better or perhaps another look at the music direction. Poor Nine Inch Nails feels like gets drowned out with the rest of the game's soundtrack but The Prodigy and the Joy Formidable are both used incredibly effectively at their respective moments in the game. Invaders must Die in particular was Perfect. That said to swing it back to the positives, They nailed combat. Especially when those two aforementioned bands kick in. Hi Fi rush is at it's best when you are headbanging to the beat with your combos and action platforming as you enter a flow state to blow through hordes of Vandelay Robots, which when it does happen thats where it feels like its hitting that GOTY Territory. Most of the time it doesnt quite hit that but its still very solid. Art direction is great, with the game world synched to the beat and characters being very expressive without going full anime-overdesign.The story is...okay, its basically a better version of Streets of Rage 4's plot which was pretty bad, the characters are all charming enough to keep you engaged and everyone has their moments of glory and shame. Comedy is generally solid and helps alleviate some of the story's rougher edges I did have a few moments where I spat out Coffee (Decaf) laughing and I don't recall cringing at any attempted jokes.Otherwise its polished, with very minor bugs if any, and is a pretty full single-player playthrough with its own post-game.So 10/10 GOTY? No but I do think its well worth the 30$ asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is a curious attempt at mixing a hack and slash action adventure in the style of Devil May Cry with a rhythm game. It was surprise released at the start of 2023 by Tango Gameworks, with the game project being directed by the same director, who previously managed the wonderful The Evil Within 2. And while I love the game’s style and energy, they are the main reason I’ve enjoyed it. Often in spite of the gameplay, not because of it.I almost never play rhythm games. I didn’t particularly enjoy the ones I’ve checked out, while the games that are usually considered to be the best in the genre are on platforms I don’t own. Not sure I would find those enjoyable either, however as while I have zero problems with rhythm and flow, I don’t really like the level of abstraction these games have in terms of transferring musical concepts to patterns. Still, I can appreciate such titles and the wave of games that tried to mix the typical rhythm game routine with other genres over the past decade has been curious. Possibly the most successful title of the kind was Crypt of the NecroDancer, which is unsurprising since that game plays like a roguelike. Transferring an already turn-based game with very simple controls and mechanics to being operated to a specific rhythm seems like natural fit. Then there were also successful Thumper and Beat Saber, which are basically a typical rhythm game, just with a different presentation. And even more recently, several titles appeared that tried to operate like a proper action game, but with rhythm game mechanics, like Metal: Hellsinger and now Hi-Fi Rush. And these don’t quite work.As mentioned, at its core Hi-Fi Rush plays like one would expect from a DMC/Bayonetta type hack and slash action adventure game. You get linear missions to go through which feature some exploration and secrets, but are more focused on platforming, light puzzle solving and locked down arenas where your performance during the fight gets rated. The game operates using the post-Bayonetta logic of not counting the time spent outside of a fight against you, instead the mission rank is calculated from those arena fights ratings. Also important to know that unlike some examples of the genre, arenas are very limited and the game doesn’t have any big set pieces with platforming and/or puzzle challenges in it that are counted as one continuous battle. Fights can have multiple phases or have additional tricks and modifiers, but you always know when it’s fighting time and when it isn’t and you can take your time.The big twist on this typical formula is the fact that the whole game world moves to the beat. And while your jumping and dodging moves can be triggered off-beat, all attacks (for both you and all enemies) always trigger on beat – you only queue them up if you press buttons off-beat. But it’s not like you have to wait long, as the beat of the game is constant, unbroken and is happening about once per second. You can, if you wish, also enable a visualizer of it just like in Crypt of the NecroDancer, but it’s optional as is even doing things perfectly to the beat. You can still play the game by button mashing, but it is going to be more difficult and you will get lower ratings. To make things simpler to remember, the game also ties the basic light and heavy attacks to a constant rule, where light attacks always require 1 beat to chain, heavy attacks require 2 beats to chain and all combos operate using this rule.Which, as any experienced player of good action titles might guess, is a potential problem. Because best action titles usually let the players control the flow and the rhythm of the fight for 90% of the time, switching up and adapting to the situation as they feel like it. Occasionally this might lead to wonderful synchronization with the beat of the music, but it doesn’t have to. In Hi-Fi Rush it must be synchronized. Now, most fights don’t do anything particularly egregious, even if they occasionally start feeling like you’re in a constant QTE rather than in an action game. But there are a few enemy attacks that just break the flow entirely and take priority. While the final boss is absolutely terrible in that you have several phases of just waiting for the boss to do a particular attack before you can do anything yourself, so they are fully in control of the pace. Though, even ignoring the rhythm aspect, the game also throws in enemies that have only one mechanic working against them, throwing the pace of the fight off as soon as they appear. And several damage types that abruptly cut anything you’ve been doing for a stun animation. In general, the more the game tries to be a technical hack and slash adventure, the worse it fairs. Which is one of the reasons I didn’t finish the optional challenges that unlock past the game completion as they’ve managed to be somehow even worse than your typical challenge rooms in DMC or Bayonetta.It doesn’t help, that other aspects of the action adventure gameplay aren’t great either. Platforming isn’t good and often times judging the jump distances is almost impossible. Special partner interactions in levels are a redundant addition of rhythm mini-games into exploration and some of the mini-games have terrible patterns that go completely against the groove of the song playing in the level. Re-exploring the missions, an ability that becomes available upon game completion, is a pain. Every mission is way too long for this to feel good and unlike the other examples in the genre, you can’t even unlock those optional challenges as a separate quick travel option if you find them during your first playthrough (they are not available until after the game is completed as well). It’s just not immediately fun to replay the same way a DMC/PlatinumGames game can be.And yet, even if the sum of its parts isn’t looking great, actually going through Hi-Fi Rush is incredibly fun. Yeah, mechanically it’s not amazing, but it’s not bad either. And most of the missteps are clearly a result of good intentions and a clear creative vision. The game is so witty, and funny, and fun – the amount of times I smiled or giggled when I saw or heard something in the cutscene or just while running through the mission is beyond counting. And even the jokes that are based on a pop culture reference are good jokes in themselves, they just get better if you get the reference. The game really knows how to do comedy well and, unfortunately, that’s a rare skill in games nowadays.Being a rhythm game it also has a very good soundtrack. There are several licensed tracks, all of which can be disabled in favor of “we have licensed music at home” versions, that are also incredibly good. While the rest of the music and soundscape is really well done too. Whenever you like the music choices or not will come down to your own musical preferences, but what’s important is that the game feels consistent and confident with its style and it fits the gameplay well. As do the wonderfully presented cutscenes that seamlessly switch between slightly different art styles from scene to scene and also add to the good comedic timing of the game.So, while it’s not a particularly good hack and slash action adventure and probably not a fantastic rhythm game, it’s a charming and endearing title with wonderful script, memorable and exciting moments and “good enough” gameplay that is definitely worth experiencing at least once. I really liked the game and wish there were more titles that channel this sort of energy.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is a rhythm hack and slash. And I must put an accent on . Pretty much everything is on the rhythm. Hits you cause are on the rhythm, hits you receive are on the rhythm, environment is on the rhythm, cutscenes are on the rhythm, everything.You could think that this would be some sort of tedious design, but it actually flows really well as a game mechanic for a hack and slash, and even becomes somewhat of a meditative experience when you're in combat and trying to get the best combo.Furthermore, everything can be parried (after unlocking), you can even block magma balls and huge robot hits with no problem - as long as it's on the beat. The gameplay is the best part of the game, and if it wasn't so good, I doubt I would've managed to finish all the achievements in this game.The game also has a significant number of platforming sections. This is where I feel that the game has some issues, you have access to a double-jump and an air-dash, but the jumping mechanic doesn't feel solid, and using all the jumps and dash doesn't really feel as if it will get you too far.This game is pretty much based on soundtrack and sound design. To start with the most surprising point, this game has songs from Nine Inch Nails and The Prodigy, unsuspected, yet welcome, and other artists. But if you want to stream this game, you also have an option for a soundtrack which shouldn't get you into DMCA trouble. Which is pretty great in case you want to not have your VOD nuked.But back to the point, this game is on the beat. All the attacks, yours and the enemies', and the environment, is on the beat. Every stage has a different track, and the environment and combat will mold around it. You will see jumping bins, boards, fences, shrubs, just in rhythm with the beat. The story is linear and lacks any choices which can be done to actually affect the ending. The story itself is corny, but in the good kind of way, and the characters are varied in their own right.There is some character progression for the main character, going from a solo act to a team player, and the story itself serves the game sufficiently to also provide comedy and even dramatic moments.I 100%'d this game, and it was a complete ride. It took me about 8 hours to do one playthrough, and then I clocked in 61 hours to reach the final challenge to unlock 100%. All in all, some achievements are ridiculously difficult, and some are ridiculously tedious, and some are both. The biggest offenders are the "Don't get hit during X boss fight" achievements. There are a few of these, and in some cases, legitimately attaining this challenge would imply redoing a level completely, which can mean up to 20 minutes of gameplay extra if you rush to the boss. Furthermore, the difficulty challenges must be done individually. As in, there are 12 sets of levels and 5 difficulties. To get all the achievements, you will need to get S rank on all the difficulties, so you could be looking at doing each stage twice, at least, for each difficulty. This is where the brunt of the hours went.I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and for 30 euros, it's a solid choice. The style is amazing, the story is charming and everything just feels complete - compared to other titles in this world where you pay 60 or even 70 dollars and then you become a slave to season passes and battle passes.

_childDocuments_.review: What a truly amazing game. I'm not usually into "beat" games, but this is like playing a Japanese styled comic book with fun mechanics and decent story. While I've only played for two and a half hours, I'm actually excited to write the review. Here are some pros and cons. PROs- Music soundtrack is GREAT! It's varied with many musicians contributing. - Graphics are seriously top notch. I mean, mind blowing. Sometimes I just stopped and looked at the scene because it was so amazing.  - The colors are bright and loud with the atmosphere being a mega corp manufacturing facility. I was completely amazed on the outright beauty of the game. - The "comic book" approach is done seamlessly without being overbearing. It uses this storytelling method to great effect. - Enemies are varied with a fun look. - The "beat" approach to combat is executed flawlessly. - Each segment of the game is graded on at least 4 categories. This means you can play for kicks, or you can take it seriously. Super nice. CONs- The mechanics don't offer many "new" options.- Combat is fun, but kind of monotonous.- The story line is linear without much variation. - Your character and story line are a bit predictable. Overall, this gorgeous game is just plain old fun. I'm having a blast with it and am amazed that same team that delivered "The Evil Within" are the same ones that developed this game. I highly recommend this game for a good time and quick play. It's superb and really delivers on the premise. Well done devs!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I had recently gotten back into this game a few days before the news broke out, having finished and enjoyed the hell out of the game when it first released. Hi-Fi Rush is, to put it simply, one of the best games to have come out in recent years, and should be the gold standard for games going forward. The game is primarily an action game, along the lines of Metal Gear Rising, Devil May Cry, or Bayonetta, but with the twist that everything moves to the beat. And I do mean everything; stage elements, your attack, enemy attacks, even cutscenes are synchronized to the beat of the background music. You aren't required to stick to the beat, but your attacks will still land on-beat, and you're rewarded with extra damage for landing on-beat.This leads to the game having a very interesting feel, as it leads to beats in the music feeling almost like frames in a fighting game. All your light attacks take one beat to execute, and your heavy attacks take two beats, and most enemies have a tell a few beats before they actually execute their attack, allowing you to perform a combo that ends right before their attack, and then bust out a parry on the next beat, before continuing your combo. The story is also extremely good, and all the characters have unique and memorable personalities that feel just over-the-top enough to not be obnoxious. Chai may feel like a protagonist you'd get tired of after a bit of time, but his personality and development lead to him being the perfect character for a game like this.Along with these, the game has incredible replay value. There's a short postgame storyline involving 16 "Challenge Rooms" that demand you to fight a wave or two of enemies with a special condition, such as not manually moving, only dealing damage with parry counters, not taking damage, or getting above a certain percentage of perfectly on-beat attacks, ending in a humorous final encounter with the game's antagonist. Afterwards, you're offered the ability to replay the game at higher difficulties, to go for higher performance ranks, or the three side modes, Rhythm Tower, BPM Rush, and Power-Up! Tower-Up!Rhythm Tower serves as a 60-floor gauntlet of the game's areas, challenging you with a short timer that you can increase by performing well in the fights, and every 10 floors, you're challenged with one of the game's corporate bosses, before facing the final boss at Floor 60 and getting your final ranking and payout based on how much time you had left.BPM Rush and Power-Up! Tower-Up! were added as part of the "Arcade Update", and are both accessed from an arcade machine in your squad's hideout. While they aren't integrated with the game's 'Achievement Mural', a large mural on the wall that fills with characters and details as you complete challenges and accept your rewards, there's a separate Arcade Reward Tracker for them, holding a bunch of exclusive rewards, such as outfits for characters, new super moves, and photo mode poses.BPM Rush has you fight an endless wave of enemies, with a bar at the bottom that fills based on your performance. Once this bar is filled, you get a "BPM Rush", where you must defeat a buffed mini-boss enemy, after which the BPM of the background music will go up and you have to repeat the process, up until you're hammering buttons at 200 BPM.Power-Up! Tower-Up! is essentially a Roguelike mode. At the start of a run, Chai is zapped, and his stats brought down to abysmal levels, but between waves of enemies, you are given the option to accept buffs that'll bring him back up to and even above form, with more powerful upgrades including a temporary "bug" that will affect the next wave of enemies, such as causing enemies to explode when they die, damaging you, or "Setting the video feed to 480p", which serves as a humorous visual impairment.Overall, Hi-Fi Rush is an AMAZING game if you're looking for something with a ton of personality and replay value. I would say I hope for a sequel, but unfortunately recent news has not only revealed that Tango was in the process of pitching one, but that they were also shut down by their parent company, essentially shuttering any hope of a good followup.EDIT: Recently news came out that Tango Gameworks, the developers of Hi-Fi Rush, was saved from closure by Krafton, with specific mention that they'll be persuing more games in the Hi-Fi series, meaning that we effectively have confirmation that we're getting Hi-Fi Rush 2, so you can ignore most of that final paragraph lmao

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the tightest game experiences I've played in a long time.Hooked me right away. The gameplay is challenging enough, but incredibly intuitive in how it combines rhythm game aspects with spectacle fighter gameplay.The combos and abilities that you can buy are just complex enough to add more depth, which slowly develops throughout the game's chapters. Nothing seems to overstay it's welcome. The platforming felt just a hint odd, but something that took only a bit of getting used to. The various elements, including sidescrolling, call-response QTAs and so on always felt fitting, and never quite annoying. The pacing felt top-notch, but the format never felt repetitive, always throwing in new things to keep it fresh for each chapter.The soundtrack is amazing. Many original compositions which always felt fitting to the stage, while the licensed tracks just amped up the hype. The streamer-mode alternatives also manage to capture the vibe of the original song perfectly without glueing onto them most of the time, allowing them to be their own unique thing.The style is cel-shaded comic, which feels incredibly polished. Joyous to look at, never seeming dull, transitions between 2D-animated cutscenes, 3D-animated cutscenes and gameplay incredibly smooth, always with a certain flair. The characters and story are simple enough, nothing crazy in terms of twists, good saturday-morning cartoon type stuff.  The personalities are charming, the voice-acting wonderful, and the comedic writing is... genuinely funny, while managing to slip in some genuinely wholesome moments.Spent about 10 hours for the main story on Hard, and the post-game opens up with plenty of replay value throughout all levels for hidden dialogue, and additional challenges.Honestly, I don't remember the last time a game fascinated me in every facet like that. 10/10, absolute recommendation to anybody who's into spectacle fighters, an incredible tight and well-crafted gameplay experience, and a funky soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the my first-ever Steam review, so I don't say this lightly: Hi-Fi RUSH is, without a doubt, one of the best video games I have ever had the pleasure of playing.If you're a fan of hack & slash action-adventure games with a ton of personality and charm akin to Devil May Cry and Bayonetta, and also enjoy-- or have been curious about-- rhythm games, please check the game out. As a long-time fan of rhythm games like Rhythm Heaven and Crypt of the NecroDancer (just to name a few), the first announcement trailer for a rock-themed rhythm based action-adventure game immediately caught my attention. Boasting a licensed soundtrack featuring bands like Nine Inch Nails and The Prodigy, BEAUTIFUL animation on *literally* almost everything in the game, and a cast of charming, funny characters, the game already had me by the balls before I'd even played it.So played it I did. And I completely fell in love.The characters: Great. The soundtrack: Amazing. The gameplay: Phenomenal. The only bad thing I can honestly say about it is when it comes to the platforming segments in levels, which is the majority of the time spent in just about every level. I know tight platforming isn't what these games are known for, even DMC and Bayonetta are just as clunky in the platforming department, but it's cause the movement is focused on fast-paced combat. Otherwise, I can't sing its praises enough. I'm working on completing the game 100%, and as of this review, it's still getting free updates and paid DLC outfits (if you care about the cosmetics).I could seriously go on forever about Hi-Fi RUSH, so just do yourself a favor and play it for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: The Definition of a perfect gameNow I know what you're thinking: "A perfect game? Really Mouse? You think this is a perfect game?" And to that I say, Yes! The combat feels funky fresh whereby you have to hit enemies to the beat of whatever song is playing in a level, the looks and details give off PS2 era love and attention to details, the game is STILL getting new content a whole year after its release and even if the new content doesn't give you a reason to come back to it, the gameplay loop is just top notch. A main complaint I see about this game is that the characters are "Too Annoying" or they're "Le Epic Cringe" for a game made in this current decade. The thing is though, the reason the characters are the way they are is that the whole vibe of the game is to not take it seriously. I mean come on. You have a guy running around beating robots with a makeshift guitar made out of scrap metal and you expect me to take it seriously? No! And that's why the characters work so well for me. They're not meant to be taken seriously and even the characters in the game know this. And that's why it works! Everyone from Robbie Daymond to Erica Lindbeck to God mother f**king ROGER CRAIG SMITH did a fantastic job in bringing these characters to life with their witty personalities and A+ voice acting. I love this game with all my heart and it showed me that games don't need to be hyper realistic to be good. Sure graphics are important. If you're intending to emphasise emotion then you obviously need to have the characters look semi decent. But the gameplay, the additional end game content, the replayability of this game has shown me that not everything is about graphics and if the game is just down to Earth and fun, then you have a perfect game of fun high octane actionIf you've been holding off playing this game and you've come across this review, let this be the one to help push you over the metaphorical edge in buying this game. You will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game as much as anyone else (and feel like it's honestly a steal at 30 bucks). The art design is gorgeous, the characters are charming, the story is engaging, and the combat is some of the best fun I've had in a game in a very long time.But I will mention a few rough spots, because the game is not flawless:1. Platforming is clunky. I don't know if the controls just are not well suited for it, or if the cel shaded environment makes it hard to judge distance (or maybe both), but you will find yourself missing platforms way more than you should. Each time you miss a jump, the game takes a small chunk of your health and puts you back at the beginning of the segment. For one off accidents, it's not too punishing. But when you miss a jump several times in a row right before a difficult fight, it's more than a little frustrating.2. Most of the world moves to the beat of the music. This is not a complaint obviously, but it makes the fact that a few things don't do this stand out, and make for a frustrating couple minutes. My main example of this would be , which I've had to sometimes repeat 20 times in a row to get right.3. The UI was very clearly designed for use with controllers. It's still usable on PC, but there's some minor annoyances like no button mouseover indication. If you're like me, you'll end up just using WASD+E to navigate menus.The following isn't a complaint, but a PSA:  Despite the bright and cheerful appearance, combat can be pretty punishing. I'm no novice to rhythm or action games, but even on normal difficulty, some of the later fights required multiple repeats to get through.
